name: Aardvark
teaser: The aardvark is Africa's night-time digger, built like no other mammal on Earth. Its name comes from Afrikaans for 'earth pig', but its closest living relatives are actually elephants and manatees, not pigs. Out at night it sniffs out termite mounds, rips them open with shovel-like claws, and flicks in a long sticky tongue that can stretch nearly a foot. A single aardvark can gulp down tens of thousands of ants and termites in one night, and its burrows become home to dozens of other animals once it moves on.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how aardvarks, whose name means earth pig in Afrikaans, dig into termite mounds with powerful claws and eat with a 30 cm sticky tongue, and their abandoned burrows shelter many other African animals. Explore their solitary night life, their secretive nature, and how their digging aerates the soil.

name: Addax
teaser: The addax is the true desert survivor of the antelope family, a pale white spiral-horned animal that lives where almost nothing else can. It roams the empty sand seas of the Sahara, getting nearly all its water from the plants it eats and from dew, and it can go for months without drinking a single drop. Its wide flat hooves spread out like snowshoes so it can walk on soft dunes. Once common across North Africa, fewer than a few hundred survive in the wild, hunted for their beautiful horns.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the addax, a pale antelope with spiral horns, survives the deep Sahara with a body that barely sweats and kidneys that extract water, once common, now critically endangered from hunting and desertification, with fewer than 100 left in the wild. Explore the reintroduction programs in fenced reserves, and their historic migrations across the dunes.

name: African Bullfrog
teaser: The African bullfrog is a heavyweight of the frog world, a huge olive-green amphibian that can weigh more than a house cat. When the dry season hits, it digs deep into the mud and wraps itself in a cocoon of shed skin, sleeping through months without rain. When the first storms come, it digs itself out and can travel miles across open ground to find new pools. Males fight ferociously over the best spots to call, and tadpoles of its own species can end up as lunch for the bigger ones.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the African bullfrog survives drought by burrowing up to a meter deep, shedding a watertight cocoon of skin, and staying dormant for years until rains come. Explore its legendary aggression, its appetite for anything it can swallow, and how males guard tadpoles by digging channels.

name: African Elephant
teaser: The African elephant is the largest land animal alive, with bulls that can top six tonnes and stand taller than a double-decker bus. A trunk of forty thousand muscles can lift a log or pick up a single peanut, and its huge ears radiate heat like radiators. Elephants live in family herds led by the oldest female, remember friends and places for decades, and grieve their dead. They shape whole landscapes by pushing over trees and digging waterholes that other animals depend on.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how African elephants, the largest land animals, use their trunks of 40,000 muscles for everything from breathing to picking up a single peanut, and their huge ears radiate heat. Explore their matriarchal herds, their memory, their grief for the dead, and the ivory trade's threat.

name: African Wild Dogs
teaser: The African wild dog is the ultimate team player — a painted, patchwork-colored hunter whose packs work together with a precision that puts other predators to shame. Wild dogs are the most successful large hunters in Africa, catching their prey on up to 80 percent of hunts (lions manage barely a quarter), and the secret is teamwork: a pack runs its quarry down in relays, with fresh dogs taking over the chase, cutting corners and anticipating the prey's turn.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how wild dog packs hunt, then explain their cooperative care of pups.

name: Albatross
teaser: The albatross is the master of endless flight, a seabird built to stay airborne for years at a time over the open ocean. It locks its long narrow wings in place and soars on wind that bounces off the waves, gliding thousands of miles while barely flapping. The wandering albatross has the largest wingspan of any living bird, over three and a half meters, and can live to sixty or beyond. It only returns to land to breed, raising one chick every year or two on remote islands battered by gales.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how albatrosses use dynamic soaring to travel 10,000 km without flapping, locking their wings with a tendon so muscles never tire. Explore how they sleep on the wing, drink seawater through a salt gland, and how plastic pollution now threatens them at sea.

name: Albatross Gliding
teaser: An albatross gliding looks effortless, but it is a masterpiece of physics. Using dynamic soaring, the bird rides the wind gradient above the waves, climbing into stronger winds and diving back down to gather speed, turning the energy of the air into forward motion. In this way an albatross can circle the planet almost without flapping, covering hundreds of kilometers a day while its heart rate stays nearly at rest. Biologists have tracked some birds making complete loops around the Southern Ocean in under two months.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how albatrosses glide for hours, then explain dynamic soaring.

name: Alligator Ponds
teaser: Alligators do not just live in the swamp, they build and maintain it. Digging with snout and tail, they create deep gator holes that hold water through droughts, giving fish, turtles, birds, and deer a place to drink when the rest of the land dries out. These ponds become nurseries for dozens of species, which is why ecologists call alligators a keystone species: remove them and whole wetlands collapse. The same holes can be used by generations of alligators over decades.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how alligators dig ponds, then explain why they help other species.

name: Alligator Snapping Turtle
teaser: The alligator snapping turtle is a living dinosaur of the rivers, North America's biggest freshwater turtle, with a shell armored in ridges like a plated tank. It hunts by lying motionless on the muddy bottom with its mouth open, wiggling a worm-like pink lure on its tongue to trick fish into swimming straight inside. Its bite can crush a broom handle, and its strong jaws and beak have no real predators as adults. It can hold its breath for nearly an hour beneath the water.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the alligator snapping turtle lies motionless on riverbeds, wiggling a worm-like lure on its tongue to draw in fish, then snaps shut with jaws that can sever a finger. Explore its armor of heavy plates, its legendary size, and how it rarely moves for years.

name: Alpine Ibex
teaser: The alpine ibex is the mountain climber of the goat family, with curved ridged horns and hooves like suction cups. It scales near-vertical rock faces and dam walls, leaping across ledges where a slip means a long fall. Its hooves have a soft rubbery pad inside a hard rim that grips wet stone, letting it rest on surfaces no bigger than a coin. Once hunted to near extinction in the Alps, careful reintroduction brought it back to the very peaks it once roamed.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how Alpine ibex, wild goats with sweeping curved horns up to a meter long, once hunted to near extinction in Europe, rebounded through protected populations and now scale the steep faces of the Alps. Explore their incredible climbing on dams and cliffs, the horn growth rings that age them, and their comeback story.

name: American Alligator
teaser: The American alligator is a survivor from the age of dinosaurs, unchanged in form for millions of years. It lives in the swamps and rivers of the southeastern United States, where it rules a slow world of warm water and mud. A large male can reach four and a half meters and weigh over four hundred kilograms, yet mothers guard their nests and carry hatchlings gently in their jaws. Alligators can slow their hearts to a few beats a minute and freeze in ice to survive bitter winters.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how American alligators, once hunted to the edge of extinction, rebounded to millions across the Southeast, living up to 50 years, growing to 4.5 meters, and building mounds that shelter many other species. Explore their cold-blooded basking, their gator holes that keep wetlands alive in drought, and the difference from crocodiles.

name: American Bison
teaser: The American bison once roamed the Great Plains in herds so vast they shook the ground, numbering in the tens of millions. A bull can weigh over a tonne, and despite their size they can outrun a horse in short bursts. Bison wallow in dust, graze the prairie into health, and their heavy bodies shape the grasslands for a hundred other species. After being hunted almost to extinction in the nineteenth century, careful conservation has brought the herds back from a few hundred survivors.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how American bison once numbered in the tens of millions, were nearly wiped out to a few hundred by the late 1800s, and have been rebuilt through protected herds, now grazing prairies again and shaping ecosystems with their wallows and grazing. Explore their shaggy winter coats, their herd defense against wolves, and their deep cultural importance.

name: American Black Bear
teaser: The American black bear is the most widespread bear in North America, at home from deep forests to suburban backyards. It is a superb climber, a strong swimmer, and mostly a shy loner that would rather run than fight. Though called black, its fur can be brown, cinnamon, or even white. It eats almost anything: berries, nuts, insects, fish, and the occasional garbage can. Before winter it packs on layers of fat, then dens up and sleeps through the cold months without eating.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how American black bears are the most common bear species, excellent climbers that flee up trees, with an extraordinary sense of smell and a diet from berries to garbage, and they've expanded their range while other bears shrink. Explore their cubs born in winter dens, their shyness around people, and the bear-proofing of campgrounds.

name: Amoeba
teaser: The amoeba is a single cell that acts like a whole animal. Found in ponds, soil, and even our own guts, it oozes its jelly-like body forward by pushing out temporary foot-like bulges called pseudopods. It hunts by flowing around a bacterium, swallowing it whole into a food vacuole, and digesting it. An amoeba has no brain or nervous system, yet it can sense food, avoid bad chemicals, and split in two to reproduce, making a perfect copy of itself in about half an hour.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how amoebas are single-celled protists that move and eat by flowing pseudopods, engulfing food by phagocytosis, and some, like the brain-eating Naegleria, are famous for the wrong reasons. Explore their reproduction by simple division, the giant deep-sea xenophyophores that grow to 10 cm, and why they're not animals or plants.

name: Amphibian Decline
teaser: Frogs, salamanders, and other amphibians are vanishing faster than almost any group of animals on the planet. More than forty percent of known species are threatened, and the causes stack up: habitat loss, pollution, climate change, and a deadly fungus called chytrid that attacks their skin. Because amphibians breathe through their skin and live between water and land, they are like canaries for the health of whole ecosystems. Scientists are racing to save species through breeding programs and disease treatments.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how a third of amphibian species face extinction from habitat loss, climate change, pollution, and chytrid fungus, a skin disease that has driven dozens of species extinct and hundreds to the brink. Explore the fungus's global spread, the rescue programs raising frogs in captivity, and what frog losses mean for ecosystems.

name: Amphibian Skin Secrets
teaser: Amphibian skin is a living chemistry lab and a breathing organ rolled into one. Frogs and salamanders take in oxygen and water directly through their thin, moist skin, which is why they need damp places to live. That same skin is packed with glands that make everything from slime to deadly poison, and some produce antibiotics that could help humans fight superbugs. The poison dart frog's skin carries enough toxin to affect a person, yet that skin is also what makes the species so fascinating to researchers.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover why amphibian skin must stay moist, then explain their gland secretions.

name: Amur Leopard
teaser: The Amur leopard is the rarest big cat on Earth, a pale spotted hunter that lives in the snowy forests of the Russian Far East and northeastern China. Its long thick coat keeps it warm in winters that drop below freezing, and its rosettes look different from African leopards, spaced more widely with thicker borders. Decades of poaching pushed it to the brink, with perhaps only dozens left in the wild, but camera traps now show the population slowly climbing again thanks to protected reserves.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how Amur leopards of the Russian Far East dropped to around 30 individuals, the rarest big cat, and have slowly recovered to over 100 through strict protection and habitat work, with camera traps documenting the comeback. Explore their thick winter coats, their prey of deer and boar, and the national park that anchors their survival.

name: Andean Cock-of-the-rock
teaser: The Andean cock-of-the-rock is a flash of impossible orange in the cloud forests of South America. The male is crowned with a huge fan-shaped crest that covers his beak, and he performs his famous lek dance on a mossy branch: hopping, sliding, and bowing in front of females, calling with grunts and whistles. The females, dull brown by comparison, watch the show and choose their partners. Fewer than a hundred males may gather at one display site, all dancing to win a mate.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how male Andean cocks-of-the-rock, vivid orange with a fan-shaped crest, gather on jungle leks to dance and display for females. Explore the lek mating system, the female's brown camouflage for nesting on cliff faces, and why Peru made it its national bird.

name: Anemonefish Partnership
teaser: The anemonefish, made famous by animated movies, lives a risky life on purpose. It settles into the stinging tentacles of a sea anemone, a creature whose touch is deadly to most fish, because the anemone's tentacles are loaded with poison. The fish builds up a protective mucus that keeps the stings from firing, turning the anemone into a fortress. In return, the fish chases off predators and keeps the anemone clean. Scientists have shown the fish can even change its mucus if it switches anemone homes.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how anemonefish, or clownfish, live safely among stinging anemone tentacles by building up a protective mucus coat the anemone doesn't recognize, while chasing off anemone-eating fish and providing nutrients with their waste. Explore the research on how they acquire immunity, their strict size hierarchy, and what happens when the anemone dies.

name: Anglerfish
teaser: The anglerfish lives in the sunless deep ocean, where food is scarce and everything glows. On its head dangles a glowing lure, made by bacteria that produce their own light, and it dangles this lantern in front of its huge mouth to tempt prey. Once a fish swims close to inspect the light, the anglerfish strikes with fang-like teeth and a stomach that can stretch to swallow prey bigger than itself. In some species the tiny male bites onto the female and fuses with her body forever, becoming a living sperm bank.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how female anglerfish lure prey in the dark deep sea with a glowing esca full of bioluminescent bacteria, and how tiny males bite onto females and fuse into permanent parasites. Explore the crushing pressures of their habitat, their enormous teeth, and the sheer weirdness of deep-sea life.

name: Animal Communication
teaser: Animals talk all the time, just not in words. Bees dance to spell out the distance and direction of flowers. Whales sing songs that travel for hundreds of miles underwater. Prairie dogs have different warning calls for different predators, even describing the color of a human's clothes. Fireflies flash coded patterns to find mates, and octopuses change color and texture to send messages. Every signal, from a bird's alarm to a wolf's howl, is a message with a meaning, shaped by evolution.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how animals communicate in astonishing ways, from whale songs that travel oceans to bee dances that describe flower locations, frog choruses, firefly flashes, and elephant infrasound rumblings felt through the ground. Explore how birds learn dialects, and what animal signals reveal about their inner lives.

name: Animal Courtship
teaser: Courtship in the animal kingdom is full of bizarre displays, and the bowerbird is the champion of romance. The male builds an elaborate structure of twigs and decorates it with blue objects, snail shells, and berries to impress females, who visit like gallery critics. Peacocks fan out dazzling tail feathers, fireflies light up in synchrony, and seahorses dance around each other for days. All this effort has one purpose: proving health, strength, and good genes to pick the best possible partner.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how animals court in spectacular ways, from bowerbirds building decorated love shacks, peacocks fanning iridescent trains, fireflies flashing coded signals, to birds of paradise dancing in costume-like plumage. Explore why females are picky, and how courtship drives some of nature's most extravagant features.

name: Animal Intelligence
teaser: Animal intelligence turns up in the most unexpected places. Crows solve puzzles with multiple steps, remember human faces for years, and hold grudges. Octopuses open jars, escape tanks, and use coconut shells as armor. Elephants recognize themselves in mirrors and mourn their dead. Dogs understand hundreds of words and read human emotions. Even humble ants run complex civilizations, and researchers now study animal minds not to rank them against ours but to understand how many different ways intelligence can evolve.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how intelligence appears across the animal kingdom, from crows that solve multi-step puzzles and remember human faces, to elephants that mourn, dolphins that recognize themselves in mirrors, pigs that play video games, and octopuses that open jars. Explore what animal minds reveal about how thought evolved.

name: Animal Migration
teaser: Migration is one of the most epic journeys in nature. The Arctic tern flies from pole to pole every year, covering enough distance in a lifetime to travel to the Moon and back. Monarch butterflies, weighing less than a paper clip, navigate thousands of miles to the same Mexican forests their great-grandparents used. Wildebeest cross crocodile-filled rivers, humpback whales cross entire oceans, and salmon fight upstream to the stream where they hatched. Migrants use the Sun, stars, magnetic fields, and even smells to find their way.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how animals migrate staggering distances, from wildebeest herds crossing crocodile-filled rivers to birds flying pole to pole, whales crossing oceans, and salmon returning to their birth streams. Explore how they navigate by stars, magnetic fields, and memory, and the dangers that make each journey a gamble.

name: Animal Mimicry
teaser: Mimicry is nature's ultimate disguise, and it saves lives every day. The harmless scarlet king snake wears the deadly coral snake's red-black-yellow warning stripes so predators leave it alone. The orchid mantis looks like a flower, luring in insects that come to sip nectar and become lunch instead. Some moths copy the eyes of owls on their wings, some butterflies copy each other, and the octopus copies whole animals, changing shape, color, and movement to mimic sea snakes and flounders in seconds.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how animals mimic everything, from harmless snakes copying venomous ones, to stick insects copying twigs, butterflies with eye patterns, and the amazing mimic octopus copying a dozen other sea creatures. Explore Batesian and Mullerian mimicry, how predators learn, and the arms race of deception.

name: Animal Rescue
teaser: Animal rescue is a global effort that brings species back from the edge. Wildlife hospitals treat injured eagles, orphaned seal pups, and oil-soaked penguins, then release them home. Rescue centers around the world have saved the California condor, the Arabian oryx, and the black-footed ferret from certain extinction, breeding them carefully until populations could be returned to the wild. Every rescue is a story: a team, a patient, and a long road back to a life in nature.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how rescue teams save animals from oil spills, floods, and poaching, from washing oiled penguins to rehabilitating orphaned elephants and releasing sea turtles with satellite tags. Explore the work of sanctuaries and clinics, the skill of caring for wild animals, and the releases that return survivors home.

name: Animal Sleep
teaser: Sleep looks different across the animal kingdom. Giraffes nap for just a few minutes at a time, totaling under two hours a day. Dolphins sleep with half their brain awake at a time so they never stop swimming or breathing. Some birds sleep while flying, and bats hang upside down for nearly twenty hours a day. Even jellyfish, which have no brain, take rest breaks. Sleep seems to be universal in some form, a mystery that scientists are still untangling across the whole tree of life.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how animals sleep in astonishing ways, from dolphins that rest one brain hemisphere at a time while swimming, swifts sleeping while flying, horses sleeping standing up, to bullfrogs that may not sleep at all. Explore why sleep matters, the trade-offs animals make, and the mystery of why we all need it.

name: Animal Vision
teaser: Animals see the world in wildly different ways. Bees see ultraviolet colors invisible to us, which is why flowers glow with patterns that guide them to nectar. Mantis shrimp have twelve types of color receptors, compared to our three, and can see polarized light. Eagles spot a rabbit from two miles away. Geckos see colors at night that humans would need a flashlight for. Cats see better in dim light but with fewer colors. Every species sees a different slice of reality.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how animals see the world very differently, from mantis shrimp with 12 color receptors to dogs with two, bees seeing ultraviolet flower patterns, snakes seeing heat, and eagles spotting prey kilometers away. Explore the physics and biology of eyes, and how each species' vision fits its life.

name: Animal World Records
teaser: The animal record books are full of extremes. The blue whale is the biggest animal that has ever lived, bigger than any dinosaur. The peregrine falcon is the fastest, diving at over three hundred kilometers an hour. The cheetah is the fastest on land, the sailfish in the sea. The Arctic tern makes the longest migration, the tardigrade survives the most extreme conditions, and the immortal jellyfish can reverse its own aging. Every champion holds its title thanks to some wild evolutionary trick.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how nature's records stagger, from the blue whale as the largest animal ever and the peregrine falcon as the fastest, to the immortal jellyfish that cheats death, the loudest animal being the pistol shrimp's sonic snap, and the longest-lived being Greenland sharks passing 400 years. Explore what each record reveals about adaptation.

name: Ant Colony Structure
teaser: An ant colony is a city with a single purpose. A queen lays the eggs, workers do the jobs, and soldiers defend the nest, but ant jobs are flexible: a worker can switch between nursing, digging, and foraging as the colony needs. They communicate with pheromone trails, chemical messages that can summon help, mark food, or declare war. Some colonies house millions of ants, yet everything runs on simple rules and chemical signals rather than a leader giving orders.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how an ant colony operates with a queen laying eggs, workers divided by age into nurses, builders, and foragers, and soldiers defending, with no single ant in charge, the colony behaving as one superorganism. Explore the pheromone trails, the communication codes, and how colonies of leafcutter ants number in the millions.

name: Ant-eating Mammals
teaser: Anteaters and pangolins both eat ants, but they could not be more different. The giant anteater of South America is a shaggy mammal with a long snout and a two-foot tongue, no teeth at all, and a huge bushy tail. The pangolin of Africa and Asia is covered in overlapping scales made of keratin, the same stuff as fingernails, and rolls into a perfect armored ball when threatened. One is fur, the other is armor, but both evolved the same odd diet of insects.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how ant and termite specialists evolved separately in different continents, from the giant anteater and tamandua of the Americas, the pangolin of Africa and Asia, and the aardvark of Africa, each developing long sticky tongues and powerful digging claws. Explore convergent evolution at work.

name: Anteater Claws
teaser: The giant anteater carries a set of the most fearsome digging claws in the animal world — long, curved talons on its front feet that can be ten centimeters long, so sharp and powerful they can tear open termite mounds as hard as concrete. The claws are the anteater's tools AND its weapons: it uses them to rip into insect nests and also to defend itself, standing upright on its hind legs and sweeping its forelimbs with a bear-like swipe that can seriously injure a jaguar.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover how anteater claws rip open nests, then explain why they knuckle-walk.

name: Antelope
teaser: Antelopes are the grace and speed of the African plains, a family of hooved mammals that includes the tiny dik-dik and the towering eland. Built for running, they have long legs, powerful hearts, and eyes on the sides of their heads to watch for predators while grazing. The impala can leap nine meters in a single bound, and the springbok pronks, bouncing high in the air to show predators it is healthy and not worth chasing. Their herds shape the grasslands as they graze.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how antelope, a family including impala, kudu, oryx, and eland, range across Africa and Asia, from tiny dik-diks to eland as big as cattle, with horns on both sexes in many species and adaptations from desert survival to swamp wading. Explore their diversity of habitats, their herding, and the predators that shape their lives.

name: Antelope Leaping
teaser: When a predator chases an antelope, the prey sometimes does the opposite of sprinting flat out: it leaps straight up with stiff legs, all four hooves leaving the ground at once. That odd bounce is called stotting, and it puzzles biologists. The best explanation is honest advertising — the leap shows the hunter how strong, fit and hard to catch this particular animal is, so the chase is abandoned before it starts. A springbok can stot nearly three meters into the air, and the display is also a signal to the rest of the herd that danger is near, sending every animal scattering in a different direction.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover why antelopes pronk, then explain what the leaps might signal.

name: Antlion
teaser: The antlion is a dragonfly relative whose larva is one of nature's sneakiest predators. The young antlion digs a perfect cone-shaped pit in dry sand and buries itself at the bottom, waiting with open jaws. When an ant slips down the loose slope, the antlion flicks sand to make the walls collapse, and the victim slides straight into its waiting pincers. After a meal, the larva flicks the empty shell out of the pit. It lives like this for up to two years before turning into a delicate flying adult.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how antlion larvae dig conical pits in sandy soil and wait at the bottom for ants to slide in, flicking sand to prevent escape, then inject digestive fluids and drink the liquefied insides. Explore the pit construction, the antlion's armor, and the adult form, a delicate lacewing-like insect that lives weeks.

name: Ants
teaser: Ants are the most successful insects on land, with an estimated twenty quadrillion individuals alive at any moment. They live in colonies that work like superorganisms, where each ant acts like a single cell of one giant body. Leafcutter ants farm fungus, weaver ants stitch nests from living leaves, and army ants march in raiding columns that clear the forest floor. They lift fifty times their own weight, lay chemical trails, and have been farming and fighting wars long before humans did.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how ants outnumber humans by millions to one, with some farming fungus, herding aphids like cattle, and building bridges with their own bodies. Explore the queen's role, the division of labor by age, and leaf-cutter colonies of millions that outrank any single animal in biomass.

name: Aphid
teaser: The aphid is a tiny sap-sucking insect that plants everywhere would love to be rid of. It pierces leaves and stems with needle-sharp mouthparts and drinks the sugary sap flowing inside. Aphids reproduce at astonishing speed: a single female can give birth to live young that are already pregnant, and one aphid's descendants can number in the billions in a single season. Some ants protect and milk them for their sweet honeydew, while ladybirds and lacewings hunt them by the dozen.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how aphids pierce plants and suck sap, multiplying so fast that a single female can produce billions of descendants in a season, giving live birth and cloning themselves, while excreting honeydew that ants farm. Explore their role as garden pests, the ladybugs and lacewings that control them, and their astonishing reproductive biology.

name: Archerfish
teaser: The archerfish hunts with a sniper's aim from below the water's surface. It spits a jet of water at an insect sitting on a leaf or branch overhead, knocking it into the water to eat. The fish calculates the bending of light as it passes from air to water, adjusting its aim for refraction with remarkable accuracy. Some can hit a target from over two meters away, and they learn to compensate for moving prey. It is one of the few animals that hunts by shooting.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how archerfish knock insects off overhanging branches by spitting jets of water, compensating for light refraction, and can even learn to knock down targets from meters away. Explore how they leap to catch falling prey, their accuracy that improves with practice, and their mangrove home.

name: Arctic Fox
teaser: The Arctic fox is built for the harshest winters on Earth. Its fur changes with the seasons, turning white in winter to vanish against the snow and brown in summer to blend with the tundra. Its short ears, thick tail, and furry paws act like a winter coat, and its body can stay warm at temperatures below minus forty degrees. When food is scarce, it follows polar bears to steal scraps, and it can sniff out lemmings beneath the snow and dive in to catch them.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how Arctic foxes change color with the seasons, white in winter for camouflage and brown in summer, with fur-covered paw pads and a thick tail used as a scarf, and they follow polar bears to scavenge kills. Explore their burrows that can be centuries old, their endurance of minus 50 degrees, and the lemming cycles that drive their numbers.

name: Arctic Tern
teaser: The Arctic tern lives more hours of daylight than any animal, chasing summer from pole to pole. Each year it flies from its Arctic breeding grounds all the way to the Antarctic, then back again, a round trip of around seventy thousand kilometers. Over a thirty-year life it travels enough to fly to the Moon several times over. It crosses oceans, rides the winds of entire hemispheres, and still returns to the same stretch of coast it hatched on, guided by an internal magnetic sense.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the arctic tern migrates from the Arctic to the Antarctic and back each year, covering up to 90,000 km and seeing more daylight than any other animal. Explore how these tiny birds navigate by the sun, stars, and magnetic field, and why they chase endless summer across the globe.

name: Armadillo
teaser: The armadillo is the only mammal with a true shell, a suit of bony plates that covers its back like armor. Found in the Americas, it digs with powerful claws for insects and grubs, and the nine-banded armadillo always gives birth to identical quadruplets from a single egg. When threatened, some species roll into an unbreakable ball, their armor locking together like a puzzle. It can hold its breath for six minutes to walk along the bottom of a riverbed.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how armadillos wear flexible bony armor, the three-banded one rolling into a perfect ball, and they dig burrows, can hold their breath underwater for minutes, and some species give birth to identical quadruplets. Explore their insect diet, their cousins, and their Texas expansion.

name: Armadillo Digging
teaser: The armadillo is nature's excavator — a small armored mammal that digs with such speed and skill that it can vanish underground in under a minute. Its front feet carry enormous claws, curved like digging picks, and its body is built for burrowing: a streamlined, armored shell that sheds dirt, strong shoulders for the claw work, and a tail that braces it as it tunnels. When danger appears, the armadillo doesn't run — it digs, going straight down in seconds, and predators that expected an easy meal are left staring at a fresh hole.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover how armadillos dig, then explain why their burrows help other animals.

name: Army Ant
teaser: Army ants run the most terrifying operation in the insect world. They have no permanent nest, instead marching in massive columns and bivouacking in a swarm of their own bodies, hanging from tree branches. Each night a colony may raid hundreds of meters of forest floor, and a million or more ants sweep everything edible from their path, from insects to small vertebrates. They communicate by scent and touch, working together so precisely that the colony acts like a single hunting animal.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how army ants live in nomadic colonies of millions, raiding in swarms that flush out insects, spiders, and even small vertebrates, with queens that lay millions of eggs and colonies that bivouac in living nests of their own bodies. Explore the swarm raids, the birds that follow to catch flushed prey, and their coordinated group hunting.

name: Arowana
teaser: The arowana is a legendary fish that leaps out of the water to catch insects, birds, and even bats from overhanging branches. Found in the rivers of South America, Asia, and Australia, it is a long, sleek predator with a mouth that opens upward for surface strikes. In Asia it is called the dragon fish and is treasured for luck and status, with some albino and golden specimens selling for tens of thousands of dollars. It can jump three meters out of the water after prey.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the Asian arowana, called the dragon fish, leaps meters out of the water to catch insects, birds, and bats from overhanging branches, carrying eggs in its mouth to protect them. Explore why albino and gold varieties sell for six-figure prices, and why it's a symbol of luck in Asia.

name: Assassin Bug
teaser: The assassin bug is a quiet killer of the insect world, stalking gardens and fields. It spears prey with a sharp beak, injects a paralyzing venom and digestive juices, then sucks the insides out like a milkshake. Some species cover themselves in the corpses of their victims to confuse predators, while others paint their legs with sticky tree resin to trap passing insects. It is not shy about size either, and it is one of the few insects known to hunt in coordinated pairs.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how assassin bugs stab prey with a dagger-like rostrum, inject digestive saliva, and suck out liquefied insides, with some species camouflaging themselves in the corpses of their prey. Explore the kissing bug's role in Chagas disease, their painful bites, and their patient ambush hunting.

name: Atlas Moth
teaser: The atlas moth is one of the largest moths in the world, with wings that span over twenty-five centimeters, wider than an adult's hand. The tips of its forewings curve like snake heads, a disguise that startles birds into keeping their distance. It has no mouth and no stomach, living its entire short adult life on fat stored as a caterpillar, just long enough to find a mate and lay eggs. Its huge silk cocoons have been used in Taiwan as purses.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the atlas moth of Southeast Asia has a wingspan of 25 cm, among the largest moths, with wing tips shaped like snake heads to scare predators, and adults that don't eat, living only days on stored fat. Explore its silent flight, its female scent that attracts males from kilometers away, and its cocoon silk.

name: Avocet
teaser: The avocet is a graceful wading bird with a black-and-white body and a long, thin, upturned bill. It sweeps that upturned beak side to side through shallow water, feeling for tiny crustaceans and insects it cannot see. Its long blue legs let it wade deeper than many shorebirds, and it nests in shallow scrapes on salt flats and wetlands. When its chicks hatch, they are up and foraging within hours, guided by parents that fiercely defend the nesting colony.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the avocet sweeps its uniquely upturned bill side to side through shallow water to catch tiny crustaceans. Explore its striking black and white plumage, its breeding colonies on salt flats, and how it defends nests with a furious distraction display.

name: Axolotl
teaser: The axolotl is a salamander that never grows up, staying in its aquatic larval form for its whole life. Native only to a few lakes near Mexico City, it keeps its feathery external gills and fins even as an adult, looking like a smiling, gilled alien. Its superpower is regeneration: it can regrow lost limbs, its tail, parts of its heart, its spinal cord, and even chunks of its brain without scarring. Scientists study it closely, hoping to unlock the same healing secrets for humans.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the axolotl keeps its juvenile gills and stays aquatic for life, a phenomenon called neoteny, and can regenerate lost limbs, spinal cords, and even parts of its heart and brain. Explore why it lives only in the canals of Mexico City, its Xochimilco habitat, and its role in regeneration research.

name: Axolotl Habitat
teaser: The axolotl's wild home is a shrinking miracle: the ancient lake system around Mexico City, especially the canals of Xochimilco. These shallow, muddy, plant-choked waters once covered the valley, but the city's growth drained most of them away. What remains faces pollution, invasive fish that eat axolotl eggs, and warmer waters. Conservationists now restore chinampas, the floating garden islands, to rebuild clean habitat, and captive axolotls bred in labs worldwide keep the species alive while the wild ones cling on.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how axolotls once thrived in the high-altitude lakes around Mexico City, including Lake Xochimilco, where chinampa farming created ideal canals, but drainage, pollution, and introduced fish nearly wiped them out, leaving only a few hundred wild animals. Explore the captive population in the millions, the refugio projects, and the effort to restore Xochimilco.

name: Axolotl Regeneration
teaser: An axolotl can regrow a lost limb in a matter of weeks, and the secret lies in how it heals. Instead of forming a scar like most animals, it grows a bud of unspecialized cells called a blastema at the wound, which then develops into a perfect new limb with bones, muscles, and nerves. It can do this dozens of times, and even regrow parts of its heart, eyes, and spinal cord. Researchers hope that decoding this trick could one day improve healing in humans.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how axolotls regrow body parts, then explain why scientists study them.

name: Axolotl Regeneration
teaser: Scientists call the axolotl the master of regeneration because it can rebuild almost any body part, and it does not stop with limbs. Remove part of its heart and it grows it back. Damage its spinal cord and it repairs it, restoring full movement. Even its brain can regenerate lost tissue. Unlike mammals, which seal wounds with scar tissue, the axolotl keeps the wound in an embryonic-like state where new cells keep dividing. Decoding this could reshape medicine for human injury and disease.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how axolotls regrow complete limbs, tails, jaws, skin, and even parts of the heart and brain, with cells near a wound reverting to a stem-like state and rebuilding the missing part with perfect function. Explore the molecular signals involved, why adult mammals lost this ability, and the human medicine hoping to borrow it.

name: Axolotl as a Pet
teaser: The axolotl has become a beloved pet, and its needs are very different from a fish or lizard. It must live in cool, clean water, ideally below twenty degrees Celsius, since warm water stresses it and invites disease. It eats worms, brine shrimp, and sinking pellets, and it cannot live with fish that might nibble its gills. Most pet axolotls are captively bred, which has helped the species survive even as its wild lakes have been destroyed, but owning one means committing to a cool-water hobby for up to fifteen years.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how axolotls make fascinating pets that stay aquatic and young-looking their whole lives, but need cool water below 20 degrees, no gravel they might swallow, and a protein-rich diet of worms and pellets. Explore why they're illegal in some places, their 15 year lifespan in captivity, and the joy of watching them regenerate.

name: Badger Setts
teaser: A badger sett is an underground fortress that can have dozens of entrances and tunnels stretching for hundreds of meters. Badgers dig with their huge front claws, passing soil back through their bodies in a relay chain, and generations of the same family may enlarge the sett for decades. The main chamber is lined with dry grass and bedding that the badgers drag down and change regularly. In winter, badgers do not truly hibernate but sleep for days at a time, waking to stretch and drink.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how badgers build setts, then explain how long a sett can be used.

name: Baiji Dolphin
teaser: The baiji, or Yangtze River dolphin, was the ghost of China's greatest river, and it may now be gone forever. A pale, shy freshwater dolphin that lived in the muddy Yangtze for twenty million years, it navigated by echolocation in water where visibility was almost zero. Industrial traffic, fishing nets, and river development proved too much: a 2006 survey found none at all, and the species was declared functionally extinct. It became the first dolphin known to be wiped out by human activity, a haunting warning.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the baiji, a freshwater dolphin of China's Yangtze River with a legend of being a river goddess, was declared functionally extinct in 2007 after the river's shipping, fishing, and dams destroyed it. Explore what makes river dolphins so vulnerable, and why the baiji is a warning for other river species.

name: Bald Eagle
teaser: The bald eagle, America's national bird, was once so rare that it almost vanished. Hunted, poisoned by pesticides like DDT that thinned its eggshells, and pushed out of its nesting grounds, only a few hundred nesting pairs remained in the lower forty-eight states by the 1960s. A ban on DDT and years of protection turned the story around, and today tens of thousands of pairs soar over lakes and coasts once again. It builds the largest tree nests of any bird, some weighing a tonne.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the bald eagle, the US national bird, builds the largest tree nests of any bird, up to 4 meters deep and weighing over a ton. Explore how its 240 degree field of vision and talons with 400 psi grip make it a master fisher, and the famous myth that its cry is a hawk's, borrowed in Hollywood films.

name: Bandicoot
teaser: The bandicoot is a small marsupial that plays a huge role in Australian soil. With a pointed snout and strong digging claws, it pokes conical holes in the ground as it hunts for grubs and insects, aerating the soil and helping plants grow. Unlike many marsupials, it has a proper placenta and tiny young that develop mostly in a backward-opening pouch. Once widespread, many bandicoot species are now threatened by foxes, cats, and habitat loss, and they are the focus of major rewilding efforts.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how bandicoots dig characteristic cone-shaped holes in gardens and bushland hunting insects and fungi, with a pouched marsupial body and a diet that spreads fungal spores vital to forests. Explore their rapid reproduction, their vulnerable status from foxes and cats, and how their digging aerates soil.

name: Barnacle
teaser: The barnacle is a tiny crustacean that lives its adult life glued to rocks, boat hulls, and even whales, standing on its head inside a volcano-shaped shell. It feeds by kicking feathery legs out of the top of its shell to sweep plankton from the water, which is why sailors call them little birds kicking. Barnacles cement themselves in place with a glue so strong that engineers study it as a model for adhesives. A larva swims freely, but once it finds a spot, it never moves again.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how barnacles are crustaceans, related to crabs, that glue themselves to rocks, ship hulls, and even whales, standing on their heads and kicking food into their mouths with feathery legs. Explore their cement that's studied for surgical glue, their penis that can stretch many times their body length, and how they choose settlement spots.

name: Barracuda
teaser: The barracuda is a sleek silver torpedo of the warm seas, built for sudden, explosive speed. It waits in the water column, often alone or in loose schools, then shoots after prey like a launched missile, striking with a mouth full of razor-sharp teeth. It can reach nearly two meters long and charges at over forty kilometers an hour. Barracudas hunt by sight and are drawn to anything shiny, which is why divers are told to remove jewelry before entering their waters.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how barracudas patrol reefs and open water with razor teeth, striking with explosive bursts of speed, sometimes following snorkelers out of curiosity. Explore their fearsome reputation vs reality, their habit of circling bait schools, and why their size can reach 2 meters.

name: Basilisk Lizard
teaser: The basilisk lizard, nicknamed the Jesus Christ lizard, can run across the surface of water. When threatened, it sprints upright on its hind legs, slapping the water with wide-fringed feet so fast that each step creates a pocket of air that keeps it from sinking. A young basilisk can dash across a pond for many meters before dropping to all fours and swimming. On land it is equally quick, and in Costa Rica's forests it is a common sight along riverbanks.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the green basilisk lizard of Central America sprints across water on its hind legs, using the speed and slap of its feet and air pockets under its toes to stay above the surface for several meters. Explore how juveniles can run farther than adults, and its crests that earned the Jesus lizard nickname.

name: Basking Shark
teaser: The basking shark is the gentle giant of the seas, the second-largest fish in the world at over ten meters long. It feeds by swimming slowly with its huge mouth open, filtering tons of plankton-rich water through gill rakers. Despite its size, it has tiny teeth and eats nothing bigger than a shrimp, and it moves no faster than a casual swimmer. It can leap clear of the water, a shocking sight for a fish that heavy, and it migrates across oceans following blooms of plankton.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how basking sharks, second only to whale sharks, cruise with mouths open wide enough to swallow a person, straining plankton through gill rakers, and migrate thousands of kilometers following blooms. Explore why they're rarely seen, the mystery of where they winter, and their vulnerability to ships and nets.

name: Bat
teaser: Bats are the only mammals that truly fly, and they make up a fifth of all mammal species. Their wings are stretched skin over long finger bones, and they can outmaneuver birds with incredible agility. Most bats are nocturnal and use echolocation, sending out high-pitched calls and reading the echoes to build a sound picture of their world. Far from being scary, they are vital: fruit bats spread seeds, and insect-eating bats can devour thousands of mosquitoes in a single night.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how bats are the only mammals that fly, with wings of skin stretched over elongated fingers, and most navigate by echolocation, emitting up to 200 calls a second. Explore their huge diversity, a quarter of all mammals, their roles eating insects and pollinating plants, and how they host but rarely spread viruses.

name: Bat Caves
teaser: A bat roost can hold hundreds of thousands of bats, a living cloud packed into a cave, attic, or hollow tree. Some caves in Texas host millions of Mexican free-tailed bats, which stream out at dusk like smoke and can eat tons of insects a night. Bats hang upside down because their wings are their arms: their clawed feet are built to grip and hold their whole body weight in that position. Roosts are vital meeting points where bats share warmth, information, and even diseases.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how millions of bats roost in caves, from Mexican free-tailed bats emerging from Bracken Cave in tornado-like streams numbering 20 million, to hibernating bats packing crevices in winter. Explore the guano that supports cave ecosystems, the white-nose fungus crisis, and why caves are critical wildlife refuges.

name: Bat Echolocation
teaser: Bat echolocation is nature's sonar, and it is incredibly precise. A bat fires out high-frequency calls, up to two hundred per second when closing in on prey, and listens to the echoes that bounce back off objects. From the timing and pitch change of the returning sound, it builds a detailed picture in the dark, detecting a mosquito-sized insect from several meters away. Some bats use constant-frequency calls to detect wing flutters, and this system is so refined that bats can hunt in complete darkness at full speed.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how bats echolocate, then explain what the returning echoes reveal.

name: Bat Echolocation
teaser: Echolocation lets bats see with sound in the dark, and their brains turn echoes into a living map. When a bat calls, sound waves bounce off obstacles and prey, and the bat reads the delay to judge distance, the shift in frequency to judge speed, and the loudness to judge size. The calls are far above human hearing, mostly, and different species use different frequencies so they can share the same sky without jamming each other. Some moths have evolved ears that hear bats coming, starting an evolutionary arms race.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how bats emit ultrasonic calls up to 200 times a second and read the echoes to map their world in the dark, catching insects mid-air with pinpoint accuracy, some detecting a mosquito-sized target at 10 meters. Explore the frequency ranges, the Doppler shifts they compensate for, and how the design inspired sonar and blind-navigation aids.

name: Bat Hibernation
teaser: Bats that hibernate pull off one of the most extreme feats of the animal world. In caves, they drop their body temperature to match the cold air, slow their heart from hundreds of beats a minute to just a handful, and take a breath only once every few minutes. They survive the whole winter on stored fat, waking rarely. This deep sleep is risky, because every wake-up burns precious energy, which is why people are urged to leave hibernating bats strictly alone in their caves.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover how bats hibernate, then explain why waking them is dangerous.

name: Bat Hunting at Dusk
teaser: At dusk, the brown bat takes to the sky on a mission that sounds like a superhero power: it can catch over a thousand insects in a single night. Flying low over fields, ponds, and streetlights, it uses echolocation to detect and intercept mosquitoes and moths in midair, sometimes catching two insects in quick succession. A nursing mother must eat nearly her own weight in bugs each night to make milk. One colony can remove enormous numbers of crop pests from the air every summer.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn why bats hunt at dusk, then explain how they catch insects on the wing.

name: Bats and Viruses
teaser: Bats carry many viruses without getting sick, and scientists are working hard to understand why. Their bodies run hot, with body temperatures that soar during flight, which may act like a fever that keeps viruses in check. Their immune systems are tuned differently from ours, always on high alert but never overreacting. Because bats fly, live in dense colonies, and sometimes share habitats with other animals, viruses can pass between species. Studying bat immunity could teach us how to make our own defenses smarter.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover why bats host many viruses, then explain their immune adaptations.

name: Bear Cubs
teaser: A bear cub is born into a world of extremes. At birth it's tiny — a black bear cub weighs under half a kilogram, smaller than a guinea pig — blind, hairless, and utterly helpless, born in the dark den while its mother hibernates. The mother nurses it on rich milk, and by spring the cub has grown into a sturdy, playful ball of fur that follows her out of the den. Cubs stay with their mother for one to two years (brown bears up to three), learning everything: what to eat, how to climb, when to avoid danger, and where the best fishing spots are.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover how small bear cubs are at birth, then explain why they stay with mothers.

name: Bear Hibernation
teaser: A hibernating bear is a medical marvel — it sleeps for months without eating, drinking, or going to the bathroom, yet loses almost no muscle or bone. That's because bear hibernation isn't true hibernation: the bear's body temperature drops only slightly, and it can wake quickly if disturbed, so scientists call it 'winter sleep' or torpor. During the deep sleep, the bear lives off its fat stores, its heart rate drops from around 50 beats per minute to about 10, and its body recycles its own waste into protein — a trick doctors would love to copy.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn what happens during bear hibernation, then explain how they survive months without food.

name: Bear Senses
teaser: The bear's most dangerous sense is its nose — a sense of smell that ranks among the best in the animal kingdom, estimated at up to 2,100 times more powerful than a human's. A bear can smell a food source from kilometers away, detect a human from far beyond sight range, and track a scent that's days old. That nose drives much of bear behavior: bears live in a world of smells, reading the forest like a newspaper, and campers are warned to store food carefully because a bear's nose will find it.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how strong bear smell is, then explain why it matters for finding food.

name: Beaver
teaser: The beaver is nature's engineer, the only animal besides humans that deliberately shapes its landscape. It builds dams from sticks, mud, and stones to slow rivers and create ponds, then lodges with underwater entrances where it raises its family. Those ponds flood the land, create wetlands, and attract fish, frogs, ducks, and deer, so beavers actually increase biodiversity wherever they build. Their incisors never stop growing, which is why they must gnaw constantly. Once nearly extinct in Europe, they are being reintroduced to restore rivers.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how beavers build dams and lodges that create wetlands, their orange teeth never stop growing, and they fell trees with chisel teeth and store branches underwater for winter. Explore how beaver ponds boost biodiversity, the near-extinction from fur trapping, and the rewilding projects bringing them back.

name: Beaver Engineering
teaser: A beaver dam is one of the great constructions of the animal world, and beavers are relentless builders. Working at night, they fell trees with their chisel teeth, drag branches into the water, and pack mud into the gaps until the dam holds. The pond it creates is the real point: deep water protects the lodge from predators and stays liquid in winter. Dams can stretch for hundreds of meters, and a single family may maintain theirs for generations, reshaping entire valleys into wetlands.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how beavers build dams, then explain why they are ecosystem engineers.

name: Beaver Lodge
teaser: The beaver lodge is a fortress with a hidden door. Built from sticks and mud in the middle of a pond, it rises above the water as a dome that can reach two meters high, with a dry sleeping chamber at its heart. All entrances are underwater, so no land predator can sneak in, and the family dries off in the chamber after swimming home. In winter the lodge traps the warmth of the family inside while ice seals the pond around it, keeping the beavers safe and snug.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how beavers build lodges of mud and sticks rising above ponds, with underwater entrances and dry chambers above water, while their dams raise water levels to flood forests for safety and food storage. Explore the engineering, the winter food caches, the young kits inside, and how a single family reshapes entire valleys.

name: Beaver Lodges
teaser: Beaver lodges are warm winter homes built in the middle of cold ponds. Beavers pile sticks, grass, and mud into a dome, then chew out a dry central chamber above the waterline with tunnels down to the submerged doors. In winter, the lodge's thick walls insulate the family, and the pond's ice keeps predators away while the beavers still swim through underwater entrances to reach food caches they sank in autumn. A single lodge can house a family for many years.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover how beaver lodges are built, then explain the underwater entrance.

name: Beaver Teeth
teaser: A beaver's front teeth are self-sharpening chisels that never wear out. The enamel on the front of each tooth is hard and orange, while the softer dentine behind it wears faster, so the tooth always keeps a sharp edge. They grow continuously, up to a meter a year if never used, so beavers must gnaw constantly just to keep them trimmed. The iron in that orange enamel makes it tougher than most mammal teeth, letting a beaver fell trees far thicker than its own body.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn why beaver teeth are orange, then explain why they never stop growing.

name: Bee-eater
teaser: The bee-eater is a dazzling hunter that turns danger into dinner. This colorful bird, decked in greens, blues, and golds, catches bees and wasps in midair, then returns to a perch to beat the sting out of the insect against a branch. It rubs the prey to squeeze out the venom, so a bee-eater can safely eat stinging insects by the hundred. It digs nesting tunnels in sandy banks and feeds its chicks with a careful diet that gets less venomous as they grow.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how bee-eaters catch bees and wasps mid-flight, rub them against a branch to remove the sting, and eat them. Explore their dazzling rainbow colors, their underground nest tunnels dug into riverbanks, and how they avoid being stung through repeated rubbing and squeezing.

name: Beekeeping
teaser: Beekeeping is one of the oldest partnerships between humans and animals, dating back thousands of years. A beekeeper manages hives, giving bees a safe home in exchange for honey, wax, and the pollinating work the bees do on nearby crops. One healthy hive can produce tens of kilograms of honey a year while its bees visit millions of flowers. Modern beekeeping is vital to agriculture, since bees pollinate a huge share of the world's food crops, and keeping hives healthy helps feed everyone.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how beekeeping dates back thousands of years, with hives from clay pots to modern boxes, beekeepers managing colonies for honey, pollination, and wax, and wearing suits and smokers to calm bees. Explore how a hive works through the seasons, the honey harvest, and the challenge of keeping bees healthy amid pests like Varroa mites.

name: Beetle Diversity
teaser: Beetles are the most diverse group of animals on Earth, with hundreds of thousands of described species and countless more undiscovered. They come in every size, shape, and color, from jewel-like weevils to stag beetles with antler-like jaws. They live almost everywhere: in deserts, rainforests, ponds, caves, and even your pantry. Their secret is a tough exoskeleton and a hard protective first pair of wings. Biologists joke that if you want to understand life on Earth, start with beetles, because there is one for everything.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how beetles make up a quarter of all known animal species, with over 400,000 described, from jewel beetles with iridescent shells to bombardier beetles that spray boiling chemicals, and their success from deserts to glaciers. Explore why they're so diverse, the beetle-collecting tradition, and the famous quote about a creator's fondness for beetles.

name: Beluga
teaser: The beluga whale is the white ghost of the Arctic seas, famous for its expressive face and high-pitched songs that earned it the nickname sea canary. Unlike other whales, its neck vertebrae are not fused, so it can nod and turn its head, and it uses its flexible melon to make a huge range of clicks, whistles, and chirps. Its skin whitens with age, babies are born grey, and it sheds its skin by rubbing on gravel. Belugas travel in pods and can dive hundreds of meters under the ice.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how belugas, the white whales of the Arctic, are called canaries of the sea for their whistles and clicks, have flexible necks that let them nod, and use echolocation under sea ice to find breathing holes. Explore their molting in estuaries, their social pods, and how their Arctic home is warming.

name: Bengal Tiger
teaser: The Bengal tiger is the big cat of the Indian subcontinent, the national animal of India and Bangladesh. Males can weigh over two hundred kilograms and stretch three meters from nose to tail, and their stripes are as unique as fingerprints. They are ambush hunters that need large territories of forest and grassland, and they are powerful swimmers, unlike most cats. Decades of poaching and habitat loss brought them to the brink, but protected reserves have seen their numbers slowly climb back.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how Bengal tigers, the most numerous tiger subspecies, roam Indian forests and mangroves, with the Sundarbans population famous for swimming between islands and a reputation built on rare but feared attacks. Explore their stripes unique as fingerprints, their territorial roaring, and the reserves like Ranthambhore that protect them.

name: Betta Fish Care
teaser: The betta, or Siamese fighting fish, is famous for flowing fins and a fierce personality, and it needs care that matches its reputation. Despite being sold in tiny bowls, it actually needs a heated, filtered tank of at least a few gallons, with water around twenty-six degrees. Males must be kept apart, since two males will fight to the death, and bettas are labyrinth fish that breathe air from the surface. With proper care, they are intelligent pets that learn to recognize their owners.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how betta fish, famous for their flowing fins and aggression toward each other, thrive in warm, planted tanks with gentle filters, not tiny bowls, eating high-protein pellets and frozen foods. Explore why males fight, the bubble nests males build, and how to keep them healthy for years.

name: Big Cat Paw Secrets
teaser: The paws of a big cat are precision tools disguised as furniture. Each paw hides retractable claws — sharp, curved blades that stay sheathed inside a protective skin fold when walking, so they stay razor-sharp and perfectly silent, then spring out when it's time to grab. Between the toes sit scent glands, so every step a lion or tiger takes leaves a chemical calling card, marking its route without a single scratch. The paw pads themselves are tough, elastic cushions that absorb the shock of sprinting and stalking, letting a 200-kilogram cat walk through dry leaves without a sound.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how retractable claws work, then explain why lions have tufted tails.

name: Bilby
teaser: The bilby is Australia's Easter bunny, a shy nocturnal marsupial with huge ears, a long snout, and silky blue-grey fur. It digs spiraling burrows to escape the desert heat and predators, and it gets all the moisture it needs from food, never drinking water. Bilbies once ranged across much of Australia, but foxes, cats, and land clearing pushed them to the edges. They now star in Australian Easter campaigns, with chocolate bilbies raising money to help bring them back.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how bilbies, rabbit-eared marsupials of the Australian desert, dig spiral burrows that shelter other species and are threatened by foxes, cats, and fire, with conservation groups selling chocolate bilbies at Easter to replace the bunny. Explore their long snouts, their nocturnal life, and the captive breeding and fence programs saving them.

name: Binturong
teaser: The binturong is a slow-moving tree dweller of Southeast Asia that smells like buttered popcorn. The scent comes from a gland under its tail, which it uses to mark its territory, and the aroma is so distinctive that zookeepers recognize each animal by smell. Also called the bearcat, it is actually related to civets, not bears or cats. It has a grasping prehensile tail like a fifth hand, and it is one of only two carnivores with a fully prehensile tail, using it to hang and climb.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the binturong, or bearcat, of Southeast Asian forests smells like buttered popcorn, a scent from a chemical in its urine, and is neither bear nor cat but a viverrid related to civets. Explore its prehensile tail used like a fifth hand, its slow tree-climbing life, and its threatened forest home.

name: Bioluminescence
teaser: Bioluminescence is living light, produced by chemicals inside animals, and it turns the dark ocean into a fireworks show. Fireflies flash to find mates, glowworms light up cave walls, and deep-sea fish dangle glowing lures to attract prey. The light comes from a chemical reaction involving luciferin and oxygen, and some animals even control the color and flash pattern. Squid release glowing ink as a decoy, and dinoflagellates make the sea glow blue when waves disturb them, a sight called the milky seas.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how hundreds of species glow through bioluminescence, from fireflies signaling mates to deep-sea fish with glowing lures, anglerfish headlights, and glowing plankton that light up waves at night. Explore the chemistry of luciferin and luciferase, and the many uses of living light, from camouflage to communication.

name: Bird Color Vision
teaser: Birds see a world full of colors we can never know, because their eyes have four types of color receptor, while humans have three. That extra type lets them see ultraviolet light, so many birds that look plain to us are patterned brilliantly in UV. Robins, for example, judge each other by ultraviolet patches invisible to the human eye. Birds of prey add even sharper detail, spotting prey from high above, and the structure of their retinas gives some of them the fastest vision of any animal.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover how bird vision differs from humans, then explain UV plumage.

name: Bird Courtship
teaser: Bird courtship is a world of dance, song, and dazzling display. Male birds of paradise turn into living sparks of color, dancing on their forest courts. Bowerbirds build and decorate elaborate structures to impress females. Grebes perform a synchronized water dance, rushing across the pond side by side. Frigatebirds inflate a huge red throat pouch like a balloon, and hummingbirds dive at breakneck speed, making their tail feathers whistle. Every display says the same thing: I am healthy, watch me.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how birds court, then explain why the male usually displays.

name: Bird Egg Science
teaser: Bird eggs are engineering marvels. Their shape is no accident: rounder eggs sit still in nests, while pointed eggs roll in a tight circle instead of falling off cliff ledges, a trick puffins and guillemots use on bare rock. The shell is mostly calcium carbonate, strong enough to hold the growing chick yet porous enough to let oxygen in. Shell color can be camouflage, and speckles can strengthen thin parts of the shell. An ostrich egg is so strong a person can stand on it.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn why bird eggs vary in color, then explain the camouflage theory.

name: Bird Migration Routes
teaser: Bird migration is one of the great spectacles of nature, with billions of birds moving between continents every year. The bar-tailed godwit flies over ten thousand kilometers without stopping, straight across the Pacific. Warblers small enough to fit in your hand cross the entire Gulf of Mexico in one night. Birds navigate by the Sun, the stars, the Earth's magnetic field, and even smells, and young birds on their first trip often fly alone to places they have never seen.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how billions of birds migrate along invisible flyways, from the Arctic tern's pole-to-pole marathon to geese flying in V-formations that save energy. Explore how birds fatten up, navigate by stars, sun, and magnetic sensing, and the stopover refueling spots whose loss can doom a species.

name: Bird Parenting
teaser: Bird parenting is a full-time job of feeding, guarding, and teaching. Both parents often share the work: one incubates the eggs while the other forages, then both stuff the gaping mouths of chicks with food from dawn to dusk. A blue tit can make over a thousand feeding trips in a day. Some birds are single parents, some have helpers, and a few, like the cuckoo, cheat entirely, dropping their eggs in other birds' nests. Nestlings are helpless, featherless, and utterly dependent.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover how birds feed chicks, then explain why some chicks leave early.

name: Birds That Mimic
teaser: Some birds are professional impersonators. The lyrebird of Australia can mimic almost any sound it hears: chainsaws, camera shutters, car alarms, and the calls of twenty other bird species, all woven into its song. Mockingbirds copy the songs of neighbors and rivals, and parrots and mynahs famously copy human speech. This mimicry is more than a party trick. Males use it to impress females, and a larger repertoire often means an older, smarter, healthier mate.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn which birds mimic, then explain why they copy sounds.

name: Birds of Paradise
teaser: Birds of paradise are the most extravagant performers in the bird world, found only in New Guinea and a few nearby islands. Males come in impossible colors, electric blue, velvet black, and gold, with long wire-like tail feathers and elaborate head plumes. Each species has its own dance: the superb bird of paradise turns into a black smiley face shape, and the Wilson's bird of paradise clears a private dance floor on the forest floor. Females watch the show and choose the best dancer.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how birds of paradise court, then explain the sexual selection.

name: Bison Wallowing
teaser: A bison's favorite pastime looks like a dirt bath, but it's a vital part of the prairie ecosystem. Wallowing — rolling and grinding in a bare patch of earth — leaves behind a shallow depression, and those depressions are ecological treasure chests. Rain collects in them, creating seasonal puddles that amphibians and insects use; the disturbed soil seeds with pioneer plants; and the wallows become hotbeds of diversity in the otherwise uniform grassland. For the bison themselves, the dust bath helps shed parasites, cool down in summer, and shed their winter coat.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn why bison wallow, then explain what the dust does for their coats.

name: Black Bear Climbing
teaser: The American black bear is the best tree-climbing bear in the world — a fact that surprises most people who think of bears as slow, ground-bound giants. Black bears climb with remarkable speed and confidence, using their powerful forelimbs and long, curved claws to scramble up trunks that would defeat most animals, and they're especially good at it when young — cubs climb trees at the first sign of danger and stay there until their mother calls them down. Adult black bears climb to escape threats, to reach fruit and nuts in the canopy, and even to sleep on high, safe branches.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover how well black bears climb, then explain why grizzlies cannot.

name: Black Mamba
teaser: The black mamba is Africa's fastest and most feared snake, but its name comes from the inside of its mouth, which is inky black. It can slither at over twenty kilometers an hour, and when cornered it rears up, spreads a narrow hood, and strikes repeatedly, delivering a neurotoxic venom that can kill in hours without treatment. Despite the reputation, mambas prefer to escape and only attack when threatened. They are also surprisingly intelligent snakes, able to learn routes and remember where they live.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the black mamba, Africa's longest venomous snake at up to 4.5 meters, moves at up to 20 km/h with a neurotoxic venom that can kill within 20 minutes untreated. Explore why its name comes from the black inside of its mouth, and how it prefers to flee, striking only when cornered.

name: Black Panthers
teaser: A 'black panther' is not its own species — it is simply a jaguar or a leopard carrying an unusual amount of dark pigment, a condition called melanism. The same way some humans have dark skin, these cats produce extra melanin, so their normally golden coats come out almost black. The spots are still there; in the right light you can see the faint rosettes glowing through the dark fur like a watermark. Melanism is far more common in rainforest populations, where the low light makes a black coat better camouflage for hunting, and less common in open savanna.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover what melanism is, then explain why black panthers are not their own species.

name: Black Widow
teaser: The black widow is the spider with the warning sign built in: a glossy black body with a red hourglass mark. Its venom is fifteen times stronger than a rattlesnake's by weight, though it delivers far less, and bites are rarely deadly to healthy adults. The female is famous for sometimes eating her smaller mate after mating, a behavior that gives the spider its name. She builds a tangled web and hangs upside down near the center, ready to pounce on anything that touches a strand.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the black widow's red hourglass warns of a neurotoxic bite that causes severe muscle pain but is rarely fatal, with antivenom available. Explore its messy tangle web, the female's size and lifespan versus the male, and why its reputation exceeds its actual danger.

name: Black-footed Ferret
teaser: The black-footed ferret is North America's rarest mammal, a comeback story built on a single lucky discovery. It was declared extinct in 1979, then a tiny wild population was found in Wyoming in 1981. All of today's ferrets, thousands of them, descend from just seven of those animals. The ferret eats almost nothing but prairie dogs, and it was saved by captive breeding and by restoring the prairie dog towns it depends on. It is a sign of how much work species recovery really takes.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how black-footed ferrets were declared extinct in the wild until a small colony was found in Wyoming in 1981, and captive breeding with prairie dog conservation has since released thousands back into the prairies. Explore their dependence on prairie dog towns, the genetic bottleneck, and the setbacks from disease.

name: Blobfish
teaser: The blobfish became an internet celebrity for its droopy, grumpy face, but that famous look is a case of decompression. The blobfish lives hundreds of meters deep, where the crushing pressure is dozens of times that at the surface. In its natural habitat, its body is shaped like a normal fish, its jelly-like flesh just slightly less dense than water so it floats above the seafloor without swimming. The squashed, sad face appears only when it is hauled to the surface, where the pressure drop makes its body collapse.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the blobfish, famous as the world's ugliest fish, looks normal in its natural habitat 1,000 meters deep where pressure holds its gelatinous body together, only sagging into the blob face when brought to the surface. Explore its low-energy life of floating and eating whatever drifts past.

name: Blue Whale
teaser: The blue whale is the largest animal that has ever lived, bigger than any dinosaur that ever walked the Earth. A single adult can reach thirty meters, longer than a basketball court, and weigh over a hundred and fifty tonnes, as much as thirty elephants. Its heart alone is the size of a small car. Despite this size, it eats some of the smallest prey, krill, filtering tons of them through its baleen plates. A newborn blue whale calf is already one of the biggest animals on the planet.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the blue whale is the largest animal ever, up to 33 meters and 190 tonnes, bigger than any dinosaur, with a heart the size of a car and a tongue that weighs as much as an elephant. Explore how it filter-feeds on krill, sings subsonic songs, and how whaling nearly erased it before protection.

name: Blue Whale Calls
teaser: Blue whale calls are the loudest sounds made by any animal, louder than a jet engine and audible across entire ocean basins.
