Their low-frequency moans, around one hundred and eighty decibels underwater, can travel hundreds of kilometers through the sea. Researchers can identify individual whales by the unique pattern of their calls, which they repeat for hours. The whales likely use these songs to keep in contact with each other across vast distances of open ocean, and shipping noise increasingly interferes with their calls.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover how loud blue whale calls are, then explain why low sounds travel far.

name: Blue Whale Feeding
teaser: A blue whale feeds by lunging into a swarm of krill with its mouth wide open, taking in a volume of water bigger than its own body. It then pushes the water out through baleen plates, leaving hundreds of kilograms of tiny shrimp-like krill trapped inside. A blue whale can eat four tonnes of krill a day during feeding season. These feasts are possible only in the cold, food-rich waters near the poles, which is why blue whales migrate between feeding and breeding grounds every year.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how blue whales filter krill, then explain the baleen plates.

name: Blue Whale Song
teaser: The blue whale's song is a deep, slow, haunting call that carries across the oceans. Each call is a long low-frequency phrase that can last up to half a minute, repeated over and over in patterns that scientists are still decoding. Whales in different ocean regions sing different dialects, and the songs slowly change over the years. Because low-frequency sound travels so far in water, a blue whale's song can reach another whale hundreds of kilometers away, keeping these giants connected in an ocean of silence.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how blue whale songs at up to 188 decibels are the loudest animal sounds, low-frequency pulses that can travel hundreds of kilometers underwater, with each population singing its own version of the song that slowly evolves over years. Explore the subsonic frequencies, the ship noise that drowns them out, and how hydrophone networks track them.

name: Blue-footed Booby
teaser: The blue-footed booby is famous for its bright blue feet, and those feet are the key to its love life. Males show off by strutting, lifting one foot at a time, and the bluer the feet, the more attractive the male, because the blue color comes from the fresh fish in his diet. Healthy boobies with vivid feet raise healthier chicks. The booby also dives spectacularly, plunging from the air into the sea like an arrow to catch fish, and it nests on the ground in noisy colonies.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how male blue-footed boobies show off bright blue feet in an elaborate high-stepping dance, with females choosing mates by the blueness of the pigment derived from fresh fish. Explore their dive-bombing fishing style, their clumsy name, and the sky-pointing greeting ritual of pairs.

name: Blue-ringed Octopus
teaser: The blue-ringed octopus is small, beautiful, and one of the most venomous animals on Earth. It lives in tide pools of the Pacific, and when threatened it flashes electric blue rings across its body as a warning. Its bite injects tetrodotoxin, the same poison as pufferfish, which can paralyze a person within minutes, and there is no antivenom. Despite its tiny size, about the length of a golf ball, its venom is potent enough to be lethal. Divers are told to admire it, never touch it.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the blue-ringed octopus, small enough to fit in a palm, carries tetrodotoxin in its bite that can paralyze a human within minutes, with no antivenom, while flashing brilliant blue rings as a warning. Explore how its venom is made by symbiotic bacteria, its shy nature, and why the flash means back off.

name: Bluefin Tuna
teaser: The bluefin tuna is the athlete of the ocean, a warm-blooded fish built for speed and endurance. It can reach three meters, weigh over six hundred kilograms, and swim at speeds above seventy kilometers an hour, crossing entire oceans on migrations. Unlike most fish, it can raise its body temperature above the surrounding water, which powers its muscles even in cold seas. Its rich flesh makes it one of the most valuable fish on Earth, and overfishing has pushed wild populations dangerously low.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how bluefin tuna are warm-blooded fish that can sprint past 70 km/h and migrate across entire oceans, traveling thousands of kilometers to spawn. Explore their streamlined torpedo bodies, their ability to heat their muscles, and how overfishing drove them to the brink for sushi.

name: Bobbit Worm
teaser: The bobbit worm is a hidden terror of the tropical seafloor. This giant marine worm can grow to three meters long, and it burrows into the sand, waiting with only its jaws exposed. When a fish swims overhead, the worm strikes faster than a blink, snapping shut with razor-sharp jaws and dragging the victim down into its burrow. It has no eyes, sensing prey by movement and water pressure instead. Divers know the feeling of a sudden tug on their line, and of the bait vanishing.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the bobbit worm, up to 3 meters long, buries itself in reef sand and strikes passing fish with five jaws that snap shut like scissors, dragging prey into its burrow. Explore its iridescent body, the aquariums it terrorized by eating fish overnight, and how little we know of its deep-sea cousins.

name: Bombardier Beetle
teaser: The bombardier beetle defends itself with a built-in chemical weapon, firing boiling hot spray from its rear. When threatened, it mixes two chemicals inside a special chamber in its abdomen, and the reaction produces a hot, explosive spray that shoots out at over one hundred degrees. The beetle can aim this spray in any direction, and it fires in rapid pulses, with each blast accompanied by an audible pop. Birds and frogs that try to eat it quickly learn to leave it alone.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how bombardier beetles defend by mixing hydroquinone and hydrogen peroxide in a reaction chamber, shooting a boiling-hot, foul spray from their rear at 100 pulses a second, accurate enough to hit a predator's face. Explore the chemistry and the debate it once sparked, and how the spray deters everything from ants to frogs.

name: Bottlenose Societies
teaser: Bottlenose dolphins live in complex societies built on alliances and friendships. Males form tight partnerships, sometimes coalitions of two or three, that work together to herd females and defend territory against rival gangs, and these alliances can last for decades. Females have their own social networks, sharing babysitting duties. Dolphins recognize each other by signature whistles, personal name-like calls they use to greet and find each other, and they can remember the whistles of friends they have not seen for twenty years.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover how male dolphins form alliances, then explain why the bonds last.

name: Box Jellyfish
teaser: The box jellyfish is one of the most venomous animals in the ocean, and it is also one of the fastest jellyfish. Unlike most jellyfish, which drift with the currents, it can swim purposefully, reaching speeds of several kilometers an hour, and it has eyes, clusters of simple eyes on each corner of its box-shaped bell. Its tentacles carry millions of stinging cells loaded with toxins that attack the heart and nerves. It lives in the warm waters of the Indo-Pacific, where beaches close when it appears.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the Australian box jellyfish is considered the most venomous animal, its tentacles carrying enough toxin to kill an adult within minutes, with a more advanced nervous system and 24 eyes, some with lenses, that let it steer toward prey. Explore the vinegar first-aid, the nets and stinger suits, and its surprising swimming ability.

name: Box Turtle
teaser: The box turtle carries its home on its back and can close it completely. Its hinged plastron, the bottom shell, folds up to seal the turtle inside its top shell like a box, so predators find a solid shell instead of a turtle. Box turtles are land dwellers that wander through forests and fields, living up to fifty years or more in the wild. They have a strong homing instinct and will travel the same routes for years, which is why moving one far from home often dooms it.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how box turtles carry a hinged shell that closes completely, sealing them into an armored box, and can live 50 to 100 years, wandering home ranges they know intimately. Explore their omnivorous appetite, their need for large wild areas, and why pet trade and roads threaten them.

name: Brittle Star
teaser: The brittle star is a relative of the starfish with long, snakelike arms that it uses to crawl quickly across the seafloor. Its central disk is small, and its five slender arms can be up to twenty times its disk's width, covered in tiny spines that help it grip. If a predator grabs an arm, the brittle star drops it and grows a new one. Some species live in vast numbers on the ocean floor, covering entire plains, and they feed on detritus and small prey, playing a huge role in recycling the seabed.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how brittle stars, more slender than sea stars, move rapidly by wriggling their five arms, some species living in the thousands on a single coral head, and they detach arms to escape predators, regrowing them. Explore their deep-sea dominance, their light-sensing arms, and the difference from true sea stars.

name: Brown Bear
teaser: The brown bear is one of the largest land carnivores on Earth, and it rules the forests and mountains of North America, Europe, and Asia. It can weigh over six hundred kilograms and run faster than a horse despite its size. Though classified as a carnivore, it eats mostly plants, berries, nuts, and roots, with fish and meat as a bonus. Before winter, it gains a hundred kilograms or more of fat and then sleeps through the cold months, its heart slowing while its cubs are born in the den.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how brown bears, including grizzlies, range from Europe to North America, weighing up to 700 kg in coastal Alaska where salmon fuel their growth, and hibernate for months without eating, drinking, or excreting. Explore their omnivorous appetites, their digging, their fishing, and their complex relationship with humans.

name: Buffalo vs Lion
teaser: The fight between a lion and an African buffalo is one of nature's great rivalries — and it's not the one-sided battle people expect. A buffalo is enormous, weighing up to a ton, and it fights back: a herd of buffalo will charge lions on sight, and lions have learned to fear the low, roaring 'hoo' call that sends the whole herd stampeding to help a member in trouble. Lions do hunt buffalo, but it takes a coordinated pride attack on a lone or sick animal, and even then the outcome is far from certain.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover how buffalo defend against lions, then explain why lions target the weak.

name: Bullet Ant
teaser: The bullet ant has the most painful sting of any insect, a bite of agony that can last for twenty-four hours. Its name is no joke: those who have felt it say the pain is like being shot. Found in the rainforests of Central and South America, it is a large ant, up to three centimeters long, with a sting that carries a potent neurotoxin. In some Amazonian tribes, young men prove their endurance by wearing gloves full of these ants, enduring the stings as a rite of passage.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the bullet ant's sting is rated the most painful of any insect, a full day of throbbing agony, and how some Indigenous Amazonian boys endure it repeatedly as a rite of passage. Explore its large size, its colony defenses, and the neurotoxin that makes the sting unforgettable.

name: Burrowing Frog
teaser: The burrowing frog survives the driest places on Earth by digging down and waiting. When the rains come, it emerges to breed in temporary pools, but when the ground dries, it digs deep into the soil, sometimes several meters down, and forms a waterproof cocoon of shed skin around itself. In this state, it can survive years without water, its metabolism slowing to a crawl. It absorbs water through its skin the moment rain returns and digs its way back to the surface to call.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how burrowing frogs dig backwards into soil with hardened feet, inflate their bodies to wedge themselves in burrows, and seal in moisture with a skin cocoon for months or years. Explore their explosive emergence after rain, their loud calls from underground, and how they store water.

name: Butterflies and Moths
teaser: Butterflies and moths make up the order Lepidoptera, and they are more alike than their looks suggest. Both start life as caterpillars, eat leaves, and transform inside a pupa or cocoon. Butterflies fly by day with club-tipped antennae, while most moths fly at night with feathery antennae, but there are day-flying moths and dull butterflies. Together they number about a hundred and eighty thousand species, and their caterpillars are the most important plant-eaters in many ecosystems, food for countless birds.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how butterflies and moths together form Lepidoptera, insects with wings covered in microscopic scales that create their colors, with butterflies generally day-flying with club-tipped antennae and moths night-flying with feathery antennae. Explore the exceptions to every rule, the scale structure behind iridescence, and their place in pollination and food webs.

name: Butterfly Garden
teaser: A butterfly garden turns a yard into a pollinator highway, and it needs just a few simple ingredients. Nectar flowers like milkweed, coneflower, and lavender feed the adults, while host plants, specific leaves the caterpillars can eat, give each species a place to lay eggs. Butterflies also need sun-warmed basking spots, shallow puddles for minerals, and shelter from wind. Plant a mix that blooms all season, avoid pesticides, and within a summer you will see monarchs, swallowtails, and skippers working the blooms.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how a butterfly garden provides nectar flowers for adults and host plants for caterpillars, from milkweed for monarchs to parsley for swallowtails, plus sunny basking spots, shelter, and puddling areas with moisture and minerals. Explore the plant choices, why pesticides undo the work, and the joy of watching full life cycles in your own yard.

name: Butterfly Metamorphosis
teaser: Butterfly metamorphosis is one of nature's strangest miracles. A caterpillar eats and grows until it is dozens of times its birth size, then attaches itself and forms a chrysalis. Inside, its body breaks down into a soupy mass of cells, and from that soup a butterfly assembles itself: wings, antennae, eyes, and all. When it emerges, it pumps fluid into its crumpled wings, dries them, and flies away within hours. Scientists are still discovering how a caterpillar's memories survive the transformation.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how a caterpillar dissolves inside its chrysalis into a soup of cells, from which imaginal discs grow the adult butterfly's wings, eyes, and legs, a transformation so complete the adult's memories may not survive. Explore the hormones timing each stage, the chrysalis breathing tubes, and how wings form and unfold.

name: Butterfly Mimicry
teaser: The viceroy butterfly wears a costume that saves its life. It looks almost exactly like the monarch, orange with black veins, but it is a completely different species. The monarch is poisonous to birds because it feeds on milkweed as a caterpillar, storing toxins in its body. The viceroy was long thought to be a harmless mimic that escapes predators by copying the monarch's warning colors, but research shows the viceroy is itself distasteful, making this a case of two toxic species copying each other's advertising.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the viceroy butterfly mimics the toxic monarch's orange and black pattern, a copycat strategy called Batesian mimicry that tricks predators into avoiding it, while the monarch's real toxicity is Mullerian, shared warning among distasteful species. Explore how predators learn to avoid the pattern, and how mimicry shaped evolution.

name: CITES
teaser: CITES, the Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species, is the world's agreement to police the wildlife trade. It lists thousands of species, from elephants and rhinos to orchids and corals, and requires permits for any cross-border trade in them. Countries that sign on agree to crack down on smuggling, and the treaty has helped reduce poaching pressure on iconic species while regulating sustainable trade in others. It is one of the oldest and most powerful environmental agreements, protecting life by controlling commerce.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species, CITES, regulates the global trade in wildlife, from ivory and rhino horn to orchids and parrots, with member countries agreeing to ban or restrict what crosses borders. Explore its three appendices, the fight against smuggling, and the loopholes smugglers exploit.

name: Caddisfly
teaser: The caddisfly is a moth-like insect whose larva is an underwater architect. The larva lives in streams and builds itself a protective case from whatever the streambed offers: tiny pebbles, sand grains, twigs, or even snail shells, all glued together with silk. Each species builds a different style of house, and some make beautiful geometric spiral cases. The case protects the soft larva while it crawls along the bottom, and it even has a small door the larva can close. When ready, the larva seals the case and emerges as a flying adult.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how caddisfly larvae build protective cases from silk and materials around them, stones, sand, twigs, and even tiny shells, each species with its own case design, and some make silk nets to filter food from streams. Explore the case architecture, their role as water quality indicators, and the adult moths they become.

name: Caecilian
teaser: The caecilian is a limbless amphibian that looks like a worm but is closer to a frog or salamander. Found in the tropics, it burrows through moist soil and leaf litter, hunting earthworms and insects with a powerful bite. Most live underground and are rarely seen, their eyes small and covered with skin. Some species skip the water entirely: the mother grows a thick, nutrient-rich skin layer that her babies tear off and eat, a form of feeding unique among amphibians.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how caecilians are limbless burrowing amphibians found in tropical soil, looking like giant earthworms, with hidden eyes and sensory tentacles, some feeding their young with skin milk. Explore how they dig with reinforced skulls, their internal fertilization, and why they're the least known amphibian group.

name: Caiman
teaser: The caiman is a crocodilian of the Americas, smaller and more numerous than its cousins the alligator and crocodile. Found from Central America to South America, including the Amazon, it hunts fish, birds, and small mammals in rivers and swamps. The black caiman is the giant of the family, growing over five meters long, while the dwarf caiman of the flooded forests stays under a meter and a half. Like all crocodilians, mothers guard their nests fiercely and carry hatchlings gently in their jaws.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how caimans, smaller relatives of crocodiles and alligators, thrive across South America, with the black caiman reaching 5 meters in the Amazon. Explore their armored belly scales used for leather, how mothers carry hatchlings in their jaws, and their role in dry-season pools.

name: California Condor Recovery
teaser: The California condor is one of the rarest birds on Earth, and its story is one of the closest calls in conservation history. By 1982, only twenty-two of these giant vultures remained, and scientists made the desperate decision to bring them all into captivity. From those twenty-two, a captive breeding program rebuilt the population, and today several hundred condors fly free again over California, Arizona, and Mexico. With a wingspan of nearly three meters, they are the largest flying birds in North America.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how California condors dropped to just 22 birds in 1982, all captured for a breeding program, and have since been released and now number over 500, though they still need lead-free ammunition rules and regular vet care to survive in the wild. Explore the hand puppets that raised chicks without imprinting, the release sites, and the lead poisoning threat.

name: Camouflage
teaser: Camouflage is the art of disappearing, and animals are its greatest masters. The leaf insect looks so exactly like a leaf that its own predators walk past it. The cuttlefish can change its color, pattern, and even the texture of its skin to match the seafloor in a fraction of a second. Arctic hares turn white with the snow, and peacock flounders become nearly invisible on sand. Some animals go further and copy other species, while others just vanish, and it is all about staying alive one more day.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how animals vanish into backgrounds through color, pattern, and texture, from snowshoe hares that turn white in winter to chameleons, flounders matching the seabed, and moths that look exactly like tree bark. Explore disruptive coloration, countershading, and how predators also use disguise to sneak up on prey.

name: Cape Buffalo
teaser: The Cape buffalo is one of Africa's most dangerous animals, a huge black beast that looks calm and can turn in an instant. A bull can weigh nearly a tonne, with horns that form a solid bony shield across its head. Herds of hundreds graze the savanna, and buffalo will mob and charge lions that threaten them, a rare counterattack among prey. Unlike most prey species, a buffalo does not forget, and lone hunters have learned to respect the revenge of a herd.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how Cape buffalo, weighing up to 900 kg, gather in large herds for protection against lions, forming circles and counter-charging predators, and are considered among the most dangerous animals in Africa when wounded. Explore their massive horns, their mud wallows, the oxpeckers that clean them, and their constant war with lions.

name: Cape Buffalo Horns
teaser: The Cape buffalo wears its helmet permanently attached to its head: a massive pair of horns that meet in the middle to form a solid 'boss' across the skull, protecting the brain like built-in armor. Those horns are the buffalo's whole identity — the boss is thick enough to stop a charging rival's horns, and the sharp, downward-hooked tips can gore almost anything. Old bulls develop fully 'hard-bossed' horns that make them look even more formidable, and the horn structure is so characteristic it's used to tell individual buffalo apart.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover why cape buffalo horns are called bosses, then explain their defensive role.

name: Captive Breeding
teaser: Captive breeding is the emergency room of conservation, saving species that are down to their last individuals. Zoos and dedicated centers breed animals under carefully managed conditions, tracking genetics to avoid inbreeding, then release young back into protected wilds. It saved the California condor, the black-footed ferret, and the Arabian oryx from extinction. The work is delicate: animals must learn to hunt and fear humans before release, and the real battle, protecting wild habitat, continues long after the first reintroduction.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how captive breeding programs keep doomed species alive, from the California condor that dropped to 22 birds and came back through hand-raised chicks, to the Arabian oryx and black-footed ferret rescued from the brink. Explore the challenges of reintroducing animals raised in captivity, and the successes and failures.

name: Capuchin Tool Use
teaser: Capuchin monkeys are the New World's tool-users — small monkeys with a surprisingly sophisticated grasp of technology. The most famous example is nut-cracking: a capuchin finds a hard palm nut, carries it to a heavy stone, places the nut on it, and smashes it with a second stone, choosing the right weight and angle with what looks like genuine planning. Some groups use sticks to probe for insects, and researchers have even watched capuchins use stones to dig and to sharpen branches.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how capuchins crack nuts with stones, then explain what it reveals about their minds.

name: Capybara
teaser: The capybara is the world's largest rodent, a gentle giant of the South American wetlands that can weigh as much as an adult human. It is semi-aquatic, with webbed feet, eyes and nostrils on top of its head for swimming, and a calm nature that lets birds perch on its back and groom it. Capybaras live in social groups, and they communicate with whistles, clicks, and barks. Its favorite pastime is lounging in water, where it escapes heat and predators.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how capybaras, the largest rodents at up to 66 kg, live in groups by rivers in South America, half-submerged with eyes, ears, and nostrils on top of their heads, and are famous for their calm, social nature that seems to make every animal their friend. Explore their swimming, their teeth, and their giant family groups.

name: Capybara Groups
teaser: Capybaras are deeply social animals that live in herds of ten to twenty, and sometimes more. The group is usually led by a dominant male who keeps watch and settles squabbles, while females and young form the core. They groom each other, rest in piles, and take turns at sentry duty, warning the herd with a sharp bark when danger approaches. Their friendships extend across species too: birds, monkeys, and even caimans share space with them peaceably at the water's edge.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover why capybaras live in groups, then explain the sentinel behavior.

name: Caracal
teaser: The caracal is a desert lynx with extraordinary athletic ability, a medium-sized cat with long black ear tufts that give it a wild, elegant look. It is famous for its jumps, leaping high into the air to knock down birds in flight, and it can catch several birds in quick succession. In some parts of its range, it has been tamed and trained for hunting, and in India it was called the cat of kings. It is a solitary ambush hunter that thrives from Africa to Asia.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how caracals leap nearly 3 meters straight up to knock birds out of the air, with black ear tufts and a face like a lynx, and their name comes from a Turkish word for black ears. Explore their savanna and desert life, their springing hunts, and their history of being tamed for hunting in ancient cultures.

name: Caribou
teaser: The caribou, known as reindeer in Europe, is the great wanderer of the Arctic. Herds of hundreds of thousands migrate up to five thousand kilometers a year, the longest land migration of any mammal, following the seasons across the frozen tundra. Both males and females grow antlers, which is rare among deer, and their wide hooves work like snowshoes in winter and paddles when swimming. For the people of the far north, caribou have been life itself for thousands of years, providing food, clothing, and tools.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how caribou of the Arctic tundra make some of the longest land migrations, herds of hundreds of thousands moving over 5,000 km a year, with hooves that change with the seasons for snow and muskeg. Explore how both sexes grow antlers, the wolves that follow them, and the decline of herds.

name: Cassowary
teaser: The cassowary is the heaviest bird in Australia and one of the most dangerous birds on Earth. It stands up to two meters tall with a helmet-like casque on its head, brilliant blue neck, and dagger-like claws on its feet that can deliver a deadly kick. It is a rainforest gardener too, swallowing fruit whole and spreading seeds across the forest in its droppings, shaping the very trees around it. When threatened, it warns with a low booming call before charging, and it can run at fifty kilometers an hour.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the cassowary of New Guinea and northern Australia is often called the world's most dangerous bird, kicking with 12 cm dagger-like claws on its inner toes. Explore how it swallows rainforest fruits whole and spreads seeds, earning the title of forest gardener, and why it's a living reminder of dinosaurs.

name: Cassowary Casque
teaser: The cassowary's casque, the bony helmet on top of its head, is a puzzle scientists are still solving. It may protect the bird's head as it pushes through dense rainforest undergrowth, act as a sound chamber that boosts its deep booming calls, or signal age and dominance to other cassowaries. The casque is made of keratin over a bony core and grows slowly with the bird. What is certain is that no two are exactly alike, and the bird cares for it carefully while it forages the forest floor.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how cassowaries wear a hollow keratin casque on their heads whose purpose is debated, possibly amplifying their booming calls, protecting the head when pushing through rainforest undergrowth, or signaling age and dominance. Explore the bone and keratin structure, the calls that vibrate the casque, and the ongoing research into its function.

name: Cat Domestication
teaser: Cats chose to live with humans, or so the evidence suggests. Wild cats began hanging around early farming villages thousands of years ago, attracted by the mice that ate stored grain, and humans welcomed them as free pest control. Unlike dogs, which were actively bred for jobs, cats domesticated themselves, and their DNA shows they were tamed multiple times in different regions. Today's house cats are still 95 percent the same animal as wild cats, and they keep many of their wild instincts.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how cats likely domesticated themselves, drawn to grain stores and the mice they attracted, with the earliest evidence in the Near East 10,000 years ago, and they remain genetically close to wildcats. Explore how cats were worshipped in Egypt, sailed the world on ships, and became the internet's favorite animal.

name: Caterpillar
teaser: The caterpillar is the eating machine of the insect world, a living stomach with legs. It hatches from an egg already hungry and spends its whole youth chewing leaves, growing so fast that it molts its skin several times to keep up. A caterpillar can increase its body weight a thousand times in a few weeks, and some eat more than a hundred times their own weight in leaves each day. Every bite is stored for the transformation ahead, because after this comes the chrysalis and the butterfly.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how caterpillars are the larval stage of butterflies and moths, eating machines that can grow 100 times their hatching size in weeks, with silk-spinning glands, and defenses from stinging hairs to eye spots and mimicry of snakes. Explore their anatomy, the legs that become butterfly parts, and the chemical defenses some carry from their food plants.

name: Cave Lion
teaser: The cave lion was a giant of the Ice Age, a lion bigger than today's African lions that prowled across Europe, Asia, and North America. It was named for the cave paintings and bones found in the caves of Ice Age Europe, and it lived alongside early humans, who painted it on cave walls and competed with it for prey. It vanished around twelve thousand years ago, at the end of the last ice age, along with the mammoths and other giants. Frozen cave lion cubs found in Siberian permafrost still have their fur intact.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how cave lions, bigger than modern lions, prowled ice age Europe and Asia, leaving claw marks and bones in the caves they denned in, painted by early humans. Explore how DNA links them closer to modern lions than thought, their prey of deer and young mammoths, and why they vanished at the ice age's end.

name: Chameleon
teaser: The chameleon is the lizard of legend, famous for changing color, and its body is packed with other superpowers. Its eyes move independently, each swiveling on its own, then lock together for perfect depth perception before it strikes. Its tongue can shoot out at twice its body length in a fraction of a second to snag an insect. Its grasping feet and curling tail make it a master climber. And the color changes are real: camouflage, but also mood, temperature, and communication signals.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how chameleons catch prey by shooting a tongue longer than their body at 26 body lengths a second, and change color not mainly for camouflage but for mood, temperature, and signaling. Explore their independently rotating eyes, their grasping feet, and how color change happens in skin cell nanocrystals.

name: Chameleon Color Change
teaser: A chameleon changes color using layers of special cells in its skin. Pigment cells shift to expose or hide different colors, and deeper cells contain microscopic crystals that reflect light, which is how the vivid greens, blues, and reds appear. The chameleon can change in under a second, but the goal is often not camouflage: brighter colors signal mood and dominance, darker colors absorb heat, and pale colors cool it down. What looks like magic is actually a super-precise system of light and cells.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover how chameleons change color, then explain what the colors mean.

name: Chameleon Eyes
teaser: A chameleon's eyes are unlike any other animal's. Each eye sits in a cone-shaped turret that rotates independently, so the chameleon can watch two directions at once, one eye scanning for predators while the other tracks prey. When it spots an insect, both eyes lock forward onto the target, giving it the binocular vision needed to judge distance exactly. Then the tongue fires. The whole strike, from aim to catch, takes a fraction of a second, one of the fastest movements in the animal kingdom.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how chameleon eyes move independently, then explain the focus trick.

name: Chameleon Tongue
teaser: The chameleon's tongue is a biological catapult that fires at incredible speed. Coiled inside its mouth like a spring, the tongue is launched by muscles that stretch it to more than twice the chameleon's body length in about a twentieth of a second. The tip is sticky and shaped like a small club, and the tongue can snatch an insect weighing more than the chameleon itself. No matter the target's size, the tongue retracts with the meal already glued on, swallowed before the insect knows it moved.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how a chameleon's tongue can shoot out at 26 body lengths per second, longer than its whole body, powered by elastic collagen and a ring of accelerator muscles, with a sticky pad that grabs insects and reels them in. Explore the physics of the projection, the mucus grip, and how high-speed cameras revealed the mechanism.

name: Cheetah
teaser: The cheetah is the fastest land animal, built for a single explosive purpose. It can accelerate from zero to one hundred kilometers an hour in about three seconds, faster than most sports cars, and its flexible spine, long legs, and semi-retractable claws give it grip like a sprinter's spikes. But these bursts last only seconds, so hunts are decided quickly. Cheetahs are also the most vulnerable of the big cats, and they are so specialized for speed that they cannot defend their kills from lions and hyenas.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how cheetahs accelerate from zero to 100 km/h in three seconds, the fastest land animal, with non-retractable claws for grip, a flexible spine, and a tail used as a rudder. Explore why they hunt by day, their high failure rate, and how cubs lose to lions and hyenas despite adult speed.

name: Cheetah Cubs
teaser: Cheetah cubs have a built-in disguise: a thick silver mane of hair down their backs that makes them look like a fierce honey badger, one of the few animals even lions avoid. For the first few weeks, the mother hides her cubs in tall grass and moves them often, hunting alone and returning to nurse. The mane fades as they grow, but the cubs stay with their mother for well over a year, learning to hunt, before striking out on their own. Mortality is high, and only a fraction of cubs survive to adulthood.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how cheetah cubs face a brutal first year, with up to 90 percent killed by lions, hyenas, and starvation while their mother hunts alone, and a mother may raise one in ten cubs to adulthood. Explore the mohawk of fur that helps camouflage them, their cub-sitting dens, and the sanctuary programs protecting orphan cubs.

name: Cheetah vs Leopard
teaser: Cheetahs and leopards are Africa's two spotted cats, but they could not be more different. Look at the spots: a cheetah's are solid black dots on a pale coat, while a leopard wears darker 'rosettes' — rings with a spot in the middle. The build tells the story too. A cheetah is built like a greyhound: long legs, small head, deep chest, all for speed, and it hunts by day in open grassland. A leopard is stockier and heavier, with a thick neck and powerful forelimbs for dragging prey up trees, and it hunts by night in the bush.

exploreAction.instruction: Compare cheetah and leopard builds, then explain how their hunting styles differ.

name: Cheetah vs Leopard
teaser: Cheetahs and leopards share the African plains but live completely different lives. The cheetah is a sprinter: slender, long-legged, and built for daylight chases, killing with a trip and a suffocating bite, then eating fast before lions steal the meal. The leopard is a heavyweight climber: stockier, stronger, and solitary, stalking by night and dragging its kills up into trees to keep them safe from scavengers. A cheetah can outrun any leopard, but a leopard can outfight any cheetah, and one on one the leopard usually wins.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how cheetahs and leopards, both spotted African cats, differ in build, spots, and lifestyle, cheetahs slim and built for speed with solid black spots and tear marks, leopards stocky with rosette spots and no tear marks, and the two rarely interact since cheetahs hunt by day and leopards by night. Explore the easy field guide to telling them apart.

name: Chest Beating
teaser: The gorilla's chest-beat is the most famous sound in the primate world — a rapid thump-thump-thump that carries over a kilometer through the forest. It is made by cupping the hands and pounding the chest while inhaling sharp breaths, and the bigger the male, the deeper and louder the drumming. Chest-beating is not just a threat: males also beat their chests when excited, when playing, when announcing their presence to rivals, and sometimes when they have simply won a fight and feel like showing off. Females and even young gorillas do it too, though far more quietly.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover why gorillas beat their chests, then explain what the sound signals.

name: Chimpanzee
teaser: The chimpanzee is our closest living relative, sharing about 98 percent of our DNA, and it is startlingly like us. It uses tools, making sticks to fish termites out of mounds and stones to crack nuts. It learns culture, with different groups using different tool traditions passed down through generations. It feels grief, plays, and forms lifelong friendships, and it also lives with politics, alliances, and even warfare between rival communities. Observing chimps is like looking into a mirror held by evolution.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how chimpanzees share about 98 percent of our DNA, use sticks to fish termites, crack nuts with stones, hunt monkeys in coordinated packs, and have distinct cultures passed between communities. Explore their politics, their capacity for empathy and war, and why Jane Goodall's work changed how we see them.

name: Chimpanzee Hunting
teaser: Chimpanzees are not the peaceful vegetarians people once assumed — they're also skilled, coordinated hunters. Troops of chimpanzees, usually led by males, launch organized hunting parties for monkeys, especially red colobus, and the hunts are spectacular team efforts: some chimps chase the monkey through the trees while others block escape routes, and one will climb in for the kill. A hunt can last over an hour, and the meat is shared — the reward goes to the hunters and their allies, which makes hunting as much about politics as food.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how chimps hunt monkeys together, then explain why meat is shared.

name: Chimpanzee Society
teaser: Chimpanzee society is a soap opera with a doctorate — the most complex social structure of any animal outside our own species. A community of dozens to over a hundred individuals is bound together by shifting alliances, lifelong friendships, grudges that last decades, and politics that decide who leads. Males climb the hierarchy by building coalitions and courting supporters; females inherit rank and form their own quiet networks. Chimpanzees console each other after fights with hugs and grooming, they reconcile with reconciliatory kisses, and researchers have watched them plan revenge, mourn their dead, and even wage small wars between rival groups.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover how chimp alliances work, then explain why grooming matters.

name: Chimpanzee Tool Use
teaser: Chimpanzees are master toolmakers, and their toolkit varies from group to group like human culture. In some forests, chimps use stone hammers and anvils to crack open nuts, a skill that takes years to learn. Elsewhere they fashion sticks into termite fishing rods, sharpen branches into spears for hunting bushbabies, and use leaves as sponges to soak up drinking water. Young chimps learn by watching their mothers, and researchers have documented over twenty distinct tool behaviors passed down the generations.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how chimps use tools, then explain what it shows about their intelligence.

name: Chipmunk Cheek Pouches
teaser: A chipmunk's cheeks are built-in grocery bags that can stretch to hold more food than its head. The cheek pouches reach back to its shoulders, and a chipmunk can stuff them with seeds, nuts, and berries, sometimes carrying a load equal to a third of its own weight. It then scurries to its burrow and empties the pouches by pushing the food out with its paws, storing it for winter. These pouches are also handy for moving nesting material, and chipmunks stay busy from dawn to dusk filling their pantry.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover how chipmunks use cheek pouches, then explain what they store.

name: Chiton
teaser: The chiton is a simple-looking mollusk that clings to rocks along the seashore, an armored slug with eight overlapping shell plates. When the tide goes out, it grips the rock so tightly that it is almost impossible to pry off, waiting for the water to return. Some chitons have a secret weapon: eyes made of aragonite, the same mineral as their shells, embedded in their armor. A few even eat with teeth made of magnetite, the hardest material any animal produces, which they use to scrape algae from stone.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how chitons wear a shell of eight overlapping plates that let them curl into a ball, clinging to rocks in crashing waves with a foot of immense grip, and some have eyes made of mineral aragonite embedded in their shells. Explore the gumboot chiton's red underside, their radula with metal-hard teeth, and their ancient lineage.

name: Cicada
teaser: The cicada is the loudest insect on Earth, and its song is a summer soundtrack in many parts of the world. Males produce sound by vibrating special membranes on their abdomens, and a single cicada can be heard over a kilometer away, with some species reaching over a hundred decibels. In North America, periodical cicadas take this to extremes: they spend seventeen years underground feeding on tree roots, then emerge by the billions in the same year, sing, mate, and die within weeks.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how periodical cicadas spend 13 or 17 years underground feeding on tree roots, then emerge by the billions in synchronized broods to sing, mate, and die in weeks. Explore why prime-number life cycles avoid predator cycles, their ear-splitting chorus, and the mystery of their timing.

name: Cicada Song
teaser: The cicada's song is produced by a pair of drum-like membranes called tymbals, buckled in and out at incredible speed by special muscles. The male is the musician; his song advertises his presence to females, who respond with a flick of their wings. Different species have different songs, a chorus that can reach deafening volume when thousands of males sing together. A cicada also has hearing organs on its abdomen, near its legs, letting it listen for rivals while singing at full volume.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how male cicadas sing by vibrating membranes called tymbals, producing calls up to 100 decibels, the loudest insect sounds, to attract mates, and different species have different songs, with the sound amplified by hollow body chambers. Explore the ear-damaging volume, the females' flicking responses, and the cicada killers that hunt them.

name: City Foxes
teaser: Red foxes have become one of the most successful city-dwellers in the animal kingdom — and they're thriving in a world of concrete. Urban foxes live in cities across Europe and North America, denning under sheds, in parks, and in abandoned lots, and they've adapted in remarkable ways: they learn traffic patterns, forage from bins and bird tables, and raise cubs within meters of busy streets. Studies show urban foxes have larger territories but smaller ranges, eat more human food, and are often bolder than their country cousins — though they're rarely aggressive and mostly avoid people.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how urban foxes adapt, then explain what they eat in cities.

name: Clouded Leopard
teaser: The clouded leopard is a medium-sized cat of the Southeast Asian forests, named for its cloud-like blotches, and it has the longest canine teeth for its body size of any cat, like a miniature saber-tooth. It is the world's best tree climber among big cats, able to climb down a tree headfirst, hang upside down from branches, and even run along the underside of a limb. Despite the name, it is not a true leopard but a separate ancient lineage. It is shy, secretive, and rarely seen.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the clouded leopard of Southeast Asian forests has the longest canine teeth relative to body size of any cat, almost sabre-like, and is the most ancient lineage of big cats, an expert climber that can hang upside down from branches. Explore its cloud-patterned coat, its near-vertical tree climbing, and the forests disappearing beneath it.

name: Clown Frog
teaser: The clown frog is a bright and poisonous performer of the Amazon rainforest, its orange and blue-black markings a warning to predators. Its skin carries toxins that make it dangerous to eat, and its colors advertise the danger, a survival trick called aposematism. It lives in leaf litter, hunts insects, and is active during the day, unusual for a rainforest frog, because its poison lets it move boldly. The same poison is being studied by scientists for its effects on the human heart and nerves.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the Bornean clown frog blends into fallen leaves with its dark blotched patterns, its oversized toe pads letting it perch on broad leaves. Explore its quiet life in peat swamps, its call, and how deforestation of Borneo threatens its leaf-litter habitat.

name: Clown Knifefish
teaser: The clown knifefish is a strange and ancient predator of Southeast Asia's rivers, shaped like a blade with a long fin running along its belly. It hunts at night, sensing the world with weak electric pulses that detect the movements of prey in murky water. It can grow over a meter long, and its unusual shape lets it slice through the water almost silently. In the aquarium trade it is prized, though it soon outgrows most tanks.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the clown knifefish of Southeast Asian rivers generates weak electric fields around its body to sense obstacles and prey in murky water, swimming with a rippling fin like a wave. Explore its knife-like body, how it hunts at night, and why it's prized by aquarists.

name: Clownfish
teaser: The clownfish is the tiny hero of the coral reef, made famous by movies, and its real life is just as dramatic. It lives among the stinging tentacles of sea anemones, immune to their venom thanks to a protective mucus coat. The fish cleans the anemone, chases away its predators, and even brings it food. Clownfish are born all male, and when the dominant female of a group dies, the largest male changes sex to replace her.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how clownfish live among the stinging tentacles of sea anemones, protected by a mucus coat the anemone doesn't recognize, while they chase off anemone-eaters and bring it food. Explore the strict hierarchy in each anemone where the biggest fish is female, and how Nemo-style males can change sex.

name: Cockatoo
teaser: The cockatoo is the rock star of the parrot world, crowned with a crest it raises and lowers to show its mood. Found in Australia and nearby islands, these intelligent birds learn words, solve puzzles, and use tools, and they form bonds with their humans that can last for decades, since some live over fifty years. Their loud calls carry for kilometers, and in the wild they gather in huge noisy flocks. A bored cockatoo is a destructive one, so they need constant mental challenges.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how sulphur-crested cockatoos lift their dramatic yellow crests in emotion, live up to 80 years, and have been seen dancing in rhythm to music, an ability once thought unique to humans. Explore their loud flocks, their tool use with sticks, and their habit of learning to open bins.

name: Coconut Crab
teaser: The coconut crab is the largest land-living arthropod on Earth, a giant hermit crab that has given up shells for armor. It can weigh four kilograms and span a meter from claw to claw, and its massive pincers can crack open coconuts, hence the name. It climbs trees, steals shiny objects, and can live for decades, growing slowly. Despite its size, it is shy and nocturnal, and its meat is so prized that it is now threatened in many places.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the coconut crab of Pacific islands is the largest land arthropod, up to 4 kg with a leg span of a meter, climbing trees and cracking coconuts with its powerful claws. Explore its return-to-sea breeding, its scavenging diet that once included Amelia Earhart theories, and how islands' giant crabs evolved from hermit crabs.

name: Coconut Octopus
teaser: The coconut octopus is the tool user of the reef, and it carries its own armor. This small octopus of the Indo-Pacific picks up two halves of a coconut shell, carries them under its arms like a backpack, and assembles them into a hiding dome when danger appears. It is one of the few animals known to use tools. It also walks on two arms, standing tall to look like a floating piece of seaweed, a disguise it uses to sneak past predators and approach prey.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the coconut octopus of tropical seas is one of the few invertebrates known to use tools, carrying coconut shells and clam halves, walking on two arms like a stilt walker, and assembling them into a portable shelter. Explore the studies that filmed this behavior, and what it says about octopus intelligence.

name: Coelacanth
teaser: The coelacanth is a living fossil, a fish that was thought to have died out with the dinosaurs sixty-six million years ago, until one turned up in a South African trawl net in 1938. It is a deep-sea fish with lobed fins that move like limbs, a hinged skull, and a slow, ancient way of life. Scientists have since found populations in the Indian Ocean, and these fish can live up to a hundred years. Seeing one swim is like watching the deep past come alive.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the coelacanth, thought to have gone extinct with the dinosaurs, was found alive off South Africa in 1938, unchanged for 400 million years. Explore its lobed fins that hint at the transition to land, its oily swim bladder, and how it gives birth to live young in deep caves.

name: Colossal Squid
teaser: The colossal squid is the heavyweight champion of the invertebrate world, heavier than the more famous giant squid, with the largest eyes of any animal, the size of dinner plates. It lives in the freezing deep waters around Antarctica, and it is armed with swiveling hooks on its tentacles as well as suckers. Its only real enemy is the sperm whale, which dives kilometers deep to hunt it, and the battles leave scars on both. No one has ever seen a live adult in its natural home.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the colossal squid of Antarctic waters is heavier than the giant squid, up to 500 kg, with swiveling hooks on its tentacles and eyes the size of basketballs, the largest eyes in the animal kingdom. Explore the few specimens ever recovered, including the frozen 8 meter female in New Zealand, and its battles with sperm whales.

name: Comb Jelly
teaser: The comb jelly drifts through the oceans like a living rainbow, its transparent body lined with rows of beating cilia that shimmer with iridescent light. It is not a true jellyfish; it.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how comb jellies are not true jellyfish but ctenophores, moving with eight rows of shimmering comb-like paddles that scatter rainbow light, and many glow, with some species cannibalistic and one that fuses with others when injured. Explore their place near the base of the animal tree, and their sticky colloblast cells instead of stings.

name: Condor
teaser: The condor is one of the largest flying birds on Earth, a vulture with a wingspan that can stretch three meters, soaring on mountain updrafts for hours without flapping. The Andean condor of South America is the biggest, while its North American cousin, the California condor, was saved from extinction by captive breeding. Condors are scavengers that clean the landscape of carcasses, and their bald heads are an adaptation for eating without matting feathers. They can fly hundreds of kilometers a day searching for food.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the Andean condor, one of the largest flying birds, weighs up to 15 kg and soars on mountain updrafts with a wingspan over 3 meters, barely flapping. Explore its bald head, its near-extinction and captive breeding comeback, and how it can live over 70 years in the wild.

name: Cone Snail
teaser: The cone snail looks like a pretty patterned shell, but it is one of the most venomous animals in the sea. Each species has a harpoon-like tooth loaded with a cocktail of toxins that it fires into fish, worms, or even other snails, paralyzing them instantly. The venom of some species can be lethal to humans, and there is no antivenom. Yet the same toxins are medical gold: one has become a painkiller hundreds of times stronger than morphine, with no addictive properties.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how cone snails hunt with a harpoon-like tooth loaded with conotoxin venom, so potent and precise that some species can kill a human, while the venom's peptides are studied as medicines for pain. Explore the geography cone's deadly reputation, the fish-hunting strategy, and why collectors handle shells with gloves.

name: Conservation Technology
teaser: Conservationists now fight extinction with drones, satellites, and artificial intelligence. Camera traps trigger automatically when an animal passes, photographing rare species that no human could track on foot; acoustic sensors listen for elephant rumbles, whale songs and chainsaw cuts in protected forests; and drones scan coastlines to count nesting sea turtles and spot poachers at night with thermal cameras. AI models sort through millions of images and sounds in hours, identifying individual animals by their stripes, spots or fin patterns. DNA from a single hair or scat sample tells scientists which species are present and how inbred a population has become.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how technology now fights extinction, from drones counting nests and thermal cameras catching poachers, to DNA analysis of ivory tracing smuggling networks, camera traps catching snow leopards, and AI identifying whale calls. Explore how cheap sensors and satellites give conservationists eyes across the wild.

name: Constriction
teaser: Constriction is how pythons and boas kill, and it is not squeezing to death but suffocation with an edge. The snake coils around its prey and tightens with each breath the animal exhales, cutting off blood flow and crushing the ribs. Prey dies in minutes, and the snake then swallows it whole, head first. Constrictors are patient ambushers, and a large python can overpower an animal far bigger than its own head, stretching its jaws and ribs to swallow it whole.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how constriction kills, then explain why it is not suffocation.

name: Coral
teaser: A coral is not a rock or a plant but a colony of tiny animals called polyps, each a soft tube with stinging tentacles. The polyps build a skeleton of calcium carbonate, and millions of them together grow the great reefs of the tropics. Inside each polyp live algae that photosynthesize and feed it, which is why reefs need clear, sunlit water. When the water gets too hot, the coral expels its algae and turns white, a stress response called bleaching. Reefs are the cities of the sea, home to a quarter of all marine species.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how corals are colonies of tiny animals called polyps that build limestone skeletons, the reefs they create housing a quarter of all marine species, and they feed at night with stinging tentacles while getting most energy from algae in their tissues. Explore how bleaching happens when warming seas expel those algae, and the race to save reefs.

name: Coral Reef Conservation
teaser: Coral reefs are dying faster than almost any ecosystem on Earth, and saving them takes every tool we have. Warmer seas cause mass bleaching, while pollution, overfishing, and ocean acidification pile on the pressure. Scientists now grow corals in nurseries and transplant them to damaged reefs, and some are breeding heat-tolerant coral strains. Marine protected areas give reefs breathing room, and clean-up projects remove invasive species. The goal is simple: keep the underwater cities of the tropics alive for the life that depends on them.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how coral reefs shelter a quarter of all marine species but face warming that causes bleaching, with the Great Barrier Reef suffering repeated mass bleaching events. Explore reef restoration with coral nurseries, the fight against ocean acidification, and why protected marine parks give reefs their best chance.

name: Cormorant Fishing
teaser: Cormorant fishing is an ancient partnership between humans and birds that still survives in parts of Asia. Fishermen raise cormorants, tie a snare around their necks that stops them swallowing big fish, and send them diving from small boats at night. The birds catch fish, bring them back, and the fishermen untie the snare to reward them with smaller catches. It is a delicate balance, and in places like China's Li River the practice now survives mostly as a living tradition for visitors.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how cormorants hunt underwater, then explain the dive time.

name: Cougar
teaser: The cougar, also called puma or mountain lion, is the most widespread cat in the Americas, roaming from Canada's forests to the tip of South America. It is a powerful ambush hunter that can take down deer much larger than itself, leaping with a force that snaps the neck of its prey. Cougars are solitary and secretive, and they are so adaptable that some now live on the edges of cities. They have the largest range of any wild cat species, and no other American land mammal has such a wide territory.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how cougars, also called mountain lions and pumas, hold records for the most names of any animal, roam the Americas from Canada to Patagonia, and leap 6 meters from a standstill. Explore their solitary territories, their ambush hunting of deer, and their remarkable comeback in populated regions.

name: Coyote Howls
teaser: The coyote's howl is the soundtrack of the American wilderness — a haunting, yipping chorus that rises and falls across the night — and it's a highly organized form of communication. Coyotes howl to keep in touch with pack members spread across a territory, to announce their presence and warn rival packs to stay away, and to call the family back together after a hunt. The famous yipping chorus is often a group effort: each coyote howls at a slightly different pitch, which makes a small pack sound like a much bigger one — a clever trick to make neighbors think twice.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn why coyotes howl in groups, then explain the sounds' purposes.

name: Crab
teaser: Crabs are the armored tanks of the shore, wearing their skeletons on the outside and walking sideways. They come in every size, from pea-sized crabs that live inside oyster shells to the Japanese spider crab with legs spanning four meters. Crabs breathe with gills that work on land as long as they stay damp, and they are masters of the beach, the reef, and the deep sea. When a crab grows, it molts, shedding its whole shell and hiding soft and vulnerable until the new armor hardens.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how crabs walk sideways on jointed legs, their first pair modified into claws, and thousands of species live from deep sea to desert, with some like the coconut crab climbing trees and others like spider crabs wearing camouflage. Explore their molting, their soft-shell stage, and their ancient armored body plan.

name: Crane Calls
teaser: The crane's call is one of the most haunting sounds in nature, a loud, rolling bugle that carries for kilometers across wetlands. It comes from a long coiled trachea that acts like a natural trumpet, giving the crane's voice its carrying power. Cranes are famous for their courtship dances too, leaping, bowing, and tossing grass in elaborate duets. These birds form pair bonds that last a lifetime, and a mated pair stays together through migrations, nesting seasons, and decades of shared life.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover why cranes call loudly, then explain the trachea coiling.

name: Cricket
teaser: The cricket is the fiddler of the insect world, its chirping song a summer night's soundtrack. Only males sing, and they make the sound by rubbing their wings together: one wing has a file, the other a scraper, and the friction produces the chirp. The rate of chirping even tracks the temperature, faster when it is warm, which is why crickets are called nature's thermometers. Females listen with ears on their front legs, choosing mates by the quality of their song.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how male crickets chirp by rubbing their wings together, one wing carrying a file, the other a scraper, with the chirp rate rising with temperature, letting you estimate the temperature in Fahrenheit by counting chirps in 15 seconds and adding 40. Explore the ears on their front legs, the burrows males dig to amplify calls, and the field cricket's aggression.

name: Crinoid
teaser: The crinoid, or sea lily, looks like a plant but is an animal, a relative of starfish that anchors itself to the seafloor on a stalk. Atop the stalk sits a crown of feathery arms that comb plankton from the current. Some crinoids abandoned the stalk entirely and swim or crawl free. Fossils of crinoids are everywhere, since their skeletons have been preserved since the Paleozoic era, and in some ancient seas they were so abundant that their remains formed thick limestone beds.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how crinoids, or feather stars and sea lilies, are ancient echinoderms that have drifted for 500 million years, arms waving to catch plankton, some anchored on stalks like lilies and others free-swimming. Explore their fossil abundance in limestone, their filtering arms, and their comeback in modern reefs and deep sea.

name: Crocodile
teaser: The crocodile is the largest living reptile, a survivor from the age of dinosaurs that has barely changed in two hundred million years. The saltwater crocodile of the Indo-Pacific can reach seven meters and weigh over a tonne, and it can live past seventy. Crocodiles are ambush hunters, lying almost invisible in the water, then exploding upward with terrifying speed. They also have an unexpected softer side: mothers guard their nests and carry their hatchlings gently to the water in their jaws.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how crocodiles have survived for over 200 million years with a bite force of 3,700 psi, the strongest of any animal, yet jaw muscles so weak you can hold them shut. Explore how they sense ripples with face pressure receptors, swallow stones as ballast, and care for their young.

name: Crocodile Hunting
teaser: A crocodile's hunting strategy is ambush perfected over millions of years. It floats with only its eyes and nostrils above the surface, motionless for hours, then launches with explosive force, grabbing prey at the water's edge. Its jaws clamp shut with enormous pressure and teeth that interlock, and it drags larger prey underwater to drown it. Because crocodiles cannot chew, they twist and roll to tear off chunks, and their stomach acid is so strong it digests bones, hooves, and shells.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how crocodiles ambush prey, then explain the death roll.

name: Crocodile Nests
teaser: A crocodile mother builds a nest like a compost heap, piling mud and vegetation that warms as it rots. She lays up to sixty eggs inside, and the rotting material keeps them at a steady temperature while she guards the mound for months. The temperature of the nest even decides the sex of the hatchlings: warmer nests produce more males, cooler nests more females. When the babies start calling from inside their eggs, the mother digs them out and carries them to the water in her mouth.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover how crocodile mothers guard nests, then explain how temperature sets sex.

name: Crocodile Tears
teaser: When a crocodile eats, it often appears to cry, a strange sight that gave us the phrase crocodile tears. The tears are real but not emotional: the reptile's tear glands drain excess salt and moisture while it feeds, since it cannot sweat. The crocodile also yawns with its mouth open to cool down, and its jaw muscles work so hard when eating that the pressure forces fluid from the tear ducts. The crying is physiology, not sadness, though the myth of the weeping predator persists.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover where the crocodile tears saying comes from, then explain the real reason crocs 'weep'.

name: Crocodilian Family
teaser: Caimans, alligators, and crocodiles are cousins that are easy to mix up. Crocodiles have narrow, V-shaped snouts with teeth that show even when the mouth is shut, and they live in salt and fresh water across the tropics. Alligators and caimans have broad, U-shaped snouts, with the alligator's teeth hidden when its mouth closes. Caimans are the smaller American relatives of alligators, found from Central to South America. All are ancient, armored, and surprisingly good mothers.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how crocodilians split into three families, true crocodiles with narrow snouts, alligators and caimans with broad snouts, and the gharial with its long thin snout, all sharing ancient ancestry with dinosaurs. Explore how snout shape fits diet, the salt glands of crocodiles that alligators lack, and the fossil giants like Sarcosuchus that dwarfed modern forms.

name: Crow Facial Memory
teaser: Crows have a memory that puts most animals to shame, and they use it to hold grudges. In a famous study, researchers who trapped and banded crows found that the birds remembered their faces and scolded them whenever they returned, years later. Crows pass this knowledge on: young crows that never met a particular person still learned to harass them, warned by their elders. They remember food caches, family members, and safe places, and their facial recognition rivals that of some primates.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover how crows recognize faces, then explain the mask experiments.

name: Crow Intelligence
teaser: Crows are among the smartest animals on Earth, with brains that solve problems like a young child's. They can use tools, bending wire into hooks to pull food from tubes, and some can plan several steps ahead, like dropping bread on water to soften it. They understand cause and effect, recognize human faces, and even hold funerals for their dead. The New Caledonian crow makes and stores its own tools, passing crafting knowledge down the generations like a cultural tradition.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn what crow experiments show, then explain the tool use.

name: Cuckoo
teaser: The cuckoo is the con artist of the bird world, famous for laying its eggs in other birds' nests. A cuckoo chick hatches early, pushes the host's own eggs and chicks out of the nest, and then begs so loudly and looks so much like a hungry mouth that the foster parents feed it more than they would their own young. The chick grows huge, often dwarfing its unwitting foster parents. Some cuckoo species mimic the eggs of their host, and hosts fight back by recognizing and ejecting the impostor eggs.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how cuckoos lay their eggs in other birds' nests, each female specializing on one host species and matching its egg color, with the cuckoo chick hatching first and pushing out the host's eggs to monopolize the foster parents' feeding. Explore the arms race with hosts that reject the eggs, and the cuckoo's hawk-like appearance.

name: Cuscus
teaser: The cuscus is a slow, round-eyed possum of the forests of New Guinea and northern Australia, with thick woolly fur and a grasping tail that works like a fifth hand. It is a marsupial, carrying its young in a pouch, and it sleeps by day curled in the treetops, hunting leaves, fruit, and insects at night. It moves so slowly that early explorers mistook it for a sloth, and its large eyes glow red in torchlight. It is a master of staying completely still among the branches.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how cuscuses are slow-climbing possums of New Guinea and neighboring islands, with thick fur, grasping tails, and a vegetarian diet of leaves and fruit, some species with striking white or spotted coats. Explore their night activity, their role in island ecosystems, and the hunting and habitat loss threatening them.

name: Cuttlefish
teaser: The cuttlefish is the shape-shifter of the sea, a cephalopod with an internal shell called a cuttlebone and an astonishing control over its own skin. It changes color, pattern, and texture in an instant, morphing into sand, coral, or even a moving ripple to blend with its surroundings or signal other cuttlefish. It has the most complex eyes of any animal and can see polarized light. When hunting, it hypnotizes prey with flashing bands of color before striking with its two tentacles.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how cuttlefish change color, pattern, and even texture, bumping skin into raised nubs to match their background in 3D, controlled by elastic pigment sacs and muscles. Explore their W-shaped pupils, their hypnosis of prey with pulsing waves, and their incredible camouflage intelligence.

name: Cuttlefish Camouflage
teaser: Cuttlefish camouflage is so good that researchers struggle to find them even when they know exactly where one is sitting. The cuttlefish reads its surroundings with its eyes, then matches color, brightness, and pattern using millions of pigment cells in its skin, plus skin texture muscles that raise bumps to imitate sand or coral. It does all this in less than a second, and it can even make different parts of its body match different backgrounds at once. Some scientists believe cuttlefish change color in their sleep, hinting they may dream.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how cuttlefish change color and texture in under a second by expanding and contracting pigment sacs and muscles that raise skin nubs, matching not just color but the 3D texture of their background. Explore the studies on their camouflage decisions, their colorblind eyes that somehow sense color, and the limits of their disguise.

name: Daddy Longlegs
teaser: The daddy longlegs, or harvestman, is not a spider, and that confusion hides a fascinating creature. Unlike spiders, it has a single fused body segment, no silk, no venom, and it eats with a mouth rather than fangs. Its famous legs are super-sensitive, acting as eyes, ears, and noses, and it can deliberately drop a leg to escape a predator. Some species gather in enormous piles, a mysterious phenomenon that still puzzles scientists. They are harmless, ancient, and everywhere.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how daddy longlegs, or harvestmen, are not spiders, with a single fused body, no silk glands, and no venom, feeding on decomposing matter, and their legs can detach and twitch to distract predators. Explore why they gather in clusters, the myth that their venom is deadly, and their eight very long legs.

name: Deathstalker Scorpion
teaser: The deathstalker is one of the most venomous scorpions on Earth, a small pale yellow hunter of the deserts of North Africa and the Middle East. Its sting delivers a potent neurotoxin that can be fatal to children and the elderly, though healthy adults usually survive with intense pain. It hunts at night, sensing prey with vibration-sensitive hairs and grabbing it with its pincers before stinging. Its venom is also valuable: researchers are studying its toxins to develop drugs, including treatments for cancer.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the deathstalker scorpion of North African deserts carries one of the most potent scorpion venoms, dangerous mainly to children and the elderly, while its venom yields molecules studied for brain cancer treatment. Explore its small size, its fluorescence under UV, and its burrow life.

name: Deep-Diving Seals
teaser: Seals are the champion divers of the mammal world, and the elephant seal holds the records. Elephant seals dive to depths of over 1,500 meters — deeper than the wreck of the Titanic — and stay under for up to two hours at a time, then surface for only a few minutes before diving again, in a rhythm they keep up for months. How do they manage it? Elephant seals are masters of oxygen management: they can collapse their lungs to survive pressure, slow their hearts to a few beats per minute, and store oxygen in their blood and muscles at levels that would poison other mammals.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover how deep seals dive, then explain their oxygen storage.

name: Deer
teaser: Deer are the gentle browsers of forests and meadows, found on every continent except Antarctica and Australia. Males of most species grow antlers, which they shed and regrow every year, the fastest-growing bone in the animal kingdom. Deer are alert and fast, able to jump high fences and sprint through woodland, and they communicate with scent, calls, and the white flash of their tails. In some places they are so abundant that they reshape the forest, which is why managing their numbers matters so much.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how deer grow and shed antlers each year, the fastest-growing tissue in the animal kingdom, used in rutting battles, and they live in herds across forests, meadows, and even suburbs. Explore the many species from whitetails to moose, the rutting season, the fawn's spotted camouflage, and their role as prey for wolves and hunters.

name: Deforestation
teaser: Deforestation clears about a football field of forest every few seconds, and its ripple effects reach the whole planet. Forests are home to most of Earth's species, so cutting them is the biggest single cause of habitat loss and extinction. They also soak up carbon dioxide, meaning their loss accelerates climate change, and they anchor soil, so cleared slopes erode and flood. Yet the story has hope: reforestation projects, protected areas, and sustainable farming are restoring forests, and countries are planting billions of trees.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how forests the size of football pitches are cleared every few seconds, driving orangutans, jaguars, and thousands of species toward extinction while releasing carbon. Explore the drivers from cattle and palm oil to logging, the difference between logging and clearing, and what sustainable choices can slow it.

name: Desert Iguana
teaser: The desert iguana is built for heat that would kill most animals, living on the hot, bare grounds of the American Southwest and Mexico. It is most active in the fiercest midday sun, when its body can reach over forty degrees, a temperature that would be fatal for many reptiles. It escapes the worst heat in rodent burrows and survives by eating the flowers and leaves of desert plants, getting water from its food. When threatened, it runs upright on its hind legs, tail streaming behind.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the desert iguana of the American Southwest tolerates body temperatures above 46 degrees Celsius, scurrying between shrubs in the midday heat that stops other animals. Explore its salt-excreting nasal glands, its diet of creosote flowers, and how it raises its body off hot sand.

name: Desert Lizards
teaser: Desert lizards are masters of surviving the world's hottest places. They have scales that trap moisture, nostrils that close against blowing sand, and bodies that tolerate temperatures that would cook other animals. The thorny devil of Australia drinks by channeling water across its spiny skin into its mouth, and the Gila monster stores fat in its tail to survive months without eating. Many burrow to escape heat, change color to regulate temperature, and hunt in the cool hours of dawn and dusk.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how desert lizards survive extreme heat by burrowing, shifting activity to dawn and dusk, standing on two legs or raising their bodies off hot sand, and some like the thorny devil collecting water through skin channels. Explore the fringe-toed lizard that dives into sand dunes, and the shingleback's slow desert life.

name: Dire Wolf
teaser: The dire wolf was the great hunter of Ice Age America, larger and heavier than today's grey wolf, with a powerful bite built to crush bone. It roamed the grasslands alongside mammoths and giant sloths, hunting in packs, and its fossils are famous from the La Brea Tar Pits of Los Angeles, where hundreds of thousands of bones have been found. Despite the name, it was not a wolf but a separate branch of the dog family. It vanished about ten thousand years ago, when its giant prey disappeared.
