exploreAction.instruction: Read how dire wolves of the American ice age were bigger-boned than gray wolves, hunting horses, bison, and giant sloths in packs, and their fossils packed the La Brea tar pits. Explore what DNA reveals about them being a separate lineage, not a gray wolf ancestor, and why they died out with their prey.

name: Do Animals Feel Emotions
teaser: Do animals feel emotions? The evidence says yes. Elephants mourn their dead, touching and circling the bones of relatives. Dogs sulk, crows hold grudges, and rats laugh, emitting high-pitched chirps when tickled. Prairie dogs grieve, and whales carry their dead calves for days. Brain scans show animals have the same structures linked to emotion in humans, and their behavior shows joy, fear, grief, and even jealousy. Science now takes animal emotions seriously, reshaping how we treat them.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how scientists now document grief in elephants that linger over the dead, joy in rats that laugh when tickled, jealousy in dogs, and comfort in chimpanzees that console friends after fights. Explore the evidence, the risks of anthropomorphism, and what brain and behavior studies reveal about animal feelings.

name: Dodo
teaser: The dodo is the world's most famous extinct animal, a flightless pigeon the size of a turkey that lived only on the island of Mauritius. It had no natural predators, so it evolved to be slow, trusting, and fearless, walking right up to sailors, who clubbed it for food. Rats, pigs, and monkeys brought to the island ate its eggs, and within a century of the first human arrival, the dodo was gone. It became a symbol of how quickly carelessness can erase a species forever.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the dodo of Mauritius, a flightless pigeon weighing up to 20 kg, vanished within a century of humans arriving in 1598, from hunting and the pigs, rats, and monkeys sailors brought that ate its ground nests. Explore what we know from rare descriptions and bones, and why its story anchors conservation.

name: Dog Domestication
teaser: Dogs were the first animals humans ever domesticated, and the partnership goes back tens of thousands of years. Wolves that scavenged near human camps gradually grew bolder and friendlier, and humans found them useful: better noses for hunting, sharp ears for warnings, and warm bodies for cold nights. Over generations, humans bred for tameness, and today's dogs come in every shape and size, from Chihuahuas to Great Danes, all descended from grey wolves. A dog reads human faces and emotions better than any other animal.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how dogs were domesticated from gray wolves at least 15,000 years ago, likely when wolves scavenged camps and self-selected for tameness, and how breeding created everything from chihuahuas to Great Danes. Explore the Siberian fox experiment, the genes for friendliness, and the ancient burials showing dogs as family.

name: Dolphin
teaser: The dolphin is the brainiac of the seas, a mammal that swims like a fish and thinks like a genius. Bottlenose dolphins live in complex social groups, call each other by name, use tools like sponges to protect their noses while foraging, and can recognize themselves in mirrors. They communicate with clicks and whistles, hunt cooperatively, and have even been seen teaching their young. Their sonar is so fine that they can detect a fish hidden in sand. Dolphins are curious about humans and have saved swimmers from sharks.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how bottlenose dolphins use echolocation to see through murky water, call each other by individual names, form lifelong alliances, and teach hunting tricks to their young. Explore their intelligence, their playful surfing and leaping, and how they sleep with half a brain awake.

name: Dolphin Echolocation
teaser: Dolphin echolocation is sonar with a musician's touch. A dolphin produces rapid clicks in its nasal passages, and the sound focuses through a fatty organ in its forehead called the melon, acting like a lens. The clicks bounce off objects, and the dolphin reads the echoes with its jaw, which conducts sound to its inner ear. From the returning signal it can tell an object's size, shape, distance, and even what it is made of, seeing with sound in dark, muddy water where eyes are useless.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how dolphins echolocate, then explain what they can detect about objects.

name: Dolphin Echolocation
teaser: Dolphins see with sound, and their echolocation is so precise it is almost like an X-ray. By sending out rapid clicks and reading the returning echoes, a dolphin can detect a three-centimeter fish from over a hundred meters away, and it can even tell whether that fish is healthy by the density of its body. It builds a sound picture so detailed that captive dolphins have been shown to distinguish between balls of different materials in total darkness. Their sonar is the best known in nature.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how dolphins send out focused clicks that bounce off objects, building detailed sound pictures that reveal fish density, seabed shape, and even a target's internal structure, with some species like the Amazon river dolphin navigating floodplains by sound alone. Explore the melon that focuses clicks, the jaw that receives echoes, and how sonar engineers borrowed the design.

name: Dolphin Pods
teaser: A dolphin pod is a family that swims together, hunts together, and protects its own. Pods can range from a few individuals to hundreds, and the members know each other by their signature whistles, individual name-like calls. They cooperate to herd fish, babysit each other's calves, and defend against sharks. Pods also have culture: different groups teach their young different hunting tricks, like strand feeding, where dolphins drive fish onto mud banks and slide out to grab them.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how dolphins live in pods with complex social structures, forming alliances within alliances, babysitting each other's calves, and learning local hunting traditions like the sponge-fishing of Shark Bay. Explore the matrilineal societies, the signature whistles that act as names, and the intelligence behind their cooperation.

name: Dolphin Signature Whistles
teaser: Every dolphin has a signature whistle, a personal call that works like its name. A baby dolphin invents its own whistle in its first months, often copying a version of its mother's, and it keeps it for life. Dolphins call out their signature when they meet, greet each other by repeating each other's whistles, and can remember the whistle of a friend they have not heard for twenty years. Researchers are decoding these calls, discovering that dolphins talk about each other in the third person.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover how dolphins develop signature whistles, then explain the evidence they use them as names.

name: Dragonfly
teaser: The dragonfly is a prehistoric predator that rules the skies, and it has not changed much in three hundred million years, when dragonflies with sixty-centimeter wingspans flew the swamps. It has nearly 360-degree vision from two huge compound eyes containing up to thirty thousand lenses each, and it can fly in any direction, hover, and reach speeds of over fifty kilometers an hour. It catches mosquitoes and flies midair, often eating them on the wing. A single dragonfly can eat hundreds of mosquitoes a day.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how dragonflies intercept prey mid-flight with a brain that predicts where the target will be, controlling four independent wings and seeing nearly all around with compound eyes of up to 30,000 lenses. Explore their nymph stage underwater, their ancient 300-million-year history with 70 cm wingspans.

name: Dragonfly Nymph
teaser: The dragonfly nymph is a lurking monster of the pond, a fierce predator that lives underwater for up to two years before its final transformation. It hunts tadpoles, small fish, and insects with a hinged, extendable jaw that shoots out to grab prey in a blink. It breathes by pumping water through its abdomen, and it can even jet-propel itself to escape danger. Then one day it climbs out of the water, its skin splits, and a winged adult dragonfly emerges, leaving its old shell behind on a reed.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how dragonfly nymphs live underwater for months to years, hunting with an extendable jaw that shoots out to grab tadpoles and fish, breathing through gills in their rectum, and jetting forward by pumping water out. Explore their final molt where they climb out and split open into flying adults, and their voracious appetite that controls mosquitoes.

name: Duck Bills
teaser: A duck's bill is a multi-tool perfected by evolution. It is covered in sensitive nerve endings that let the duck feel for food in muddy water, and the comb-like edges called lamellae work like a sieve, filtering tiny plants and animals from the water. The bill even has a slightly hooked tip called the nail, used for grooming and gripping. Baby ducks hatch with their bills already packed with sensors, and a mother duck guides her ducklings to food-rich water, where they dabble, tip, and sieve all day.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how duck bills filter food, then explain the comb-like edges.

name: Duck Waterproofing
teaser: A duck stays dry because it spends hours waterproofing itself. It spreads oil from a gland at the base of its tail over its feathers, and this oil makes the feathers shed water, keeping the down beneath warm and dry. The feather structure itself is a marvel: tiny hooks zip the barbs together, so after preening the duck's coat is one smooth, waterproof sheet. Ducks preen constantly, and the oil also keeps the feathers flexible and helps with display, since a healthy sheen signals good health.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how preen oil waterproofs ducks, then explain the preen gland.

name: Dugong
teaser: The dugong is a gentle sea cow that grazes on seagrass meadows across the warm waters of the Indian and western Pacific oceans. It is one of only four living sea cows, and legend says sailors once mistook it for a mermaid. A dugong can grow three meters long and live for seventy years, and it spends its days slowly cropping seagrass, moving its flexible lips like a vacuum cleaner. Seagrass meadows are its only home, so protecting them protects the dugong.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how dugongs of the Indian Ocean and Australia graze seagrass meadows, the only strictly marine herbivorous mammal, slow and gentle, and are thought to have inspired sailors' mermaid tales. Explore their migrations, their breathing every few minutes, and how seagrass loss and nets threaten them.

name: Dung Beetle
teaser: The dung beetle is the recycler of the savanna, and its life is built around poop. It finds fresh dung by smell, shapes it into a ball, and rolls it away, pushing it backward with its hind legs while walking head down, always following the stars or the Milky Way to roll in a straight line. It buries the ball and lays its eggs inside, giving its young a ready food supply. A dung beetle can pull over a thousand times its own body weight, making it one of the strongest animals on Earth.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how dung beetles roll balls of dung far larger than themselves, navigate in straight lines using the Milky Way, the sun, or the moon, and some even climb on their ball to cool their feet. Explore their role in fertilizing soil and controlling flies, and their surprising strength.

name: Eagle Nests
teaser: Eagles build the biggest nests of any bird, and they reuse them for decades, adding new branches every year until they can weigh over a tonne and stretch several meters across. The bald eagle's nest is a platform of sticks in a tall tree, often near water, and the pair returns to it each season, repairing and expanding. Some nests are so old that entire generations of eagles have used them. The chicks stay in the nest for months, growing from tiny fluffballs to the size of adults.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover how big eagle nests grow, then explain why they are reused.

name: Eagle Species
teaser: Eagles are the rulers of the sky, and there are about sixty species across the planet. The golden eagle of the northern hemisphere hunts foxes, rabbits, and even young deer in mountain country. The harpy eagle of the Amazon, with talons like bear claws, takes monkeys and sloths from the treetops. The bald eagle of North America lives near water and dives for fish. All eagles are raptors with hooked beaks, superb eyesight, and powerful feet, but each species has its own hunting style and home.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how eagle species differ, then explain the sea eagle group.

name: Eagle Vision
teaser: An eagle's eyesight is legendary, and the science backs it up. Its eyes are large, packed with dense photoreceptors, and its retinas have a fovea that gives it sharp, detailed vision. An eagle can spot a rabbit from over two kilometers away and track a moving target while diving at high speed. Its field of view is wide, and its eyes are so big relative to its skull that they barely move, so the eagle turns its whole head to look around. Humans would need binoculars to match its clarity.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how eagle eyes achieve sharp vision, then explain the two foveas.

name: Earthworm
teaser: The earthworm is one of the most important animals you never see, a silent engineer of the soil. It tunnels through the earth, swallowing soil, digesting the organic matter in it, and casting the rest back up, aerating the ground and turning it into rich, fertile humus. Charles Darwin calculated that worms move tons of soil per acre every year. Their tunnels let water and air reach plant roots, and their casts are packed with nutrients. A field without worms is a dying field.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how earthworms tunnel through soil, aerating it and recycling organic matter into fertile castings, with a single acre of healthy soil holding up to a million worms. Explore their five hearts, their regeneration, how they sense light, and Charles Darwin's lifelong study of their importance.

name: Echidna
teaser: The echidna is one of only two living mammals that lays eggs, the monotreme, an egg-laying, milk-producing oddity of Australia and New Guinea. It is covered in spines like a hedgehog but is actually a distant relative of the platypus. It hunts ants and termites with a long sticky tongue and a beak-like snout packed with electro-sensors. When threatened, it rolls into a ball of spikes or digs straight down, vanishing in seconds. Baby echidnas, called puggles, hatch from eggs and suckle from milk patches.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how echidnas are monotremes that lay eggs, then carry the puggle in a pouch, covered in spines with a long snout for lapping ants and termites, and males have a four-headed penis used in rotation. Explore their brain structure shared with the platypus, and their odd breeding behavior.

name: Echidna Spines
teaser: An echidna's spines are its armor and its offense. They are modified hairs made of keratin, stiff and sharp, and when the echidna is threatened it curls into a ball or wedges itself into a crevice, spines bristling. The animal can also raise its spines to jab an attacker that gets too close. Its body is covered in thousands of them, and between the spines grows woolly fur that keeps it warm. Even its powerful digging legs, tipped with strong claws, double as weapons when cornered.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover how echidnas use their spines, then explain their digging.

name: Echidna Spines
teaser: The echidna is the porcupine of the monotreme world, its back a bristling suit of spines that deters almost everything. When danger appears, it curls into a ball with only spikes showing, or it digs frantically, sinking into the earth until only its spines remain above ground. The spines are hollow, sharp modified hairs, and the echidna can even raise them to increase the threat. Its muscle power while digging is astonishing: it can break through packed dirt so fast it seems to melt into the ground.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how echidnas defend with up to 5,000 modified hairs that are sharp spines, rolling into a spiky ball or digging into the ground leaving only spikes exposed, and males use spines in mating rivalry. Explore how spines grow from fur follicles, the difference from hedgehog quills, and the echidna's prehistoric spiky relatives.

name: Echolocation
teaser: Echolocation is nature's sonar, used by animals to see with sound in darkness and murky water. Bats fire high-frequency clicks and read the echoes to catch insects midair in pitch blackness. Dolphins and whales do the same underwater, and even some shrews and birds use it. The animal sends a sound, the sound bounces off objects, and the returning echo carries information about distance, size, and movement, all processed in a brain wired for sound. It is one of evolution's greatest inventions.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how bats, dolphins, and some birds and shrews navigate and hunt by echolocation, sending out clicks and reading the echoes, with bats detecting a mosquito-sized target in complete darkness and dolphins seeing through murky water. Explore the biology of sound vision and how humans borrowed the idea for sonar.

name: Egg-Cracking Mongooses
teaser: The mongoose is famous for fighting venomous snakes, but it also has a trick for breakfast: cracking eggs. Some mongooses pick up an egg, rear up, and throw it down hard between their legs, or against a rock, to smash it open. Others learned to drop eggs from a height or roll them against a hard surface. Banded mongooses have been seen tossing eggs backward through their legs to break them. It is a tool-using skill passed down by watching and practicing, generation after generation.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover how mongooses crack eggs, then explain why the technique varies.

name: Eggs or Live Birth
teaser: Snakes raise families in two very different ways. Most snakes lay eggs, and the mother often wraps around them or guards them until they hatch, keeping them warm and safe. But many others, including vipers, boa constrictors, and sea snakes, give birth to live young, keeping the eggs inside their bodies until the babies are ready. Some even nourish their developing young through a placenta-like structure. Live birth helps snakes in cold climates, where buried eggs would freeze.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn why some snakes lay eggs and others give birth, then explain the cold-climate link.

name: Electric Eel
teaser: The electric eel is not an eel but a knifefish, and it is one of the most electrifying hunters in the Amazon. Three organs in its body generate electricity: a low-voltage radar for sensing, and high-voltage blasts of up to six hundred volts to stun prey and defend itself. It can deliver repeated shocks, and it hunts by stunning fish, then gulping them before they recover. The electricity also works as a taser on predators, and its shocks can even be strong enough to affect a horse in the water.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the electric eel of Amazon rivers generates up to 600 volts from three electric organs, using low-voltage pulses to sense prey and high-voltage bursts to stun it. Explore how they drive prey into a panic to force it out of hiding, and why they're not actually eels but knife fish.

name: Elephant Bird
teaser: The elephant bird was the giant of Madagascar, a flightless bird that stood up to three meters tall and weighed over half a tonne, the heaviest bird that ever lived. It was so big that its eggs alone were bigger than a basketball, the largest eggs of any known animal. Related to the ostrich, it survived on the island until humans arrived around a thousand years ago, hunting it and clearing its forest home. Within a few centuries, the elephant bird was gone, leaving its giant eggs and bones behind.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how elephant birds of Madagascar stood up to 3 meters and laid eggs with 9 liter capacity, the largest eggs of any animal, and were hunted to extinction by settlers. Explore how their huge eggs were used as water containers, their ostrich-like build, and what eggs and bones tell us about island life.

name: Elephant Communication
teaser: Elephants are talking to each other right now in a language you can't hear. Beyond the trumpets and rumbles that humans can hear, elephants produce low-frequency calls around 20 hertz — infrasound — that travel through the ground and air for many kilometers. A matriarch can warn her herd of an approaching storm or a pride of lions from miles away, and the herd answers with rumbles of its own, forming a rolling conversation across the savanna.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover how elephants communicate over distance, then explain what infrasound is.

name: Elephant Ears as Radiators
teaser: An elephant's huge ears are the animal's radiator, and they work on a simple principle: blood and air. Beneath the thin skin of the ear run dense networks of blood vessels, so the ears are loaded with warm blood. When the elephant flaps them — slowly and deliberately on a hot day — the moving air cools the blood, and the cooled blood circulates back through the body. An African elephant's ear can be nearly two meters across and weigh tens of kilograms, and the flap-flap rhythm picks up exactly when the temperature does.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how ears radiate heat, then explain why African elephants have bigger ears.

name: Elephant Feet
teaser: An elephant's feet are engineering marvels built for walking on eggshells while carrying five tons. Under each foot lies a thick, jelly-like cushion of fat and tissue that spreads out as the elephant steps, distributing its weight so evenly that an elephant leaves barely a sound and only a shallow print — and can walk through terrain where a human would sink. These soft cushions act like shock absorbers, and elephants are surprisingly silent walkers for their size.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how elephant feet absorb impact, then explain why they barely make noise.

name: Elephant Memory
teaser: The saying 'an elephant never forgets' turns out to be close to the truth. Elephants have the largest brains of any land animal, and their memory is genuinely remarkable: matriarchs remember the routes to water holes they last visited decades earlier, and they recognize the calls and scents of individuals they have not seen for many years. Older matriarchs guide their herds through droughts because they remember where to find food when everything else is dry. Studies even show elephants can remember people who harmed or helped them long ago, responding with fear or affection accordingly.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn what studies show about elephant memory, then explain why it matters for survival.

name: Elephant Memory
teaser: An elephant never forgets, and the science says the memory is real. Elephants recognize individual elephants and humans even after decades apart, and they remember the locations of waterholes and migration routes across vast distances, passing this knowledge down through the generations. The matriarch of a herd holds the collective memory, and herds with older matriarchs make better decisions in droughts. Elephants also remember kindness and cruelty, greeting old friends with joy and avoiding those who harmed them.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how elephants have exceptional memories, remembering water sources across decades of drought and individuals they met years earlier, guided by matriarchs whose knowledge keeps herds alive, and how science confirms their long-term social memory. Explore the studies of recognition, the role of the matriarch, and why elephant brains are wired for memory.

name: Elephant Mud Baths
teaser: An elephant's favorite bath is made of mud, not water, and it's not just for fun. After a wallow, the drying mud cakes onto the skin and acts like natural sunscreen, protecting the elephant's thick but sun-sensitive hide from UV rays and insects. It also seals in moisture and helps the elephant shed heat. If mud isn't around, elephants use dust — flinging clouds of dirt over their backs with their trunks — and then they'll follow with a proper water bath, spraying themselves with dozens of trunkfuls of water.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover why elephants coat themselves in mud, then explain what it protects against.

name: Elephant Seal
teaser: The elephant seal is the heavyweight of the ocean, and the males wear their size like a crown. A bull can weigh over three tonnes, far larger than the females, and he battles rival males on the beach, rearing up and crashing chest to chest until one submits. His name comes from the trunk-like nose that inflates as he roars. Elephant seals dive deeper and longer than almost any other mammal, plunging over a kilometer and staying under for up to two hours, hunting squid in the dark abyss.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how elephant seals dive deeper and longer than almost any other seal, past 1,500 meters for up to two hours, and males grow enormous inflatable noses and battle for harems on beaches with bloody fights. Explore the northern and southern species, their molting on beaches, and the researchers that track their oceanic wanderings.

name: Elephant Trunk
teaser: An elephant's trunk is the most versatile limb in the animal kingdom, a fusion of nose and upper lip containing about forty thousand muscles. It can lift a tree trunk, pluck a single blade of grass, peel fruit, sip water, and give itself a dust bath. It is strong enough to knock down a branch and gentle enough to cradle a newborn calf. Elephants use their trunks to smell, touch, trumpet, and even blow water like a hose. They are left-trunked or right-trunked, just like humans have a dominant hand.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the elephant trunk is a fusion of nose and upper lip with up to 40,000 muscles, able to lift a log, pick a single blade of grass, snorkel, spray water, and smell water kilometers away, with a fingertip-like tip that can pluck a peanut. Explore the trunk's development in calves, its use in greeting and comfort, and the watering can technique.

name: Elephant Trunk Abilities
teaser: An elephant's trunk is one of the most versatile tools in nature — a nose, hand, hose, trumpet, and snorkel all in one. It contains around 40,000 muscles and not a single bone, and the tip is so dexterous that an elephant can pick up a single blade of grass, yet strong enough to uproot a tree. The trunk is used for everything: breathing and smelling (with nostrils at the tip), drinking up to ten liters of water at a time, spraying mud and dust over the body, trumpeting alarm calls, caressing a calf, and delicately plucking fruit from branches.

exploreAction.instruction: List what an elephant can do with its trunk, then explain how it drinks.

name: Elk
teaser: The elk, called wapiti in some regions, is one of the largest members of the deer family, and its bugle call is one of the most thrilling sounds of the mountains. Males grow huge antlers, up to a meter and a half long with many points, shedding and regrowing them every year. During the rut, bulls bugle, wallow, and clash antlers to win harems of females. Elk live in herds that migrate with the seasons, and they are so adaptable that some now live in parks and forests near towns.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how elk, or wapiti, bugle with high-pitched whistles that carry across valleys during the rut, gathering harems of females, and males spar with massive antlers, while herds migrate between summer meadows and winter ranges. Explore their Yellowstone reintroduction, their role as prey for wolves, and the antler cycles.

name: Emperor Moth
teaser: The emperor moth is a European giant, and the male can smell a female from several kilometers away. His feathery antennae are packed with scent receptors tuned to the female's pheromone, and he flies cross-country, even across cities, to reach her. The female, flightless in some species, waits and calls. The caterpillar is equally striking, a big green beast with colored spots that looks like a miniature dragon, and it feeds on heather and bramble before spinning a tough silk cocoon.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the emperor moth flashes large eyespots on its hind wings to startle predators, and females release pheromones that attract males from kilometers away, some males detected at 11 km in experiments. Explore the feathery antennae that sense pheromones, the caterpillar's green body, and the short adult life without feeding.

name: Emperor Penguin
teaser: The emperor penguin is the only animal that breeds in the dead of the Antarctic winter, and its story is one of endurance. After the female lays a single egg, she walks up to a hundred kilometers back to the sea to feed, leaving the male to balance the egg on his feet, under a flap of skin, through months of darkness and storms that reach minus sixty degrees. The males huddle together, taking turns in the warm center, fasting the whole time. When the females return, the chick hatches into a world of ice and survival.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how emperor penguins breed during the darkest, coldest months of the Antarctic winter, with males incubating the single egg on their feet under a brood pouch while females travel up to 100 km to feed. Explore how they huddle against minus 60 degrees, and how fathers survive months without eating.

name: Emperor Penguin Deep Dives
teaser: The emperor penguin is the deepest-diving bird on Earth, plunging over five hundred meters beneath the Antarctic ice to hunt fish and squid. It can stay under for more than twenty minutes, slowing its heart to a few beats a minute and letting its blood chemistry protect it from the crushing pressure and freezing water. Its feathers trap a layer of warm air, and its body shuts down non-essential systems while diving. No other bird comes close to its underwater endurance.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how emperor penguins dive deeper than any other bird, past 500 meters, holding their breath for over 20 minutes, with muscles that work on stored oxygen and a heart rate that drops to a few beats a minute. Explore how they hunt fish and squid in the dark depths and return to breathe through breathing holes in the ice.

name: Endangered Species
teaser: An endangered species is one that is at risk of vanishing forever, and more than forty thousand species now face that threat. The causes are almost always human: habitat loss, pollution, climate change, poaching, and invasive species. But the story is not all doom. The panda, the humpback whale, and the bald eagle have all bounced back thanks to protected areas and conservation laws. Every species saved is proof that with will and effort, we can tip the balance back toward survival.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how species go extinct at up to 1,000 times the natural rate, from rhinos poached for their horns and tigers losing forests to amphibians dying from a spreading fungus. Explore the Red List, the difference between endangered and critically endangered, and the rescue programs fighting to save species one by one.

name: European Badger
teaser: The European badger is a bold, black-and-white bandit of the woods, built for digging and family life. It lives in an underground sett that can have dozens of tunnels, passed down through generations of the same clan. Badgers are social, grooming each other and sharing sleeping quarters, and they mark their territory with strong-smelling scent. By night they forage for worms, grubs, and fruit, using their powerful claws. Their famous black-and-white face stripes may warn rivals or simply break up their outline in the dark.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how European badgers live in extended family groups called clans within vast underground setts that can have dozens of entrances and be centuries old, marking territory with latrines and scent. Explore their nocturnal foraging, their famous fights with beekeepers over hives, and the tuberculosis debate that drives culls.

name: Falcon Hunting Skills
teaser: A falcon hunts with speed that breaks records: the peregrine falcon is the fastest animal on Earth, diving at over three hundred kilometers an hour. From a high perch or from circling flight, it spots prey, folds its wings, and stoops, becoming a living missile. As it hits its target, it clenches its feet and strikes the bird out of the sky, then catches it or fetches it from the ground. Falcons also hunt by level flight, chasing down pigeons and ducks with relentless speed.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how falcons hunt on the wing, then explain the notch in their beaks.

name: Falconry
teaser: Falconry, the art of hunting with birds of prey, is thousands of years old, practiced from the steppes of Central Asia to the deserts of Arabia. Falconers raise and train falcons, hawks, and eagles, teaching them to return to the fist or glove and to hunt wild quarry. It is a partnership of trust, built on patience and reward, and in many cultures it is a mark of prestige and tradition. UNESCO lists falconry as an intangible cultural heritage, and modern falconers also use birds to scare birds away from airports.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover how falconry works, then explain why the bird chooses to return.

name: Fastest Animals
teaser: The animal kingdom has a speed champion for every arena. On land, the cheetah tops out around a hundred kilometers an hour, but only in short bursts. In the air, the peregrine falcon is unbeatable, diving at over three hundred. In the water, the sailfish is the fastest, racing past a hundred kilometers an hour. The black marlin, pronghorn, and quarter horse all claim their own titles, and the humble cockroach is the fastest land insect. Speed is survival, and evolution keeps raising the bar.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how speed records are set across the animal kingdom, from the peregrine falcon stooping at 300 km/h and the cheetah sprinting to 100 km/h on land, to sailfish at 110 km/h in water and dragonflies accelerating harder than fighter jets. Explore the physics of their bodies, and how speed trades off with endurance.

name: Feather Duster Worm
teaser: The feather duster worm is a living bouquet on the seafloor, a tube-dwelling worm that unfurls a crown of feathery tentacles in brilliant colors. It builds a tube of sand and mucus, and from its safe home it extends its tentacles to catch plankton and particles from the current. When danger passes, the whole crown vanishes back into the tube in an instant. If a tentacle is nipped off, the worm simply grows a new one. It is one of the most beautiful animals on the reef, and also one of the simplest.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how feather duster worms live in leathery tubes and extend crowns of feathery tentacles to filter plankton, retreating instantly into their tubes when disturbed. Explore how they regenerate lost crowns, their reef and aquarium lives, and the difference between worms that look like flowers and the flowers that look like nothing else.

name: Finch Beak Variety
teaser: The finches of the Galapagos are famous because their beaks tell the story of evolution. Each species has a beak shaped for its food: thick, strong beaks for cracking seeds, slender beaks for picking insects, and even a tool-using finch that probes cactus spines into holes to dig out grubs. Darwin noticed these beaks on his famous voyage, and decades of study have shown that in dry years, finches with bigger beaks survive better, proof of evolution happening in real time on a handful of islands.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how finch beaks vary, then explain the natural selection story.

name: Fire Ant
teaser: The fire ant is a tiny invader with a painful sting and a talent for teamwork. Native to South America but now spread across the world, it builds massive mound nests and floods out when disturbed, each worker stinging repeatedly, leaving burning welts that give the ant its name. Fire ants also use teamwork to survive floods, linking their bodies into rafts that float on water until the colony reaches dry land. They are fierce competitors that push out native ants wherever they arrive.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how fire ants, named for their burning stings, build colonies that survive floods by linking together into floating rafts that can drift for weeks, and their invasive spread has made them a costly pest in the US. Explore their mound building, the venom's alkaloid chemistry, and the control methods from baits to phorid flies.

name: Fire-bellied Toad
teaser: The fire-bellied toad is small, warty, and green on top, but flip it over and its belly blazes orange and black, a warning of the toxins in its skin. When threatened, it arches its back in a pose called the unken reflex, showing off the bright belly as a clear signal: I taste terrible. The display is honest, since its skin does carry irritants, and predators that try it once rarely try again. In spring, these toads gather in ponds and call with a soft, melodic trill.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how fire-bellied toads, when threatened, arch their bodies and flash bright red or orange bellies in a pose called the unken reflex, warning predators of skin toxins. Explore their green camouflage on top, their toxin secretion that tastes awful, and their bobbing nasal calls.

name: Firefly
teaser: The firefly is the original living light bulb, flashing to find a mate on summer nights. The light comes from a chemical reaction inside its abdomen, where luciferin combines with oxygen in a controlled glow with almost no heat, making it one of the most efficient light sources known. Each species has its own flash pattern, a code of pulses and pauses, and the female answers from the grass with her own signal. Some fireflies even mimic other species' codes to lure in males, then eat them.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how fireflies produce cold light through bioluminescence to attract mates, each species flashing its own coded pattern, and some females mimic other species' flashes to lure and eat males. Explore the chemistry of luciferin, the glow of larvae called glowworms, and why light pollution dims their signals.

name: Firefly Species
teaser: There are over two thousand species of fireflies, and not all of them fly or glow the same way. Most glow as larvae too, earning the name glowworms, and some species hardly glow at all by day, relying on pheromones instead of light to find mates. A few females are wingless and stay on the ground, glowing like beacons. Fireflies also have hidden talents: their larvae are predators that hunt snails and worms with a paralyzing bite. Wherever fireflies vanish, the night grows quieter.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the world's 2,000 firefly species flash in different patterns, colors, and rhythms, from the synchronous fireflies of the Smokies that blink in unison to the blue ghosts of Appalachia that glow steadily, each pattern a private code. Explore how females choose by pattern, the species that don't flash, and the tourism drawn to synchronous shows.

name: Flamingo
teaser: The flamingo is pink because of what it eats: the shrimp and algae in its wetland home are packed with pigments called carotenoids, which the bird's body deposits in its feathers. A flamingo's color is a health certificate, with the pinkest birds the best fed. It feeds upside down, its head dipping into the water while its tongue pumps and its comb-like bill filters out tiny food. Flamingos stand on one leg to save heat, and they live in enormous colonies that can number in the millions.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how flamingos get their pink from carotenoid pigments in the algae and shrimp they filter, and how their upside-down feeding with a tongue acting like a pump separates food from mud. Explore their one-legged standing habit, still not fully explained, and their huge noisy breeding colonies of millions.

name: Flamingo Filter Feeding
teaser: A flamingo feeds with its head upside down, and its bill is a masterpiece of filter engineering. The bird sweeps its upside-down head through the water while its tongue moves back and forth like a piston, pumping water in and out through the comb-like lamellae in its bill. Tiny shrimp, algae, and mud are sieved out by these fine plates, and the food is swallowed. The bend in the flamingo's bill mirrors the upside-down feeding position, so the bird can filter even in shallow, crowded water.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover how flamingos feed upside down, then explain the lamellae.

name: Flounder
teaser: The flounder is the flatfish that rewrote its own anatomy. It hatches as a normal-looking fish with an eye on each side, swimming upright, but as it grows, one eye migrates across its skull until both eyes sit on the same side of its body. It then lies flat on the seabed, both eyes facing up, its lower side pale and its upper side colored to match the sand. It can even change its pattern to blend with new surroundings, becoming nearly invisible while it waits to ambush prey.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how flounders start life swimming upright with eyes on both sides, then one eye migrates over the top of the skull as they settle onto the seafloor, both eyes ending on the same side. Explore how they change color to match the seabed and bury themselves in sand.

name: Flying Squirrel
teaser: The flying squirrel does not truly fly, but it comes close, gliding through the forest with astonishing grace. Stretches of loose skin between its wrists and ankles form a parachute, and it launches from high branches, steering with its tail and limbs to glide over fifty meters between trees. It lands softly, feet first, then scrambles up to launch again. Flying squirrels are mostly nocturnal, and a family may share a tree hole, curling up together for warmth. Their glides are the forest's secret night flights.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how flying squirrels glide up to 90 meters using furry membranes stretched between wrists and ankles, steering with their tails, and they're nocturnal, unlike daytime tree squirrels. Explore the physics of their gliding, their nests in tree hollows, and the Japanese giant flying squirrel the size of a cat.

name: Flying Squirrels
teaser: Flying squirrels glide to move between trees faster and safer than walking, and they have perfected the art. Their gliding membrane turns their body into a wing, and they can steer, brake, and even change direction midair by adjusting their limbs and tail. Some species can glide a hundred meters or more, covering a football field in a single leap. At night, infrared cameras show them crisscrossing forests like silent shadows. Scientists have even used their technique to inspire flying robots.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how flying squirrels glide, then explain the parachute membrane.

name: Fossa
teaser: The fossa is Madagascar's top predator, a cat-like carnivore that is actually a distant cousin of the mongoose. It is the largest carnivore on the island, stretching two meters from nose to tail, and it hunts lemurs through the trees with a combination of agility and strength. It can rotate its ankles to climb down trees headfirst, and it uses its long tail for balance. Because Madagascar evolved in isolation, the fossa fills the role that big cats fill elsewhere, and lemurs have no other enemy like it.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the fossa of Madagascar is the island's largest predator, a cat-like mongoose relative that hunts lemurs through the trees with semi-retractable claws and a tail for balance. Explore why Madagascar evolved such unique predators, the fossa's endangered status, and its secretive life.

name: Frilled Lizard
teaser: The frilled lizard is the dragon of the Australian outback, and its defense is pure theater. When threatened, it opens a huge frill of skin around its neck that spreads like an umbrella, making it look twice as big, and it stands tall, hissing and flashing its bright mouth. It then sprints away on its hind legs, running upright like a tiny dinosaur. The frill is also used to impress females and to regulate temperature. Despite the display, the frilled lizard would rather run than fight.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the frilled lizard of Australia and New Guinea erects a large frill around its neck to startle predators, gaping its mouth and hissing, then runs off on two legs. Explore how the frill is also used in courtship and temperature control, and its habit of fleeing up trees.

name: Frilled-neck Lizard vs Basilisk
teaser: The frilled-neck lizard and the basilisk are two reptiles that run on two legs, but for different reasons. The frilled lizard of Australia sprints upright on its hind legs to escape danger, its big frill snapping open to scare off attackers, and it prefers life in the trees. The basilisk of Central America runs across water on its hind feet, using its speed and wide-fringed toes to stay on the surface. Both are runners first and thinkers second, evolution's answer to the question of getting away fast.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how Australia's frilled lizard scares predators with a neck frill and runs on two legs, while Central America's basilisk runs across water, both famous for dramatic escapes. Explore how each evolved its own extreme, the frill's display role, and the water-running trick of the basilisk's wide-fringed toes.

name: Frog Calls
teaser: Frog calls are the voices of spring, and every species has its own song. Males call to attract females, each species singing a unique chorus of croaks, peeps, trills, and even whistles, so that frogs can find mates without confusion even when many species share the same pond. The calls are made by air pushed over vocal cords, and many frogs amplify them with inflatable throat sacs that balloon out like balloons. Some calls carry a kilometer or more, and a pond full of calling frogs can be heard from a long way off.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover how frogs call, then explain why males call at night.

name: Frog Calls
teaser: A frog's call is one of the most recognizable sounds of the natural world, and it is a serious business. Male frogs call to advertise themselves to females and to warn off rival males, and each species has its own distinct song. The call is produced as air passes over the vocal cords, and throat sacs amplify it, turning a small frog into a surprisingly loud singer. Females listen for the calls of their own species, and in some species the females even prefer the deeper, larger, and stronger-sounding males.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how frogs call to attract mates, defend territory, and warn of rain, each species with a distinctive call, from the deafening roar of bullfrogs to the ultrasonic calls of some Chinese frogs and the peeps of spring peepers that signal spring's arrival. Explore the vocal sacs that amplify sound, the males that call in choruses, and how scientists identify species by ear.

name: Frog Skin Superpowers
teaser: Frog skin is a superpower in disguise. It is thin, moist, and packed with blood vessels, letting frogs breathe and drink through it, which is why they must stay damp. It is also a chemical factory, producing everything from mucus to powerful toxins: the poison dart frogs carry enough poison to stop a heart, yet their skin also makes antimicrobial peptides that kill bacteria and viruses. Scientists are studying frog skin to develop new medicines, from antibiotics to painkillers, making these little amphibians pharmacists of the wild.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover how frogs breathe through their skin, then explain why they need damp habitats.

name: Frog Tongues
teaser: A frog's tongue is one of the fastest weapons in nature. It is attached at the front of the mouth, not the back, so it can shoot out like a slingshot, extending to nearly its full body length in about a hundredth of a second. The tip is covered in sticky saliva that is actually a soft, fluid-like glue, and it wraps around the prey, holding it fast. Then the tongue snaps back, pulling the insect into the frog's mouth before it can react. Frogs see prey with eyes that bulge, giving them 3D vision to aim the strike.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover how frog tongues attach to prey, then explain the saliva trick.

name: Frogs That Freeze
teaser: Some frogs survive winter by freezing solid. The wood frog of North America can have up to sixty-five percent of its body water turned to ice, its heart and breathing stop completely, and it stays that way for months. In spring, it thaws from the inside out and hops away as if nothing happened. The secret is a natural antifreeze: glucose and other sugars flood its cells, protecting them from ice damage while the spaces between cells freeze. It is one of the most extreme survival tricks in the animal kingdom.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how wood frogs survive freezing, then explain the glucose antifreeze.

name: Fruit Bat
teaser: The fruit bat is the gardener of the tropics, a flying mammal that spreads the seeds of entire forests. It feeds on fruit and nectar at night, and as it flies, it drops seeds in its droppings, planting new trees across huge areas. Some fruit bats can carry seeds many kilometers, making them vital to rainforest regeneration. They also pollinate flowers, including crops like durian and agave. Despite their big eyes and dog-like faces, they are gentle, intelligent, and essential, not the villains of vampire legend.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how fruit bats, or flying foxes, feed on nectar and fruit, pollinating flowers and spreading seeds across vast distances, some with wingspans over 1.5 meters and faces like foxes. Explore their roosts of thousands, their role in regenerating forests, and the threats from hunting and habitat loss that make them conservation priorities.

name: Fruit Bats
teaser: Fruit bats, also called flying foxes, are the largest bats in the world, with wingspans over a meter and a half. They do not echolocate like insect-eating bats, relying instead on excellent eyesight and a strong sense of smell to find ripe fruit and flowers. At dusk, colonies stream out of their roosts by the thousands to feed, and their faces, with pointed ears and bright eyes, look almost dog-like. Flying foxes pollinate plants and spread seeds across entire islands, making them keystone species of the tropics.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover how fruit bats help forests, then explain their role as gardeners.

name: Fur Seals
teaser: Fur seals are the acrobats of the cold seas, sleek swimmers with the thickest fur of any animal, up to three hundred thousand hairs per square centimeter. That dense fur traps air for warmth, which is why fur seals were hunted almost to extinction for their pelts. They are closely related to sea lions, and like them they can walk on their hind flippers, hauling out onto rocky shores and forming huge noisy colonies. In the water they are torpedoes, chasing fish and squid with speed and agility.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover why fur seals were hunted, then explain their thick double coats.

name: Galapagos Tortoise
teaser: The Galapagos tortoise is the largest tortoise in the world, a slow-moving giant that can weigh over four hundred kilograms and live past a hundred years, with some reaching one hundred and fifty. Each island in the Galapagos has its own distinct shell shape, adapted to its food: dome-shelled tortoises graze low grass, while saddleback tortoises raise their heads high to reach cactus. Once hunted by sailors and threatened by introduced goats and rats, careful conservation has brought their numbers back from the brink.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how Galapagos tortoises can exceed 150 years and weigh over 400 kg, storing water and fat to survive months without food or drink. Explore the island-specific shell shapes Darwin noted, the near-extinction from whalers, and the breeding programs that brought species back.

name: Garter Snake
teaser: The garter snake is one of the most widespread and familiar snakes in North America, found from gardens to mountains. It is harmless to humans, though its saliva is mildly toxic to its prey of worms, slugs, and amphibians. Garter snakes give birth to live young, and in Canada, red-sided garter snakes gather by the tens of thousands in limestone dens each spring, in the largest snake aggregations on Earth, a writhing mass that emerges together to mate in the brief northern summer.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how garter snakes are among the most common and harmless snakes of North America, eating slugs, worms, and frogs, gathering in huge mating balls each spring, and some even give birth to live young. Explore their range across Canada and the US, their mild musk defense, and why they're great neighbors.

name: Gazelle
teaser: The gazelle is the elegant sprinter of the African and Asian plains, built for beauty and speed. Its long legs and light body let it sprint at nearly a hundred kilometers an hour, and it can zigzag to escape predators that are faster in a straight line. When a lion approaches, gazelles stot, bounding high in the air with stiff legs, a signal that they are healthy and not worth the chase. Gazelles also have a trick called pronking, springing straight up with all four feet off the ground.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how gazelles are among the fastest and most graceful antelopes, Thomson's gazelles sprinting at 80 km/h with bounding leaps called stotting that signal fitness to predators, living on the dry plains of Africa. Explore their herding, their drought survival, and the cheetah hunts they must outrun.

name: Gazelle Speed
teaser: The Thomson's gazelle is the cheetah's favorite meal — and the fastest thing in its weight class. It can sprint at around 80 kilometers per hour, but its real talent is agility: the gazelle weaves, dodges, and cuts at full speed with jinking turns that a chasing cheetah simply can't match. It also uses a special zigzag run that opens up distance, and it can sustain a fast gallop far longer than a cheetah can sprint. There's even a built-in early-warning system: when a gazelle spots a predator, it 'stots' — jumps stiff-legged — and the whole herd takes the hint.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how fast gazelles run, then explain why they zigzag when chased.

name: Gecko
teaser: The gecko is the wall-crawler of the tropics, famous for running up glass and across ceilings without falling. Its feet are covered in millions of microscopic hairs, each splitting into even finer spatula-shaped tips, that grip surfaces using weak molecular forces called van der Waals forces. This lets a gecko climb smooth glass and even hang from a single toe. Geckos are also champion vocalists among lizards, with species that chirp, click, and bark. Their tails can regrow, and their eyes see color in near-darkness.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how geckos climb smooth glass using millions of microscopic hairs called setae that create van der Waals forces, enough to hold 130 kg in theory. Explore their tails that drop off, their toe pads that self-clean, and how this biology inspired real climbing robots and adhesives.

name: Gecko Calls
teaser: Geckos are the talkative ones of the lizard world, and most species make sounds, which is rare among lizards. The tokay gecko gets its name from its loud, two-syllable call, TO-KAY, that rings through the night. Others chirp, click, squeak, or bark, using their voices to defend territory and attract mates. These calls are especially common at night, when geckos are most active, hunting insects on walls and in trees. A house with geckos is a house with a nightly soundtrack.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how some geckos are among the most vocal lizards, the tokay gecko named for its loud tokay call that echoes through tropical nights, with males calling to claim territory and attract mates, and some species defending territory with chirps. Explore the different calls, why geckos are named after their sounds, and the nocturnal chorus of Southeast Asian walls.

name: Gecko Eyes
teaser: Gecko eyes are built for the dark. Unlike most reptiles, geckos are often nocturnal, and their eyes have huge pupils that open wide at night, with many more rod cells than daytime lizards, letting them see colors even in dim light. Their eyes have no eyelids, so they clean them with their long tongues. Some geckos can see colors at night up to three hundred and fifty times better than humans. Their vertical slit pupils close to near-pinholes in bright light, protecting their night vision.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how gecko eyes work at night, then explain the vertical pupil.

name: Gecko Feet
teaser: A gecko's feet are nature's miracle of adhesion, letting it walk up walls and across ceilings. Each toe is covered with millions of microscopic hairs called setae, and each seta splits into hundreds of even tinier spatula-shaped tips. These tips create weak molecular attractions, van der Waals forces, that collectively grip any surface, even smooth glass. The gecko can attach and detach in a fraction of a second by changing the angle of its toes, and it even cleans its feet by walking on leaves. Engineers study gecko feet to design new adhesives and climbing robots.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover how gecko feet grip, then explain van der Waals forces.

name: Giant African Land Snail
teaser: The giant African land snail is one of the biggest snails on Earth, growing up to twenty centimeters long, and it is one of the world's worst invasive species. It eats over five hundred kinds of plants, damages crops, and can even gnaw through plaster to eat the lime in walls. It carries a parasite that can cause meningitis in humans, and it reproduces at a stunning rate, laying hundreds of eggs at a time. Where it invades, it pushes out native snails and costs billions in damage.

exploreAction.targetName: Meet the giant African land snail
exploreAction.instruction: Read how the giant African land snail grows to 20 cm and 1 kg, eats hundreds of plant species, lays hundreds of eggs, and spreads diseases, making it one of the world's worst invasive species, repeatedly intercepted at ports. Explore how it arrived in Florida and was eradicated twice, and its dual life as pest and food.

name: Giant Anteater
teaser: The giant anteater of South America is a walking vacuum cleaner, built entirely around eating ants and termites. Its snout is a long tube with no teeth, its tongue is over half a meter long and covered in sticky saliva, and it flicks that tongue up to a hundred and fifty times a minute, gulping down thousands of insects a day. Its powerful front claws, which look like they should be on a bear, rip open rock-hard termite mounds. It has one of the lowest body temperatures of any mammal, conserving energy for its slow, deliberate life.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how giant anteaters lick up to 30,000 ants and termites a day with a 60 cm tongue that whips in and out 150 times a minute, and fend off jaguars with razor-sharp front claws. Explore their strong smell, their shaggy tails used as blankets, and their solitary wanderings.

name: Giant Anteater Details
teaser: The giant anteater is a walking contradiction: a fierce-looking animal with a gentle feeding habit. Its claws are long and sharp enough to fight off a jaguar, yet it uses them to rip open termite mounds, then flicks its meter-long tongue in and out up to a hundred and fifty times a minute to lap up insects. It has no teeth, and its sense of smell is forty times stronger than a human's, letting it find a termite nest from a distance. It walks on its knuckles to keep its claws sharp.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how fast giant anteaters flick their tongues, then explain their smell.

name: Giant Clam
teaser: The giant clam is the heavyweight of the reef, and some can grow over a meter long and weigh more than two hundred kilograms. It lives embedded in coral, and its colorful mantle is home to symbiotic algae that photosynthesize and feed it, which is why it needs sunlit water. It also filter-feeds plankton, pulling water through its siphons. The myth that giant clams trap divers is false, but their shells have been treasured for centuries, and they are now protected across much of the tropics.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how giant clams of Indo-Pacific reefs grow over a meter long and 200 kg, hosting algae in their colorful mantles that feed them sugars while they filter feed, growing reef structure. Explore their strong shell muscle, the overharvesting that shrank populations, and their role in reef ecology.

name: Giant Ground Sloth
teaser: The giant ground sloth was one of the strangest giants of the Ice Age, a bear-sized plant-eater that walked on its knuckles with huge curved claws. It lived across the Americas until about ten thousand years ago, alongside mammoths and saber-toothed cats, and some species weighed several tonnes. It may have dug burrows, and its claws suggest it could rear up to pull down branches. Cave paintings and fossil tracks show it shared the land with early humans. It was one of the last great megafauna to vanish.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how giant ground sloths, the size of elephants, shuffled across the Americas for millions of years, walking upright and maybe standing on hind legs to reach leaves. Explore how they survived ice ages, the debate over whether humans hunted them, and their ancient dung caves.

name: Giant Panda
teaser: The giant panda is the world's most famous conservation icon, a black-and-white bear that eats almost nothing but bamboo. It is a carnivore by ancestry, with the digestive system of a meat-eater, yet it survives on a diet of tough plant stalks, spending up to fourteen hours a day eating, consuming over a dozen kilograms of bamboo. Its famous thumbs are actually modified wrist bones that help it grip the stalks. Decades of protection in China have brought its numbers back, and it is no longer considered endangered.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how giant pandas, bears with a carnivore's gut, survive almost entirely on bamboo, eating up to 38 kg a day, and their slow digestion means constant eating, while their famous black-and-white markings may aid camouflage and communication. Explore their solitary life, their cubs born tiny and pink, and how conservation pulled them back from the brink.

name: Giant Squid
teaser: The giant squid is the stuff of sea monster legend, a deep-sea giant that can grow over twelve meters long, with eyes the size of basketballs and arms armed with suckers lined with sharp teeth. It lives in the dark depths, and almost everything we know about it comes from dead specimens washed ashore or found in sperm whale stomachs. The first video of a live giant squid in its natural habitat was only captured in 2012. It remains one of the last great mysteries of the ocean.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the giant squid, a legend of the deep for centuries with arms reaching 13 meters and eyes the size of dinner plates, was only filmed alive in its natural habitat in 2012 after decades of searching. Explore its battles with sperm whales, its suckers ringed with teeth, and what we still don't know about it.

name: Giant Trapdoor Spider
teaser: The giant trapdoor spider is the silent sentinel of the bush, a large, slow-growing spider that builds a burrow with a hinged lid. It waits inside with the door slightly open, sensing vibrations through silk trip-lines stretched around the entrance. When an insect walks by, the spider bursts out, grabs it, and drags it inside before the door falls shut. The female may live twenty years in the same burrow, rarely leaving it, and the trapdoor is camouflaged with soil and leaves to look like bare ground.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how trapdoor spiders dig burrows with hinged silk doors they hold shut, waiting under the lid to grab passing insects, and how females spend their whole lives in one burrow, living up to 40 years. Explore their armor, their docile reputation despite looks, and their ancient lineage.

name: Gibbon
teaser: The gibbon is the acrobat of the Asian rainforests, swinging through the treetops with the fastest locomotion of any non-flying mammal. Its long arms, hook-like hands, and powerful shoulders let it brachiate, swinging hand over hand at speeds that blur, covering ten meters in a single swing. Gibbons live in family groups and are famous for their songs: mated pairs sing duets that carry through the forest, strengthening their bond and defending their territory. Their calls are among the most beautiful in nature.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how gibbons swing through trees with arm-swinging brachiation at speeds that would break human shoulders, and sing duets with mates that echo through the forest, some pairs harmonizing perfectly. Explore their small ape size, their monogamy, and why they're called lesser apes.

name: Gibbon Brachiation
teaser: The gibbon is the trapeze artist of the primate world, and its flying style has a name: brachiation — swinging from arm to arm through the trees. Gibbons are so good at it that they're the fastest of all tree-dwelling mammals, launching themselves ten meters or more between branches, moving with a grace that looks almost effortless. Their arms are disproportionately long, their hands hook-shaped, and their shoulders rotate freely in a way ours can't, letting them reach and release with perfect rhythm.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how gibbons swing through trees, then explain the power of their arms.

name: Gibbon Duets
teaser: Gibbons are the opera singers of the animal kingdom — the only apes that truly sing, and the sound is a piercing, haunting melody that carries for kilometers through the forest. Pairs of gibbons perform duets at dawn, and the song is a duet in the real sense: male and female each have their own parts, weaving together in a synchronized performance that strengthens their pair bond and announces their territory to neighboring families. Each pair develops a song so individual that researchers can tell exactly which gibbon family is singing, and the duet grows more perfectly coordinated the longer a pair has been together.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover why gibbons sing duets, then explain what the song announces.

name: Gigantopithecus
teaser: Gigantopithecus was the largest ape that ever lived, a giant relative of orangutans that stood up to three meters tall and weighed over two hundred kilograms. It roamed the forests of southern China and Southeast Asia for millions of years, and scientists know it almost entirely from its teeth and jaws, which are huge. It likely ate mostly bamboo and fruit, and it vanished around three hundred thousand years ago, possibly unable to cope with changing forests and climate. Its story is written in fossils and a few giant molars.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how Gigantopithecus, a giant ape of ancient Asia standing up to 3 meters tall and weighing 300 kg, is known only from teeth and jaws, yet was the largest primate ever. Explore why it likely died out when forests shrank, the bamboo diet theory, and how it inspired King Kong legends.

name: Gila Monster
teaser: The Gila monster is one of only two venomous lizards in the world, a thick, bead-covered reptile of the American Southwest that looks like it crawled out of a myth. Its venom flows from grooves in its teeth, and once it bites, it clamps down and chews, working the venom into the wound. Despite its scary reputation, it is slow and shy, spending most of its life hidden underground, and it stores fat in its tail to survive months without food. Its venom has even produced a drug used to treat diabetes.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the Gila monster is one of only two venomous lizards, gripping and chewing venom into wounds with grooved teeth, and how its venom inspired the diabetes drug exenatide. Explore its slow desert life, its fat-storing tail, and how it can survive months between meals.

name: Giraffe
teaser: The giraffe is the tallest animal on Earth, a walking skyscraper that can reach nearly six meters, with a neck that holds seven vertebrae, the same number as a human's. Its heart is huge, pumping blood up that long neck against gravity, and its blood pressure is twice that of a human, yet special valves keep its brain safe. Giraffes browse the treetops that no other animal can reach, and males fight by swinging their heads and necks in powerful blows called necking. Despite its size, it can gallop at fifty kilometers an hour.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how giraffes reach 5.5 meters on necks of just seven vertebrae, each 25 cm long, with a heart that pumps blood up two meters against gravity using pressure valves in the neck. Explore their blue-black prehensile tongues, their dangerous necking fights, and how they sleep only minutes a day.

name: Giraffe Calf Life
teaser: A baby giraffe enters the world with a two-meter fall. Calves are born standing up, dropping from their mother's height to the ground, and within an hour of that rude welcome they can stand; within a day they're running. The first weeks are the most dangerous of a giraffe's life, so the calf's mother stays close and a herd of aunts keeps watch — giraffe mothers famously babysit each other's young in a crèche while the rest of the herd feeds. A calf can double its height in the first year, growing up to a meter in a single year, fueled by up to three liters of milk a day.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how giraffe calves grow, then explain why they stay in nursery groups.

name: Giraffe Neck
teaser: The giraffe's neck is one of evolution's most famous puzzles. It has only seven vertebrae, the same as a human, but each one is stretched to over twenty centimeters. Darwin and others long thought the neck evolved to reach high leaves, but the giraffe also uses it in mating battles, swinging it as a weapon, and it is the only mammal that consistently feeds above shoulder height. The neck's blood vessels are a marvel too, with special valves and a pressure-regulating system that keeps the giraffe from fainting when it drinks.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how giraffe necks reach 2 meters to browse treetops out of reach of rivals, yet the classic competition theory has been debated, with recent research suggesting necks may have evolved for male neck-swinging fights, and their unique cardiovascular system handles the extreme height. Explore the blood pressure pumps, the valve system, and the necking combat.

name: Giraffe Necking Battles
teaser: Giraffe fights don't look like any other animal fight. Males 'neck' — they stand side by side, swing their long necks, and batter each other with the heavy, bony bumps on their skulls called ossicones, aiming blows at the neck and body. The fights are slow-motion duels that can go on for twenty minutes, with each swing building momentum until a hit lands with real force. Sometimes it escalates to full contact, with both animals leaning into each other to push and twist.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover how male giraffes fight with their necks, then explain what they are proving.

name: Giraffe Pattern Camouflage
teaser: A giraffe's spots aren't decoration — they're a living disguise, and every pattern is unique, like a fingerprint. Under a giraffe's skin runs a network of blood vessels that follows the exact pattern of its spots, and the dark patches act like thermal windows, helping the animal dump heat on hot days. In the dappled light of the savanna, the irregular blotches break up the giraffe's outline so effectively that a lion can walk past a still giraffe and never notice it. A calf inherits a pattern that is always different from its mother's, so a mother can recognize her own baby by sight.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover how giraffe spots break up their outline, then explain the pattern's uniqueness.

name: Giraffe Sleep Habits
teaser: Giraffes are the insomniacs of the animal kingdom, sleeping less than almost any other mammal. An adult giraffe averages only about half an hour of deep sleep a day, and it never sleeps in one long stretch — instead it takes a series of tiny power naps that last just a few minutes each. When it does sleep deeply, it curls its neck back over its body to rest its head on its hip, an awkward position it holds for only minutes at a time, because lying down makes a giraffe slow and vulnerable to predators.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how little giraffes sleep, then explain why they nap standing.

name: Glass Frog
teaser: The glass frog is a tiny jewel of the tropical forests of Central and South America, and its most remarkable feature is see-through skin. Look at one from below and you can see its beating heart, its liver, and its intestines through the transparent skin of its belly, hence the name. The males call from leaves over streams, and the females lay their eggs on the leaves, with fathers guarding them until the tadpoles drop into the water below. Their camouflage is so good that they can be almost invisible.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how glass frogs of Central and South America have translucent belly skin that reveals their beating heart and organs, while their backs are leaf-green for camouflage. Explore why the transparency evolved, how males guard eggs over streams, and the threat of chytrid fungus.

name: Glass Frog Transparency
teaser: Glass frog transparency is a biological mystery and a masterstroke of camouflage. Seen from above, a glass frog is bright green, blending with leaves, but from below, its belly is nearly transparent, letting light pass through and making it almost invisible to predators looking up. Scientists studying this transparency have found that the frogs' red blood cells concentrate in the liver while they sleep, clearing the blood from the rest of the body, and the frogs somehow do this without forming dangerous clots. It is one of the wildest tricks in biology.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how glass frogs' transparent bellies let observers watch their organs, including the beating heart, and researchers found they hide red blood cells in the liver during sleep, making them far more transparent, possibly to avoid casting shadows for predators. Explore the camouflage advantage and the science of reversible transparency.

name: Glass Sponge
teaser: The glass sponge is one of the oldest and strangest animals in the sea, building its skeleton from silica, the same material as glass. Its delicate lattice of glassy spicules can stand over a meter tall on the deep seafloor, and some are so old that scientists have estimated one species to live for thousands of years, among the longest-lived animals known. It filters food from the water and provides shelter for tiny shrimp. Found in deep, cold water, glass sponges thrive where few other animals can.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how glass sponges of the deep sea build skeletons of silica spicules so intricate they've inspired optical fiber design, and some reefs of these sponges off Canada are over 9,000 years old, the oldest living animal communities. Explore how they trap plankton with their glass lattices, and the trawling that destroys them.

name: Gnu: Another Name
teaser: The wildebeest answers to two names, and both fit: wildebeest, from the Dutch for 'wild beast,' and gnu, from the Khoikhoi name that imitates the animal's own call. That call — a rolling, guttural 'gnu' — is one of the most recognizable sounds of the African plains, and it carries across the grass like a foghorn. The name is a reminder of how the animal got its reputation: the gnu was seen by early European settlers as a strange, shaggy, unmanageable creature, neither cattle nor horse, and the 'wild beast' label stuck.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover where the name gnu comes from, then explain the Khoikhoi origin.

name: Goblin Shark
teaser: The goblin shark is a living fossil from the deep sea, a pinkish shark with a flattened, blade-like snout and jaws that shoot forward like a spring-loaded trap. When it strikes, its jaw unhinges and thrusts out to grab prey with needle teeth, then retracts. It lives in deep water around the world, down to over a thousand meters, and is rarely seen, since it stays far below the reach of divers. Its strange look has earned it a reputation as the ocean's ugliest, and strangest, predator.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the goblin shark of the deep sea shoots its jaw forward like a slingshot to grab prey, a pink snout packed with electroreceptors for sensing prey in darkness. Explore how rarely humans see it, why it's called a living fossil, and how its flabby body suits crushing depths.

name: Golden Eagle
teaser: The golden eagle is the great hunter of the northern hemisphere's mountains and open country, one of the most powerful birds of prey on Earth. With a wingspan over two meters, it can strike down prey as large as foxes, deer fawns, and young mountain goats, diving at over a hundred and fifty kilometers an hour. It builds enormous stick nests on cliffs, returns to them for years, and pairs stay together for life. Its golden nape feathers give the eagle its name, and it has been a symbol of power for millennia.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the golden eagle hunts from a mile up, folding into a stoop that can exceed 240 km/h, and has been recorded killing foxes, goats, and even young deer. Explore its pair bond that lasts a lifetime, its enormous eyries reused for generations, and its use in falconry for thousands of years.

name: Golden Lion Tamarin
teaser: The golden lion tamarin is a tiny burst of flame in the Brazilian rainforest, a monkey the size of a squirrel with a brilliant orange mane. It lives in family groups that share parenting, with fathers and older siblings carrying the babies while the mother feeds. Its forest home shrank so drastically that by the 1970s only a few hundred remained, but a famous breeding and reintroduction program has brought the population back, making it a symbol of conservation success in the Atlantic rainforest.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how golden lion tamarins of Brazil's Atlantic forest dropped to a few hundred before a famous captive breeding and reintroduction program rebuilt their numbers, with conservationists carrying young monkeys into the forest in boxes to release them. Explore the golden mane, the family groups, and the forest corridors now connecting isolated populations.

name: Goliath Beetle
teaser: The goliath beetle is one of the heaviest insects on Earth, a giant of the African rainforest that can weigh as much as a small apple and grow to eleven centimeters long. Its thick, armored body comes in striking patterns of black, white, and brown, and males use their forked horns to wrestle rivals for the best spots to feed. Despite its size, it eats mostly fruit, sap, and nectar, and its grubs are even bigger, feeding on decaying wood and protein-rich food.
