exploreAction.instruction: Read how goliath beetles of African rainforests weigh up to 100 grams, among the heaviest insects, with larvae that outweigh adults and shells so hard they're used as jewelry. Explore their swift flight, their sap and fruit diet, and their dramatic black and white patterns.

name: Goose Pair Bonds
teaser: Geese form some of the strongest pair bonds in the bird world, mating for life. A bonded pair stays together year after year, migrating together, sharing parenting, and greeting each other with synchronized calls and head-bobbing ceremonies. When one partner dies, the survivor often grieves, and some never pair again. Geese also care for their goslings as a family, with parents leading them in single file and guarding them fiercely. Their famous V-formation flight is teamwork, with the leader rotating to share the work.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how geese pair for life, then explain the family structure.

name: Gorilla
teaser: The gorilla is the largest living primate, a gentle giant of the African forests that can weigh two hundred kilograms yet is mostly a peaceful plant-eater. It lives in family groups led by a silverback male, who protects and guides the troop, settling disputes with a show of chest-beating rather than violence. Gorillas build nests to sleep in, use tools, and teach their young. They share about 98 percent of their DNA with humans, and watching a mother groom her baby is like watching family life almost like our own.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how gorillas, our closest relatives after chimpanzees, live in family troops led by silverback males that can be 10 times stronger than a human, yet are gentle vegetarians. Explore their knuckle walking, their nests built fresh each night, their sign language abilities, and the fight to save mountain gorillas.

name: Gorilla Family Life
teaser: A gorilla family runs on the calm authority of one enormous male — the silverback, named for the silver saddle of hair that spreads across his back once he reaches maturity. He leads a family of several females and their young, deciding when the group feeds, rests, and moves, and settling disputes with a glance rather than a fight. Silverbacks are patient fathers: they play with infants, let them climb on them, and intervene in their squabbles, and the family unit is so stable that members may stay together for years.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how gorilla troops are organized, then explain the silverback's role.

name: Gouldian Finch
teaser: The Gouldian finch is one of the most brilliantly colored birds in the world, a small Australian finch with a rainbow of red, green, purple, yellow, and turquoise feathers. It is so dazzling that it is sometimes called the rainbow finch, and it is popular in aviaries worldwide. In the wild it lives in the tropical savannas of northern Australia, where it nests in tree hollows and feeds on grass seeds. Wild populations have declined, and conservationists now manage their habitat and fire regimes carefully.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the Gouldian finch of northern Australia flashes red, black, yellow, purple, and turquoise in one small body, with heads in three color morphs that once were traded as separate species. Explore its seed diet, its seasonal nesting in tree hollows, and threats from fire and trapping.

name: Grasshopper
teaser: The grasshopper is the jumper of the meadow, a champion leaper that can cover twenty times its own body length in a single bound. Its powerful hind legs act like springs, and its wings let it fly to escape danger. Grasshoppers eat plants, and their chewing mouthparts can strip a field, with huge swarms of locusts, which are grasshoppers in swarm form, devastating crops across whole continents. Their hearing organs sit on their abdomens, and they communicate by stridulating, rubbing their legs against their wings.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how grasshoppers leap 20 times their body length with spring-loaded hind legs, hear with membranes on their abdomen, and sing by rubbing legs against wings. Explore their huge appetite that can swarm into locust plagues, their camouflage from green to brown, and the difference from crickets and katydids.

name: Gray Whale
teaser: The gray whale makes one of the longest migrations of any mammal, swimming up to twenty thousand kilometers round trip each year from the feeding grounds of the Arctic to the warm lagoons of Mexico's Baja coast. It is a bottom feeder, rolling on its side and sucking up mouthfuls of mud to filter out tiny shrimp-like amphipods through its baleen. Gray whales are famous for approaching boats, lifting their heads to look at people, a curiosity that has made whale watching a huge industry along their migration route.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how gray whales make one of the longest mammal migrations, 20,000 km round trip between Arctic feeding grounds and Mexican lagoons, and feed by rolling on their sides to scoop mud from the seabed, filtering amphipods through baleen. Explore the friendly whales of San Ignacio lagoon, the calf journeys, and the eastern population's recovery.

name: Great Ape Conservation
teaser: Great apes, our closest living relatives, are in deep trouble. Chimpanzees, gorillas, bonobos, and orangutans are all endangered, threatened by deforestation, the bushmeat trade, and disease, with some populations down by more than half in a generation. Conservation groups work on every front: protecting rainforests, fighting poaching, rescuing orphaned apes, and helping local communities find sustainable livelihoods. Every great ape saved is a piece of our own family tree preserved, and the fight goes on across three continents.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how orangutans, gorillas, chimpanzees, and bonobos all face habitat loss, poaching, and disease, with mountain gorillas surviving a scare to under 1,000 individuals before patient protection doubled them. Explore the rangers, vets, and communities behind the comebacks, and what great ape survival means for forests.

name: Great Auk
teaser: The great auk was the penguin of the north, a flightless seabird of the cold North Atlantic that stood nearly a meter tall and waddled in huge colonies on rocky islands. It was a superb swimmer, but it was utterly defenseless on land, and sailors, fishermen, and feather hunters slaughtered it by the thousands. The last two known individuals were killed on an Icelandic island in 1844. The great auk became the first European bird driven to extinction in modern times, a lesson about how quickly carelessness can erase a species.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the great auk, a flightless seabird of the North Atlantic that stood a meter tall and nested in huge colonies, was hunted for food, feathers, and specimens until the last two were killed in Iceland in 1844. Explore how its vulnerability on land doomed it, and its place as an extinction symbol.

name: Great Horned Owl
teaser: The great horned owl is the tiger of the night skies, one of the most powerful and adaptable owls in the Americas. Its yellow eyes and feather tufts, which are not ears but decoration, give it a fierce look, and its talons squeeze with hundreds of pounds of pressure, enough to crush a skunk's spine, a favorite prey. It hunts from perches in near-total darkness, its hearing so fine it can catch mice beneath snow. Its deep hooting call, a classic of the night, echoes through forests, deserts, and even city parks.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the great horned owl hunts at night with hearing so acute it can strike prey under snow, its serrated feather edges make flight silent, and its grip can crush a rabbit's spine. Explore why it's called the tiger of the sky, taking prey from mice to skunks, and its deep resonant hooting.

name: Great White Hunting Strategy
teaser: The great white shark is an ambush predator of extraordinary patience and power. It hunts seals and sea lions by attacking from below at high speed, often breaching fully out of the water with the prey in its jaws, then lets the victim bleed out before feeding. It uses all its senses: smell, hearing, and special electro-receptors that detect the heartbeat of prey hidden in the sand. After a big meal, it can go weeks without eating. Its bite force is among the strongest of any animal alive.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how great white sharks hunt seals by launching from below at high speed, sometimes breaching fully out of the water, using the seal's dark silhouette against the surface to target it, and biting first to investigate. Explore the elephant seal colonies that draw them, and the reasons attacks on humans are often mistaken identity.

name: Great White Shark
teaser: The great white shark is the most famous predator in the ocean, a cold-blooded killing machine that is actually warm-blooded in key parts of its body, letting it hunt in cold waters. It can reach six meters and over two tonnes, and it has rows of serrated, triangular teeth that constantly replace themselves. Despite its reputation, attacks on humans are rare and usually cases of mistaken identity, since humans are not part of its diet. Great whites are now protected in many waters, and scientists are working to understand and conserve them.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how great white sharks grow to 6 meters, hunt with rows of serrated teeth that regrow constantly, and detect prey's heartbeat through electroreception. Explore their warm-blooded muscles for cold-water hunting, the mystery of breaching attacks, and how they learn by biting first.

name: Green Anaconda
teaser: The green anaconda is the heaviest snake on Earth, a giant of the South American swamps that can weigh over two hundred kilograms and grow to more than nine meters. It lives in and around water, where its bulk is supported and it can move with surprising speed. It hunts by ambush, coiling around caimans, capybaras, and deer, squeezing until the prey suffocates, then swallowing it whole. Despite its fearsome reputation, it is shy and rarely attacks humans, and its greatest threat is habitat loss.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the green anaconda of South American rivers can weigh over 200 kg and reach 9 meters, constricting prey with pressure that stops blood flow within minutes. Explore its aquatic life, eyes and nostrils on top of the head, and how females are far larger than males.

name: Green Iguana
teaser: The green iguana is the giant lizard of the American tropics, a plant-eater that can grow two meters long, most of it tail. It is a superb climber, dropping from high branches into water to escape predators and swimming powerfully away. Young iguanas are bright green and fast, while old males grow heavy jowls and duller colors. Iguanas bask in the sun to warm up, and they have a third eye on top of their heads that senses light and movement, warning them of predators from above.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how green iguanas grow to 1.8 meters, basking in treetops and dropping into water with a splash when threatened, with a third eye on their forehead that senses light and shadows. Explore their mostly leaf diet, their territorial displays, and their spread as pets gone wild in Florida.

name: Green Sea Turtle
teaser: The green sea turtle is the ocean's great grazer, a reptile that can weigh over two hundred kilograms and live to eighty years. Its name comes from the green fat beneath its shell, the result of its plant diet: it is one of the few marine animals that eats seagrass, acting like an underwater lawnmower that keeps the meadows healthy. It migrates thousands of kilometers between feeding and nesting beaches, and females return to the same beach where they hatched to lay their eggs, guided by the Earth's magnetic field.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how green sea turtles migrate thousands of kilometers between feeding grounds and nesting beaches, with females returning to lay eggs on the exact beach where they hatched decades earlier. Explore how they navigate by magnetic fields, why hatchlings race to the sea, and threats from plastic and light pollution.

name: Grizzly Salmon Fishing
teaser: When the salmon run, the grizzly bear throws a feast — and watching a grizzly fish is one of the great spectacles of the natural world. In Alaska and western Canada, grizzlies gather at rivers and waterfalls as salmon fight their way upstream to spawn, and the bears take up positions in the water, catching fish with their paws, mouths, or a spectacular leaping snatch. A grizzly can eat dozens of salmon in a day, and the timing is everything: the fish are fat with eggs and energy, the perfect fuel to fatten the bear for its long winter hibernation.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how grizzlies catch spawning salmon, then explain the role of the falls.

name: Hammerhead Shark
teaser: The hammerhead shark wears its head like a radar dish, and the strange shape is pure function. Its flattened, wing-like head spreads its eyes and nostrils wide apart, letting it scan a wider area and pinpoint prey from the electric signals their bodies give off. It swings its head like a metal detector to find stingrays buried in the sand, its favorite food. Hammerheads gather in huge schools of hundreds, one of the great mysteries of the ocean, and the scalloped hammerhead is now endangered from overfishing.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how hammerhead sharks use their wide hammer-shaped heads to improve electroreception and vision, swinging their heads like metal detectors to scan the seafloor for rays, and some species school in the hundreds. Explore why the head evolved, their deep dives, and the fin trade's threat to them.

name: Harbor Seal
teaser: The harbor seal is the familiar, spotted face of the world's coasts, found in bays and estuaries across the northern hemisphere. It is a graceful swimmer, reaching speeds over thirty kilometers an hour, and it can dive for up to half an hour, slowing its heart to conserve oxygen. On land it hauls out onto sandbars and rocks to rest and warm up, and mothers nurse their pups on land, teaching them to swim within weeks. Harbor seals sleep underwater, rising to breathe without waking, and they can even sleep with half their brain at a time.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how harbor seals, with spotted coats and puppy-like faces, haul out on rocky shores and sandbars along northern coasts, diving for fish and holding breath for 20 minutes, and mothers nurse pups that can swim within hours. Explore their wide distribution, their wariness of boats, and the pupping seasons on protected beaches.

name: Hare vs Rabbit
teaser: Hares and rabbits look alike but live different lives. Hares are larger, with longer ears and legs, and they are born fully furred with open eyes, able to run within hours of birth. Rabbits are born naked, blind, and helpless, and they raise their young in burrows underground. Hares live above ground in shallow scrapes called forms, relying on speed to escape, while rabbits dig warrens and hide. Hares are loners for most of the year, while rabbits live in colonies. Even their running styles differ: hares bound high, rabbits sprint low.

exploreAction.instruction: Compare hares and rabbits, then explain why leverets are born ready.

name: Hawk Soaring
teaser: A hawk soaring is one of the great sights of the open sky, a bird riding columns of rising warm air called thermals without flapping. The hawk spreads its broad wings, circles into the rising air, and climbs hundreds of meters on the invisible updraft, then glides to the next thermal, covering huge distances for almost no energy. Migrating hawks use this trick to travel thousands of kilometers, and they can stay aloft for hours. Watching them circle ever higher, you are watching a master of physics.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover how hawks ride thermals, then explain why they circle.

name: Hawk vs Falcon
teaser: Hawks and falcons are both birds of prey, but they are built for different ways of hunting. Hawks have broad, rounded wings and long tails, built for soaring and agile maneuvering through forests, and they catch prey with powerful talons in a strike. Falcons have long, pointed wings, built for speed, and they kill in the air with a swift dive or a punch from their feet, or by slicing prey with their hooked beak. Hawks often chase prey through cover, while falcons own the open sky.

exploreAction.instruction: Compare hawks and falcons, then explain the wing shape difference.

name: Hedgehog
teaser: The hedgehog is the spiky, snuffling gardener of the night, a small mammal covered in up to six thousand hollow spines. When threatened, it rolls into a tight ball, spines pointing in every direction, so that predators find only an impenetrable spiky sphere. Hedgehogs are insect-eaters that also snack on snails, worms, and even small snakes, and they are immune to many poisons. In Europe they are beloved garden visitors, though their numbers are falling as habitat disappears and road traffic rises.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how hedgehogs are covered in up to 5,000 hollow spines, roll into a ball to sleep and defend, and snuffle through gardens at night eating insects, with a skill for climbing and even swimming. Explore their hibernation, their decline from traffic and gardens without holes, and how to help them.

name: Hedgehog Hibernation
teaser: Hedgehogs hibernate through the cold months, and it is a marathon of survival. Before winter, they fatten up, then find a safe nest of leaves, and their body temperature drops to nearly match the cold air, their heart rate falling from two hundred beats a minute to a handful, and they may take just a few breaths a minute. They wake periodically, and a hedgehog can lose a third of its body weight by spring. A hedgehog that enters hibernation underweight, or wakes too often, may not survive the winter.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn when hedgehogs hibernate, then explain how they survive winter.

name: Hellbender
teaser: The hellbender is one of the largest salamanders in the world, a wrinkled, flat-bodied giant that can grow over seventy centimeters long, found in the clear, fast rivers of the eastern United States. Despite its scary name, it is harmless, spending its days under rocks and its nights hunting crayfish. Its loose, folded skin is full of blood vessels, letting it breathe through its skin in the cold, oxygen-rich water it needs. Pollution and damming have made it endangered, and it is now a symbol of clean rivers.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the hellbender, North America's largest salamander at up to 74 cm, lives under rocks in fast Appalachian rivers, breathing through its wrinkled skin. Explore how it got the nickname snot otter from its slimy mucus, how males guard nests, and why it's a sensitive indicator of clean water.

name: Herd Protection
teaser: When danger comes for an elephant family, everyone has a job. The matriarch assesses the threat; the older females move the calves into the center; and the adults face outward in a circle, ears spread wide to look bigger and trunks raised to smell and threaten. If the threat is real, the herd charges as one — a wall of several tons of muscle and ivory moving together, which usually sends predators running long before contact. Calves learn to run to the middle of the herd at the first alarm call, and aunts and grandmothers guard them as fiercely as their own mothers.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover how herds protect calves, then explain why elephants circle up.

name: Hermit Crab
teaser: The hermit crab is a soft-bodied crab that carries its home on its back: the empty shell of a snail. As it grows, it must find a bigger shell, and shell-hunting is the drama of its life, with crabs lining up by size to trade up when a new shell appears. Its abdomen is curled to fit the spiral shell, and its first pair of legs are adapted to grip the shell's opening. Some hermit crabs live on land, far from the sea, and the coconut crab is a giant hermit that outgrew shells entirely.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how hermit crabs have soft unprotected abdomens and must find empty snail shells to live in, swapping as they grow and lining up in queues to trade shells, sometimes fighting for a good one. Explore their shell-changing rituals, the sea anemones they carry for protection, and how plastic litter tricks them into deadly shell homes.

name: Hibernation
teaser: Hibernation is a deep sleep that saves animals from winter's scarcity. Before the cold arrives, animals like bears, hedgehogs, and ground squirrels fatten up, then drop their body temperature and slow their heart and breathing to a fraction of normal, living off stored fat for months. True hibernators, like woodchucks, drop their temperature nearly to freezing, while bears' temperature barely falls but their heart slows dramatically. It is not just sleep: it is a controlled shutdown, and waking from it burns precious energy.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how animals survive winter by hibernating, dropping their body temperature and heart rate, from bears that don't eat for months to ground squirrels that cool to near freezing and marmots that wake to shiver every few weeks. Explore the difference from torpor, how fat is stored, and the science of suspended life.

name: Hippo Blood Sweat
teaser: The hippo has a secret weapon that looks like blood but works like sunscreen. Glands in its thick skin ooze an oily red liquid — the famous 'blood sweat' — which was a mystery for centuries. Scientists finally cracked it: the red pigment is a natural sunscreen that absorbs ultraviolet light, and a second compound in the same fluid works as an antibiotic, killing bacteria and helping the hippo's wounds heal clean in muddy, bacteria-rich water. So the hippo's 'sweat' is really a self-applied protective coating, sealing its skin against sunburn and infection.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover what hippo sweat really is, then explain its two jobs.

name: Hippo Calves
teaser: A hippo calf's first act is a crash course in holding its breath. Calves are born underwater after about eight months of gestation, and a newborn — weighing around thirty to fifty kilograms — takes its first breath only after its mother nudges it to the surface. From then on, the calf nurses underwater, closing its nose and ears to suckle at the river bottom while its mother keeps watch. For the first weeks, the mother guards her calf jealously, sometimes keeping it apart from the pod, and calves stay close to their mothers for years.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how hippo calves are born, then explain how they nurse underwater.

name: Hippo Communication
teaser: A hippo's grunts and honks aren't random noise — they're a rich underwater phone network. Hippos are constantly talking: loud grunts and roars above water, and a whole extra conversation happening below the surface, where their calls travel through the water far better than through air. They call to announce their presence, to keep the pod together, to warn off intruders, and to check in on calves, and a hippo can recognize the voice of a specific neighbor or relative. The dominant bull uses a distinctive 'wheeze-honk' to announce his territory, and mothers answer their calves' squeaks.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover how hippos communicate, then explain why they make so much noise in water.

name: Hippo Dung Ecology
teaser: A hippo's toilet is a lifeline for an entire river. Hippos spend their days in the water and release vast amounts of dung there — each hippo produces hundreds of kilograms of waste, and a pod concentrates it in the pools where they rest. For years scientists dismissed it as pollution, but the dung is actually a fertilizer pipeline: it feeds algae and aquatic plants, which feed fish, and the whole river's food web runs on hippo output. When hippos are removed from a stretch of river, the fish populations collapse.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover how hippo dung feeds river life, then explain why too much can harm fish.

name: Hippo Pods
teaser: A group of hippos is called a pod, a bloat, or a herd, and it runs on a strict pecking order. In the water, dozens of hippos pack together in a lazy-looking crowd, but the surface calm hides a social ladder: one dominant bull owns the territory and the mating rights, while younger males are pushed to the edges, and the females and calves hold the safest center. Every day starts and ends with a ritual — the 'dung shower,' where hippos spin their tails like propellers to fling droppings far and wide, marking territory and announcing status.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover how hippo groups work, then explain why males fight.

name: Hippo Skin
teaser: A hippo's skin looks tough, but it is surprisingly delicate and needs constant care. It is nearly five centimeters thick, yet it has no fur and must stay wet to avoid cracking and overheating in the African sun, which is why hippos spend their days submerged. Their skin oozes a red oily liquid, the famous blood sweat, that is not blood but a natural sunscreen and antibiotic that protects the hippo from sunburn and infection. This remarkable secretion is being studied for human medicine.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how hippo skin is up to 5 cm thick, nearly hairless, and secretes a red oily fluid that acts as sunscreen and antibiotic, the famous red sweat that isn't sweat, protecting them under the African sun. Explore the skin's sensitivity, why hippos wallow to stay wet, and how the secretion's pigments inspired sunscreen research.

name: Hippopotamus
teaser: The hippopotamus is one of the most dangerous animals in Africa, a massive creature that can weigh three tonnes, and it is not as slow as it looks. It spends days submerged in rivers and lakes, coming out at night to graze, and it can run faster than a human on land. Its mouth opens wide enough to swallow a person, with tusks-like canines that grow over half a meter. Hippos live in groups in the water, and despite their bulk, they are surprisingly agile swimmers and can even walk along the riverbed.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how hippos, weighing up to 3 tonnes, spend days submerged with just eyes and nostrils out, their skin secreting a red sunscreen, and gallop surprisingly fast on land. Explore why they're among Africa's most dangerous animals, how they breathe underwater, and their vital role fertilizing rivers with dung.

name: Honey Badger
teaser: The honey badger is famous for a reason: it is one of the toughest animals on Earth, pound for pound. This stocky African and Asian mustelid fights lions, steals from leopards, and shrugs off snake venom, and it has been recorded attacking vehicles and digging through concrete. Its loose, thick skin lets it twist and bite back even when grabbed, and its claws are built for digging. It is also smart, using tools to escape enclosures. Its fearless attitude has made it an internet legend.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how honey badgers of Africa and Asia are legendary for fearlessness, attacking snakes, stinging bee hives, and even fighting off lions and hyenas, with thick loose skin that lets them twist and bite back. Explore their intelligence, their tool use, and their name from a mutual bird partnership.

name: Honey Pot Ant
teaser: The honey pot ant is a living pantry. In the deserts of Australia, Mexico, and the American Southwest, a special caste of workers called repletes are filled with nectar until their abdomens swell to the size of grapes, then they hang from the ceiling of the nest as living storage jars. When food is scarce, the colony taps the repletes and drinks the stored honey. Some Aboriginal people in Australia prize these ants as a sweet treat, digging them up to eat the honey directly from the living jar.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how honey pot ants gorge on nectar until their abdomens swell into translucent amber orbs, hanging from nest ceilings as living food storage, regurgitating sweetness for the colony in lean times. Explore where Aboriginal people and desert peoples harvest these ants as sweet treats, and their underground nests.

name: Honeybee
teaser: The honeybee is the world's most important pollinator, a social insect that lives in colonies of tens of thousands, and it is a masterpiece of teamwork. Each bee has a job: the queen lays eggs, workers forage, nurse, build, and guard, and drones mate. Bees communicate with dances, share food mouth to mouth, and make honey by concentrating nectar, and a single colony can produce dozens of kilograms a year. About a third of the food we eat depends on bee pollination, making the honeybee essential to our dinner tables.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how honeybees pollinate a third of the food we eat, dance to tell hive mates where flowers are, and live in colonies of tens of thousands ruled by a queen. Explore the waggle dance's coded directions, how bees make honey from nectar, and colony collapse threats.

name: Honeybee Decline
teaser: Honeybees are dying at alarming rates, and the causes are many and overlapping. Pesticides poison them, the parasitic varroa mite spreads disease, and habitat loss removes the flowers they need, all compounded by climate change. Beekeepers report losing a third or more of their colonies every winter, a crisis called colony collapse. The stakes are huge, since bees pollinate much of our food, but there is hope: reducing pesticide use, planting wildflowers, and supporting healthy hives can turn the tide.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how honeybee colonies have been dying at alarming rates from Varroa mites, pesticides, habitat loss, and colony collapse disorder, threatening pollination of a third of our food. Explore the role of neonicotinoids, the beekeeper losses, the native bee alternatives, and what a world without bees would cost.

name: Honeybee Waggle Dance
teaser: The honeybee waggle dance is one of the most famous forms of animal communication, a coded message inside the hive. A forager that finds a rich patch of flowers returns and dances on the comb, waggling her body in a figure-eight pattern. The angle of the dance tells other bees the direction of the food relative to the sun, and the duration of the waggle tells them the distance, with each second roughly corresponding to a kilometer. Other bees read the dance and fly straight to the flowers.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how honeybees perform a waggle dance to tell hive mates the direction and distance of flowers, the angle of the waggle relative to vertical encoding the sun's bearing, the duration encoding distance, all information decoded by following bees. Explore the studies that decoded the language, the accuracy of the distance estimates, and what the dance says about insect minds.

name: Hornbill
teaser: The hornbill is a big, bright-beaked bird of Africa and Asia, and its most famous habit is a form of family security. The female seals herself inside a tree cavity with mud and droppings, leaving only a small slit through which the male feeds her and the chicks. She stays sealed for months, molting and raising the young in safety, while the male works hard to bring food. Hornbills have huge bills topped with a hollow casque, and they play a vital role in forests by spreading the seeds of the fruits they eat.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how female hornbills seal themselves inside tree cavities with mud, leaving only a slit through which males pass food, to protect chicks from predators. Explore the casque on top of the beak, its role in calls and courtship, and how some hornbills use the same nest hole for decades.

name: Horned Lizard
teaser: The horned lizard is the spiky, flat-bodied reptile of the American deserts, and it has the most bizarre defense in the reptile world: it squirts blood from its eyes. When threatened by a coyote or dog, it increases blood pressure in its head until jets of blood shoot from special vessels near its eyes, startling the predator and tasting foul. It also camouflages brilliantly with the desert, and it eats almost nothing but ants. Despite its dragon-like look, it is harmless to people.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how horned lizards defend against canids by squirting blood from their eye ducts up to 1.5 meters, the blood laced with chemicals that repel dogs and coyotes. Explore their flattened bodies, their armor of scales and horns, and their favorite food, harvester ants.

name: Horseshoe Crab
teaser: The horseshoe crab is older than the dinosaurs, a living fossil that has crawled the ocean shallows for over four hundred and fifty million years. It is not a crab but a relative of spiders, and its blood is a strange, valuable blue, colored by copper, and it contains a chemical that detects bacteria so reliably that the pharmaceutical industry uses it to test medicines. Every year, hundreds of thousands of horseshoe crabs come ashore to spawn on Atlantic beaches, an ancient ritual that still draws millions of migrating shorebirds.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how horseshoe crabs have survived over 450 million years with blue copper-based blood that clots on contact with bacteria, the basis of the Limulus amebocyte lysate test used to check every injectable medicine for contamination. Explore their role as shorebird food, the bleeding and return program, and the synthetic alternatives in development.

name: How Birds Navigate
teaser: How do migrating birds find their way across continents? They use every tool available. By day, many navigate by the position of the sun; by night, by the stars, learning star patterns as chicks. Their brains also sense the Earth's magnetic field, acting like a built-in compass, and they can detect polarized light, even the faint smell of home. Young birds on their first migration often fly alone to destinations they have never seen, guided by instinct and these invisible maps.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn the navigation tools birds use, then explain the magnetic sense.

name: How Dolphins Sleep
teaser: Dolphins sleep with one eye open, literally. Because they must surface to breathe, they cannot go fully unconscious, so they sleep with only half their brain at a time, letting one hemisphere rest while the other keeps them swimming and breathing. They often float at the surface, one eye closed, and may circle slowly. This unihemispheric sleep lets dolphins rest for hours each day while staying alert to danger. Even their calves sleep this way from birth.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover how dolphins sleep with one eye open, then explain why they cannot fully stop swimming.

name: How Giraffes Walk
teaser: A giraffe walks like nothing else on Earth because it moves both legs on the same side of its body at once — a gait called pacing. While a horse or a human crosses its legs alternately, the giraffe's front left and back left swing forward together, then the right pair, giving it that distinctive rolling, rocking motion. The gait looks clumsy but it's perfectly adapted: with such long legs, an alternating walk would make the giraffe trip over its own feet, while pacing keeps the body steady and lets the animal cover ground efficiently.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover the giraffe's unique gait, then explain why it cannot trot.

name: How Snakes Move
teaser: Snakes move in four completely different ways, and each is a marvel of engineering. Serpentine locomotion is the classic S-shaped slither, pushing against rocks and grass. Sidewinding lets desert snakes cross loose sand, throwing loops of their body sideways. Concertina movement bunches the body and extends forward, perfect for tunnels and branches. And rectilinear motion, used by heavy snakes like boas, moves in a straight line by rippling the belly muscles, each scale gripping like a tiny foot.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn the four snake movement styles, then explain sidewinding in sand.

name: How Snakes Swallow Big Prey
teaser: A snake can swallow prey far bigger than its head because its jaws are not fused at the front. Its lower jaw splits in two, and each half moves independently, walking over the prey in a ratchet-like motion while skin and muscle stretch. The snake's ribs spread wide, and its trachea extends out so it can breathe while its throat is full. Digestion takes days or weeks, and a python can eat a deer, an alligator, or even a leopard, then not need to eat again for months.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how snake jaws separate, then explain how they breathe while eating.

name: How Songbirds Learn Songs
teaser: Songbirds learn their songs the way human children learn language: by listening, imitating, and practicing. A young bird hears its father's song in its first weeks and memorizes it, then spends months practicing, making mistakes and gradually refining, until its song matches the local dialect. Some species even have regional accents, with birds in different valleys singing different variations. The song learning window closes early in life, and a bird raised in silence never learns to sing properly.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover how young birds learn songs, then explain the critical period.

name: How Zebras Sleep
teaser: Zebras are champions of the power nap, sleeping a total of only about two to three hours a day — and almost always standing up. A standing zebra can lock its legs so it doesn't fall over, catching light dozes with its ears still swiveling for danger, and it rarely lies down to sleep, because a lying zebra is a vulnerable zebra. When zebras do lie flat, it's usually in shifts — one or two animals resting while the rest of the harem stands guard. Foals sleep more than adults, but even they learn the standing-sleep trick early.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover how zebras sleep standing, then explain why they sleep so little.

name: Howler Monkey Calls
teaser: The howler monkey is the loudest land animal in the Americas, and its call is a genuine weapon: a deep, booming howl that can travel over three kilometers through the forest. The sound comes from an oversized hyoid bone in the throat that acts like a built-in megaphone, resonating chamber, and bass amplifier — a howler monkey's howl is so deep it's almost a roar, more like a big cat or a foghorn than anything you'd expect from a small monkey.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover how howler monkeys produce their roar, then explain the enlarged hyoid bone.

name: Hummingbird
teaser: The hummingbird is the smallest bird in the world and one of the most extreme. The bee hummingbird of Cuba weighs less than a coin, and its heart beats over a thousand times a minute, its wings beating up to eighty times a second, which is why they hum. Hummingbirds can fly backward, sideways, and even upside down, and they must eat constantly, visiting hundreds of flowers a day, drinking nectar with a long, specialized tongue. At night they slow their bodies into torpor, a mini-hibernation, to survive.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how hummingbirds beat their wings up to 80 times a second, hover in place, and even fly backwards, powered by nectar they lap up at up to 15 licks a second. Explore their sky-high metabolism, torpor at night to save energy, and how their iridescent feathers flash color from tiny air pockets, not pigment.

name: Hummingbird Flight
teaser: A hummingbird's hovering flight is one of the great feats of the animal world. Unlike other birds, it beats its wings in a figure-eight pattern, generating lift on both the upstroke and the downstroke, which lets it hang motionless in midair, even in the wind. It can fly backward, sideways, and straight up, and it moves with such precision that it can hold its beak perfectly still while drinking from a swaying flower. Its wing muscles make up a third of its body weight, and its heart races to power the constant motion.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover how hummingbirds hover, then explain their wing speed.

name: Hummingbird Migration
teaser: The ruby-throated hummingbird makes one of the most astonishing journeys in the bird world: a nonstop flight across the Gulf of Mexico, over eight hundred kilometers of open water, with no place to land. Weighing only a few grams, it must double its body weight in fat before leaving, then fly for up to twenty hours straight, its tiny heart pounding at over a thousand beats a minute. It arrives exhausted, then spends the summer raising two or three broods before doing it all over again.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover how far hummingbirds migrate, then explain how they fuel the trip.

name: Hummingbird Nests
teaser: A hummingbird nest is one of the smallest and most beautiful structures in the bird world. Built by the female alone, it is about the size of a walnut shell, woven from plant down and spider silk, which stretches as the chicks grow, and covered with lichen and moss for camouflage. The two eggs are the size of peas, and the chicks hatch blind and naked, fed on a diet of regurgitated nectar and insects. The nest expands to hold the growing family, then is abandoned after a single use.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how hummingbird nests are built, then explain the stretchy material.

name: Hummingbird Territory
teaser: Hummingbirds are tiny but fiercely territorial. A male stakes out a patch of flowers and defends it against all comers, including birds ten times his size, diving at intruders with his needle-sharp bill and driving them away with chattering calls. Some species even defend entire feeding territories from the same perch, chasing off butterflies and bees. The females, meanwhile, slip in to feed between the males' patrols. For a bird that weighs less than a coin, attitude is everything.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn why hummingbirds chase rivals, then explain their aggression.

name: Humpback Bubble Nets
teaser: Humpback whales hunt with teamwork and a net made of bubbles. A group of whales circles a school of fish, blowing a ring of bubbles from their blowholes that rises to form a wall, trapping the fish in a tightening cylinder. Then the whales surge upward through the middle with mouths open, lunging together to scoop up tons of fish in a synchronized strike. Some humpbacks even slap the water with their tails to herd fish first. It is one of the most sophisticated hunting strategies in the ocean.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how humpbacks corral fish with bubbles, then explain who leads the group.

name: Humpback Bubble Netting
teaser: Bubble netting is the humpback's signature hunting trick, a cooperative feat passed down through the generations. One whale dives below a school of fish and blows a spiral of bubbles, while others call and circle to herd the fish into a tight ball. As the bubble net rises, the whales surge up through the center with mouths wide open, and the fish have nowhere to go. Young whales learn the technique by watching their elders, and each population has its own variations, a true marine culture.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how humpback whales hunt herring and krill by swimming in an upward spiral while releasing a curtain of bubbles that corrals prey into a tightening cylinder, then lunging through the middle with mouths open, sometimes working in teams. Explore the coordination, the timing, and the aerial acrobatics of the lunge.

name: Humpback Songs
teaser: Humpback whale songs are among the most complex sounds in the animal kingdom, long, structured sequences of moans, cries, and chirps that can last twenty minutes and repeat for hours. Only males sing, mostly during the breeding season, and all the males in one ocean population sing the same evolving song, which changes gradually over the years like a living tradition. The song may attract females or organize males, and its beauty has inspired musicians and scientists alike for decades.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover how humpback songs change over years, then explain why only males sing.

name: Humpback Whale Song
teaser: The humpback whale song is a mystery and a masterpiece, a vocal display that can travel hundreds of kilometers through the ocean. Male humpbacks sing the same song as their neighbors, but the song slowly changes each season, so that after a few years the whole population is singing something new. Scientists record these songs to track populations, and the whales themselves seem to learn from each other across entire oceans. Every humpback song is a snapshot of an evolving, cultural tradition.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how humpback whales sing complex songs that evolve over years, with all males in a population singing the same version, and populations far apart even sharing new verses. Explore why they sing, the song's structure from phrases to themes, and how hydrophones reveal whales carrying songs across oceans.

name: Huntsman Spider
teaser: The huntsman spider is a fast-moving hunter that does not build a web, chasing down its prey instead. Found in warm regions worldwide, it can be huge, with legs spanning up to thirty centimeters in some species, and it can run at blistering speed, moving sideways like a crab. It hunts insects at night and often turns up in houses and cars, giving people a fright, but it is harmless to humans. In its home range, it is a useful pest controller, and it is even kept as a pet in some places.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how huntsman spiders, with leg spans up to 30 cm, are fast, flat, and commonly found inside warm homes and cars in Australia and Asia, but their venom is mild and they help control cockroaches and other pests. Explore their sideways running, their egg guarding, and why they frighten people more than they harm them.

name: Hyena Clans
teaser: Spotted hyenas live in clans that can number eighty individuals, run by the females, and they have one of the most complex societies in the animal kingdom. Females are larger and dominant, and their social rank is inherited, passed from mother to daughter. Clan members greet each other with elaborate rituals, and they cooperate to defend territory and raise cubs communally. The cubs are born with their eyes open and teeth already sharp, and they fight fiercely from birth, since rank is won in the nursery.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how hyena clans are structured, then explain why females dominate.

name: Hyena Hunting Power
teaser: Spotted hyenas are among the most successful hunters in Africa, and their jaws are among the most powerful in the mammal world. A clan can run down a wildebeest or zebra, chase it for kilometers, and bring it down, and their bone-crushing bite lets them eat every part, including bones and hooves, leaving almost nothing behind. People long thought hyenas were only scavengers, but studies show they hunt most of their food themselves, and lions and hyenas steal from each other in a constant rivalry.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how hyenas hunt and scavenge, then explain their powerful jaws.

name: Immortal Jellyfish
teaser: The immortal jellyfish is the only known animal that can reverse its own aging. When it is old, sick, or stressed, this tiny jellyfish shrinks back into a ball of cells and transforms into its juvenile polyp stage, then grows up again, a process it can repeat indefinitely, making it biologically immortal. It does this through transdifferentiation, turning one cell type into another. Scientists study it to understand aging, though even immortals can be eaten by predators. It drifts in oceans worldwide, a tiny miracle.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how Turritopsis dohrnii, the immortal jellyfish, can revert from its adult stage back to a polyp when stressed, restarting its life cycle and potentially living forever, the only animal known to do this. Explore how the process works, whether it truly avoids death, and what it teaches about aging and regeneration.

name: Impala
teaser: The impala is one of the most graceful and athletic antelopes of the African savanna, and its leaps are legendary. It can jump over three meters high and ten meters long, a single bound that clears bushes and dazzles predators, and when startled, whole herds scatter in a synchronized fountain of leaping animals. Impalas are also sprinters, reaching eighty kilometers an hour. They live in mixed herds, grazing by day and resting in the shade, always alert to the danger that surrounds them on the open plains.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how impalas leap up to 3 meters high and 10 meters long, clearing bushes and scattering in all directions to confuse predators, and they use scent glands to mark territory and alarm snorts to warn the herd. Explore their herding structure with bachelor groups and territorial males, and their place at the heart of the savanna food web.

name: Ivory-billed Woodpecker
teaser: The ivory-billed woodpecker was the largest woodpecker north of Mexico, a striking black-and-white bird with a red crest, sometimes called the Lord God bird because of the way people exclaimed when they saw it. Logging destroyed its old-growth swamp forests, and it was declared extinct in the twentieth century, though unconfirmed sightings in the American South keep the hope, and the search, alive. Its disappearance helped launch the modern conservation movement, and its ghost still haunts the cypress swamps.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the ivory-billed woodpecker, North America's largest, called the Lord God bird for the awe of its sighting, lost its swamp forests to logging and was declared extinct, though occasional unconfirmed sightings spark hope. Explore its dependence on old-growth dead trees, and the debates over whether it survives.

name: Jabiru Stork
teaser: The jabiru is the giant stork of the Americas, standing over a meter and a half tall with a wingspan of two and a half meters and a distinctive black head and neck with a red throat pouch. It stalks the wetlands of Central and South America, spearing fish, frogs, and snakes with its enormous bill. It builds huge platform nests on tall trees, returning to them year after year, and its chicks are among the largest of any bird, growing fast on a diet of whole fish fed by both parents.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the jabiru stork of South American wetlands stands up to 1.5 meters tall with a black neck and massive bill, wading for fish and small animals. Explore its huge stick nests reused for years, its silent flight, and how it's a flagship of the Pantanal.

name: Jacana
teaser: The jacana is the Jesus bird of the tropics, famous for walking on water. Its enormous feet and long toes spread its weight so evenly that it can step across floating lily pads without sinking, striding over ponds where other birds must swim. It feeds on insects and seeds plucked from the water plants, and it is one of the few birds where the males do most of the parenting, incubating the eggs and carrying the chicks under their wings. Its bright colors flash as it walks across the green pads.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how jacanas walk across floating lily pads on incredibly long toes that spread their weight, earning nicknames like lily trotter, and in some species the males build the nests and incubate the eggs while females defend territory. Explore the reversed sex roles, the toes' length relative to body size, and their tropical wetland homes.

name: Jaguar
teaser: The jaguar is the largest cat in the Americas, a powerful ambush hunter of the rainforests, and its bite is the strongest of any cat, capable of piercing a turtle's shell or cracking a skull. It hunts on the ground and in the water, and it is a superb swimmer, catching fish, caimans, and capybaras. Its rosettes, spots within spots, set it apart from leopards, and it roams territories in the Amazon and Pantanal. Its name comes from a word meaning he who kills with one leap, and it is a symbol of the wild.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how jaguars of the Americas have the strongest bite of any big cat, piercing skulls with their canines, and unlike other big cats they love water, swimming and hunting caiman and fish. Explore their rosette spots, their solitary territories, and their role as rainforest guardians.

name: Jellyfish
teaser: The jellyfish is one of the simplest animals in the ocean, a drifting bell of jelly with stinging tentacles, and it has been around for over five hundred million years, older than the dinosaurs. It has no brain, no heart, and no bones, yet it moves by pulsing its bell and catches prey with stinging cells that fire like tiny harpoons. Some glow in the dark, some are larger than a person, and their population is booming in seas where their predators have vanished. They are ancient, strange, and everywhere.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how jellyfish, up to 95 percent water, drift through oceans using pulsing bells, their stinging tentacles firing microscopic harpoons, and how the immortal jellyfish can revert to its baby stage forever. Explore their blooms that clog beaches, and how they thrive where fish decline.

name: Jerboa
teaser: The jerboa is the kangaroo of the desert, a tiny rodent of North Africa and Asia that hops on two legs like a miniature kangaroo. Its enormous back feet and long tail let it leap several meters, outrunning predators across the open sand, and it can cover great distances with energy-saving bounces. It digs burrows to escape the desert heat, and its huge ears and eyes help it survive nights on the dunes. Some species never drink water, getting everything from seeds and plants.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how jerboas of Asian and African deserts hop on elongated hind legs like tiny kangaroos, covering 3 meters a leap, and can survive without drinking, getting water from seeds. Explore their huge ears that radiate heat, their burrow life avoiding the heat of day, and their extraordinary leaps to escape predators.

name: Jumping Spider
teaser: The jumping spider is a tiny predator with remarkable eyesight and charisma. It has four pairs of eyes, including two huge forward-facing ones that give it sharp, binocular vision, and it can see in color, even ultraviolet. It stalks its prey like a cat, then pounces, and it can leap many times its own body length, using a safety line of silk. Some species dance for mates with elaborate moves and colors, and they are intelligent enough that scientists study their problem-solving abilities.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how jumping spiders have eight eyes including large forward-facing ones with binocular depth perception, stalking prey like tiny cats and leaping with a safety dragline. Explore their courtship dances, their ability to see color and even UV, and their unexpectedly sharp vision for creatures so small.

name: June Bug
teaser: The June bug, also called the May beetle, is a chunky, brown beetle that blunders into porch lights on summer nights with a heavy thud. It spends most of its life underground as a white grub, feeding on plant roots, sometimes damaging lawns and crops. After a year or more, it emerges as an adult to mate, flying noisily and clumsily. Birds, bats, and raccoons feast on them during their brief adult season, and their larvae are an important food source for moles and other diggers.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how June bugs, heavy scarab beetles, clumsily bump into windows and lights on summer evenings, their grubs feeding on grass roots underground for years before emerging as adults that eat leaves. Explore why they fly into lights, their short adult lives, and how they're food for owls, skunks, and raccoons.

name: Kangaroo
teaser: The kangaroo is Australia's great hopper, the largest marsupial on Earth, and it is built to bounce. Its powerful hind legs and elastic tendons act like a spring, letting it cover huge distances with barely any extra energy, reaching speeds over sixty kilometers an hour. It cannot walk backward, and it balances with its thick tail. Kangaroos live in mobs, and females carry their joeys in a pouch for months. They graze at dawn and dusk, and they have become icons of the Australian bush.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how red kangaroos hop at up to 60 km/h using elastic tendons that store energy, cover 8 meters in a bound, and can't walk backwards. Explore the pouch where tiny jelly-bean sized joeys develop, their boxing fights, and how they survive drought by pausing embryo development.

name: Kangaroo Boxing
teaser: Kangaroo boxing is a real thing, and it is how males settle their differences. Two males stand upright, balance on their tails, and grapple with their forearms, kicking with their powerful hind legs, blows strong enough to break bones. These fights decide rank and access to females, and they end when one male submits and hops away. Despite the violence, they are ritualized, rarely fatal, and the defeated male simply lives to fight another day. The boxer's stance is a classic image of the Australian outback.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how kangaroos fight, then explain the tail support.

name: Kangaroo Pouches
teaser: A kangaroo's pouch is a built-in nursery with a remarkable system. A newborn joey is the size of a jellybean, blind and hairless, and it claws its way from the birth canal to the pouch, where it latches onto a teat for months. The mother can produce two different kinds of milk at once, one for the newborn and one for her older joey, and she can pause a pregnancy until the pouch is free. The joey stays in the pouch for up to a year, then returns to it head-first for milk as it grows.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how kangaroo pouches work, then explain why joeys climb in and out.

name: Katydid
teaser: The katydid is a master of disguise, an insect so well camouflaged as a green leaf that it is almost invisible among the foliage. It lives in trees and bushes around the world, and its males sing at night with a rhythmic chirp, their ears located on their front legs. Some katydids imitate leaves so perfectly, with veins and even bite marks on their wings, that predators walk right past them. Others mimic twigs, bark, or even other insects, and a few are fierce predators themselves.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how katydids, named for their katy-did calls, are leaf-shaped insects that sing from treetops at night, with ears on their front legs, and some species mimic leaves so perfectly they even have leaf-like veins and bite marks. Explore their long antennae, their green camouflage, and their role as bird food.

name: Kestrel
teaser: The kestrel is the hovering hunter of the open country, a small falcon that can hang motionless in midair, facing into the wind, while scanning the ground below for mice and insects. It is one of the few birds that can hover, and it uses its keen vision, which includes ultraviolet sensitivity, to spot the urine trails of voles in the grass. It dives to strike its prey, then returns to a perch to eat. The American kestrel is the smallest falcon in North America, and a favorite of birdwatchers.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the kestrel hovers almost motionless by facing into the wind, adjusting its head with tiny movements to keep perfectly still while scanning for voles, and can even see ultraviolet light to spot mouse urine trails. Explore why it's one of the most adaptable birds of prey.

name: Killer Whale Pods
teaser: Killer whales, or orcas, live in family pods that stay together for life, and each pod has its own culture. Pods in the Pacific Northwest hunt salmon together, while others specialize in hunting seals, and some pods even hunt other whales. The pod is led by the oldest female, who remembers migration routes and hunting grounds. Different pods speak different dialects, with calls passed down through generations, and researchers can tell which pod a whale.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how orca pods pass down hunting knowledge, then explain the resident and transient divide.

name: King Cobra
teaser: The king cobra is the longest venomous snake in the world, reaching over five meters, and it is also one of the most intelligent snakes, able to learn and remember. When threatened, it rears up a third of its body length, spreads its hood, and hisses with a sound like a growling dog. Unlike most snakes, the king cobra builds a nest of leaves for its eggs and guards them until they hatch. Its venom is potent enough to kill an elephant, yet it prefers to eat other snakes, including other cobras.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the king cobra, the world's longest venomous snake, is the only snake that builds a nest, the female coiling leaves into a mound and guarding it until eggs hatch. Explore how it feeds almost entirely on other snakes, its hood and hiss, and why its venom is a neurotoxin that can kill an elephant.

name: King Penguin
teaser: The king penguin is the second-largest penguin, a stately bird of the sub-Antarctic with a bright orange-gold patch on its neck, and it is a champion of endurance. It raises its chick through the Antarctic winter, and its parenting schedule is so long that a pair can raise only two chicks every three years. The chick sits on the parents' feet, kept warm by a brood pouch, while the adults take turns walking up to a hundred kilometers to the sea to fish. Kings dive deep and can stay under for ten minutes hunting squid and fish.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how king penguins take 14 to 16 months to raise a single chick, breeding on sub-Antarctic islands with a crowded crèche system where parents find their own chick by call. Explore their teardrop shape for swimming, diving past 300 meters, and their bright orange ear patches.

name: Kingfisher
teaser: The kingfisher is a flash of electric blue that dives like an arrow, one of the most brilliant birds on Earth. It perches above the water, watches for fish, then plunges headfirst, entering the water with barely a splash thanks to its streamlined bill, and grabs its prey with its dagger-like beak. It returns to a perch, beats the fish against a branch, and swallows it headfirst. Its eyes are specially adapted to see clearly underwater, and its dive is timed to the split second.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how kingfishers spot fish from a branch, hover, then plunge headfirst with eyes shielded by a nictitating membrane, rarely missing. Explore how the shape of their beak inspired bullet-train nose design in Japan, and why their feathers can appear blue without any blue pigment.

name: Kingfisher Burrows
teaser: Kingfishers are tunnel diggers that nest in the earth. The pair chooses a sandy riverbank and digs a tunnel up to a meter long, using their bills as picks, with a chamber at the end where the eggs are laid. The tunnel slopes upward so floodwater cannot reach the nest, and the fish bones and droppings pile up inside, giving the tunnel a strong smell. Both parents take turns incubating and feeding the chicks, which grow fast on a steady diet of fish brought back from the river.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover how kingfishers dig nest tunnels, then explain why they choose riverbanks.

name: Kingfisher Family
teaser: The kookaburra is a giant kingfisher, which surprises many people, since it rarely eats fish. This Australian bird is the largest of the kingfisher family, and its famous laughing call is one of the most recognizable sounds of the bush. Instead of diving for fish, it hunts on land, sitting on a branch and pouncing on snakes, lizards, and insects, killing them by bashing them against a tree. Its laughing chorus, often at dawn and dusk, is a family group announcing its territory.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the kingfisher family spans 120 species worldwide, from tiny African dwarf kingfishers that catch insects to the giant kookaburra that hunts snakes, proving the name undersells their varied diet. Explore how some dive for fish while others hunt on land, and how they dig nest tunnels.

name: Kingfisher Variety
teaser: There are about ninety species of kingfishers, and they are far more varied than the fish-eating bird most people picture. Many live in forests, far from water, and hunt insects and lizards on the ground, like the kookaburra. Some are tiny, like the African dwarf kingfisher, smaller than a sparrow, while the giant kingfisher is nearly half a meter long. What unites them is the big head, long bill, and brilliant colors, from electric blues to shimmering green and purple.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover how kingfishers differ, then explain why some do not eat fish.

name: Kinkajou
teaser: The kinkajou is a honey-loving acrobat of the Central and South American rainforests, a golden mammal related to raccoons. It has a prehensile tail it uses like a fifth hand, and it can rotate its ankles backward to climb down trees headfirst. It is mostly nocturnal, spending nights reaching into flowers with its long tongue to drink nectar, which makes it an important pollinator, and it also eats fruit and honey. It lives in the high canopy, where it moves with surprising speed and agility.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how kinkajous, called honey bears, of Central and South American rainforests use 40 cm tongues to lick nectar and honey, living in trees with prehensile tails, and are related to raccoons, not bears. Explore their night activity, their social fruit-feeding groups, and their vocal repertoire from barks to screams.

name: Kiwi
teaser: The kiwi is New Zealand's national bird and one of the strangest birds on Earth. It is flightless, about the size of a chicken, with feathers more like hair, no tail, and nostrils at the very tip of its long bill, the only bird with nostrils on its beak. It hunts at night by smell, probing the forest floor for worms, and its eggs are enormous, up to a fifth of the female's body weight, the largest egg-to-body ratio of any bird. Its chicks are born feathered and independent, and it survives nowhere else on Earth.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the kiwi, New Zealand's national bird, has tiny useless wings, whiskers like a cat, and lays an egg a quarter of its own body weight, the largest egg relative to body size of any bird. Explore how it hunts by smell at night, and why it behaves more like a small mammal than a bird.

name: Knuckle Walking
teaser: Gorillas don't walk on their palms like most four-legged animals — they walk on their knuckles, a gait so distinctive it has its own name: knuckle-walking. Their front limbs are much longer than their back ones, so they fold their fingers under and support their weight on the middle knuckles, letting the long arms swing forward as they move. It's an efficient way for a giant to travel: a 200-kilogram silverback can knuckle-walk for miles through the forest, and young gorillas practice it almost as soon as they can walk.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover how gorillas walk on their knuckles, then explain why they do not stand often.

name: Koala
teaser: The koala is the sleepy icon of Australia, a marsupial that spends up to twenty hours a day resting. It lives almost entirely on eucalyptus leaves, which are tough, low in nutrition, and toxic to most animals, but the koala's long gut and special bacteria break them down. It rarely needs to drink, getting water from its food, though it drinks when necessary, and its name is thought to mean no water in an Aboriginal language. Koalas are not bears, and their closest living relative is the wombat.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how koalas survive almost entirely on eucalyptus leaves that are toxic to most animals, thanks to a long gut and special microbes, and sleep up to 20 hours a day because the leaves are poor fuel. Explore the difference between koalas and bears, the joey's pouch life, and chlamydia's threat.

name: Koala Pouch Life
teaser: A koala joey is born the size of a jellybean, blind, and hairless, and it crawls into the pouch on its own, where it latches onto a teat for six months. It spends those months growing, feeding on milk, and later on a special substance called pap, a pre-digested eucalyptus mix that transfers the mother's gut bacteria, teaching the joey's own gut how to digest the toxic leaves. When it finally leaves the pouch, the joey rides on its mother's back, returning for comfort and milk.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover how koala joeys develop, then explain the pouch direction.

name: Komodo Dragon
teaser: The Komodo dragon is the largest living lizard, a powerful predator that can grow over three meters long and weigh ninety kilograms. It lives on a few Indonesian islands, where it hunts deer, pigs, and even water buffalo, using serrated teeth that slice flesh like knives. Its bite carries venom that prevents blood clotting and drops prey's blood pressure, so even animals that escape soon collapse. It swallows huge meals whole or in chunks, and it can eat up to eighty percent of its body weight in one sitting.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the Komodo dragon, the largest living lizard at up to 3 meters, hunts with serrated teeth and venom glands that lower blood pressure and prevent clotting, weakening prey over days. Explore how it senses carrion from kilometers away, and how it attacks everything from deer to water buffalo.

name: Komodo Dragon Senses
teaser: The Komodo dragon hunts with senses that turn it into a living sniffer dog. Its forked tongue flicks out to sample the air, carrying scent particles to a special organ in its mouth that detects prey from kilometers away, including the smell of blood and carrion. It can also sense vibrations in the ground through its feet, feeling the footsteps of approaching animals. Its eyesight is sharp, and it can even see in color at night. Once it locks onto a trail, it rarely lets go.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how Komodo dragons detect carrion from 10 km away using a forked tongue and vomeronasal organ, flicking scents out of the air, and their vision and hearing are sharp enough to track prey, with venom glands studied only in 2009. Explore the taste buds in their throats, their tongue-flicking behavior, and how they locate wounded prey over days.

name: Kookaburra
teaser: The kookaburra is famous for its laughing call, a loud, rolling chorus that sounds like human laughter and echoes through the Australian bush at dawn and dusk, earning it the nickname the bushman's clock. It is the largest of the kingfishers, and unlike most of its family, it hunts on land, perching quietly and pouncing on snakes, lizards, and insects, killing them by beating them against a branch. Its laugh is used by filmmakers the world over as a soundtrack of the jungle.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the kookaburra's territorial call sounds like a raucous human laugh, sung in chorus at dawn and dusk across Australia. Explore how it hunts snakes, lizards, and insects with a heavy beak, nests in hollows, and why its laugh is used in movies to set jungle scenes, even in Africa.

name: Krill
teaser: Krill are tiny shrimp-like crustaceans that form the foundation of the ocean's food web, and there are more of them by weight than any other animal group. They swarm in schools so dense they turn the sea pink, and they are the main food of blue whales, which can eat millions in a single day, as well as seals, penguins, fish, and seabirds. Krill feed on algae, and they migrate from the depths to the surface daily in a mass movement that scientists track from space. Without krill, the whole ocean would starve.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how Antarctic krill, shrimplike crustaceans just 6 cm long, swarm in billions and form the foundation of the Antarctic food web, eaten by whales, seals, penguins, and fish. Explore their daily vertical migrations, their glowing swarms, the fishing industry harvesting them, and how climate change affects their sea-ice nursery.

name: Lacewing
teaser: The lacewing is a delicate, green insect with wings like frosted glass, and it is a garden's best friend. Its larvae, called aphid lions, are fierce predators that hunt aphids, mites, and other pests, sometimes covering themselves with the husks of their victims for camouflage. A single lacewing larva can eat hundreds of aphids as it grows, and gardeners release them to control pests naturally. The adults sip nectar, and their eggs are laid on stalks, protecting them from predators.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how adult lacewings are delicate green insects with lacy wings, while their larvae, called aphid lions, are voracious predators that impale aphids with hollow jaws, and some species cover themselves in debris and prey corpses for camouflage. Explore their garden benefits, their chemical defenses, and the green lacewing's ultrasonic hearing.

name: Ladybug
teaser: The ladybug, or ladybird, is one of the most beloved insects, and it is a gardener's ally. Its bright red-and-black spots warn predators that it tastes terrible, and when threatened it oozes a bitter, yellow fluid from its legs. Its larvae, which look like tiny alligators, are voracious predators of aphids, and a single ladybug can eat thousands of pests in its lifetime. Ladybugs hibernate in large groups in winter, clustering in cracks and under bark, and they wake with the spring to hunt.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how ladybugs devour aphids, a single beetle eating thousands in its life, which is why gardeners love them, and why they flash red with spots, a warning of bitter defensive blood. Explore how they play dead, release yellow fluid from their knees, and huddle in hibernation masses.

name: Leaf Insect
teaser: The leaf insect is nature's ultimate camouflage, an insect that looks so much like a leaf that it is practically invisible among real leaves. Its body is flat and green, with wings marked like leaf veins, and even its legs look like stems, with leaf-shaped lobes. When it sways gently, it mimics a leaf in the breeze. It stays perfectly still by day, feeding at night, and it is so well disguised that predators walk right past it. Even its eggs look like seeds.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how leaf insects mimic leaves with flattened bodies, leaf-shaped wings with veins, and even bite marks and decay spots, some species swaying like a leaf in the breeze, the ultimate camouflage in Southeast Asian forests. Explore how they avoid being eaten by birds, their defensive stillness, and their display behavior when disturbed.

name: Leaf-tailed Gecko
teaser: The leaf-tailed gecko of Madagascar is one of the masters of camouflage, a lizard so well disguised as a dead leaf that it disappears among the branches. Its tail looks like a chewed leaf, its body is flattened and veined like foliage, and it can even change color to match its surroundings. By day it presses itself against a branch and waits, its mottled pattern breaking up its outline completely. At night it hunts insects, and its eyes, which lack eyelids, are cleaned with its tongue.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how Madagascar's leaf-tailed geckos flatten their bodies against tree trunks, their tails shaped like decaying leaves, their camouflage so perfect they're nearly impossible to spot by day. Explore their huge lidless eyes for night hunting, their color that matches specific bark, and their threatened habitat.

name: Leafcutter Ant
teaser: The leafcutter ant is a farmer that grows its own food, and it does not eat the leaves it cuts. Workers carry leaf fragments back to the nest and chew them into a pulp, feeding them to a fungus garden that the colony cultivates underground. The fungus is the ants' only food, and the two species have co-evolved for millions of years. Leafcutter colonies are among the largest insect societies, with millions of ants in nests that can cover an area bigger than a house, and their trails can stretch for hundreds of meters.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how leafcutter ants cut and carry leaf pieces up to 50 times their body weight back to underground gardens, not eating the leaves but feeding them to fungus they cultivate as their only food. Explore their mega-colonies of millions, their highway systems, and how their farming predates human agriculture by 50 million years.

name: Lemur
teaser: The lemur is a primate found only on Madagascar, a world of its own that split from the main primate family tree tens of millions of years ago. Lemurs come in all sizes, from the tiny mouse lemur, which weighs less than a mouse, to the indri, which sings like a whale. The ring-tailed lemur sunbathes in troops, holding its striped tail up like a flag. Madagascar's isolation let lemurs evolve into many forms, but deforestation now threatens most of them, and they are among the most endangered mammals on Earth.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how lemurs exist only in Madagascar, evolving in isolation into over 100 species from tiny mouse lemurs to the howling indri, with ring-tailed lemurs sunbathing in troops and stink-fighting with their tails. Explore why Madagascar is a primate ark, and the deforestation endangering every species.

name: Lemurs of Madagascar
teaser: Lemurs are Madagascar's native primates, and the island's isolation turned them into something unique: a whole family of primates that evolved with no monkeys competing against them. As a result, lemurs took over every role monkeys play elsewhere, from tiny mouse lemurs that weigh 30 grams to the giant lemurs of the past, which were the size of gorillas. With no monkeys to compete with, lemurs became the island's gardeners, seed-spreaders, and tree-dwellers, and nearly 100 species still survive — every single one found only in Madagascar.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn why lemurs exist only in Madagascar, then explain how they got there.

name: Leopard
teaser: The leopard is the adaptable survivor of the big cats, found across Africa and Asia, from rainforests to mountains. It is the strongest climber of the big cats, hauling kills twice its weight up into trees to keep them safe from lions and hyenas. It hunts by stealth, its spotted coat breaking up its outline in the dappled light, and it can take prey from small rodents to antelopes much bigger than itself. Solitary and secretive, it thrives where other big cats have vanished.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how leopards are the most widespread big cat, hauling prey heavier than themselves into trees to keep it from lions and hyenas, with spots called rosettes and near-night vision. Explore their adaptability from rainforest to city edge, their stealth, and the melanistic black panther form.

name: Leopard Seal
teaser: The leopard seal is the top predator of the Antarctic, a sleek, spotted seal with a huge head and jaws like a reptile. It hunts penguins, grabbing them at the water's edge and thrashing them to tear them apart, and it also feeds on fish, squid, and even other seals. It is powerful and curious, and divers describe its visits as awe-inspiring and unsettling. Despite its fierce reputation, it can be playful, and it spends the winter hunting in the pack ice, the undisputed boss of the southern ocean's shallows.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how leopard seals, the only seals that hunt warm-blooded prey, ambush penguins at the water's edge with immense jaws, and also filter krill with specialized teeth, while curious encounters with divers reveal a complex personality. Explore their solitary life, their vocal underwater songs, and their feared yet fascinating role in Antarctica.

name: Leopards and Trees
