The brown pelican dives spectacularly from the air, plunging headfirst into the sea, while white pelicans cooperate, herding fish into shallows with their wings. Their pouches were once thought to hold food for their young, and the birds are beloved icons of coasts worldwide.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how pelicans scoop fish with a throat pouch that can hold 13 liters of water, then drain it and swallow. Explore their coordinated fishing in flocks, the myth of carrying fish in the pouch (they don't), and how chicks feed by reaching into the parent's pouch.

name: Penguin Call Recognition
teaser: Penguins recognize each other by voice, an essential skill in colonies of thousands where every bird looks the same. Each penguin has a unique call, and chicks learn their parents' calls within days of hatching, calling out when they are hungry and recognizing the reply among thousands of others. Parents returning from sea find their chick among hundreds by listening for its distinctive voice, and mated pairs also recognize each other's calls across the colony. In the noise of a penguin colony, voice is identity.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover how penguins recognize each other's calls, then explain the individual signature.

name: Penguin Colonies
teaser: A penguin colony is one of the most crowded places in nature, with hundreds of thousands of birds packed onto rocky shores and ice. Emperor penguins form colonies in the Antarctic winter, huddling together for warmth, while king penguins gather in vast, noisy rookeries where every square meter holds several birds. The colonies are organized chaos: pairs defend tiny territories, chicks form crèches, and the noise is deafening. Scientists use satellite images to count the colonies, and the largest can hold over a million birds.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover how penguin colonies organize, then explain why they nest so close.

name: Penguin Dive Depths
teaser: Penguins are champion divers, and the emperor penguin holds the record for birds, diving over five hundred meters deep and staying under for more than twenty minutes. Its body is built for the deep: it slows its heart to a few beats a minute, stores oxygen in its muscles, and lets its blood shift to protect its organs from the pressure. King penguins routinely dive three hundred meters for food, and even the small Adelie penguin dives to one hundred and fifty. For penguins, the ocean is a deep pantry.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how deep penguins dive, then explain their oxygen storage.

name: Penguin Feathers
teaser: A penguin's feathers are an engineering marvel that keeps it warm in the coldest places on Earth. They are tiny, dense, and stiff, layered so thickly that they form a waterproof, windproof suit, with an underlayer of soft down trapping warm air against the body. Penguins also have a layer of fat beneath the skin, and they oil their feathers with a special gland. Emperor penguins face temperatures of minus sixty degrees and storms, yet their feather suit keeps them warm while their brood patches, bare skin patches, warm the eggs.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how penguin feathers stay dry, then explain the oil gland.

name: Penguin Huddling
teaser: Emperor penguins survive the Antarctic winter by huddling, packing together in a tight mass that can hold thousands of birds. The huddle is so dense that the birds inside are sheltered from the wind, and the temperature inside the group can be twenty degrees warmer than outside. Penguins on the edge, coldest and most exposed, slowly shuffle toward the center, while the warm birds on the inside move to the outside, so everyone takes turns at the worst spot. The huddle is a living, moving shelter of bodies.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how penguins share warmth, then explain why the huddle rotates.

name: Penguin Leaps
teaser: Penguins leap from the water onto ice shelves and rocks with a technique called porpoising, swimming fast then launching into the air in a graceful arc. The leap can carry them two meters high, letting them clear the ice edge and land safely, and the same technique helps them breathe while swimming fast and escape predators in the water. They also toboggan on their bellies across the ice, sliding on their stomachs and pushing with their feet, a faster way to travel than waddling upright.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn why penguins leap out of water, then explain the breathing theory.

name: Penguin Parenting
teaser: Penguin parenting is a team effort with one of the hardest jobs in nature. In emperor penguins, the female lays one egg, then walks to the sea to feed, leaving the male to balance the egg on his feet through months of Antarctic winter, fasting the whole time. When she returns, the chick is just hatching, and the parents then take turns traveling to the sea to fish and returning to feed the chick, until it can join the crèche. In most penguin species, both parents share incubation and feeding equally.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover how emperor penguins incubate eggs, then explain the chick crèche.

name: Penguin Swim Speeds
teaser: Penguins may waddle on land, but in the water they are torpedoes. The fastest, the gentoo penguin, swims at speeds up to thirty-six kilometers an hour, faster than any other penguin, and even the big emperor penguin can cruise at fifteen kilometers an hour. Their bodies are streamlined, their wings are stiff flippers, and they can leap out of the water like dolphins. When they need to move fast on land, they toboggan, sliding on their bellies. The waddle is just the land side of a water-speedster.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover how fast penguins swim, then explain the porpoising.

name: Penguin Swimming
teaser: Penguins swim by flying underwater, using their stiff, flattened wings like flippers to power themselves through the water, and they are among the fastest swimming birds in the world. Their dense bones reduce buoyancy, letting them dive deep, and their streamlined bodies slip through the water with little drag. They can turn sharply, leap out of the water to breathe, and accelerate quickly to catch fish. On land they waddle and hop, but in the ocean they are as graceful as dolphins, and their underwater speed is their greatest defense.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover how penguins swim so fast, then explain the flipper motion.

name: Penguin vs Puffin
teaser: Penguins and puffins look alike but are not related, and their similarities are an example of convergent evolution, where different animals evolve the same solutions to the same problems. Both are black-and-white seabirds that swim underwater using their wings, both nest in colonies, and both are excellent divers. But penguins live in the southern hemisphere, mostly in the Antarctic, cannot fly, and are often much larger, while puffins live in the northern hemisphere, can fly, and are small. They are cousins by trade, not by blood.

exploreAction.instruction: Compare penguins and puffins, then explain why they look alike.

name: Peregrine Falcon
teaser: The peregrine falcon is the fastest animal on Earth, and its hunting dive is a feat of pure physics. It climbs high above its prey, folds its wings, and stoops, reaching speeds over three hundred kilometers an hour, faster than a Formula One car. As it strikes, it clenches its feet and hits the prey with the force of a bullet, stunning or killing it instantly, then catches it in midair. Peregrines live on every continent except Antarctica, and they even nest on skyscrapers, diving after pigeons between the buildings.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the peregrine falcon tucks its wings into a teardrop and stoops at over 300 km/h, making it the fastest animal on the planet. Explore how its nictitating membranes protect the eyes at speed, how it knocks prey out of the sky with a closed talon, and why cities full of pigeons have become its favorite hunting ground.

name: Pistol Shrimp
teaser: The pistol shrimp is the loudest animal in the ocean, pound for pound, and its weapon is a bubble. It snaps its oversized claw shut so fast that it creates a cavitation bubble that collapses with a sound louder than a gunshot and a flash of heat nearly as hot as the sun's surface, stunning or killing prey and shattering small glass. The snap can reach two hundred decibels, louder than a jet engine. Pistol shrimp live in burrows in coral reefs and mudflats, and their snaps are so loud that they interfere with submarine sonar.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the pistol shrimp snaps a giant claw so fast it creates a collapsing bubble that produces a shockwave hotter than the sun's surface and a sound louder than a gunshot, stunning or killing prey. Explore the sonoluminescence of the snap, the flash of light it makes, and how snapping shrimp colonies hum through the sea.

name: Planarian
teaser: The planarian is a flatworm with a superpower that has fascinated scientists for a century: it can regrow its entire body from a tiny fragment. Cut a planarian into pieces and each piece grows into a complete new worm, complete with a brain and eyes, thanks to powerful stem cells called neoblasts. It can even regrow a new head, and experiments have shown that a trained planarian cut in half produces two worms that both retain the memory. It is one of the most studied animals in biology.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how planarians can regrow an entire body from a fragment of 1/279th of themselves, thanks to powerful stem cells called neoblasts, and even regrow heads with functional brains, storing memories across regeneration in some experiments. Explore their light-sensitive eyespots, their flat ribbon bodies, and their role in regeneration research.

name: Platypus
teaser: The platypus is one of the strangest animals on Earth, a mammal that lays eggs, has a duck-like bill, webbed feet, a beaver-like tail, and venomous spurs on its ankles. It is a monotreme, one of only two mammal groups that lay eggs, and it lives in the rivers of eastern Australia, where it hunts by sensing electricity with its bill. Its young, called puggles, hatch from eggs and lap milk from the mother's skin. When the first platypus was sent to Europe, scientists thought it was a hoax stitched together from other animals.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the platypus is a mammal that lays eggs, has a duck-like bill that detects electricity, a beaver-like tail, webbed feet, and venomous spurs on males' ankles. Explore why it confused early scientists, how it hunts blind underwater with electroreception, and its monotreme relatives.

name: Platypus Electrosense
teaser: The platypus hunts with a sixth sense: electroreception. Its duck-like bill is packed with thousands of sensors that detect the tiny electric fields produced by the muscles of its prey, letting it find shrimp, worms, and insects in dark, murky water where it cannot see. It also senses touch and pressure, and it closes its eyes, ears, and nostrils while diving, hunting entirely by the electric picture its bill paints. It is one of the few mammals with this ability, and its electro-sense is finer than a shark's.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how platypuses hunt with electrosensitive receptors in their bills, sensing the tiny electrical fields of muscles twitching in hidden prey, closing their eyes, ears, and nostrils underwater to hunt entirely by electricity and touch. Explore how the bill's receptors work, the underwater head-sweeping hunting motion, and the echidna's similar but weaker sense.

name: Platypus Venom
teaser: The male platypus carries a venomous spur on each hind ankle, and it is one of the few venomous mammals. The spur delivers a venom that causes intense, long-lasting pain in humans, pain so severe that no painkiller reliably stops it, and in smaller animals it can be lethal. The male uses the spurs mainly in fights with rivals during the breeding season, wrestling and stabbing each other. The venom is a cocktail of proteins, some of which are also found in other animals, and scientists study it for potential new medicines.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how platypus venom works, then explain why only males have spurs.

name: Play in Animals
teaser: Animals play, and it is not just for fun: play is practice for life. Lion cubs wrestle to learn hunting skills, lambs race to build strength, and dolphins surf waves, perhaps just for joy. Rats laugh when tickled, crows slide down snowbanks, and octopuses blow water at objects, a behavior researchers call play. Play builds muscles, hones skills, and strengthens social bonds, and young animals that play more often grow into better hunters and more flexible thinkers. It is one of the clearest signs that animals have rich inner lives.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how animals play across species, from dogs and dolphins to crows, octopuses, and even spiders, practicing skills, testing social rules, and building bonds. Explore the theory that play is training for real life, how play signals differ from aggression, and why young animals play more.

name: Poaching
teaser: Poaching is the illegal killing of wild animals, and it pushes some of the world's most iconic species to the edge of extinction. Rhinos are killed for their horns, elephants for their ivory tusks, pangolins for their scales, and tigers for their bones and skins, all feeding black markets that can be worth billions. Poachers use snares, traps, and automatic weapons, and rangers risk their lives to stop them. Conservationists fight back with drones, tracking collars, sniffer dogs, and community programs, and progress is real, but the battle continues.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how poaching kills tens of thousands of elephants and rhinos for ivory and horn, pangolins for scales, and tigers for traditional medicine, funding criminal networks. Explore the demand that drives it, the rangers risking their lives, and how technology, tracking, and awareness are turning the tide.

name: Poison Dart Frog
teaser: The poison dart frog is one of the most toxic animals on Earth, a tiny, brilliantly colored frog of the Central and South American rainforests. Its skin carries enough poison to kill a human, and indigenous peoples have used its toxins to tip blowdart darts, hence the name. The frogs do not make their own poison: they get it from the toxic ants and mites they eat, so captive frogs, fed a normal diet, are harmless. Their bright colors warn predators of the danger, and each species wears a different pattern.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how poison dart frogs pack enough toxin in their skin to kill predators, the most toxic species carrying enough to kill ten humans, the poison used by Indigenous hunters on blow darts. Explore how their bright colors warn predators, and the mystery that frogs raised in captivity lose their toxicity.

name: Poison Dart Frogs
teaser: Poison dart frogs come in a rainbow of warning colors, and their toxin comes from their diet. Wild frogs eat poisonous ants, mites, and beetles, and they concentrate the alkaloid toxins in their skin, becoming deadly to touch. Each species of the Amazon and Central America has its own color pattern, from golden yellow to electric blue, and predators learn to avoid them all. Interestingly, frogs raised in captivity on harmless food are not poisonous at all. Scientists study their toxins for potential medicines, including painkillers.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn why poison frogs are colorful, then explain where their toxins come from.

name: Polar Bear
teaser: The polar bear is the largest land carnivore on Earth, a marine mammal that spends most of its life on the Arctic sea ice, and it is built for the cold. Its fur is not actually white but transparent and hollow, trapping warmth, and under it lies black skin that absorbs heat. It is a powerful swimmer, covering hundreds of kilometers across open water, and it hunts seals by waiting at their breathing holes for hours. Climate change is melting its ice home, and the polar bear has become the symbol of the warming Arctic.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how polar bears, the largest land carnivores weighing up to 700 kg, hunt seals from sea ice, with black skin under translucent fur and paw pads that grip ice. Explore their incredible swimming, their dependence on shrinking sea ice, and why they're the symbol of climate change.

name: Polar Bear Fur Facts
teaser: A polar bear's white fur is an optical illusion — the hairs are actually transparent and hollow. Each hair is a clear, pigment-free tube that scatters and reflects light, which is why the bear appears white against the snow, and the hollow structure also traps air, providing insulation so effective the bear barely loses body heat. Under that coat, the polar bear's skin is black — a dark surface that absorbs the sun's heat, adding to the bear's warmth. On a warm day, a polar bear can appear yellowish, and on rare occasions algae growing inside the hairs can make one look green.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn what polar bear fur is really like, then explain how it traps heat.

name: Polar Bear Hunting
teaser: The polar bear is the Arctic's apex predator, and its hunting is a study in patience and power. Its favorite prey is the ringed seal, and it hunts with two main strategies: still-hunting, where the bear waits silently beside a breathing hole in the ice for hours, sometimes days, until a seal surfaces — then the paw comes down like a sledgehammer; and stalking, where it creeps across the ice and charges the last few meters. A polar bear can smell a seal's breathing hole from nearly a kilometer away through a meter of snow.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover how polar bears hunt seals, then explain the challenges of melting ice.

name: Porcupine
teaser: The porcupine is the prickliest mammal on Earth, covered in up to thirty thousand sharp quills that are modified hairs. It cannot shoot its quills, but when threatened it raises them, rattles them, and charges backward, driving them into the attacker. The quills are barbed and detach easily, and a porcupine can regrow them. It is a slow, peaceful animal that eats bark, leaves, and fruit, and it is an excellent climber. Most predators learn quickly to leave the porcupine alone.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how porcupines are covered in up to 30,000 quills, modified hairs that detach easily and are barbed, sticking into attackers, and contrary to myth they can't shoot them. Explore the new world porcupines that climb trees with prehensile tails, their salt cravings that lead them to chew axe handles, and the predators like fishers that flip them over.

name: Porcupine Quills
teaser: A porcupine's quills are its defense and its curse. Each quill is a sharp, barbed spine, and when an attacker gets close, the porcupine slaps with its tail, driving dozens of quills into the predator's face. The barbs make the quills hard to pull out, and they can work deeper into the wound over time. Porcupines cannot shoot them, but they can regrow lost quills. Even the porcupine itself can be hurt by its own quills if it falls, and every porcupine injury is a reminder that its armor cuts both ways.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn what porcupine quills are made of, then explain why they are hard to remove.

name: Porcupine Varieties
teaser: There are about thirty species of porcupines, and they come in two very different families. The Old World porcupines of Africa, Asia, and Europe are ground dwellers with long, banded quills, and some grow a meter long. The New World porcupines of the Americas, like the North American porcupine, are smaller, better climbers, and have shorter quills, often with a yellowish tint. Despite the name, they are not closely related to hedgehogs, and they range from desert to rainforest, all armed with the same prickly defense.

exploreAction.instruction: Compare old and new world porcupines, then explain the climbing difference.

name: Portuguese Man o' War
teaser: The Portuguese man o' war is not a jellyfish but a colony of tiny animals working together, and it is one of the most dangerous creatures in the ocean. It floats on the surface with a gas-filled bladder that acts like a sail, and beneath it trail tentacles that can stretch thirty meters, armed with stinging cells packed with venom. Its sting is extremely painful and can be life-threatening, and washed-up man o' war on beaches still sting. The name comes from its resemblance to an old Portuguese warship under sail.

exploreAction.targetName: Meet the Portuguese man o' war
exploreAction.instruction: Read how the Portuguese man o' war is not a jellyfish but a siphonophore, a colony of specialized animals working as one, with a gas-filled float, stinging tentacles that can trail 30 meters, and venom that can hospitalize swimmers. Explore its wind-driven sailing, the beaches it washes onto, and the painful stings it leaves.

name: Prairie Dog
teaser: The prairie dog is the keystone of the American grasslands, a chubby ground squirrel that lives in vast underground towns and shapes the whole ecosystem. Its burrows aerate the soil, its grazing keeps the prairie healthy, and it is food for eagles, hawks, ferrets, and foxes, with dozens of species depending on it. Prairie dogs are deeply social, greeting each other with kisses, grooming, and elaborate calls, and their colonies once stretched for hundreds of kilometers. Their decline has hurt the entire prairie ecosystem.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how prairie dogs build vast underground towns with separate chambers for nurseries and bathrooms, and have one of the most sophisticated animal alarm systems, with different calls for different predators. Explore their role as keystone species feeding ferrets, eagles, and badgers, and the ranching conflicts over their grazing.

name: Prairie Dog Language
teaser: Prairie dog language is among the most sophisticated of any animal, with calls that describe the world around them. Researchers have found that prairie dogs have different alarm calls for different predators, and their calls even describe the color of a human's clothing, the size and shape of an approaching animal, and whether a person is carrying a gun. A prairie dog can say, in effect, tall human in blue is coming. The calls are learned, with different colonies speaking slightly different dialects, a discovery that amazed science.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn what prairie dog calls encode, then explain the predator descriptions.

name: Prairie Dog Towns
teaser: A prairie dog town is a city under the grass, and the largest ever recorded stretched over sixty thousand square kilometers and held an estimated four hundred million prairie dogs. The town is divided into wards and neighborhoods, each with its own family groups called coteries, usually one male, several females, and their young. The burrows have bedrooms, nurseries, and lookout posts, and the town is a bustling society of grooming, playing, and gossiping with calls. Prairie dogs are among the most social animals in North America.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover how prairie dog towns are organized, then explain the sentinel system.

name: Praying Mantis
teaser: The praying mantis is a master of ambush, a patient predator that can sit motionless for hours, waiting for prey to wander within reach. Its name comes from its front legs, which fold in a posture that looks like praying, but those legs are weapons, armed with spines that snap shut on insects in a fraction of a second. Its triangular head swivels to follow movement, and its compound eyes give it sharp vision and depth perception. It eats pests in gardens, and its famous habit of the female eating the male after mating is real, though not universal.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how praying mantises wait motionless with folded raptorial arms, strike in 50 milliseconds, and swivel their heads nearly 180 degrees, the only insect that can look over its shoulder. Explore the famous and rare sexual cannibalism, their camouflage, and how they catch bees and even hummingbirds.

name: Prehensile Tails
teaser: Some monkeys have a secret fifth limb: a prehensile tail — a tail so strong and skilled it can grip, swing, and even hold weight, acting like an extra arm. Prehensile tails are the specialty of New World monkeys like spider monkeys, howlers, and capuchins, and they're a family innovation that the Old World monkeys of Africa and Asia never evolved. The underside of the tail has a bare patch of skin with ridge patterns that grip like a fingerprint, and a monkey can hang by its tail alone, freeing both hands to gather fruit.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn which monkeys have prehensile tails, then explain why Old World monkeys do not.

name: Pufferfish
teaser: The pufferfish is the balloon of the reef, and its defense is a dramatic transformation. When threatened, it gulps water in seconds, inflating into a spiky ball several times its normal size, making it impossible for predators to swallow. Many species also carry tetrodotoxin, one of the most toxic substances in nature, in their skin and organs, and the poison can kill a human. Yet in Japan, fugu, a pufferfish dish, is a delicacy prepared only by licensed chefs who know exactly how to remove the deadly parts.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how pufferfish gulp water to inflate into a spiky ball when threatened, while carrying tetrodotoxin, one of the most poisonous substances in nature. Explore why chefs train for years to serve fugu safely, and how these slow swimmers rely on defense over speed.

name: Puffin
teaser: The puffin is the clown of the sea, a small seabird with a rainbow-striped bill that looks like a parrot's, and it is one of the most beloved birds in the world. It spends most of its life at sea, but returns to coastal cliffs each spring to nest, and it is an expert diver, using its wings to fly underwater in pursuit of fish, carrying dozens in its bill at once. Its bill is brightly colored during breeding season and dulls in winter. Puffins dig burrows in cliff tops, and their chicks, called pufflings, leave the nest at night.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how Atlantic puffins spend the winter at sea, then return to cliff-top burrows they dig with beaks and feet, carrying up to 60 fish at once held crosswise by a spiny tongue. Explore their colorful breeding beaks that shed in winter, and how they mate for life and return to the same burrow.

name: Puffin Burrows
teaser: Puffins nest in burrows they dig into the grassy tops of sea cliffs, using their beaks and feet to tunnel up to a meter deep. Each pair returns to the same burrow year after year, and the burrow protects the single egg and chick from predators and storms. The chick, called a puffling, is fed a steady supply of small fish that the parents carry back crosswise in their bills, and it can eat over a hundred fish a day as it grows. When it is ready, the puffling leaves the burrow at night, heading out to sea alone.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover why puffins nest in burrows, then explain the single egg.

name: Purple Martin
teaser: The purple martin is North America's largest swallow, and it is one of the few wild birds that has come to depend on human-provided housing. Almost all purple martins east of the Rockies now nest in multi-room birdhouses that people put up for them, and the birds return to the same colony year after year. They are aerial acrobats, catching insects on the wing, and a single martin can eat thousands of mosquitoes and flies a day. Their cheerful gurgling calls announce spring in much of the eastern United States.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how purple martins in North America now nest almost entirely in human-made gourds and apartments, a relationship that goes back to Indigenous peoples hanging hollow gourds centuries ago. Explore their acrobatic insect-catching, their communal roosts of hundreds of thousands, and their full migration to South America.

name: Python Hunting
teaser: Pythons are ambush hunters that kill by constriction, and the largest, the reticulated python and the Burmese python, can overpower prey far bigger than themselves. The python lies in wait, often in water or tall grass, senses the heat of warm-blooded prey with pit organs on its face, and strikes, coiling around the victim in a lightning move. It tightens with each exhale, suffocating the prey, then swallows it headfirst, a meal that can last for months. Its jaws and skin stretch enormously, and it can eat deer, pigs, and even alligators.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how pythons and boas kill by constriction, coiling around prey and tightening with each exhale until the heart and blood flow fail, then swallowing prey whole with jaws that unhinge and stretch. Explore how they sense warm prey, how big their meals can get, and the record Burmese pythons swallowing deer in Florida.

name: Quagga
teaser: The quagga was a zebra of southern Africa with stripes only on its head and neck, fading to plain brown on its body, like a zebra that forgot to finish painting itself. It lived in huge herds and was hunted relentlessly for its meat and hide, and the last wild quagga died in the 1870s, with the final captive one passing away in Amsterdam in 1883. It was once thought to be a distinct species, but DNA shows it was a subspecies of the plains zebra. A project is now trying to breed zebras back toward the quagga's look.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the quagga, a zebra relative with stripes only on its front, roamed South African plains in huge herds and was hunted to extinction by 1883, the last one dying in a zoo. Explore the famous photos, the quagga DNA that proves it a plains zebra subspecies, and the breeding project trying to bring its look back.

name: Quokka
teaser: The quokka is the happiest animal on Earth, a small wallaby of Western Australia with a face that seems to smile permanently, and selfies with quokkas have made it famous. It lives on Rottnest Island, where it is tame and curious, and it is a herbivore that grazes and browses. Quokkas carry their young in a pouch, and they can climb small trees to reach food. The smile is just the shape of its mouth, but the quokka has become a symbol of joy, and its island home protects it from the foxes and cats that threaten mainland populations.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how quokkas, small wallaby-like marsupials of Rottnest Island, Australia, became internet famous for their apparent smiles, which are actually a feature of their muzzle, not a mood. Explore their plant diet, their fearlessness around people that made selfies possible, and why tourists flock to see them.

name: Rabbit Communication
teaser: Rabbits communicate with their feet: they thump the ground with a hind foot to warn the warren of danger. The thump creates vibrations that travel through the ground, and the sound alerts other rabbits to freeze or dive for cover. It is not the only rabbit signal: rabbits also snort, grunt, and scream in extreme fear, and they signal with body language, like a white tail flashing as it runs. A pet rabbit thumping at night is usually telling its humans, in the only way it can, that something startled it.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover how rabbits communicate, then explain the foot thump warning.

name: Rabbit Ears
teaser: A rabbit's ears are more than just cute: they are radar dishes and radiators. Each ear can swivel independently, catching sounds from all directions, and rabbits can hear frequencies far beyond human range, letting them detect predators long before they are visible. The ears are also packed with blood vessels, and rabbits use them to cool down: in hot weather, blood flows to the ears and releases heat, so rabbits in warm climates have longer ears. In the cold, they press their ears flat to keep warm.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover how rabbit ears regulate temperature, then explain their hearing range.

name: Raccoon
teaser: The raccoon is the masked bandit of the Americas, a clever, adaptable animal that has thrived alongside humans in cities and forests alike. Its black mask and ringed tail are its trademarks, and its front paws are almost like little hands, so dexterous that raccoons can open latches, jars, and even doors. It washes its food, hence its name, and it eats almost anything, from berries and insects to garbage and fish. Raccoons are mostly nocturnal, and their intelligence is famous: they can remember solutions to problems for years.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how raccoons are famous for their mask-like face markings and dexterous front paws that can open latches, jars, and doors, washing food before eating it, a behavior that gives them their name. Explore their night raids on trash cans, their city adaptation, and their den life in hollow trees and attics.

name: Radula
teaser: The radula is the secret weapon of snails and slugs, a ribbon of tiny teeth that works like a conveyor belt. It is found in almost all mollusks, from garden snails to squid, and it scrapes, cuts, or drills food. A garden snail's radula has tens of thousands of teeth, and it rasps away at leaves, while the radula of a cone snail is a single harpoon tooth loaded with venom. Some deep-sea snails even use their radulas to drill through the bones of whales. It is one of the most versatile tools in the animal kingdom.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the radula, a ribbon of thousands of microscopic teeth found in most molluscs, works like a conveyor-belt rasp, used by snails to scrape algae, cone snails to harpoon fish, and chitons to grind rock with teeth reinforced with iron. Explore the variety of radula designs and how each fits its owner's diet.

name: Rainforest Alliance
teaser: The Rainforest Alliance is a global organization working to protect forests and the people and animals that depend on them. It certifies farms that meet environmental standards, from coffee and cocoa to bananas and tea, so that products bought with its green frog seal are grown without destroying rainforests. The program helps farmers use sustainable methods, protect wildlife, and earn fairer incomes. Buying Rainforest Alliance certified products is one of the simplest ways people can help protect the world's rainforests.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the Rainforest Alliance certification labels coffee, chocolate, tea, and bananas grown with standards that protect forests, wildlife, and worker rights, working with small farms across the tropics. Explore how the frog seal began in 1987, the audit system, and how consumer choices can shift whole industries.

name: Raptor Talons
teaser: A raptor's talons are its primary weapons, four toes armed with sharp, curved claws, and they are built to grab and kill. The talons close with crushing force, powered by leg muscles that can exert hundreds of pounds of pressure, and the razor-sharp tips pierce the prey's vital organs. Eagles have some of the strongest grips in the bird world, strong enough to break bone, and their toes are covered in spiky scales that help grip slippery fish. A raptor's feet are the reason the whole bird is feared.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover how raptor talons grip, then explain the killing grip strength.

name: Ready Birds and Helpless Chicks
teaser: Bird chicks come in two very different packages. Precocial chicks, like ducklings, geese, and chickens, hatch with open eyes and fluffy down, and they can walk, swim, and feed themselves within hours of hatching, following their parents everywhere. Altricial chicks, like robins, owls, and songbirds, hatch blind, naked, and helpless, entirely dependent on their parents to feed and warm them. Precocial parents guard and guide, while altricial parents work as nonstop feeding machines. Both strategies work, and the whole bird world is split between them.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn the difference between precocial and altricial chicks, then give an example of each.

name: Red Fox
teaser: The red fox is the most widespread wild carnivore on Earth, found across the northern hemisphere, from Arctic tundra to city streets. It is a clever opportunist that eats almost anything, from mice and rabbits to berries and garbage, and it is famous for its intelligence and cunning in folklore around the world. It hunts by pouncing, leaping high into the air and diving onto prey hidden beneath snow or grass, guided by hearing so acute it can pinpoint a mouse underground. Its bushy tail, called a brush, wraps around it as a warm blanket in winter.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how red foxes are the most widespread carnivore, found across northern continents and even in cities, with a legendary cunning, hunting by sound with ears that pin down mice under snow. Explore their dens, their omnivorous diet, their mating pair bonds, and why they thrive alongside humans.

name: Red Knot
teaser: The red knot is a small shorebird that makes one of the most extraordinary migrations on Earth, flying up to fifteen thousand kilometers from the Arctic to South America and back every year. It is famous for its stop at Delaware Bay, where it must double its weight in just two weeks by feasting on horseshoe crab eggs before continuing its journey. If the crab eggs are late, the knots cannot fatten up and may not survive the flight. This tiny bird links continents, and its survival depends on the beaches where it refuels.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how red knots migrate up to 30,000 km a year between Arctic breeding grounds and southern wintering beaches, fattening on horseshoe crab eggs at Delaware Bay, a critical refueling stop, and their populations crashed when the crab harvest collapsed. Explore the epic journey, the fuel loads, and the conservation that restored the stopover.

name: Red Panda
teaser: The red panda is a flame-colored mammal of the Himalayan forests, and despite the name, it is not a panda. It is the only living member of its own family, Ailuridae, and its closest relatives are raccoons, weasels, and skunks. It eats mostly bamboo, like its giant namesake, using a false thumb to grip the stalks, and it is an expert climber that spends its days sleeping in trees, its reddish coat camouflaging it among the moss. It is shy, gentle, and threatened by habitat loss, and it is the original panda, discovered before the giant panda.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how red pandas of Himalayan bamboo forests are not closely related to giant pandas, more like raccoons and weasels, using a false thumb to grip bamboo and a tail with ring patterns for balance. Explore their bamboo-heavy diet, their shy tree life, and how they gave the Firefox browser its name.

name: Red-eyed Tree Frog
teaser: The red-eyed tree frog is the poster child of the rainforest, a bright green frog with huge red eyes, orange toes, and blue-and-yellow stripes, and it is a master of surprise. By day it sleeps flattened against a leaf, its green back blending perfectly with the foliage, hiding its bright colors. When disturbed, it snaps its eyes open and flashes its brilliant body, startling predators long enough for it to escape. The flash is called startle coloration, and the frog is harmless, though it carries mild toxins in its skin.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the red-eyed tree frog of Central American rainforests sleeps flattened on leaves, hidden by green skin, then flashes startling red eyes and orange feet to startle predators when disturbed. Explore its gelatinous egg masses over water, the race of tadpoles to the pond, and its night insect hunts.

name: Red-eyed Tree Frog Life Cycle
teaser: The red-eyed tree frog lives its life in two worlds. It begins as a tadpole in a temporary pool, then transforms into a tree frog that spends its days sleeping on leaves high in the canopy. Mating happens during the rainy season, and the female lays her eggs on a leaf hanging over the water: when the tadpoles hatch, they drop into the pool below. The eggs can hatch early if a snake attacks, tumbling the tadpoles to safety. From leaf to pool and back again, it is a life of daring escapes.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how red-eyed tree frogs lay eggs on leaves over ponds, hatchlings drop into the water as tadpoles within a week, grow, and climb back to the canopy as adults that sleep on leaves by day and hunt insects by night. Explore how eggs can hatch early when threatened, and the frog's famous flash coloration.

name: Reef Sharks
teaser: Reef sharks are the guardians of the coral reef, a group of sleek predators that includes the blacktip, whitetip, and grey reef sharks. They patrol the reef, hunting sick and slow fish, which keeps the reef healthy, and they are generally shy around divers. The blacktip reef shark is famous for leaping clear of the water while feeding, and the whitetip rests in caves by day, hunting at night. Overfishing has emptied many reefs of their sharks, and their loss has cascading effects on the whole reef community.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how blacktip, whitetip, and grey reef sharks patrol coral reefs, keeping fish populations healthy, and their presence is a sign of reef health. Explore the shark feeding frenzies when fishing boats arrive, their daytime resting caves, and how overfishing empties reefs of their sharks.

name: Regent Honeyeater
teaser: The regent honeyeater is one of Australia's rarest birds, and it is losing its voice. Its population has fallen to only a few hundred, and so many young birds are raised away from their parents that many have never heard the adult song, and they sing improvised, garbled versions instead. Conservationists now play recorded songs to teach the young birds to sing properly, an extraordinary effort to save a species' culture as well as its numbers. It is a striking black-and-yellow bird of the eucalyptus woodlands.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the regent honeyeater of southeastern Australia, with fewer than 400 left, is so rare that young males learn songs from other species instead of their own, producing hybrid calls, and researchers now tutor captive birds with recorded songs before release. Explore the eucalyptus woodland loss, the captive breeding program, and the urgent conservation work.

name: Reindeer
teaser: The reindeer, called caribou in North America, is the domesticated deer of the far north, and it has lived alongside humans for thousands of years. Both males and females grow antlers, unique among deer, and they shed them each year. Reindeer have wide, cloven hooves that work as snowshoes in winter and paddles when swimming, and their noses are specially adapted to warm the freezing air they breathe. They migrate in vast herds, and their thick coats, with hollow, insulating hairs, keep them warm at minus forty degrees.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how reindeer, called caribou in North America, are the only deer where both sexes grow antlers, with noses adapted to warm inhaled air and hooves that change with seasons, and they've been domesticated for thousands of years pulling sleds in the far north. Explore the migrations, the lichen diet, and the winter snow craters they dig.

name: Resplendent Quetzal
teaser: The resplendent quetzal is one of the most beautiful birds on Earth, a jewel of the Central American cloud forests with iridescent green and red feathers and, in males, tail feathers that stream behind for up to a meter. The Aztecs and Mayas revered it, using its feathers in royal headdresses, and it is the national bird of Guatemala, whose currency is even named after it. It feeds on wild avocados and is a key seed spreader, and it nests in tree cavities, leaving the forest only when the fruit runs out.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the resplendent quetzal, sacred to the Maya and Aztecs, trails tail feathers up to 65 cm long from its back, molting them only after nesting. Explore why it was worshipped as the god Quetzalcoatl, why killing one was a capital crime, and its dependence on cloud forests with wild avocado trees.

name: Reticulated Python
teaser: The reticulated python is the longest snake in the world, with records over nine meters, and its name comes from the beautiful net-like pattern of its scales. It lives in the rainforests and rivers of Southeast Asia, where it hunts by ambush, coiling around rodents, birds, and even deer, and it is an excellent swimmer that sometimes ventures into coastal waters. It is not venomous, killing by constriction, and it is a popular, though demanding, snake in captivity, growing too large for most keepers.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the reticulated python of Southeast Asia is the longest snake, with verified specimens over 7 meters and folklore of longer ones, a constrictor that climbs trees and hunts mammals and birds. Explore its beautiful diamond pattern, its heat-sensing labial pits, and how females coil around eggs to incubate them.

name: Rewilding
teaser: Rewilding is the bold idea of letting nature heal itself by restoring the animals and processes that once shaped the land. It means bringing back missing species, like wolves to Yellowstone, where their return changed the rivers by controlling elk, or beavers to British rivers, whose dams created wetlands that teemed with life. Rewilding can also mean simply leaving land alone to recover. It is not about going back in time but about restoring the natural engines that keep ecosystems healthy, and it is spreading across the world.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how rewilding projects restore ecosystems by bringing back keystone species, from wolves returning to Yellowstone and reshaping rivers by controlling elk, to bison, lynx, and beavers returning across Europe. Explore the debate over what wild means, and how small reintroductions ripple through whole landscapes.

name: Rhino Mud Wallows
teaser: A rhino's favorite spa treatment is a wallow — a muddy pit it rolls in for hours, caking its thick hide with wet mud. It's not just for fun: the mud acts as sunscreen and insect repellent, protecting the rhino's sensitive skin from the brutal African sun and from biting flies, ticks, and parasites. The mud also helps the rhino shed heat, since rhinos can't sweat much. A wallow is a shared resource, with several rhinos using the same pits in turn, and the mud baths leave behind enough scent that the wallow becomes a kind of message board where rhinos read who's been around.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn why rhinos need mud, then explain how it protects their skin.

name: Rhino Senses
teaser: A rhino's eyesight is famously terrible — it can barely make out a person standing still a few dozen meters away — so it relies on its other senses to build its world. Its sense of smell is phenomenal: a rhino can pick up scents from far away, read the age and identity of other rhinos through their dung piles, and smell water or danger on the wind. Its hearing is almost as sharp, with ears that rotate independently to pin down every sound.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover how rhinos compensate for weak eyesight, then explain their charging behavior.

name: Rhino and Oxpecker Birds
teaser: The rhino has a small, feathered entourage: oxpeckers, little birds that perch on its back and hop around its face picking off ticks, flies, and other parasites. It looks like a perfect deal — the bird gets a meal, the rhino gets pest control — and mostly it is. But scientists discovered the relationship has a darker side: oxpeckers sometimes peck at open wounds and keep them from healing, lapping up blood. Still, the birds give the rhino something almost as valuable as grooming: a warning system.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover what oxpeckers do on rhinos, then explain what each gets from the deal.

name: Rhinoceros
teaser: The rhinoceros is a prehistoric-looking giant, one of the last of the great land mammals, and its name means nose horn. Five species survive, from the tiny Sumatran rhino to the white rhino, which can weigh over two tonnes. Despite its size, the rhino can run at fifty kilometers an hour and turn surprisingly quickly, and its skin is thick armor, though it is sensitive to sunburn, which is why rhinos wallow in mud. All five species are threatened, and poaching for their horns, made of keratin like fingernails, drives them toward extinction.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how rhinos, weighing up to 2.5 tonnes, have horns made of compressed keratin like fingernails, thick skin like armor, and poor eyesight but sharp hearing and smell. Explore the five rhino species, the poaching crisis for their horns worth more than gold, and the armed guards protecting the last northern whites.

name: Rhinoceros Senses
teaser: Rhinos have famously poor eyesight, and they see the world as a blur beyond a few dozen meters, which explains their sometimes startling behavior: a rhino that looks like it is charging may simply be trying to see what you are. To compensate, rhinos rely on superb hearing and an extraordinary sense of smell, using their prehensile upper lip to sniff the air and ground. Their ears swivel independently, and their noses can detect scents from far away. They also have a wide field of vision, and their horns, made of compacted hair-like keratin, are used for defense and display.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how rhinos have poor eyesight, barely seeing a person at 30 meters, but superb hearing that swivels their ears toward sounds and an excellent sense of smell used to read territory and detect danger. Explore why they sometimes charge humans, how their eyes are placed for grazing, and how the senses balance the blind spots.

name: River Otter Play
teaser: River otters are the most playful animals in North America, and their play is serious business. They slide down muddy banks and snow slopes on their bellies, over and over, not just for fun but to practice the fast, slippery movements they need to escape predators and chase fish. They wrestle, chase, and play games of keep-away with sticks and fish, and mothers teach their pups to swim and hunt through play. Play builds the strength, coordination, and social bonds otters need, and it makes them the most joyful animals on the river.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover why otters play, then explain how play sharpens hunting.

name: Rotifer
teaser: The rotifer is one of the smallest animals on Earth, a microscopic creature with a wheel of cilia that spins like a motor, sweeping food into its mouth. It lives in ponds, moss, and soil almost everywhere, and it is nearly indestructible. Rotifers can survive complete drying, freezing, and even radiation, reviving after decades in a dormant state. Some have even been revived after being frozen for twenty-four thousand years in Siberian permafrost. Tiny as they are, they are masters of survival, and they have been on Earth for millions of years.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how rotifers are microscopic aquatic animals with ciliated crowns that look like spinning wheels, and bdelloid rotifers can survive freezing, drying, and radiation for years, reviving with DNA repair, and have reproduced without sex for millions of years. Explore their ability to survive in the Antarctic permafrost for decades.

name: Ruby-throated Hummingbird Migration
teaser: The ruby-throated hummingbird migrates between North America and Central America, and its journey includes a nonstop flight of over eight hundred kilometers across the Gulf of Mexico. Weighing only three grams, it must nearly double its weight in fat before leaving, then fly for up to twenty hours without rest, its heart pounding at over a thousand beats a minute. It times its departure with the winds and flower blooms, and it returns north in spring to the same backyard feeders it visited the year before, an astonishing feat of navigation for a bird smaller than a coin.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how ruby-throated hummingbirds, weighing about the same as a coin, fatten up and fly nonstop across the Gulf of Mexico, some 800 km of open water. Explore how they almost double their weight beforehand, how scientists confirmed the crossing, and the risks of storms and exhaustion.

name: Sabre-toothed Cat
teaser: The sabre-toothed cat, often called the sabre-toothed tiger, was one of the most iconic predators of the Ice Age, with fangs up to twenty centimeters long. It was not a tiger but a member of a separate, now-extinct cat family, and its name comes from its curved, blade-like canine teeth. It used those fangs to slice the throats of giant prey like mammoths, bison, and ground sloths, and it went extinct about ten thousand years ago, along with the megafauna it hunted. Its fossils, found in huge numbers at the La Brea Tar Pits, are among the most famous in paleontology.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how sabre-toothed cats like Smilodon grew 20 cm canine teeth, too long to bite with, instead using powerful forelimbs to pin prey and slash the throat. Explore how their bites worked, why they vanished at the end of the ice age, and the famous La Brea tar pit fossils.

name: Saiga Antelope
teaser: The saiga antelope is a living fossil of the Eurasian steppes, famous for its bizarre, trunk-like nose that hangs down over its mouth. The nose warms and filters the dusty air in summer and the freezing air of winter, acting like a built-in climate control, and it gives the saiga its distinctive snuffle. Herds once numbered in the millions across the grasslands of Central Asia, but hunting and disease have brought them to the edge of extinction. Conservation efforts are working to save this strange, ancient survivor.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how saiga antelopes of Central Asian steppes wear huge inflatable noses that filter dust and warm cold air, and their mass migrations once numbered millions, crashing to tens of thousands from hunting and disease. Explore the mass die-offs that puzzled scientists, the nasal cooling system, and the fences that block their ancient routes.

name: Sailfish
teaser: The sailfish is the fastest fish in the ocean, reaching speeds over a hundred kilometers an hour, and its giant dorsal fin, the sail, rises when it hunts or threatens. It uses its speed and long bill to slash through schools of fish, stunning and injuring many at once, then turning back to eat the wounded. Sailfish sometimes work together, herding baitfish into tight balls before striking. Their bill is a spear of fused bone, and their sleek, streamlined bodies are built for pure speed, making them one of the most exciting fish in the sea.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how sailfish are clocked at speeds over 110 km/h, the fastest fish, using a tall retractable dorsal fin and a bill to slash through bait balls. Explore how they hunt in coordinated groups, taking turns to stun sardines, and their migrations across warm oceans.

name: Salamander
teaser: The salamander is the quiet amphibian of the forest floor, a lizard-like creature that is actually a frog's relative, and it is a master of regeneration. It can regrow lost limbs, tails, and even parts of its heart and brain, and it can regenerate the same limb dozens of times. Salamanders breathe through their skin, which must stay moist, so they live in damp places. Some, like the tiger salamander, can survive years in drought by staying in their larval form, and the fire salamander's bright yellow spots warn predators of its skin toxins.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how salamanders can regrow complete limbs, tails, jaws, and even parts of the heart and brain, a regeneration superpower scientists study to help human healing. Explore their moist skin breathing, the difference from lizards, and the giant Japanese and Chinese salamanders that reach 1.8 meters.

name: Sand Dollar
teaser: The sand dollar is a flattened sea urchin, a relative of starfish that lives buried just beneath the sand, and its delicate skeleton is a beachcomber's treasure. It has a five-petaled pattern on its upper surface, its flower, which is actually a system of pores for its tube feet, and it uses tiny spines to move and burrow. It feeds on sand grains, scraping off the algae and bacteria, and the little holes on its edges are where its tube feet emerge. The white disks washed up on beaches are its cleaned skeletons, and it is one of the ocean's quietest workers.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how sand dollars are flattened sea urchins that burrow in sandy seabeds, using tiny spines to move and tube feet to pass food to their mouths, their five-petaled patterns are breathing pores. Explore how they feed on sand grains, the keyhole sand dollar's slits, and why beachcombers love their skeletons.

name: Saving the Rhinos
teaser: Rhinos are in a war for survival, and the battlefield is the poaching crisis. Their horns can sell for more than gold on the black market, which drove rhino populations down from over half a million a century ago to tens of thousands today, with the Javan and Sumatran rhinos nearly gone. The fight to save them is a full-contact effort: heavily armed rangers patrol reserves, some rhinos are dehorned to make them worthless to poachers, and dedicated breeding programs have pulled the southern white rhino back from the brink.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover why rhinos are poached, then explain the conservation strategies being used.

name: Scimitar Oryx
teaser: The scimitar-horned oryx was once a common sight across the Sahara, a pale desert antelope with long, curved horns, but hunting and drought wiped it out in the wild by the 1990s. It survived thanks to captive herds in zoos, and in a historic move, conservationists reintroduced hundreds of them to fenced reserves in Chad, where the species had not been seen for decades. The oryx can go weeks without drinking, getting water from its food, and its pale coat reflects the desert heat. Its story is one of the most hopeful in conservation.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the scimitar-horned oryx, declared extinct in the wild in 2000, has been reintroduced to Chad from captive herds through a pioneering rewilding program, with GPS-collared herds monitored across the Sahel. Explore the desert adaptations, the herding into release pens, and the poaching and drought challenges the comeback faces.

name: Scorpion
teaser: The scorpion is one of the oldest land animals, a predatory arachnid that has prowled the Earth for over four hundred million years, long before the dinosaurs. It is armed with pincers and a venomous stinger at the end of its curved tail, and it hunts insects, spiders, and even small lizards at night. Some scorpions glow blue-green under ultraviolet light, and the female carries her young on her back. Most scorpion stings are painful but not deadly, though a few species are dangerous. They can survive a year without food and freeze solid, then revive.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how scorpions have survived for 400 million years, glowing blue-green under ultraviolet light, sensing vibrations through leg hairs, and some going a year without food. Explore their venom stings, how mothers carry young on their backs, and the pale desert species that hide by day.

name: Sea Anemone
teaser: The sea anemone looks like a flower but is a predatory animal, a relative of jellyfish and corals that lives attached to rocks, reefs, and even crab shells. Its crown of tentacles, armed with stinging cells, waves in the current and fires when prey touches it, paralyzing fish and shrimp that swim too close, then drawing them into its mouth. Some anemones host clownfish, which are immune to their sting and bring them food. Despite their soft, beautiful look, they are patient, venomous hunters of the seafloor.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how sea anemones look like flowers but are predators, stinging with tentacles packed with harpoon-like nematocysts, and can live for decades or centuries, some splitting in half to clone themselves. Explore their partnership with clownfish, their slow gliding over rocks, and their relatives, corals and jellyfish.

name: Sea Cucumber
teaser: The sea cucumber is the vacuum cleaner of the ocean floor, a sausage-shaped relative of starfish that crawls along the seabed eating sand and mud, digesting the organic matter in it, and excreting clean sand. A single sea cucumber can process huge amounts of sediment, and their activity turns over the seafloor like earthworms turn over soil. When threatened, some expel their internal organs as a decoy and regrow them, and others fire sticky threads at attackers. They are also a prized food, dried and eaten across Asia, and their populations are now managed carefully.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how sea cucumbers crawl across the seafloor vacuuming sediment for food, defend by ejecting sticky organs or their own guts to distract predators, and some breathe through their rear ends. Explore their role recycling ocean nutrients, the alarming trade in them for Asian cuisine, and their farming in marine ponds.

name: Sea Lion
teaser: The sea lion is the acrobat of the shore, a sleek marine mammal with external ear flaps and flippers it can turn under its body to walk on land. It is built for swimming, reaching speeds over thirty kilometers an hour, and it can dive to three hundred meters hunting fish and squid. Sea lions are famously intelligent, trainable, and playful, and they gather in huge noisy colonies on the coast. They use their long whiskers to detect vibrations in the water, and the Steller sea lion can weigh over a tonne.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how sea lions are the loud, social members of the pinniped family, with visible ear flaps and flippers they use to walk on land, gathering in noisy colonies, and they're the famous balancing performers in marine shows. Explore their swimming agility, their deep dives, and the difference from true seals.

name: Sea Lions
teaser: Sea lions are the circus performers of the ocean — and their famous balancing act is no trick, it's biology. A sea lion can balance a ball on its nose with total ease, and even balance its whole body on one flipper, because of two remarkable adaptations: an exceptionally mobile neck and spine that let it arch and adjust its center of gravity, and superb proprioception — an internal sense of exactly where its body is in space. In the wild, that balance helps sea lions move on rocks and ice, and in the water they use the same control for spectacular acrobatics.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how sea lions differ from seals, then explain their flipper movement on land.

name: Sea Otter
teaser: The sea otter is the smallest marine mammal and one of the only animals that uses tools: it floats on its back, places a stone on its chest, and cracks open clams and sea urchins against it. It has the densest fur of any animal, up to a million hairs per square inch, since it has no blubber, and it wraps itself and its pup in strands of kelp to keep from drifting away while it sleeps. It eats a quarter of its body weight daily, and it is a keystone species, keeping sea urchins from devouring entire kelp forests.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how sea otters float on their backs, cracking clams and urchins with stones on their chests, wrap themselves in kelp to anchor while sleeping, and their fur is the densest in the animal kingdom, a million hairs per square inch. Explore their role keeping kelp forests healthy by eating sea urchins, and their near extinction from the fur trade.

name: Sea Otter Rafts
teaser: Sea otters sleep on the water, and they've solved the problem of drifting apart in the cutest way possible: they hold hands. When a group of otters rests, they float together in what's called a raft — sometimes hundreds of animals — and many of them link paws so they don't drift away from each other while asleep. Mothers wrap their pups in seaweed, or carry them on their chests while dozing, and single otters wrap themselves in kelp like a blanket to anchor themselves to the seafloor's edge.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn why sea otters hold hands, then explain the kelp anchoring trick.

name: Sea Otter Tool Use
teaser: The sea otter is one of the only animals in the world that uses a tool to eat — and it treats the ocean like a kitchen. Sea otters dive to the seafloor and bring up hard-shelled prey: clams, mussels, abalone, and sea urchins, along with a flat rock they choose carefully and carry under their armpit, sometimes for the whole dive. Then, floating on their backs, they place the rock on their chest like an anvil and smash the shell against it until it cracks — a technique they repeat hundreds of times a day.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover how sea otters crack shells, then explain the pouch under their arms.

name: Sea Snail
teaser: The sea snail is a slow, shelled traveler of the ocean, and it comes in astonishing variety, from tiny periwinkles on the shore to giant whelks in deep water. It moves on a single muscular foot, gliding over rocks and sand, and it feeds with a radula, a ribbon of tiny teeth, scraping algae or drilling into other shells. Some sea snails, like the cone snail, are venomous hunters, and their spiral shells, in every color and pattern, are among the most beautiful objects in nature, prized by collectors for centuries.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how sea snails graze shores and reefs with radula teeth, many in spiraled shells, from the tiny periwinkle to the giant whelk that drills into clams with acid and a rasping tongue. Explore how shells grow, the spiral geometry of their homes, and the roles they play from tide pool to deep sea.

name: Sea Snake
teaser: The sea snake is the most fully aquatic reptile in the world, a venomous snake that lives its whole life in the warm oceans of the Indo-Pacific. It swims with a flattened, paddle-like tail, can hold its breath for hours, and even drinks fresh water, which it collects when rain forms a lens on the sea surface. Its venom is among the most potent known, but sea snakes are shy and bites are rare. They give birth to live young in the water, and they must surface to breathe, though some can absorb oxygen through their skin.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how sea snakes are among the most venomous snakes, fully adapted to ocean life with paddle tails, the ability to absorb oxygen through skin, and the capacity to dive deep and hold breath for hours. Explore why they rarely bite humans, their live birth at sea, and the myths surrounding their venom.

name: Sea Snakes
teaser: Sea snakes are the ocean's most specialized reptiles, and there are about sixty species, all in the Indo-Pacific. They evolved from land snakes and adapted so fully to water that some, like the true sea snakes, can barely move on land, with flattened bodies and paddle tails. They hunt fish and eels in reefs, using venom to subdue prey, and they are fearless but not aggressive: they rarely bite, even when handled. The yellow-bellied sea snake drifts on ocean currents across the whole Pacific, the most widely distributed snake in the world.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how sea snakes breathe and dive, then explain their venom.

name: Sea Star
teaser: The sea star, or starfish, is one of the most familiar and remarkable animals of the tide pools, and it is not a fish at all. It moves on hundreds of tiny tube feet powered by water pressure, and it can regenerate lost arms, even growing a whole new body from a single arm with part of the center. It eats by pushing its stomach out through its mouth to digest prey, like clams, which it pries open with its arms. Some species have dozens of arms, and all of them are masters of the seafloor.
byline: The star of the tide pool

exploreAction.instruction: Read how sea stars are echinoderms with tube feet that grip, a stomach they push outside to digest prey, and the superpower of regrowing lost arms, with some species splitting in half to reproduce. Explore the crown-of-thorns that devastates coral, and why they're not fish.

name: Sea Turtle Homing
teaser: Sea turtles navigate the open ocean with a built-in compass and map. After years at sea, adult turtles return to the exact beach where they hatched to lay their eggs, sometimes traveling thousands of kilometers to get there. Scientists believe they sense the Earth's magnetic field, learning the magnetic signature of their home beach as hatchlings, and they use it as a beacon. Their magnetic memory is so precise that turtles from the same beach are all found at the same location, an extraordinary homing instinct that still amazes researchers.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how sea turtles navigate home, then explain the magnetic sense theory.

name: Sea Turtle Nesting
teaser: Sea turtle nesting is one of the great natural spectacles, a nighttime ritual repeated for millions of years. The female hauls herself up the beach, digs a deep hole with her flippers, lays up to a hundred leathery eggs, covers them, and returns to the sea, never seeing her hatchlings. Two months later, the hatchlings emerge together at night and race to the ocean, guided by the moonlight on the water, while predators pick off many along the way. Only a tiny fraction survive to adulthood, and the survivors return to nest on the same beach decades later.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover how sea turtles nest, then explain why they return to the same beach.

name: Sea Urchin
teaser: The sea urchin is a slow-moving pin cushion of the ocean floor, a relative of starfish covered in long, movable spines. It crawls on hundreds of tiny tube feet, and it grazes on algae, scraping it off rocks with a five-toothed mouth called Aristotle's lantern. Its spines defend it and help it wedge into crevices, and it can regrow lost spines. In healthy numbers, urchins keep reefs clean, but when their predators, like sea otters, disappear, they can multiply and strip entire kelp forests bare.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how sea urchins move on tube feet among spines, graze algae with a five-toothed jaw called Aristotle's lantern, and can devastate kelp forests when their predators vanish. Explore the purple urchin explosion along Pacific coasts, their roe prized as uni sushi, and their role in reef ecosystems.

name: Seagrass Grazers
teaser: Dugongs are the world's only strictly marine grazing mammals, and they spend their days cropping seagrass like underwater cattle. A dugong grazes by sinking its flexible, trunk-like snout into the meadow, and its rough lips tear up whole plants, roots and all, leaving distinctive feeding trails across the seabed. This grazing actually keeps seagrass healthy, encouraging new growth, and the dugong's constant movement spreads seeds. Seagrass meadows are among the most productive habitats on Earth, and dugongs are their gardeners.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how dugongs and manatees graze seagrass meadows like underwater cows, with dugongs feeding in long furrows that stimulate regrowth, and their grazing maintaining healthy seagrass for fish nurseries. Explore the seagrass ecosystems that store carbon, the threats from boats and pollution, and the protected zones that shelter the grazers.

name: Seahorse
teaser: The seahorse is one of the strangest fish in the sea, and its strangest trick is how it reproduces: the male gives birth. The female deposits her eggs into a pouch on the male's belly, and he fertilizes, carries, and nurtures them for weeks before releasing tiny fully-formed seahorses into the water. Seahorses are terrible swimmers, drifting with currents and gripping seaweed with their curling tails, and they hunt by waiting and sucking in tiny prey with their snouts. They are masters of camouflage, changing color to match their surroundings.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how male seahorses carry fertilized eggs in a brood pouch and give birth to hundreds of live young, the only animal where males undergo pregnancy. Explore how they swim upright, grip coral with prehensile tails, and how their monogamous courtship includes daily greetings.

name: Seal
teaser: Seals are the acrobats of the cold seas, sleek marine mammals that spend their lives between ocean and ice. They are superb swimmers, using their hind flippers like a fish tail and closing their nostrils to dive deep, some staying under for over an hour. True seals, like the harbor seal, cannot walk on their flippers and haul out like caterpillars, while fur seals and sea lions can walk upright. They are intelligent, curious, and vocal, and they were once hunted so heavily that many species nearly vanished.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how seals are marine mammals that dive for fish, some like the elephant seal diving 1,500 meters for up to two hours, sleeping underwater, and coming ashore to breed and molt. Explore the difference between true seals and sea lions, their whiskers that sense fish wakes, and their clumsy-yet-graceful double life.

name: Seal Life
teaser: Seals are the split personalities of the animal kingdom — sleek, graceful torpedoes in the water and clumsy, plodding sunbathers on land. They belong to a group called pinnipeds ('fin-feet'), and their bodies are built entirely for the water: streamlined, with flippers instead of legs, and the ability to hold their breath for dramatic lengths of time. At sea, seals are expert hunters, chasing fish and squid in the dark depths; on land, they haul out to rest, molt, and raise their young, moving with an awkward wiggle that looks almost comical next to their underwater grace.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how seals divide time between sea and shore, then explain why they haul out.

name: Seal Pups
teaser: Seal pups are born on ice, beaches, and rocks, and their first weeks are a race to grow. A harp seal pup is born on the pack ice with a white coat that hides it from polar bears, and its mother's milk is so rich, up to sixty percent fat, that the pup triples its weight in under two weeks. Then the mother returns to sea, and the pup is on its own, learning to swim, fish, and survive. Grey seal pups, born on British and Canadian shores, stay with their mothers for a few weeks before the same sudden independence.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how seal pups are born on ice or beaches with white or golden coats, nursing milk so rich they double their weight in weeks, then abruptly weaned when their mothers return to sea, left to learn swimming and hunting alone. Explore the harp seal's white coat, the hooded seal's brief nursing, and the dangers from ice loss and predators.

name: Seal Species Around the World
teaser: There are about thirty species of seals, and they span the globe, from the Arctic to the Antarctic and everywhere between. The walrus is the giant of the family with tusks, the elephant seal can weigh four tonnes, and the tiny ringed seal fits in a bathtub. The leopard seal of Antarctica hunts penguins, the crabeater seal eats krill with its sieve-like teeth, and monk seals live in warm waters. What unites them is the marine life, the blubber, and the diving skill, and each species has its own way of surviving the sea.

exploreAction.instruction: List three seal species, then explain how earless and eared seals differ.

name: Seal Whiskers
teaser: A seal's whiskers are super-sensors that work like a second set of eyes in murky water. Each whisker is packed with nerves that detect the tiny water movements made by swimming fish, and a seal can follow the wake of a fish it cannot see, tracking it through dark or muddy water. Researchers have shown seals can tell the size and shape of an object just from the ripples it makes, and even distinguish a fish by its wake. In total darkness, a seal hunts with its whiskers.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how seals and sea lions use whiskers called vibrissae to detect water movements, allowing a blindfolded seal to follow a fish's wake minutes after it passed, and how some can sense the pressure trail of a submarine. Explore the whisker follicle structure, the physics of wake tracking, and how the design inspires underwater robots.

name: Secretary Bird
teaser: The secretary bird is the strangest of birds of prey, a long-legged raptor of the African savanna that hunts on foot, walking up to thirty kilometers a day. Its name comes from the quill-like feathers behind its head, which look like the pens a secretary once tucked behind an ear. It hunts snakes, small mammals, and insects, and it is famous for its snake-killing stomps, kicking with powerful legs at up to two hundred strikes per minute. The kick is so fast that the snake has no time to strike back.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the secretary bird of African savannas hunts snakes by stomping them with powerful kicks of up to 195 Newtons, delivered in rapid succession. Explore its long eyelash-like feathers, its name from the quill pens behind 19th-century secretaries' ears, and its habit of walking up to 20 km a day on foot.

name: Secretary Bird Kicks
teaser: The secretary bird's kick is one of the deadliest strikes in the bird world. It hunts snakes, including venomous ones, on the African plains, and it stamps with its long, powerful legs, delivering kicks that can crush a snake's skull in a single blow. The kick is delivered with such speed that it is nearly invisible, and the bird's feet are protected by thick scales that venomous fangs cannot easily pierce. It even uses its wings as shields, flaring them to distract the snake before the final stomp.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how secretary birds deliver kicks with up to 195 Newtons of force, five times their own body weight, delivered in less than 15 milliseconds, stunning snakes so quickly they can't strike back, before the bird finishes them with more stomps or holds. Explore the high-speed footage that measured the kicks, the accuracy of the timing, and the snake-hunting strategy.

name: Seed Banks
teaser: Seed banks are the world's insurance policies for plants, vaults where millions of seeds are dried, frozen, and stored so that species can never truly be lost. The Svalbard Global Seed Vault, buried in an Arctic mountain, holds over a million crop varieties from every country, a backup copy of the world's agriculture. If a crop fails, a variety is lost, or a plant goes extinct, seeds can be withdrawn and regrown. Seed banks are also botanical arks, preserving rare wild plants alongside the staple crops that feed humanity.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how seed banks freeze seeds from hundreds of thousands of plant species as insurance against extinction, from the Svalbard Global Seed Vault carved into Arctic permafrost to national banks worldwide. Explore how seeds are dried and frozen, why crop diversity matters for food security, and how banks help restore damaged landscapes.

name: Serval
teaser: The serval is a tall, elegant wild cat of the African grasslands, with the longest legs relative to its body of any cat, and ears so large they can pinpoint the rustle of a rodent in tall grass. It is a specialist hunter of rats and mice, and it listens, then leaps high into the air, pouncing down onto its prey with a precise strike, sometimes catching birds mid-flight. Its long legs and neck let it see over the grass, and its spots break up its outline as it stalks. It is one of the most successful small hunters in Africa.
