exploreAction.instruction: Read how servals have the longest legs relative to body size of any cat, leaping 3 meters into the air to catch birds, and using huge ears to hear rodents underground before pouncing. Explore their grassland home in Africa, their near 60 percent hunting success, one of the highest of cats, and their spotted coats.

name: Shoebill
teaser: The shoebill is a prehistoric-looking bird of the African swamps, standing up to a meter and a half tall with a huge, clog-shaped bill that gives it its name. It hunts by standing completely still in the water for hours, then lunging forward to grab lungfish, catfish, and even baby crocodiles in its enormous beak. Its bill is one of the largest of any bird, and it makes a strange clattering sound with it. Its slow, motionless hunting style and unblinking stare make it one of the most memorable birds on Earth.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the shoebill of African papyrus swamps stands motionless for hours like a statue, then strikes with its enormous shoe-shaped bill to grab lungfish and even baby crocodiles. Explore its unsettling stare, its bill-clattering greeting, and why it's considered a living fossil.

name: Shrew
teaser: The shrew is a tiny mammal with a terrifying metabolism, and it must eat constantly just to stay alive. Some shrews eat more than their own body weight in insects and worms every day, and their hearts beat over a thousand times a minute. They are ferocious for their size, attacking prey bigger than themselves, and some have venomous saliva. The Etruscan shrew is one of the smallest mammals alive, weighing less than two grams, yet it hunts like a tiny tiger. Most live less than two years, burning through life at full speed.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how shrews have the highest metabolism of any mammal, eating up to three times their body weight daily, and some like the water shrew and short-tailed shrew carry venom in their saliva. Explore their constant eating, their heart rates over 1,000 beats a minute, and how they survive winter by shrinking their own skulls and organs.

name: Siberian Tiger
teaser: The Siberian tiger, also called the Amur tiger, is the largest cat in the world, with males weighing over three hundred kilograms, and it lives in the snowy forests of the Russian Far East. Its thick coat and layer of fat protect it from brutal winters, and its pale stripes blend into the snow and birch trunks. It needs a huge territory, up to a thousand square kilometers, to find enough deer and wild boar. Decades of protection have brought it back from the brink, though poaching and logging still threaten it.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how Siberian or Amur tigers are the largest cats, males reaching 300 kg, surviving in the snowy forests of Russia's Far East with thick fur and fat, hunting wild boar and deer across huge territories. Explore their comeback from near extinction under strict protection, and the corridors needed to connect their scattered populations.

name: Silk Moth
teaser: The silk moth is the insect that clothed the world, domesticated for five thousand years for the silk in its cocoon. The Bombyx mori, the domestic silk moth, is so specialized that it cannot fly or survive in the wild, and it lives only where humans raise it. Its caterpillar spins a single continuous silk thread up to a kilometer long, and the cocoon is carefully harvested, with the thread unraveled to weave silk fabric. The secret of silk production was guarded by China for millennia, one of history's most valuable trade secrets.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the domesticated silkworm moth was bred over thousands of years for a single job, spinning a continuous silk cocoon thread up to a kilometer long that became the fabric of empires along the Silk Road. Explore how silk is unwound, why the moth can't fly, and the secret of its Chinese origin.

name: Silverback Gorilla
teaser: The silverback is the leader of a mountain gorilla family, a mature male named for the silver saddle of hair that grows on his back when he reaches adulthood. He is the family's protector, guide, and peacemaker, deciding when the group eats, sleeps, and travels, and settling squabbles among the younger gorillas. He fights off threats, and his powerful chest-beating display can be heard for a kilometer. Despite his size, he is gentle with his family, playing with the young and grooming his mates, and he may lead the group for decades.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how a silverback gorilla leads his troop through the forest, deciding when to feed, rest, and travel, breaking up squabbles, and protecting his family from threats, even dying to defend them. Explore how his silver hair signals maturity, his huge strength, and how Dian Fossey's studies revealed his gentle leadership.

name: Skunk
teaser: The skunk is the mammal with the chemical defense, and its spray is one of the most effective weapons in nature. Glands under its tail produce a foul-smelling oil that can be aimed with accuracy up to three meters, and the smell lingers for days, warning every predator in the area. Before spraying, the skunk gives clear warnings: it stamps its feet, raises its tail, and hisses, and only sprays as a last resort. The spray is not just stinky but can sting the eyes, and a skunk can spray several times before its glands empty.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how skunks defend with a foul musk sprayed from glands under their tail, accurate to 3 meters and potent enough to be smelled a kilometer away, after giving unmistakable warnings by stamping and raising their tails. Explore why predators learn to avoid their black-and-white warning colors, and why skunks are beneficial pest eaters.

name: Sloth
teaser: The sloth is the slowest mammal on Earth, and it has built its whole life around moving slowly. It sleeps up to twenty hours a day, and it moves so slowly that algae grows in its fur, turning it green and camouflaging it in the rainforest canopy, where it spends almost its entire life. It descends to the ground about once a week to relieve itself, a slow and dangerous journey. Sloths can swim, surprisingly well, and their slow pace is an energy-saving strategy for a diet of leaves that barely nourishes.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how sloths move so slowly that algae grows in their fur, camouflaging them and providing nutrients, and they descend from trees only once a week to poop. Explore their upside-down life, their three-toed claws, their slow metabolism, and how slowness is an energy-saving survival strategy.

name: Sloth Claws
teaser: A sloth's claws are its ticket to the canopy — long, curved hooks up to ten centimeters long that lock onto branches and let the sloth hang securely while it sleeps, eats, and even gives birth. The claws aren't retractable like a cat's; they're permanently extended, and the sloth's limbs are built around them: its front legs are longer than its back legs, and its hands are fused into a hook-like shape. The claws are so specialized for hanging that sloths are nearly helpless on the ground, where they drag themselves along on their elbows.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how sloth claws work, then explain why they come down from trees at all.

name: Sloth Digestion
teaser: A sloth's stomach is a slow-cooker that turns the world's worst food into a meal. Leaves are tough, low in nutrition, and full of defensive chemicals, so the sloth has evolved one of the slowest digestive systems of any mammal: a multi-chambered stomach, like a cow's, where the food ferments for days — up to a month — while symbiotic bacteria break down the cellulose. The payoff is that the sloth can survive on leaves that would starve most other animals, which lets it live high in trees where the food is safe from competition.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover why sloth digestion takes so long, then explain how often they descend to defecate.

name: Slow Worm
teaser: The slow worm looks like a snake but is actually a legless lizard, and it has the telltale signs: eyelids that blink, ear openings, and the ability to shed its tail when grabbed. Found in gardens and grasslands across Europe, it is harmless, feeding on slow prey like slugs and worms. When threatened, it drops its tail, which wriggles to distract the predator, then grows a new, shorter one. Slow worms are actually more closely related to skinks than snakes, and they can live over thirty years.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how slow worms are legless lizards, not snakes, with eyelids, ear openings, and the ability to shed their tails, and they live in gardens and grasslands eating slugs and snails. Explore why they're gardeners' friends, their blue-spotted males, and how to tell them from snakes.

name: Snail
teaser: The snail is the patient traveler of the garden, carrying its home on its back and gliding on a single muscular foot. It moves on a layer of mucus that it secretes as it goes, and the slime protects its foot and lets it climb walls and even glass. A snail's shell grows with it, and it can retreat inside and seal the opening to survive drought and winter. Snails have thousands of microscopic teeth on a ribbon called a radula, and they are hermaphrodites, each one able to lay eggs. They have lived on Earth for over five hundred million years.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how snails glide on a single muscular foot with slime, retreat into spiral shells, and use a rasping radula tongue with thousands of microscopic teeth, with some species like the cone snail hunting fish with venom harpoons. Explore the giant African land snail, the garden snail's homing, and how snails helped map human brain cells.

name: Snake Senses
teaser: Snakes sense the world in ways humans cannot. They taste the air with their forked tongues, flicking scent particles to a special organ in the roof of their mouths, building a detailed chemical map of their surroundings. Many have pit organs that detect the infrared heat of warm-blooded prey, letting them hunt in total darkness. They have no external ears, feeling vibrations through their jawbones instead, and some see well while others see little. Every sense is tuned for one thing: finding prey and avoiding becoming prey.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover how snakes smell with their tongues, then explain heat pits.

name: Snake Senses
teaser: A snake experiences the world through smell, heat, and vibration. Its forked tongue samples the air constantly, delivering scent particles to the Jacobson's organ in its mouth, and the fork lets it detect the direction of a smell. Pit vipers, pythons, and boas have heat-sensing pits on their faces that build a thermal image of their surroundings, letting them strike at warm prey in pitch darkness. Snakes feel footsteps through the ground, since they have no ears, and their whole bodies are sensitive to vibration. They are ambush predators with senses built for one purpose.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how snakes sense the world through flicking tongues that carry scent molecules to a vomeronasal organ, some with heat-sensing pits that see infrared, jaw bones that hear ground vibrations, and some like sea snakes with vision sharpened underwater. Explore the combination of senses that makes them such precise hunters in darkness.

name: Snow Leopard
teaser: The snow leopard is the ghost of the high mountains, a cat that lives above three thousand meters in the peaks of Central Asia, where oxygen is thin and winters are brutal. Its thick, smoky-grey coat with dark rosettes camouflages it among the rocks, and its huge, furred paws work like snowshoes. Its long tail, nearly as long as its body, wraps around it like a scarf and balances it on cliff edges. It hunts ibex and blue sheep, and it is so elusive that it is called the ghost cat, rarely seen even by researchers who study it.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how snow leopards of the Himalayas leap 15 meters between cliffs, wrap their tails around themselves like scarves, and are so elusive locals call them ghosts. Explore their thick spotted fur, their bluish-grey eyes, their shrinking habitat, and the camera-trap studies trying to count them.

name: Snow Leopard Cubs
teaser: Snow leopard cubs are born in the harsh heart of winter, in a den high in the mountains, usually two or three to a litter. They are born blind and helpless, covered in thick grey fur, and they stay in the den for weeks while their mother hunts. They begin exploring at around two months, following their mother on hunts and learning to stalk the ibex and sheep of the high peaks, and they stay with her for nearly two years. Their survival rate is low, but each surviving cub carries on the ghost cat's lineage in the roof of the world.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how snow leopard mothers raise cubs in remote mountain dens, nursing them for months, teaching them to stalk through steep terrain, and keeping them hidden for their first year while defending territory that can span 1,000 square kilometers. Explore the cubs' smoky coats, their stay with mothers into their second year, and the camera traps that finally documented dens.

name: Snow Leopard Survival
teaser: The snow leopard is the ghost of the high Himalayas, living where the air is thin and the cold bites at minus 40 degrees. Everything about it is built for that world: a coat of dense, woolly fur with a pale smoky color that vanishes against the rock; a thick, meter-long tail that wraps around its face like a scarf when it sleeps; and huge, fur-padded paws that act like snowshoes. It hunts blue sheep and ibex on slopes so steep that a fall would be fatal, and it can leap six times its own body length.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover how snow leopards survive thin air and cold, then explain their camouflage.

name: Snow Monkey Hot Springs
teaser: The Japanese macaque, better known as the snow monkey, has found the ultimate winter luxury: hot springs. In the mountains of northern Japan, where winter temperatures plunge and snow buries the forest, troops of snow monkeys soak in natural geothermal pools — sitting in the steaming water, grooming each other, and looking, to any human observer, profoundly relaxed. The behavior is a recent invention, first seen in the 1960s when one monkey discovered the warm pools, and it spread through the troop as others copied her — a textbook example of animal culture spreading through imitation.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover how snow monkeys use hot springs, then explain how the habit spread.

name: Snowy Owl
teaser: The snowy owl is the white hunter of the Arctic, a bird so adapted to the tundra that it breeds on the open ground of the far north. Its pure white feathers, more in males and heavily speckled in females, camouflage it against the snow, and thick feathering covers even its toes for warmth. It hunts lemmings and voles by day, since the Arctic summer has almost no night, perching on mounds and diving down on its prey. In years when lemmings crash, snowy owls fly south, sometimes reaching the United States, delighting birdwatchers.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how snowy owls breed on the Arctic tundra, nesting on the ground in sync with lemming booms, and hunt around the clock under the midnight sun. Explore how their white feathers provide camouflage, their yellow eyes, and how hungry years send them irrupting far south.

name: Snowy Owl and Lemmings
teaser: The snowy owl's life is tied to the lemming, its favorite food, and its breeding success follows the lemming cycle. In years when lemmings are abundant, snowy owls lay more eggs, up to eleven in a clutch, and raise large families. When lemming populations crash, as they do cyclically every few years, the owls may lay few or no eggs at all, and many fly south in search of food. The owls even defend their nesting territory by driving off predators like arctic foxes, and their lives are a mirror of the lemming's boom-and-bust world.

exploreAction.targetName: Explore the snowy owl's prey cycle
exploreAction.instruction: Read how snowy owl breeding success tracks lemming populations, with owls nesting and laying more eggs in lemming boom years and skipping breeding entirely in bust years, a boom-bust cycle that also drives Arctic foxes and other predators. Explore the lemming population crashes and spikes, the owl's nomadic movements to find prey, and the irruptions south in hungry years.

name: Social Insects
teaser: Social insects, like bees, ants, wasps, and termites, live in colonies that work like a single superorganism. Each colony is built on a division of labor: a queen lays eggs, workers forage, build, and care for the young, and soldiers defend, with each individual acting like a cell of one giant body. They communicate with chemical signals, dances, and sounds, and their cooperation lets them build nests, farm fungus, and wage war. Their colonies can last for decades and number in the millions, and together they outweigh and outnumber all other insects.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how ants, bees, termites, and wasps build societies that function like a single superorganism, with queens, workers, soldiers, and complex division of labor, from bee waggle dances to ant bridges and termite towers with air conditioning. Explore how simple individuals create collective intelligence.

name: Spadefoot Toad
teaser: The spadefoot toad is the desert's waiting game champion, a toad named for the sharp, shovel-like growths on its hind feet that it uses to dig. It spends almost its whole life buried underground, sometimes for years, waiting for rain, then emerges in a sudden frenzy when desert storms hit. It breeds explosively in temporary pools, its tadpoles racing to metamorphose before the water evaporates, and some tadpoles even eat their smaller siblings to grow faster. In the desert, the spadefoot's whole life is a race against the sun.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how spadefoot toads use sharp keratin spades on their hind feet to dig backwards into desert soil, emerging in explosive breeding frenzies after rare rains. Explore how tadpoles can metamorphose in just two weeks to beat drying pools, and how some species wait years between rains.

name: Sperm Whale
teaser: The sperm whale is the largest toothed predator on Earth, a deep-sea giant with the biggest brain of any animal, weighing up to nine kilograms. Males can reach twenty meters and weigh fifty tonnes, and they dive deeper than almost any mammal, plunging over two thousand meters to hunt giant squid in the cold dark. Its huge head holds a reservoir of spermaceti oil, once hunted for lamps and lubricants, and its skin bears the circular scars of squid sucker battles. It is the deepest-diving whale, and it is still full of mysteries.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how sperm whales dive over 2,000 meters for up to 90 minutes hunting squid, carrying the largest brain on Earth and a head full of spermaceti oil that helps with buoyancy and echolocation. Explore the matriarchal pods, the scars from giant squid battles, and how their clan dialects vary like human cultures.

name: Sperm Whale Dives
teaser: The sperm whale is the champion deep diver of the animal kingdom, plunging over two thousand meters in search of giant squid. A dive lasts about ninety minutes, and the whale slows its heart, stores oxygen in its muscles, and collapses its ribcage and lungs to withstand the crushing pressure. It hunts in near-total darkness, finding squid with echolocation, and its huge head may help it focus sound. After a deep dive, it rests at the surface for up to ten minutes, breathing and rebuilding oxygen before diving again.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how deep sperm whales dive, then explain their adaptations for pressure.

name: Sperm Whale Sonar
teaser: The sperm whale produces the loudest sound of any animal, a series of clicks that can reach over two hundred decibels, loud enough to stun or even kill prey. The clicks are made by air forced through structures in its huge head, which focuses the sound like a giant acoustic lens, and they are used as sonar to scan the dark depths for squid. Different clicks have different uses: some for echolocation, some for communication between whales, and each whale has its own click pattern, a personal signature. The click is powerful enough to vibrate the water for kilometers.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover how sperm whales use echolocation clicks, then explain the spermaceti organ.

name: Spider Bites
teaser: Despite their fearsome reputation, spiders are far less dangerous than most people think. Of the tens of thousands of species, only a handful can seriously harm humans, and most bites happen when a spider is trapped against skin. The black widow and brown recluse in North America and the funnel-web in Australia are the ones to treat seriously, with antivenoms available. Most other spiders cannot even pierce human skin, and spiders eat enormous numbers of pests. The best bite safety is simple: shake out shoes, check dark corners, and leave spiders alone.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how only a few spiders worldwide have venom dangerous to humans, like the widow and recluse, with most bites harmless, and spider bite myths vastly exaggerate the danger, while insect stings and wasps cause far more medical visits. Explore the symptoms of widow and recluse bites, the antivenoms, and why doctors see so few real spider bites.

name: Spider Courtship
teaser: Spider courtship is a high-stakes performance, since the female is often bigger and sometimes hungrier than the male. Male jumping spiders dance, waving their colorful legs and abdomens in intricate routines to convince the female they are suitors, not snacks. Male peacock spiders flash iridescent colors, and male wolf spiders tap rhythms on the ground. Some males offer gifts, wrapping insects in silk, and the nursery web spider male even ties the female down with silk before mating. The famous black widow name comes from the female occasionally eating the male afterward.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how male spiders risk being eaten during courtship, so they signal with plucked web vibrations, offer prey gifts, dance with patterned legs, and some even tie females down with silk, while others like the redback perform a somersault onto the female's fangs. Explore the mating strategies, sexual cannibalism, and why males so often die young.

name: Spider Silk
teaser: Spider silk is one of the strongest materials in nature, stronger by weight than steel and tougher than Kevlar, and it is also elastic, stretching without breaking. A spider produces it as liquid protein in glands, pulling it out through spinnerets to form the thread, and different silks have different uses: dragline silk for frames, sticky capture silk for prey, and soft silk for egg sacs. The orb weaver's web is a masterpiece of engineering, and scientists are working to produce synthetic spider silk for medical stitches, bulletproof vests, and lightweight materials.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how spider silk is five times stronger than steel by weight and more elastic than rubber, spun as liquid protein that solidifies into fiber, with different silks for webs, draglines, and egg cases, and orb-weavers recycling their webs by eating them. Explore the attempts to farm and synthesize silk for armor and medical sutures.

name: Spiders vs Insects
teaser: Spiders are often called insects, but they belong to a completely different group, the arachnids. Spiders have eight legs, while insects have six; spiders have two body parts, while insects have three; and spiders have no antennae or wings, while most insects have both. Spiders are predators, most with venom and silk, while insects include plant-eaters, pollinators, and scavengers. In fact, spiders eat enormous numbers of insects, making them farmers' best friends. The two groups are ancient cousins, but they could not be more different.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how spiders differ from insects in body plan, with two body parts instead of three, eight legs instead of six, no antennae or wings, and simple eyes, and spiders belong to arachnids with scorpions and mites. Explore the common confusion, the counting legs trick, and how both groups dominate the invertebrate world.

name: Sponge
teaser: The sponge is the simplest animal on Earth, a living sieve that has existed for over six hundred million years. It has no brain, no nerves, no heart, and no muscles, and it feeds by pumping water through its porous body, filtering out bacteria and tiny particles. A large sponge can filter thousands of liters of water a day, and it is built from special cells that can change jobs and even reassemble if the sponge is strained through a sieve. Sponges are found everywhere, and their skeletons, natural sponges, have been used by humans for bathing for centuries.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how sea sponges are animals despite lacking brains, muscles, or organs, pumping seawater through their bodies to filter food, some species with skeletons of glass needles and others harvested for bathing. Explore how they can regrow from single cells, their chemical defenses that inspire drugs, and their ancient 600-million-year history.

name: Spotted Hyena
teaser: The spotted hyena is one of the most misunderstood animals in Africa, and it is also one of the most successful predators. It has one of the strongest bites of any mammal, strong enough to crush bones, and its jaws can eat almost every part of a carcass, including skin and skeleton. It is a skilled hunter that runs down wildebeest and zebra, and it lives in female-led clans that cooperate to hunt, defend territory, and raise cubs. Its famous laugh is actually an excited call, and its intelligence rivals that of primates.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how spotted hyenas are powerful hunters, not just scavengers, with clans ruled by dominant females larger than males, and their famous laugh is a call of submission or excitement. Explore their bone-crushing jaws, their cubs that fight from birth, and their matriarchal society.

name: Springbok
teaser: The springbok is the acrobat of the African plains, a gazelle famous for pronking, leaping up to three meters in the air with its back arched and legs stiff, a display that can fill the horizon when a herd does it together. The jumps are a signal of health and fitness, showing predators that the herd is strong and not worth chasing, and they are also a way to scan the surroundings for danger. Springboks can run at nearly ninety kilometers an hour and go without water for long periods in the dry savanna.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how springboks leap up to 3.5 meters in stiff-legged jumps called pronking, displaying a crest of white hair, and historically gathered in herds of millions that streamed across the veld. Explore their drought survival on desert shrubs, their speed, and the mass migrations that once rivaled the Serengeti.

name: Squid
teaser: Squid are the jet-powered rockets of the ocean, and they are masters of speed, camouflage, and escape. They swim by sucking water into their mantle and forcing it out through a funnel, jetting backward at high speed, and they change color and texture in an instant. When threatened, many squid release a cloud of ink that acts as a smoke screen, and the deep-sea firefly squid glows blue to confuse predators. Some squid school in enormous numbers, and the colossal squid of the deep is one of the largest invertebrates alive.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how squid are torpedo-shaped cephalopods that jet backward by blasting water through a funnel, changing color with pigment cells, and some species flash and school in coordinated shoals. Explore their three hearts, their ink defense, their fast growth, and the giant squid's deep-sea cousins.

name: Squirrel Food Caching
teaser: Squirrels are famous hoarders, and their food caching is a serious science. They hide hundreds of nuts in the autumn, burying each one in a shallow hole, and they find them again in winter by memory, smell, and even spatial patterns. Some squirrels scatter-hoard, hiding each nut separately, while others, like red squirrels, build a single great store called a midden. A squirrel can remember the locations of thousands of buried nuts, and the ones it forgets grow into new trees, making squirrels accidental forest gardeners.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how squirrels cache nuts, then explain how they find them again.

name: Squirrel Tail Signals
teaser: A squirrel's bushy tail is a multi-purpose tool. It acts as a parachute, helping the squirrel balance during its spectacular leaps between branches, and it works as a blanket, wrapping around the body for warmth in winter. The tail also communicates: a flicking tail signals agitation, and some species flag their tails to warn of predators. In hot weather, squirrels use their tails as sunshades, and a wet tail can even be used as a towel. It is one of the busiest body parts in the animal kingdom.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover how squirrels use their tails, then explain the alarm signals.

name: Stag Beetle
teaser: The stag beetle is the heavyweight of the insect world, a large beetle whose males carry enormous antler-like jaws that give it its name. The jaws are used in dramatic fights between males for the best breeding spots, wrestling and flipping each other like tiny stags. Despite the fearsome look, the jaws are for display and combat with rivals, not for biting humans. The larvae live in rotting wood for years, growing to the size of a finger, before emerging as adults for a brief few weeks of summer life.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how stag beetles duel with enormous mandibles shaped like deer antlers, males wrestling to win mates, while females' jaws are small and strong for chewing wood. Explore their six-year larval life chewing rotten wood, their size record in the insect world, and their decline as dead wood disappears.

name: Stag Beetle Fights
teaser: Male stag beetles fight with their huge jaws, and the battles are wrestling matches worthy of their namesake. Two males face off on a tree trunk, each trying to grip the other with its mandibles and flip him off the branch, and the winner earns the right to mate with the females nearby. The fights are intense but rarely deadly, and the jaws, though massive, are used more for lifting and flipping than for biting. The males' jaws are also used to signal size and strength, and bigger jaws usually mean a better fighter.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how male stag beetles use their huge mandibles to wrestle rival males, lifting and throwing them from branches to win mating rights, while females have small jaws for chewing wood. Explore the fight rituals, the energy cost of the weapons, and how size determines the outcome of the jousts.

name: Starling Murmurations
teaser: A starling murmuration is one of the most breathtaking sights in nature: hundreds of thousands of starlings swirling together at dusk, forming shapes that ripple and change like a living cloud. The birds fly so close together that they seem to move as one, yet each starling is reacting only to its nearest neighbors, a system of simple rules that creates incredible complexity. Scientists study murmurations to understand collective behavior, and the flocks gather before roosting, possibly to confuse predators or to share information about good feeding grounds.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how starlings form murmurations, then explain why they gather.

name: Stick Insect
teaser: The stick insect is the ultimate disguise artist, an insect that looks so exactly like a twig that it disappears among the branches. Its body is long and thin, colored like bark, and it holds perfectly still by day, swaying gently like a twig in the breeze. Some species look like leaves, others like lichen, and when disturbed they play dead. The largest, from Southeast Asia, can grow over half a meter long, the longest insect in the world. Its eggs even look like seeds, dropped to the forest floor to hatch unseen.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how stick insects mimic twigs so perfectly, with body segments like nodes and legs held like branches, that predators pass them by, some species swaying in the wind to complete the disguise, and the longest can reach 60 cm. Explore parthenogenesis where females lay eggs without males, their camouflage molts, and the eggs that look like seeds.

name: Stonefish
teaser: The stonefish is the most venomous fish in the world, a master of camouflage that sits on the seabed looking exactly like a rock. It has thirteen spines along its back, each carrying venom that can be fatal to humans, and it strikes when stepped on, injecting a toxin that causes excruciating pain. Its venom is so potent that it is studied for its effects on nerves. It hunts by ambush, lunging at fish that swim past, and divers are taught to watch their step in the waters where it lives.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the stonefish of Indo-Pacific reefs is the most venomous fish, camouflaged as an encrusted rock, delivering agonizing venom through dorsal spines that can kill within hours untreated. Explore the antidote, why divers must watch their step, and how its camouflage is nearly perfect.

name: Stork Migration
teaser: Storks are the great travelers of the bird world, and the white stork is famous for its epic migrations between Europe and Africa. Every autumn, European storks fly thousands of kilometers south, crossing the Mediterranean and the Sahara to winter in Africa, soaring on warm thermals to save energy, then returning north in spring to nest on chimneys and rooftops. A stork can travel over three hundred kilometers in a day, and its migrations are so regular that people once believed they were following a compass. Its return is a sign of spring across Europe.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover how far storks migrate, then explain why they ride thermals.

name: Strongest Animals
teaser: The strongest animals in the world are not the biggest. The dung beetle can pull over a thousand times its own body weight, the equivalent of a human dragging six double-decker buses. The leafcutter ant carries fifty times its weight in its jaws, and the rhinoceros beetle can lift eight hundred times its mass. Among the big animals, the elephant can push over trees, and the gorilla is several times stronger than the strongest human. Relative to size, the tiny arthropods are the true powerlifters of nature.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how strength scales wildly, with the dung beetle pulling over 1,100 times its body weight, leafcutter ants carrying 50 times theirs, and elephants moving fallen trees, while the blue whale's sheer power dwarfs all. Explore why small animals seem strongest relative to size, and the physics of scaling.

name: Surinam Toad
teaser: The Surinam toad has one of the strangest parenting strategies in nature: it carries its eggs on its back, in pockets of skin. During mating, the pair rises in the water and somersaults together, and the eggs are pressed onto the female's back, where skin grows over them, forming individual pouches. The tadpoles develop inside these pockets and emerge as fully formed toadlets, popping out one by one. The female looks like a flat, speckled leaf, and her strange, window-like back holds her whole brood until the great emergence.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the Surinam toad embeds its eggs into the spongy skin of the female's back, where they develop into fully formed toadlets that burst out, a strategy found nowhere else. Explore its flattened leaf-like body, its star-tipped fingers for sensing prey in murky water, and its bizarre underwater life.

name: Swan Aggression
teaser: Swans may look graceful, but they are fiercely territorial, and a swan defending its nest is one of the most intimidating sights in nature. A male swan, the cob, patrols his territory and will confront intruders with spread wings, hissing, and powerful wing strikes that can break a person's bone. The wings are the real weapon, driven by strong muscles and capable of hitting with enormous force. Swans are also devoted parents, building huge nests and guarding their cygnets for months, chasing off foxes, dogs, and even boats that come too close.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover why swans hiss and chase, then explain the wing display.

name: Swift
teaser: The swift is the speed champion of the bird world, a bird so built for flight that it even sleeps on the wing. It can stay airborne for almost its entire life, up to ten months at a time, eating, drinking, and even mating in the air, and it only lands to nest. It flies at speeds over a hundred kilometers an hour and can travel thousands of kilometers during migration. Its small feet are barely used, and it is one of the few birds that cannot perch. The common swift may fly millions of kilometers in its lifetime.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the common swift can stay airborne for up to 10 months, eating, sleeping, and even mating on the wing, only landing to nest. Explore how it drinks by skimming water, sleeps with half its brain awake, and racks up millions of kilometers in a lifetime.

name: Swimming Tigers
teaser: Most cats treat water like a punishment, but tigers are the swimmers of the family. They happily wade into rivers, paddle across wide channels, and even hunt in the water, and a tiger has been recorded swimming almost 30 kilometers in a single day. The Bengal tiger of the Sundarbans mangrove forest lives its whole life among rivers and tidal creeks, and big males will sometimes attack prey while chest-deep in water. A tiger's muscular build and partially webbed paws make it a strong, comfortable swimmer, and on hot days a soak is its favorite way to cool down.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover which big cats swim well, then explain why tigers take to water.

name: Sydney Funnel-web Spider
teaser: The Sydney funnel-web spider is one of the most dangerous spiders in the world, a large, aggressive Australian spider with venom that can kill a human within hours. It is named for the funnel-shaped silk entrance to its burrow, and it is most active after rain, when males wander looking for mates. Unlike most spiders, it will readily attack when provoked, rearing up and striking repeatedly. An antivenom developed in 1981 has saved many lives, and its venom is now studied for potential medicines.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the Sydney funnel-web is one of the world's most dangerous spiders, with large fangs and potent neurotoxic venom, aggressive when threatened, but no deaths have occurred since antivenom in 1981, and males roam in warm months. Explore the bite first-aid, the venom research, and the milking program that saves lives.

name: Symbiosis
teaser: Symbiosis is the partnership of different species living together, and it drives much of life on Earth. The clownfish and anemone protect each other, the oxpecker rides rhinos and eats their ticks, and the cleaner wrasse picks parasites off bigger fish, which line up politely to be cleaned. Some partnerships are lopsided: the cuckoo forces other birds to raise its young, a parasitic symbiosis. The most important of all may be the fungi that partner with plant roots, feeding nearly every tree and crop on Earth.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how species partner in symbiosis, from clownfish and anemones, oxpeckers cleaning rhinos, cleaner wrasse fish servicing reef clients, to the fungi and algae inside lichens and the bacteria in our own guts. Explore mutualism, commensalism, and parasitism, and how these partnerships shaped life on Earth.

name: Tadpole
teaser: The tadpole is the larval stage of frogs and toads, a swimming, breathing machine that is almost a different animal from the adult. It hatches from an egg in the water, breathing with gills and feeding on algae, and it grows legs, absorbs its tail, and develops lungs in the process called metamorphosis. The change is dramatic: its gut shortens, its mouth changes from a scraper to a jaw, and its diet changes from plants to insects. In weeks, the pond-dwelling tadpole becomes a land-hopping frog, one of nature's great transformations.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how tadpoles are aquatic larval frogs that breathe through gills, graze on algae with tiny teeth, and undergo metamorphosis that rearranges their whole body into a frog. Explore the hormones driving the change, how some tadpoles eat meat or even siblings, and the fastest metamorphosis in desert pools.

name: Tadpole Life
teaser: Tadpole life is a race against time. Frogs lay their eggs in ponds, often temporary pools that may dry up in weeks, so tadpoles must grow and transform before the water vanishes. They graze constantly on algae, and some species form huge swarms, thousands of black tadpoles wriggling together in the shallows. In crowded pools, some tadpoles turn cannibalistic, and spadefoot toad tadpoles grow carnivorous jaws and eat their siblings for fast growth. The tadpole stage is short, intense, and decisive for the frog's survival.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how tadpoles live, then explain what triggers their transformation.

name: Tapir
teaser: The tapir is a strange, ancient mammal of the tropics, a plant-eater with a short, flexible trunk and a body like a small hippo. It is a living fossil, related to rhinos and horses, and it has changed little in twenty million years. It lives in the rainforests of South America and Southeast Asia, and it is a superb swimmer, often feeding in rivers. The tapir is a gardener of the forest, eating fruit and spreading seeds, and it is important to the rainforests it calls home, though it is threatened by habitat loss.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how tapirs are large forest mammals of South America and Asia with short prehensile trunks, excellent swimmers that dive to feed on river plants, and a conservation status threatened across all four species. Explore their calves with striped coats that fade with age, their seed-spreading role, and their ancient lineage unchanged for 50 million years.

name: Tapir Calf Stripes
teaser: Tapir calves are born with a coat of white stripes and spots, a pattern that looks completely unlike the adult's plain dark coat. The stripes break up the calf's outline in the dappled forest light, camouflaging it from predators while it rests in the undergrowth, and the mother leaves it hidden while she feeds. After a few months, the pattern fades to the adult's solid color. The tapir's camouflage trick is a classic example of how young animals are protected differently from adults.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover why tapir calves are patterned, then explain when the pattern fades.

name: Tarantula
teaser: The tarantula is the giant of the spider world, a large, hairy hunter found on every continent except Antarctica. Despite its fearsome look, its bite is about as dangerous as a bee sting to humans, and it would rather flee than fight. It hunts by ambush or chase, and it has no web, using its thick leg hairs as sensors and weapons, flicking irritating hairs at attackers. Females can live over twenty years, growing huge, while males often die within months of mating. Tarantulas are gentle giants, popular as pets around the world.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how tarantulas, despite their fearsome looks, mostly flee, flicking barbed urticating hairs at threats and only biting in defense with venom rarely dangerous to humans. Explore their molting to grow, their silk-lined burrows, and how females can live 30 years while males often die after mating.

name: Tarantula Hawk
teaser: The tarantula hawk is a huge wasp with one of the most painful stings in the insect world, rated among the worst pain any animal can inflict. It hunts tarantulas, the spider's worst nightmare: the wasp stings the spider, paralyzing it, then drags it to a burrow, lays an egg on it, and seals the entrance. The larva hatches and feeds on the living, paralyzed tarantula, slowly, over weeks. The female wasp is a brilliant metallic blue, and despite its fearsome reputation, it is not aggressive toward humans.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how tarantula hawk wasps, with one of the most painful stings in the insect world, hunt tarantulas, paralyzing them with a precise sting and dragging them to a burrow to lay an egg, the larva eating the still-living spider. Explore the sting rating scale, the iridescent blue-black body, and the battle between wasp and spider.

name: Tardigrade
teaser: The tardigrade, or water bear, is the most indestructible animal on Earth, a microscopic creature that can survive almost anything. It can withstand temperatures from near absolute zero to over one hundred and fifty degrees, survive in the vacuum of space, endure radiation thousands of times the lethal human dose, and go without water for decades, shriveling into a dormant ball called a tun, then reviving when water returns. It has eight stubby legs, a bear-like waddle, and it lives in moss and water everywhere. Scientists study it to understand extreme survival.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how tardigrades, or water bears, microscopic eight-legged animals, survive boiling, freezing, vacuum of space, radiation, and decades without water by drying into a tun state and reviving when wet. Explore where they live from moss to deep sea, their DNA-copying heat-shock proteins, and what makes them nearly indestructible.

name: Tarsier
teaser: The tarsier is a tiny primate with enormous eyes, each one as big as its brain, and it is one of the strangest creatures of the Southeast Asian rainforests. Its eyes are fixed in its skull, so it turns its head almost all the way around, and its huge ears can hear the faint sounds of insects. It is a pure carnivore, leaping between trees at night to catch insects, lizards, and even birds, killing them with a bite to the neck. A tarsier can leap over forty times its own body length, one of the greatest jumpers in the animal kingdom.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how tarsiers of Southeast Asia have eyes bigger than their brains, each eye the size of their whole eyeball, letting them hunt insects in darkness, and can rotate their heads almost 360 degrees. Explore their leaping between trees, their high-pitched calls, and why they're fragile in captivity.

name: Tasmanian Devil
teaser: The Tasmanian devil is the largest surviving carnivorous marsupial, a stocky, black scavenger of Tasmania with a bite so strong that its jaws are among the most powerful for its size of any mammal. It is named for its ferocious screeches and its habit of devouring entire carcasses, bones and all, and its famous gape, a huge, wide yawn.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how Tasmanian devils, the largest carnivorous marsupials, scavenge with bone-crushing jaws and unleash ear-splitting screams and snarls, with a contagious face cancer that nearly wiped them out. Explore their pouch babies, their island home, and the breeding programs and vaccine research fighting devil facial tumor disease.

name: Termite
teaser: The termite is the great builder of the insect world, a social insect that constructs some of the most impressive structures in nature. Termite mounds can tower six meters high, with sophisticated ventilation systems that keep the nest cool and fresh, and the mounds are built from soil, saliva, and droppings, harder than brick. The colony has a king and queen, workers, and soldiers, and some termites farm fungus in underground gardens. Termites recycle dead wood, returning nutrients to the soil, and their mounds are landmarks across Africa and Australia.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how termites build mounds up to 8 meters with internal ventilation that keeps the colony cool, farm fungus gardens, and digest wood through symbiotic microbes. Explore their queen that lays millions of eggs, their soldier castes, and how a single colony can contain millions.

name: Terror Bird
teaser: The terror bird was one of the most fearsome predators ever to walk the Earth, a giant flightless bird that ruled South America for millions of years. It stood up to three meters tall with a massive hooked beak and powerful legs, and it hunted by kicking and slashing, or by grabbing prey in its beak and smashing it against the ground. Some species were the apex predators of their time, chasing down mammals across the grasslands. They went extinct around two million years ago, when the continents connected and new predators arrived.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how terror birds were flightless predators up to 3 meters tall that ran down prey across South America, striking with huge hooked beaks before mammals became top predators. Explore how they dominated for 60 million years, the possible arms race with early mammals, and the mystery of their final extinction.

name: The Aardvark
teaser: The aardvark is Africa's original digger, a strange mammal whose name means earth pig in Afrikaans, even though it is not related to pigs at all. It spends its nights alone, using its powerful claws to tear open termite mounds and ant nests, lapping up the insects with a long, sticky tongue. It has a long snout, rabbit-like ears, and a thick tail, and it can dig a burrow faster than a person with a shovel. Its burrows provide shelter for dozens of other species, making the aardvark a keystone of the savanna.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn what an aardvark really is, then explain its digging power.

name: The Aardvark's Tongue
teaser: The aardvark's tongue is a remarkable tool, up to thirty centimeters long, covered in sticky saliva, and shaped to reach deep into the tunnels of termite mounds. It flicks in and out up to a hundred and fifty times a minute, and it can lap up tens of thousands of ants and termites in a single night. The aardvark's snout is a tubular extension of its face, and its nostrils have special flaps that close against dust and stinging insects while it feeds. It is a living vacuum cleaner, perfectly adapted to a diet of insects.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover how aardvarks eat, then explain why they dig so many holes.

name: The Aardwolf
teaser: The aardwolf is the termite specialist of the hyena family, a shy, striped animal that looks like a small hyena but eats almost nothing but termites. Unlike its big cousins, it has weak jaws and small teeth, built for lapping up termites rather than crushing bones, and it can lick up thousands in a night with its broad, sticky tongue. It lives in pairs that defend a shared territory, marking it with scent, and it raises its cubs in a burrow. It is harmless, gentle, and completely devoted to its insect diet.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover how aardwolves eat termites, then explain why they are shy.

name: The Addax
teaser: The addax is the true ghost of the Sahara — a pale, spiral-horned antelope that once roamed the great desert in the millions and is now one of the rarest large mammals on Earth. Everything about it is built for emptiness: its coat turns nearly white in summer to reflect the sun and grey-brown in winter, and it can survive for months without drinking, getting all the moisture it needs from the sparse desert grasses and tubers it digs up. The addax's hooves are broad and flat, perfect for walking on soft sand, and it follows a nomad's route across the dunes in search of rare rainfall.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover why addax are so endangered, then explain how they survive without drinking.

name: The African Buffalo
teaser: The African buffalo lives in some of the biggest, most organized herds of any large animal — groups of hundreds, sometimes thousands, that move and defend themselves as one. The herd's heart is a tight core of females and calves, protected by an outer ring of bulls, and when a threat appears, the buffalo don't scatter; they face it together. Buffalo are famously unpredictable and aggressive, and they've earned a reputation as one of the most dangerous animals to hunt in Africa — they attack with head lowered, horns ready, and they can circle back and ambush their pursuers.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn why buffalo are considered dangerous, then explain their herd behavior.

name: The African Grey
teaser: The African grey parrot is widely considered the most intelligent bird in the world, with a vocabulary that can exceed a thousand words and a remarkable ability to use them with understanding. The famous parrot Alex could count, name colors and shapes, and answer questions about objects he had never seen before. African greys solve puzzles, mimic sounds, and form deep bonds with their owners, and they can live for fifty years. Their intelligence has made them beloved pets, and tragically, hugely popular, driving heavy trapping in the wild.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover what African greys can learn, then explain the studies on their cognition.

name: The Agouti
teaser: The agouti is a large rodent of the Central and South American rainforests, and it is one of the most important gardeners in the jungle. It feeds on fallen fruit and nuts, especially the huge seeds of the Brazil nut tree, and it buries surplus seeds for later, forgetting many of them, which grow into new trees. A single agouti can scatter seeds over a wide area, and researchers call them the movers of the forest. It has orange-brown fur, a pointed face, and it barks like a dog when alarmed.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover how agoutis scatter seeds, then explain why they help forests.

name: The Albatross Wingspan
teaser: The wandering albatross has the largest wingspan of any living bird, up to three and a half meters, wider than a small plane. Its long, narrow wings are built for gliding, and it locks them in place and soars on the winds of the Southern Ocean, covering enormous distances with barely a flap. It can stay at sea for years, circling the globe on the roaring forties, and it only lands to breed. Its wings are so specialized that it is a poor flyer in calm conditions, but in the ocean winds it is king of the skies.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover how wide albatross wings get, then explain why they are so long.

name: The American Bison
teaser: The American bison is a comeback story written in muscle. Tens of millions once darkened the Great Plains, so many that their migrations literally shook the ground; then, in one of history's great slaughters, hunters reduced them to under a thousand by the 1890s. From that sliver, the bison has clawed back to hundreds of thousands through a century of careful conservation, and it now stands as the national mammal of the United States. A bull can weigh a ton, sprint at fifty kilometers an hour, and plow through prairie snow with a head built like a battering ram.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover the bison's near-extinction and recovery, then explain their ecological role.

name: The Amphibian Crisis
teaser: Amphibians are the most threatened group of vertebrates on Earth, with over forty percent of species at risk of extinction, and they are disappearing faster than any other animal group. Their thin, permeable skin makes them acutely sensitive to pollution, climate change, and the chytrid fungus that is wiping out frog populations worldwide. Amphibians are also vital: they control insect pests, feed birds and fish, and their health reflects the health of their ecosystems. Their decline is a warning sign that the environment is in trouble.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn why amphibians are declining, then explain the chytrid fungus threat.

name: The Andean Condor
teaser: The Andean condor is one of the largest flying birds in the world, with a wingspan of over three meters, and it soars over the Andes and along the coasts of South America. It is a scavenger, riding the mountain updrafts for hours without flapping, scanning for carcasses, and it can fly hundreds of kilometers a day. It is black with a white collar and a bare head, and the male has a fleshy comb. It is a symbol of the Andes, and it is now threatened by poisoning, with conservation programs working to protect it.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how Andean condors glide, then explain their wingspan.

name: The Anhinga
teaser: The anhinga is the snakebird of the American wetlands, a diving bird that swims with only its long, S-shaped neck and spear-like bill above the water. It hunts fish underwater, spearing them with its sharp bill, then surfaces and tosses them into the air to swallow them headfirst. Unlike ducks, its feathers are not waterproof, which lets it dive deep, but means it must dry its wings after fishing, sitting spread-winged in the sun, a pose that gives it another name: the water turkey. It is a superb swimmer and a silent hunter.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover why the anhinga swims with only its neck showing, then explain its sharp bill.

name: The Arctic Fox
teaser: The Arctic fox is a master of extreme camouflage, wearing two coats a year to match its world. In winter, its fur turns pure white to vanish against the snow; in summer, it molts to a brown-grey that blends with the tundra's rocks and plants. The winter coat isn't just white — it's the warmest fur of any animal in the Arctic, with a dense underlayer so effective that the fox can sleep in the open at minus 40 degrees without shivering. Its body is built for the cold: short muzzle, small ears, furry paws that act like snowshoes, and a compact shape that conserves heat.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how arctic foxes change color, then explain their cold-weather adaptations.

name: The Arctic Hare
teaser: The Arctic hare is a survivor of the frozen tundra, a large hare that turns white in winter to vanish against the snow and brown in summer to blend with the rocks. It has shorter ears than other hares, conserving heat, and its thick fur covers even its feet, working like snowshoes. It digs snow burrows for shelter, and it feeds on woody plants, moss, and even frozen grass, scraping through the ice with its claws. Herds of Arctic hares can number in the thousands, moving together across the white landscape.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover how arctic hares change color, then explain their cold survival.

name: The Arctic Tern
teaser: The Arctic tern is the champion of animal travel, migrating between the Arctic and Antarctic every year, a round trip of about seventy thousand kilometers, the longest migration of any animal. It nests in the Arctic summer, then flies south to spend the Antarctic summer, experiencing more daylight than any creature on Earth. Over a thirty-year life, it flies about two and a half million kilometers, the distance to the Moon and back several times. It is guided by the sun, the stars, and the Earth's magnetic field, and it can navigate across oceans with astonishing precision.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how far arctic terns travel, then explain the pole-to-pole route.

name: The Armadillo's Armor
teaser: The armadillo is the only mammal with a built-in suit of armor — and one species, the three-banded armadillo, is the only one that can roll into a perfect ball to protect itself. Its shell is made of bony plates covered in a horny skin, connected by flexible bands that let it curl into a near-impenetrable sphere, tucking its vulnerable head and feet safely inside, leaving predators with nothing to grab except smooth armor. It's such a complete defense that the ball can even roll downhill, and a dog or jaguar will simply give up trying to pry it open.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn what armadillo shells are made of, then explain which species roll into balls.

name: The Axolotl
teaser: The axolotl is the smiling salamander of Mexico, a critically endangered amphibian famous for its ability to regenerate almost any body part. It keeps its larval features for life, feathery gills and all, and it can regrow lost limbs, tails, and even parts of its heart and brain without scarring. It lives only in the canals and lakes around Mexico City, which face pollution and invasive fish. Axolotls are bred in labs worldwide, where they are helping scientists study regeneration, wound healing, and development.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover how axolotls keep larval features, then explain their regeneration.

name: The Aye-Aye
teaser: The aye-aye is one of the strangest animals on Earth — a lemur that looks like a cross between a bat, a rat, and a gremlin, with giant eyes, enormous ears, and a long, skeletal middle finger. That finger is the aye-aye's secret weapon: it uses echolocation-style tapping, knocking rapidly on tree bark with its skinny finger and listening with its huge ears for the hollow echo that reveals an insect grub tunneling inside. Then it bites through the wood and uses the same finger, thin as a twig, to fish the grub out.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how the aye-aye finds grubs, then explain its unusual middle finger.

name: The Babirusa
teaser: The babirusa is a wild pig with a bizarre feature: its canine teeth grow up through the top of its snout and curve backward toward its forehead, in males sometimes curving so far they touch or even pierce the skull. The purpose of these tusks is still debated, but they likely serve as weapons and displays in fights between males. The babirusa lives in the rainforests of the Indonesian island of Sulawesi, and it swims well, sometimes crossing to offshore islands. It is an ancient and unusual member of the pig family.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover why babirusa tusks grow upward, then explain the mystery of their use.

name: The Bald Eagle
teaser: The bald eagle is the national bird of the United States, a symbol of freedom chosen for its majesty and its American habitat. It is not actually bald: its white head feathers appear at maturity, around five years old, and its name comes from an old word meaning white-headed. It is a powerful hunter and scavenger that lives near water, building the largest tree nests of any bird, some weighing a tonne. Saved from extinction by the DDT ban and protection, it has made a spectacular comeback across North America.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn why bald eagles are called bald, then explain their recovery story.

name: The Bandicoot
teaser: The bandicoot is a small, pointy-snouted marsupial of Australia and New Guinea, and it is one of the most important soil engineers on the continent. It digs small, conical holes as it hunts for grubs and insects, aerating the soil and improving water absorption, and a single bandicoot can turn over large areas of earth in a night. It has a backward-opening pouch for its tiny young, and it is an omnivore, eating insects, fungi, and roots. Several species are now endangered, threatened by foxes, cats, and habitat loss.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover how bandicoots forage, then explain their cone-shaped holes.

name: The Barking Sea Lion
teaser: Sea lions are the most vocal of the marine mammals, and their bark is one of the defining sounds of the coast. They bark to communicate across the noisy colonies, males barking to mark territory and challenge rivals, females and pups calling to find each other in the crowd. A sea lion's bark carries over the roar of the surf, and mothers and pups recognize each other's voices even in a colony of thousands. Their barking, honking, and grunting make a rookery one of the loudest places in nature.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how sea lions differ from true seals, then explain their use of front flippers.

name: The Barn Owl
teaser: The barn owl is one of the most widespread birds in the world, a ghostly pale owl that hunts over farmland and grassland on every continent except Antarctica. It is a mouse machine, eating thousands of rodents a year, and its heart-shaped face is a sound collector, funneling the faintest rustle of a vole to its ears. Its hearing is so precise it can catch mice in total darkness. It is silent in flight, and its blood-curdling screech and white, floating appearance gave it a place in folklore as a ghost.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn why barn owls hunt so effectively by sound, then explain their silent approach.

name: The Bat Family
teaser: There are over fourteen hundred species of bats, a fifth of all mammal species, and they live on every continent except Antarctica. They range from the bumblebee bat of Thailand, the smallest mammal on Earth, to flying foxes with two-meter wingspans. Most eat insects, catching them on the wing, while others eat fruit, nectar, fish, frogs, and even blood. They are the only mammals that fly, and their echolocation has inspired sonar technology. Bats are everywhere, and they are vital to almost every ecosystem.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how many bat species exist, then explain the mega and micro bat split.

name: The Bear Family
teaser: The bear family is small but mighty: eight species scattered across the Northern Hemisphere and one in South America. They range from the sun bear, which can weigh as little as a large dog, to the polar bear, the largest land carnivore on Earth, and the Kodiak brown bear, which can top a ton. Bears are surprisingly fast for their bulk, sprinting faster than a racehorse over short distances. Most are omnivores and spend the warm months eating constantly to build fat, then sleep through winter in a state of deep torpor in which they neither eat, drink, nor urinate, living off that stored energy for months.

exploreAction.instruction: List the eight bear species, then explain how they are related.

name: The Beaver's Tail
teaser: The beaver's flat, scaly tail is a multi-purpose tool, one of the most distinctive in nature. It acts as a rudder when swimming, a prop when standing upright, and a signal: the beaver slaps the water with it to warn the family of danger, a crack that echoes across the pond. In summer, the tail releases heat to cool the beaver, and in winter it stores fat. It is also used as a seat, and to balance loads of mud and branches. It is a jack-of-all-trades built for a life in the water.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover what a beaver uses its tail for, then explain the warning slap.

name: The Bee Hummingbird
teaser: The bee hummingbird is the smallest bird in the world, weighing less than two grams and measuring barely five centimeters, smaller than some insects. Found only in Cuba, it is so tiny that its eggs are the size of coffee beans, and its heart beats over a thousand times a minute. It hovers at flowers, drinking nectar with its needle-like bill, and it can beat its wings up to eighty times a second. Despite its size, it is fearless, and it migrates across the island to follow the blooming flowers.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover how small the bee hummingbird is, then explain its habitat.

name: The Beluga
teaser: The beluga is the white whale of the Arctic, one of the most recognizable and social whales in the world. Its pure white color develops with age, and its flexible neck lets it nod and turn its head, giving it an expressive face. It is called the sea canary for its rich repertoire of clicks, whistles, and chirps, and it uses them to communicate within its pod. Belugas have no dorsal fin, an adaptation for swimming under ice, and they can dive over eight hundred meters. They live in the cold Arctic waters, traveling in pods of up to hundreds.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn why belugas are white, then explain their flexible neck.

name: The Bilby
teaser: The bilby is Australia's Easter bunny, a shy, nocturnal marsupial with huge ears, a long snout, and silky blue-grey fur. It digs spiraling burrows to escape the desert heat and predators, and it gets all the moisture it needs from food, never drinking water. Bilbies once ranged across much of Australia, but foxes, cats, and land clearing pushed them to the edges. They now star in Australian Easter campaigns, with chocolate bilbies raising money to help bring them back.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how bilbies survive the desert, then explain their burrow digging.

name: The Black Mamba
teaser: The black mamba is the fastest snake in the world, capable of slithering at over twenty kilometers an hour, and in a straight line across open ground, few animals can outrun it. It is also one of the longest venomous snakes, reaching four meters, and its venom is a fast-acting neurotoxin that can kill a human within hours without treatment. Despite its fearsome reputation, it prefers to flee, and it only attacks when cornered. Its name comes from the black lining of its mouth, which it shows when threatened.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover how fast mambas move, then explain why they are feared.

name: The Blackbird
teaser: The blackbird is one of the most familiar and beloved birds of Europe and Asia, a garden singer with a rich, fluting song that fills the spring evenings. The male is glossy black with a yellow-orange beak, while the female is brown, and both are ground feeders, tilting their heads to listen for worms before pulling them from the soil. Blackbirds are fiercely territorial, and their song, heard at dawn and dusk, is one of the finest in the bird world, a sound of early summer across parks and gardens.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how blackbirds defend territory, then explain the song's role.

name: The Blue Jay
teaser: The blue jay is the loud, clever, and strikingly handsome bird of the eastern United States, with bright blue plumage, a white chest, and a black necklace. It is a member of the corvid family, the cleverest of birds, and it is known for mimicking hawk calls, hoarding acorns by the thousands, and recognizing human faces. It is bold and noisy, and it will mob predators, screaming to drive them off. Its blue color comes not from pigment but from the structure of its feathers scattering light.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how blue jays mimic hawks, then explain their caching.

name: The Blue-Footed Booby
teaser: The blue-footed booby is the clown of the Galapagos, a seabird with bright blue feet that are central to its love life. Males show off their feet in a high-stepping dance, and the bluer the feet, the more attractive the male, since the color comes from the fresh fish in his diet. Boobies are expert divers, plunging from the air into the sea like arrows to catch fish, and their name comes from the Spanish word for clumsy, from their awkward, comical walk on land. They nest on the ground in noisy colonies.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn why boobies have blue feet, then explain the dance.

name: The Bonobo
teaser: The bonobo is the peacekeeper of the great apes — a chimpanzee cousin that runs its society on empathy, cooperation, and sex instead of aggression. Where chimpanzee groups are male-dominated and violent, bonobo groups are led by females, who form alliances that keep the peace, and conflicts that would turn into fights among chimps are resolved with grooming, sharing, and sexual contact. Bonobo societies are famously egalitarian: food is shared, females dominate through social bonds, and even strangers are welcomed rather than attacked.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover how bonobo societies differ from chimps, then explain the female-led structure.

name: The Booby Dance
teaser: The blue-footed booby's courtship dance is one of the most entertaining in the bird world. The male struts, lifting one bright blue foot high, then the other, in a high-stepping march, whistling and pointing his beak at the sky, and the female joins in, mirroring his moves. The dance is a health test: the bluest feet come from a diet of fresh fish, and females choose the males with the brightest feet, since they are the best providers. The pair may dance for years, and the ritual is performed every breeding season.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover what the booby dance signals, then explain the foot color's role.

name: The Bowerbird
teaser: The bowerbird is the interior decorator of the bird world, a plain-looking bird that builds an extraordinary structure just to impress females. The male clears a stage on the forest floor and builds an elaborate bower, a tunnel or avenue of twigs, decorated with objects he collects: blue flowers, berries, snail shells, stones, and even human items like bottle caps and glass. Females visit the bowers like gallery critics, inspecting the display, and the males perform dances and songs around them. The best-decorated bower wins the mate.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover how bowerbirds build bowers, then explain what females judge.

name: The Budgerigar
teaser: The budgerigar, or budgie, is the most popular pet bird in the world, a small, friendly parrot native to the Australian outback. In the wild, budgies travel in huge, wheeling flocks over the grasslands, and they are one of the few birds that breed in response to rain rather than season. They are tiny parrots, and their ability to mimic speech, their playful nature, and their bright green and yellow wild plumage have made them beloved companions for over a century. Wild budgies are still common across most of Australia.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover where budgies live in the wild, then explain their flock behavior.

name: The Burrowing Owl
teaser: The burrowing owl is the underground owl of the Americas, a small, long-legged owl that lives in burrows instead of trees. It often moves into abandoned prairie dog and ground squirrel holes, and it is active by day, standing guard at the burrow entrance on its long legs. It hisses like a rattlesnake when threatened, mimicking the sound to scare off predators, and it decorates its burrow entrance with dung to attract the beetles it eats. It nests, roosts, and raises its young underground.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how burrowing owls use ground squirrel holes, then explain their daytime hunting.

name: The Burrowing Owl's Dance
teaser: The burrowing owl's dance is one of nature's strangest spectacles: a bird that appears to be dancing on the ground. When alarmed or excited, the owl bobs, weaves, and turns, leaning in and out with a jerky motion, and a group may all dance together, a behavior that looks comical but is serious communication. The dance may intimidate predators or signal between owls, and researchers still debate its exact meaning. Whatever the reason, a field of dancing burrowing owls is unforgettable.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how burrowing owls mimic rattlesnakes, then explain why the trick works.

name: The Bush Dog
teaser: The bush dog is the dog family's bulldog — a small, stocky, short-legged canid of Central and South American forests that looks like a cross between a teddy bear and a sausage dog, with a stout body built for one purpose: chasing prey through dense undergrowth. Bush dogs are pack hunters with webbed feet, perfect for wetlands, and they'll take on prey much bigger than themselves, hunting capybaras — animals twenty times their size — through the forest. A pack of bush dogs can bring down prey that would seem impossible for their size, using teamwork and relentless pursuit.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover where bush dogs live, then explain their pack hunting.

name: The Caecilian
teaser: The caecilian is a legless, worm-like amphibian that lives buried in the soil of the tropics, and it is almost never seen. It hunts earthworms and insects underground, sensing them with tentacles on its head, and it is actually a relative of frogs and salamanders. Some caecilians give birth to live young and feed them with a special skin milk, and the young are born with teeth to scrape it off. They are among the least known animals on Earth, and new species are still being discovered.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn what caecilians are, then explain why they are rarely seen.

name: The Caiman
teaser: The caiman is a crocodilian of the Americas, a smaller, sleeker cousin of the alligator and crocodile. It lives in rivers, lakes, and swamps from Central to South America, hunting fish, birds, and small mammals, and the black caiman of the Amazon can grow over five meters long, the largest predator in the river. Caiman mothers build nests and guard their young, and the species was once hunted heavily for its hide. In some areas, caimans have recovered so well that they now shape the whole wetland ecosystem.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how caimans differ from alligators, then explain their size range.

name: The California Condor
teaser: The California condor is one of the rarest birds on Earth and one of the largest flying birds in North America, with a wingspan of nearly three meters. By 1982, only twenty-two remained, and scientists took them all into captivity for breeding. Today, over five hundred condors live in zoos and in the wild, flying free over California, Arizona, and Mexico. They are scavengers that soar for hours, and each bird is tracked with numbered tags. Their recovery is one of the greatest conservation stories ever told.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover how close condors came to extinction, then explain the captive breeding program.

name: The Canary
teaser: The canary is the singer of the bird world, a small finch domesticated for centuries for its beautiful song. Wild canaries live on the Canary Islands, and the bright yellow color of the domestic bird was bred by humans, since wild canaries are olive-green. Canaries were once carried into coal mines as living gas detectors: if the bird collapsed, the miners knew the air was dangerous, giving rise to the phrase canary in a coal mine. Their song, learned and practiced, is one of the finest in the cage bird world.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover why canaries were used in mines, then explain the warning role.

name: The Capybara
teaser: The capybara is the world's largest rodent, a gentle giant of the South American wetlands that can weigh as much as an adult human. It is semi-aquatic, with webbed feet, eyes and nostrils on top of its head for swimming, and a calm nature that lets birds perch on its back and groom it. Capybaras live in social groups, and they communicate with whistles, clicks, and barks. Its favorite pastime is lounging in water, where it escapes heat and predators.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how big capybaras get, then explain their semi-aquatic life.

name: The Caracal
teaser: The caracal is the cat with the world's most striking ears — long, black-tipped tufts that stand up like a desert radio antenna. Those ears are not decoration: the caracal can hear a rodent moving underground from meters away, and it uses that hearing to hunt with a jump that would impress an Olympic athlete. A caracal can leap nearly three meters straight up into the air and knock a flying bird out of the sky with both paws — a move so famous that falconers in ancient India trained caracals to catch birds for them.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover how caracals leap for birds, then explain the ear tufts' possible purpose.

name: The Cardinal
teaser: The cardinal is the red jewel of North American gardens, a songbird so striking that it is the state bird of seven states. The male is brilliant crimson with a black mask and crest, while the female is a warm brown with red accents, and both sing, unusual among songbirds. Cardinals stay year-round, their red feathers blazing against the winter snow, and they are devoted parents, raising several broods a year.
