They are dabblers — they tip forward to graze underwater plants without diving — and they can take off almost vertically from a tiny patch of water. A mallard's quack, famously, does not echo, and the female's quack is louder than the male's.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover why mallards are so widespread, then explain their migration.

name: The Manatee
teaser: The manatee is the gentle giant of warm rivers and springs, a slow-moving marine mammal that can reach four meters and weigh over 500 kilograms, yet eats nothing but plants. It grazes on seagrass and river vegetation, consuming up to ten percent of its body weight every day, and its closest living relatives are elephants. Manatees must surface to breathe every few minutes, but they can rest underwater for up to twenty minutes by holding their breath. They are famously docile and curious, and their low-frequency calls keep mothers and calves in contact in murky water. Boat strikes are their greatest threat, scarring and killing many each year.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover how manatees stay warm in winter, then explain their slow pace.

name: The Mandrill
teaser: The mandrill wears the most colorful face in the animal kingdom — a blaze of electric blue and red that looks like warpaint, and it's not decoration: it's a status report. The colors come from blood vessels and pigment arranged in ridges, and the brighter and more saturated a male's face, the higher his rank and the better his health — females and low-ranking males are noticeably duller. The blue in particular is structural color, the same physics that makes a blue jay blue, and it's a signal of testosterone and dominance.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn why mandrills have such bright faces, then explain what the color signals.

name: The Maned Wolf
teaser: The maned wolf looks like a fox on stilts — a long-legged, golden-furred canid from the grasslands of South America that stands nearly a meter tall at the shoulder, with legs so long they seem to belong to a different animal. Those legs are the maned wolf's survival tool: they let it see and move over the tall grass of its savanna home, peering above the vegetation and traveling long distances with an almost mechanical gait.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn what the maned wolf really is, then explain its unusual diet.

name: The Marabou Stork
teaser: The marabou stork is the bald scavenging stork of Africa, a huge, unlovely bird that stands over a meter and a half tall with a wingspan of nearly three meters — among the largest of any land bird. Its bare head and neck, like a vulture's, are an adaptation for scavenging: feathers would become fouled with blood and gore as it feeds. The marabou has a balloon-like throat pouch that inflates during display, and it is one of the few birds that eats carrion alongside vultures, sometimes bullying them off kills. It also eats fish, frogs and even flamingo chicks, and it soars on thermals like a vulture, looking for the next meal.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn why marabou storks are called undertaker birds, then explain their scavenging.

name: The Marine Iguana
teaser: The marine iguana is the only sea-swimming lizard on Earth, found only in the Galápagos Islands. It dives into the cold Pacific to graze on underwater algae, holding its breath for up to half an hour and using its flattened tail to swim. Because the water is so cold, the iguanas bask on black volcanic rocks to warm up, and when they are too cold to swim, they simply stop — they can even shrink their skeletons to survive food shortages. When they sneeze, they spray out concentrated salt they have absorbed from the sea, leaving white crusts on their heads like a crown of salt.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover how marine iguanas forage underwater, then explain their sneeze.

name: The Marmot
teaser: The marmot is the whistling alpine rodent, a chunky ground squirrel of mountains and steppes that lives in colonies of dozens, sharing elaborate burrow systems with separate chambers for nesting, storing food and hibernating. Marmots are famous for their sentinel whistle: the first to spot a predator — eagle, fox or bear — stands on its hind legs and lets out a piercing whistle, and the whole colony dives for cover. They are among the deepest hibernators, sleeping up to eight months a year with body temperatures near freezing and heart rates of just a few beats a minute. Some species weigh over eight kilograms.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover how marmots whistle warnings, then explain their hibernation.

name: The Meadowlark
teaser: The meadowlark is the grassland bird with the yellow chest, a member of the blackbird family that fills the prairies of the Americas with song. Its bright yellow breast marked with a black V is a display feature, and its flute-like, bubbling song is one of the most beloved sounds of the open country. Meadowlarks are ground birds that walk through the grass hunting insects and seeds, and they nest on the ground in a domed grass cup. In winter they gather in flocks of hundreds, and the eastern and western meadowlarks look almost identical but sing completely different songs.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover how meadowlarks nest on the ground, then explain their song perches.

name: The Meerkat Sentinel
teaser: The meerkat sentinel is the lookout who guards the mob, standing on its hind legs on the highest rock or termite mound, scanning the sky and horizon for danger. While the rest of the group forages for insects and small animals, the sentinel watches, calling out a different alarm for each predator — a short bark for a snake, a whistle for an eagle, a chattering call for a jackal — and the mob responds accordingly, diving into burrows or scattering. Sentinels take turns, and research shows they are more likely to sound a false alarm to snatch the best food for themselves, a small act of meerkat selfishness.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how meerkat sentinels warn the group, then explain the warning calls.

name: The Moa
teaser: The moa were the giant flightless birds of New Zealand, some species standing over three meters tall and weighing more than 250 kilograms — the tallest birds ever to exist. With no native land mammals, moa filled the roles of deer, antelope and giraffe, browsing the forests with no natural enemies except the huge Haast's eagle, which could take down a full-grown moa. When Polynesian settlers arrived around 1300, the birds' large flightless bodies and slow breeding made them easy prey, and within a few centuries every species of moa was extinct. They were among the last great flightless birds to vanish, and their bones still turn up in caves.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover how moa species went extinct, then explain their size.

name: The Mockingbird
teaser: The mockingbird is the songbird that copies others, and it does so brilliantly: a single northern mockingbird can learn and perform over 200 different songs, imitating cardinals, blue jays, car alarms, frog calls and even the creak of a gate. Males sing constantly, day and night, especially under bright moonlight, and they keep adding new sounds throughout their lives. Mockingbirds are bold defenders of their nests, dive-bombing cats, dogs and even humans who get too close. Their scientific name means 'many-tongued mimic', and they are the state bird of five US states.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover how mockingbirds imitate, then explain why they add new songs.

name: The Mole
teaser: The mole is the underground insect hunter, a tunneling machine built for life in the dark. Its front paws are enormous, paddle-like shovels with extra thumbs, and it can dig tunnels at a rate of several meters an hour, pushing soil aside with a swimming motion. Moles are nearly blind — their eyes are tiny and covered — and they navigate by feel and smell, with super-sensitive whiskers and a snout that detects vibrations. They are voracious eaters of earthworms, consuming more than their own body weight every day. A single mole's tunnel system can stretch for hundreds of meters and be reused for years.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how moles dig tunnels, then explain their tiny eyes.

name: The Mouse Lemur
teaser: The mouse lemur is the world's smallest primate — a tiny, big-eyed night creature that weighs about the same as a golf ball, small enough to curl up in the palm of your hand. It's a miniature marvel of adaptation: by day it sleeps rolled into a tight ball in a tree hole, and by night it prowls the forest, hunting insects and sipping nectar, its enormous eyes gathering every photon of moonlight. A mouse lemur can live for over a decade, and it uses fat storage to survive Madagascar's dry season, sometimes even entering a short period of torpor.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover how small mouse lemurs are, then explain their nocturnal life.

name: The Musk Ox
teaser: The musk ox is the Arctic's living fortress — a shaggy, prehistoric-looking beast that has weathered the ice age with a two-layer coat: a dense underfur called qiviut, eight times warmer than sheep's wool, beneath long guard hairs that hang to the ground. It roams the tundra of Greenland and Canada in herds, and when wolves attack, the herd forms a defensive circle with adults facing outward and calves protected in the middle, a formation so effective that wolves usually give up. Musk oxen can survive temperatures of minus 50°C, and both sexes carry the heavy curved horns that give the circle its deadly edge.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover how musk oxen survive the arctic, then explain the defensive circle formation.

name: The Narwhal Tusk
teaser: The narwhal's tusk is one of the most mysterious teeth in nature: a spiral canine that can grow up to three meters long, protruding from the upper lip of Arctic whales. For centuries it was sold as the horn of the mythical unicorn. The tusk is packed with millions of nerve endings, leading scientists to believe it is a sensory organ that lets the whale detect changes in temperature, salinity and pressure in the water. Males mostly grow tusks, and the spiral pattern is unique to each animal, like a fingerprint. Rarely, a narwhal grows two, and some females grow one too.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the narwhal's tusk, a spiraled tooth with up to 10 million nerve endings, may sense water salinity, temperature, and pressure, with males possibly using it to assess rivals and even duel, and occasional double-tusked and female tusks exist. Explore the sensory studies, the flexing tusk, and the enduring mystery of its purpose.

name: The Narwhal's Tusk
teaser: The narwhal's spiral tooth is the closest thing the ocean has to a unicorn horn, and it has fascinated humans for centuries — Viking traders sold it to European kings as proof of the unicorn. Only the male narwhal usually grows the tusk, a canine that erupts through the upper lip and can reach three meters, and it is packed with living nerve tissue, suggesting it works as a sensory organ reading the water's temperature, pressure and chemistry. The tusk is also used in displays of dominance, with males occasionally crossing and rubbing tusks in what may be a form of swordplay for status. A few narwhals grow two, and some females grow one.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover what the narwhal tusk really is, then explain the leading theories for its purpose.

name: The Newt
teaser: The newt is the water-loving salamander with a toxic skin, a small amphibian that lives the strangest double life: it spends winter on land, spring breeding in ponds, and summer both. In spring, male newts grow spectacular crests and dance in front of females, fanning pheromones with their tails. The European great crested newt is protected by law across much of Europe. Newts defend themselves with bright bellies and toxic skin secretions, and some species, like the Japanese fire-bellied newt, can regenerate lost limbs, tails, eyes and even parts of their hearts and brains — abilities scientists study closely for clues to human medicine.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover how newts defend themselves, then explain their rough skin.

name: The Nightingale
teaser: The nightingale is the famous night singer, a plain, brown bird whose song has inspired poets for a thousand years — Keats, Coleridge and Shakespeare all wrote odes to it. The males sing at night to attract mates and defend territory, and their songs are among the most complex in the bird world: a single bird can produce over a thousand different phrases, and some individuals learn more than 250 distinct song types. The nightingale sings louder and more elaborately the closer a rival comes, and its voice can carry half a kilometer. Ironically, the singer is drab — all the color is in the song.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn why nightingales sing at night, then explain their song complexity.

name: The Numbat
teaser: The numbat is the striped termite-eating marsupial of Western Australia, a small, squirrel-like animal covered in bold white and black stripes with a bushy tail. Unlike most marsupials, it has no pouch — the young cling to the mother's fur and are carried on her back. The numbat is one of the most specialized eaters in the world: its diet is almost entirely termites, and it uses a long, sticky tongue that can extend up to ten centimeters to lick them out of shallow tunnels. It sleeps in hollow logs and can eat up to 20,000 termites a day. Once widespread, it survives in a few protected reserves.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how numbats eat termites, then explain their daytime activity.

name: The Nuthatch
teaser: The nuthatch is the upside-down climbing songbird, the only bird that regularly walks head-first down tree trunks. While woodpeckers and treecreepers only climb upward, the nuthatch's oversized hind toe and strong legs let it descend head-first, scanning the bark from a different angle and finding insects other birds miss. It is famous for wedging nuts and acorns into bark crevices and hammering them open with its sharp bill — hence its name. Nuthatches are plump, short-tailed birds with a habit of creeping around branches, and they are bold visitors to garden feeders, often caching seeds for winter.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how nuthatches climb down trunks, then explain the difference from woodpeckers.

name: The Nyala
teaser: The nyala is one of Africa's most beautiful and most confusing-looking antelopes because the two sexes look like completely different animals: males are large, dark grey-brown with spiraled horns, white stripes and a shaggy mane; females are small, chestnut red with white stripes and no horns. They live in dense thickets near water, and their striking stripe pattern breaks up their outline in dappled shade. Nyala are shy and usually stay hidden, feeding at dawn and dusk on leaves and fruit. Only the males carry the long, twisted horns, and they are so handsome that they are among the most photographed antelope in Africa.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover the nyala's habitat, then explain the difference between male and female coloring.

name: The Ocelot
teaser: The ocelot is a wild cat of the Americas that looks like a miniature leopard wearing a designer coat — a pattern of dark rosettes, spots, and stripes so beautiful that people once killed thousands of them for fur. About twice the size of a house cat, the ocelot is a shy, mostly nocturnal hunter of the rainforest undergrowth, stalking small mammals, birds, and reptiles on the forest floor. Unlike many cats, it is comfortable in both day and night, and it is a superb climber that often rests high in the branches.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover the ocelot's habitat and hunting, then explain why its coat was once hunted.

name: The Okapi
teaser: The okapi looks like a cross between a zebra and a deer, but it's actually the giraffe's only living relative — a secret of the Congo rainforest so hidden that Western scientists didn't confirm it existed until 1901. It shares the giraffe's long, prehensile, dark tongue, built for stripping leaves, and the same basic body plan, but everything else is adjusted for the jungle: a shorter neck, reddish-brown coat, and bold white stripes on the legs and rump that break up its shape in the dappled forest light.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover how okapis were discovered, then explain their surprising stripes.

name: The Okapi Discovery
teaser: The okapi was hidden from science for nearly a century — local people in the Congo rainforest knew it well, but European explorers searched for it for decades, chasing rumors of a 'forest zebra' or a unicorn-like beast. When the first skin reached London in 1901, scientists were stunned: it had zebra-like stripes on its legs but the body shape and gentle face of a giraffe, its closest relative. The okapi's dark, velvety coat and striped hindquarters keep it camouflaged in the dappled forest light. Today it is endangered, threatened by habitat loss and poaching in the war-torn forests of its homeland.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how okapis were finally documented, then explain the mystery around them.

name: The One-Legged Stand
teaser: Why do flamingos stand on one leg? The most likely answer is simple physics: standing on one leg halves the heat the bird loses through its legs in cold water, saving energy, and a one-legged stance requires no muscular effort at all — flamingos have a locking mechanism in the hip that holds the leg in place, so the position is literally effortless. Flamingos even sleep on one leg, and they fall over so rarely that researchers suspect the stance is a default resting pose. It may also help them balance in mud and keep both feet out of the water's chill.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn the theories for the one-leg stand, then explain the energy saving idea.

name: The Opossum's Venom Immunity
teaser: The opossum has a remarkable superpower: near-total immunity to snake venom. The Virginia opossum's blood contains a protein that neutralizes the toxins of pit vipers like rattlesnakes and copperheads, and tests show the protein also blunts scorpion, bee and even plant toxins. Because opossums are marsupials — more distant from mammals like humans — their immune system produces this broad-spectrum defense that researchers hope to adapt into a universal antivenom. A bite from a rattlesnake that would kill a dog barely slows an opossum down. The opossum is also North America's only marsupial and famously plays dead under stress.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how opossums resist venom, then explain what scientists learned from them.

name: The Orangutan
teaser: The orangutan is the world's largest tree-dwelling animal — an ape that treats the rainforest canopy as a home, a bedroom, and a highway, spending nearly all its life high above the forest floor. Its arms span two meters, its hands are made for gripping branches, and it moves through the trees with a slow, deliberate grace, testing each branch before committing its weight. Orangutans are famously solitary: males live alone, and mothers raise a single infant for nearly a decade — the longest childhood of any animal after humans, which is why the orangutan's population grows so slowly.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how orangutans live alone, then explain their arboreal adaptations.

name: The Osprey Fisher
teaser: The osprey is the fish-hunting raptor of the waterways, a bird so specialized for fishing that its entire body is built for it. Its outer toe is reversible, letting it grip fish with two toes forward and two back; its feet are covered in sharp, spiny scales that lock onto slippery prey; and its oily feathers shed water so it can dive and take off again while soaked. An osprey hovers, then plunges feet-first, sometimes completely submerging, and emerges clutching a fish aligned head-forward to reduce drag. It succeeds on about one in four dives, and it hunts on every continent except Antarctica.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how ospreys catch fish, then explain their reversible toes.

name: The Ostrich
teaser: The ostrich is the giant flightless bird of Africa, standing up to 2.7 meters tall and weighing over 150 kilograms, the largest bird alive. It cannot fly, but it is the fastest bird on land, sprinting at up to 70 kilometers an hour with a stride of up to five meters, and its powerful two-toed legs can deliver a kick fatal to a lion. Its eyes are the largest of any land animal, bigger than its own brain. Ostriches live in flocks and lay the largest eggs of any living bird — a single egg equals about two dozen chicken eggs. The myth that they bury their heads in the sand is false; they lower their heads to the ground to look and listen.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how fast ostriches run, then explain their two-toed feet.

name: The Ostrich Egg
teaser: The ostrich egg is the largest egg on Earth — a single one weighs about 1.4 kilograms, equivalent to roughly two dozen chicken eggs, and is so strong that an adult can stand on it without it breaking. It takes an ostrich chick about two days to hatch, chipping through the shell with a special egg tooth before flopping out exhausted. In the wild, the male and female ostrich take turns incubating: the female sits by day, her brown feathers camouflaging the nest, and the dark male takes over at night. Ostrich eggs are so prized that people have long carved the thick shells into containers and jewelry.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover how big ostrich eggs are, then explain why they are so hard to break.

name: The Owl's Facial Disk
teaser: The owl's face is a sound-collecting dish. The ring of stiff feathers around each eye forms a concave facial disk that funnels sound toward the owl's ears, and the two ears sit asymmetrically — one higher and one slightly forward of the other — so the owl can detect the vertical and horizontal position of a sound simultaneously with pinpoint accuracy. A barn owl can locate a mouse by sound alone in total darkness, striking within a centimeter of the target. Its silent flight comes from feather edges so soft that they muffle the air passing over the wings, letting the owl hear without its own noise drowning out the prey.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover how the facial disk captures sound, then explain the owl's hearing accuracy.

name: The Paca
teaser: The paca is the spotted forest rodent of the Americas, a large, guinea-pig-like animal weighing up to 12 kilograms that lives near rivers and streams from Mexico to Argentina. Its coat is covered in rows of white spots, which break up its outline in the dappled forest light, and it is the second-largest rodent in the world after the capybara. Pacas are nocturnal and shy, swimming well and diving to escape predators. They are also important seed dispersers, carrying large fruits and nuts away from parent trees. Their meat is highly prized, and hunting pressure has made them wary and hard to see.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how pacas hide from predators, then explain their burrow life.

name: The Panda's Sixth Finger
teaser: The giant panda has six fingers, and the sixth one isn't really a finger at all — it's an enlarged wrist bone covered in a pad of skin, forming a 'false thumb' that works like a real opposable digit. The panda's true five fingers are fused into the palm, leaving the false thumb free to grip bamboo stalks from the other side, letting it strip leaves and hold stems with surprising precision. The false thumb is one of evolution's most famous examples of adaptation: Stephen Jay Gould wrote a classic essay about it, marveling that a carnivore's wrist bone became a tool for eating plants.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover how the panda grips bamboo, then explain the evolutionary story of its thumb.

name: The Pangolin's Scales
teaser: The pangolin is the only mammal in the world covered in scales — rows and rows of overlapping keratin plates, the same material as fingernails and rhino horn, that make it look like a walking pinecone. When threatened, it curls into a tight, armored ball that even a lion cannot pry open, and it can slash predators with the sharp edges of its scales by flexing its muscles. Pangolins have no teeth and feed entirely on ants and termites, using a tongue longer than its own body to reach into nests. They are the most trafficked animals in the world, poached for their scales, and all eight species are threatened.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn what pangolin scales are made of, then explain why they are the most trafficked animals.

name: The Pangolin's Tongue
teaser: The pangolin's tongue is one of the longest in the animal world relative to its body — up to 40 centimeters, longer than its entire head and body combined. It is anchored not in the mouth but far back in the chest, attached to the pelvis, and it can extend deep into ant and termite nests, coated in sticky saliva, to pull out thousands of insects. The pangolin has no teeth, so it swallows small stones and sand that grind up its food in the stomach. The tongue is so long that when retracted it folds back into the pangolin's chest cavity, past its heart and lungs.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn where a pangolin's tongue anchors, then explain how it reaches ant nests.

name: The Patagonian Mara
teaser: The Patagonian mara is the rabbit-like rodent of the plains, a strange animal that looks like a cross between a rabbit, a deer and a kangaroo — long legs, big ears and a body that runs with a bouncing gait. It lives in the open grasslands of Argentina in bonded pairs that stay together for life, and it is one of the few mammals that is strictly monogamous. Maras raise their young in communal warrens where several pairs share a burrow and cooperate to defend the crèche of pups. They are among the largest rodents in the world, weighing up to 16 kilograms, and they graze like small deer.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn why maras look like rabbits, then explain their mating bonds.

name: The Peacock's Display
teaser: The peacock's display is one of the most extravagant courtship rituals in the animal kingdom: the male fans out his train of up to 200 iridescent feathers into a shimmering, eye-covered wheel and quivers it, producing a low rustling sound, while pacing and turning to show it from every angle. The 'eyes' on the feathers are optical illusions — microscopic structures that reflect light to create shifting blues, greens and golds. Females inspect the display closely and choose the male with the most eyespots and the best symmetry, and they mate with the males whose trains are largest and most vivid, driving the feathers to become more extravagant generation after generation.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover why peacocks spread their trains, then explain the eyespots.

name: The Peacock's Train
teaser: The peacock's magnificent train is not its tail at all — it is elongated upper-tail coverts, feathers that grow from the bird's back and drape over the true tail, which is plain underneath. The train can be over 1.5 meters long, nearly two-thirds of the male's body length, and is replaced each year after the breeding season. When a peacock fans it out, the shimmering 'eyes' are not pigment but microscopic crystal-like structures that reflect light, shifting color as the bird moves. The train is costly to grow and heavy to carry, which is exactly the point: only a healthy male can afford such an absurd display, so it honestly signals quality to the females.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn what the peacock train actually is, then explain why it is molted.

name: The Peccary
teaser: The peccary is the wild pig-like mammal of the Americas, a stocky, bristly animal that has roamed the New World for over 30 million years but is not a true pig — it.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how peccaries differ from pigs, then explain their herd life.

name: The Peregrine Dive
teaser: The peregrine falcon is the fastest animal on Earth: in its hunting stoop it folds its wings and drops, reaching speeds over 300 kilometers an hour — faster than any other animal in motion. It strikes its prey in mid-air with a closed fist of a foot, killing or stunning it instantly, then catches the falling bird. Peregrines are so fast that their nostrils have evolved bony cones to let them breathe at speed, and their eyes have a special membrane that keeps them clear. They hunt from high perches over open country and cities alike, and their population recovered dramatically after the ban on DDT.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover how fast peregrines dive, then explain the adaptations for the plunge.

name: The Petrel
teaser: The petrel is the ocean wanderer of the stormy seas, a seabird built for a life that barely touches land. Some petrels spend years at sea, flying over every ocean on Earth, drinking seawater and eating fish, squid and krill caught from the surface. They are named for St. Peter because they appear to walk on water — pattering their feet across the waves as they take off. The snow petrel is one of only three birds that breed in Antarctica, and the storm petrels are among the smallest seabirds alive. Many species nest in burrows and return to the same colony, even the same burrow, year after year.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how petrels survive storms, then explain their oil stomach.

name: The Pheasant
teaser: The pheasant is the colorful long-tailed game bird, a bird so handsome that humans have spread it around the world: the common pheasant, originally from Asia, now lives on five continents, and the golden pheasant of China is one of the most striking birds alive, with a gold crest, scarlet body and a tail more than a meter long. Male pheasants are showy and loud, crowing from forest edges in spring; females are camouflaged brown. Pheasants run more than they fly, exploding into the air only when startled. They scratch the ground for seeds and insects, and in winter they gather in small flocks.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover why male pheasants are so colorful, then explain the display.

name: The Platypus
teaser: The platypus is one of the strangest animals alive — a duck-billed, beaver-tailed, egg-laying mammal with venomous spurs. It is a monotreme, one of only two mammals that lay eggs, and when the first stuffed specimen reached Europe in 1799, naturalists thought it was a hoax stitched together from different animals. The male has a spur on each hind ankle that delivers a painful venom, and the duck-like bill is actually packed with electroreceptors that detect the electrical pulses of prey underwater. The platypus closes its eyes and ears when diving, trusting its bill to find shrimp, worms and insect larvae in the dark riverbed.

exploreAction.instruction: List the platypus's surprising traits, then explain how it hunts with electricity.

name: The Platypus Bill
teaser: The platypus's bill is a living metal detector. Its soft, leathery surface is packed with thousands of electroreceptors and touch receptors that sense the tiny electrical fields given off by the muscles of prey, so the platypus can hunt in total darkness and murky water where its eyes and ears are useless. When it dives, it shuts its eyes, ears and nostrils and sweeps its bill from side to side across the riverbed like a metal detector, homing in on the electrical signature of a wriggling shrimp or worm. The bill is so sensitive that the platypus can detect prey buried in sand and even tell the direction a signal is coming from.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover how the platypus bill detects electricity, then explain why it closes its eyes underwater.

name: The Platypus Foraging
teaser: The platypus hunts the way no other mammal does: it dives into rivers and streams, shuts its eyes, ears and nostrils, and relies entirely on its bill's electroreceptors to find food. A foraging platypus sweeps its bill through the mud and gravel like a mine detector, snapping up shrimp, worms and insect larvae at a rate of several captures per minute. It stores its catch in cheek pouches and surfaces to chew — it has no teeth, so it grinds food with horny pads. Platypuses dive about every minute for thirty to sixty seconds at a time and can spend twelve hours a day foraging in cold water.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover how platypuses forage blind, then explain the electro-sense.

name: The Porpoise
teaser: The porpoise is the shy smaller cousin of the dolphin, a compact, blunt-snouted cetacean that rarely performs the acrobatic leaps dolphins are famous for — instead it makes a rolling, barely noticeable surfacing. The harbor porpoise, one of the smallest cetaceans at around 1.5 meters, is found in coastal waters across the Northern Hemisphere. Porpoises hunt small fish with high-frequency sonar clicks so fast they sound like a buzz, and they are among the quietest, most elusive marine mammals, often seen only as a fleeting dark fin. They travel in small groups and are threatened by fishing nets and underwater noise.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how porpoises differ from dolphins, then explain why they are rarely seen leaping.

name: The Possum
teaser: The possum is the adaptable marsupial of the Americas, one of nature's great survivors — the Virginia opossum has thrived for 70 million years and is now expanding its range northward in the US and Canada. It is famous for 'playing possum': when terrified, it collapses, drools, and feigns death so convincingly — stiff body, glazed eyes, foul-smelling anal secretion — that predators lose interest. Possums eat almost anything, including ticks, and a single opossum can eat thousands of ticks a year. They have 50 teeth, more than any other North American land mammal, and they carry their babies in a pouch.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover how opossums survive in cities, then explain their playing dead.

name: The Proboscis Monkey
teaser: The proboscis monkey is the animal with the world's most unforgettable nose — a long, pendulous, fleshy nose that can hang down past the mouth on adult males, and scientists still debate what it is for. The leading theory is sexual selection: females prefer the biggest noses, and the huge nasal chamber may amplify the male's loud, honking calls, making a big nose a signal of a healthy, impressive mate. The nose grows throughout a male's life, becoming more exaggerated with age. Proboscis monkeys live only on the island of Borneo, in riverside forests, and they are excellent swimmers that will leap into rivers to escape predators, sometimes diving completely underwater.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover why male proboscis monkeys have huge noses, then explain their swimming ability.

name: The Puffin
teaser: The puffin is the clown-faced sea bird of the cliffs, instantly recognizable by its orange beak, black-and-white body and penguin-like waddle. That colorful beak is seasonal — it brightens in spring for breeding and sheds its outer sheath in winter, becoming smaller and duller. Puffins nest in burrows on cliff tops, laying a single egg, and both parents fly out to sea to catch small fish, carrying up to a dozen at a time held crosswise in their beaks. They fly by beating their wings up to 400 times a minute, and they 'billing' — touching beaks — as part of courtship. Atlantic puffins return to the same colony, and often the same burrow, year after year.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how puffins carry fish, then explain the colorful beak.

name: The Quail
teaser: The quail is the ground-dwelling game bird, a plump, short-tailed bird that would rather run than fly. It lives in grasslands and farm fields, where its streaky brown camouflage makes it nearly invisible until it erupts at your feet with a startling whirring burst of wings. Quail feed on seeds and insects, scratching the ground like tiny chickens, and they nest in a simple scrape lined with grass. Some species, like the California quail, live in coveys of up to 60 birds and are famous for their social calls and the male's bobbing topknot. The common quail is one of the few birds that migrates across the Sahara each year.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how quails avoid predators, then explain their camouflage.

name: The Quokka
teaser: The quokka is the smiling marsupial of Rottnest Island, a small wallaby with a face that appears to be permanently smiling — which made it an internet celebrity and the selfie star of Western Australia. The smile is just the shape of its mouth, but the quokka is genuinely friendly: on Rottnest Island, where it has no natural predators, it approaches people and poses for photos. Quokkas are nocturnal, sleeping in the shade during the day and grazing on grass and leaves at night. They climb small trees and shrubs to reach food, and females carry a single joey in their pouch for about six months.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover why quokkas look like they smile, then explain their island life.

name: The Quoll
teaser: The quoll is the spotted carnivorous marsupial of Australia and New Guinea, a cat-sized hunter with a coat covered in white spots and a fierce appetite. Despite its cute face, it is a top predator of small animals — insects, lizards, birds and small mammals — and it has one of the strongest bites for its size of any mammal. Quolls are nocturnal and solitary, denning in hollow logs and rock crevices. The tiger quoll, the largest, weighs up to seven kilograms. Quolls are threatened by cane toads, which poison them when they bite, and by habitat loss, and conservation programs are working to protect them.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover how quolls hunt, then explain their tree climbing.

name: The Rabbit
teaser: The rabbit is the fast-breeding herbivore of fields and burrows, famous for its ability to multiply: a single pair can produce dozens of offspring in a year, and a female can conceive again within hours of giving birth. Rabbits live in warrens — networks of burrows with multiple entrances — where a hierarchy decides who gets the best nesting spots. Their eyes sit high on their heads for near-360-degree vision, their ears swivel independently, and their powerful hind legs let them zigzag at speed to escape predators. They constantly re-ingest soft droppings called cecotropes to extract extra nutrition from their food.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how rabbits live in warrens, then explain their breeding speed.

name: The Raccoon's Hands
teaser: A raccoon's front paws are the closest thing to human hands in the animal kingdom — dextrous, sensitive, five-fingered tools that can open latches, unscrew lids, and pick up a coin from a table. The paws have about four to five times more sensory receptors than a cat's, and the raccoon 'feels' its food before eating it, using its paws like eyes. That tactile genius makes raccoons legendary problem-solvers: they've been filmed undoing complex locks, opening trash bins with multiple latches, and solving puzzle boxes that stump other animals.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn why raccoon paws are so sensitive, then explain the washing behavior.

name: The Raccoon's Mask
teaser: The raccoon's black face mask is one of the most recognizable patterns in nature — and like the bandit reputation it inspired, it's a survival adaptation. The dark mask around the eyes reduces glare and cuts down reflection in the dark, helping the nocturnal raccoon see clearly at night, much like the black marks football players paint under their eyes. The mask also makes the raccoon look more menacing to rivals, which may help it hold its ground.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover what the raccoon's mask does, then explain their night vision.

name: The Rattlesnake's Rattle
teaser: The rattlesnake's rattle is a built-in alarm system made of hollow keratin segments that interlock loosely. When the snake vibrates its tail up to 90 times per second, the segments knock together to produce the signature buzz, and the sound is a genuine warning: 'stay back'. Each time the snake sheds its skin, a new segment is added — though segments also break off, so the number of rattles is not a reliable age count. A rattlesnake is born with a single 'button' and adds its first full rattle after its first shed. The rattle warns large animals away, saving the snake from being stepped on.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover how rattles work, then explain what they warn.

name: The Raven
teaser: The raven is the largest songbird with a big brain — the common raven is the size of a hawk, and its intelligence rivals that of chimpanzees and dolphins. Ravens solve puzzles that stump most animals, plan for the future, and use tools; they have been seen dropping stones on people who threatened their nests and rolling snowballs down slopes for fun. They can imitate human speech and even mimic the calls of other animals, and they remember individual human faces for years, treating kind people and rude people differently. A pair of ravens bonds for life and works as a team, defending a territory that can span many square kilometers.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how intelligent ravens are, then explain their problem-solving.

name: The Red Panda
teaser: The red panda is one of nature's most lovable mistakes — an animal so unique that it's not really a bear and not really a raccoon; it.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn what red pandas really are, then explain why they eat mostly bamboo.

name: The Red Panda's Tail
teaser: The red panda's tail is a blanket, a balance pole, and a disguise all in one. Long and bushy, with a pattern of nine pale rings, the tail makes up nearly half the animal's body length, and the red panda puts it to constant use. In the cold Himalayan mountains, it wraps its tail around its body like a scarf when it curls up to sleep, and when it's feeding in the trees, the tail acts as a counterbalance for reaching maneuvers. The tail's ringed pattern even helps camouflage the red panda among the mossy trees and lichens it lives among.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover how red pandas use their tails, then explain the counter-shading.

name: The Red-Tailed Hawk
teaser: The red-tailed hawk is the most common hawk of North America, the broad-winged raptor you see perched on highway poles and circling in thermals. Its signature scream — a hoarse, descending screech — is so emblematic that Hollywood uses it as the voice of every eagle in every movie. The red tail appears only in adults; young birds have brown tails with fine bars. Red-tails are versatile hunters, taking rodents, rabbits, snakes and birds, and they are famous for the aerial courtship display in which a pair locks talons and spirals down together. They build large stick nests high in trees and reuse them for years.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn what red-tailed hawks hunt, then explain their famous cry.

name: The Rhea
teaser: The rhea is the South American ostrich cousin, a large, flightless bird that roams the grasslands of Brazil, Argentina and Patagonia in flocks. Smaller than the ostrich but standing up to 1.5 meters tall, it runs at speeds over 60 kilometers an hour using its wings as rudders for sharp turns. Unusually among birds, it is the male who does almost all the parenting: he mates with several females who lay eggs in his nest, then he incubates the clutch of up to 50 eggs for six weeks and raises the chicks alone. Rheas graze on plants and eat insects, and farmers sometimes keep them like livestock.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover how rheas live on the plains, then explain the male parenting.

name: The Ring-Tailed Lemur
teaser: The ring-tailed lemur is the celebrity of the lemur family, famous for its dramatic striped tail, which it waves like a flag. It lives in troops of up to 30 in the dry forests of Madagascar, and it is the most terrestrial of lemurs, spending much of its time on the ground. Females rule the troop — they eat first, lead the group, and choose their mates. In a ritual called 'stink fighting', males anoint their tails with scent and wave them at rivals. Ring-tails sunbathe in groups with arms spread, and their haunting, cat-like calls carry through the forest.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover how ring-tailed lemurs sunbathe, then explain the stink fights.

name: The Robin
teaser: The robin is the red-breasted songbird of gardens, one of the most beloved birds in Europe and a year-round companion that sings even in winter, defending its territory with song all year long. The European robin's orange-red breast is not for the females' eyes only — it is a badge of aggression shown to rivals, and robins will fight their own reflection in a window for hours. They follow gardeners to eat freshly turned worms, and they are famously tame, perching close to people. The American robin is a different bird entirely, a member of the thrush family with a cheery caroling song that announces spring.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover why robins sing in early morning, then explain the red breast display.

name: The Rook
teaser: The rook is the bare-faced corvid of the rookeries, a large black bird of the crow family that nests in noisy colonies called rookeries, often containing hundreds of nests in a single grove of tall trees. Rooks are instantly recognizable by the bare, pale patch of skin at the base of their adult beaks — the face feathers wear away from digging in soil for grubs and worms. They are highly social and intelligent, cooperating to mob predators and sharing information about food. Rooks were long considered pests by farmers, but studies show they are remarkably smart, capable of solving puzzles and understanding cause and effect.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how rooks nest in colonies, then explain the bare face.

name: The Sable Antelope
teaser: The sable antelope is often called Africa's most beautiful antelope, and with good reason — its jet-black coat, white facial markings, and sweeping, back-curved horns make it look like it walked out of a fantasy novel. Both sexes carry the horns, which can reach over a meter, and the sable is famously fierce: it will fight to the death, and a sable cow has been known to kill a lion defending her calf. Herds are led by a dominant female, with a single bull guarding the group, and calves are hidden in dense bush for their first weeks.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn why sable antelopes are so striking, then explain their fighting style.

name: The Salamander
teaser: The salamander is the tailed amphibian of damp places, a shy, moist-skinned animal that lives under logs, rocks and leaf litter, hunting worms, insects and slugs at night. Salamanders are masters of regeneration: they can regrow lost tails, limbs, jaws and even parts of their hearts and eyes, a superpower scientists study intensely. Their skin must stay moist for them to breathe through it, so they avoid sunlight and dry air. The fire salamander's bright yellow-and-black warning colors advertise the toxins in its skin, and some species, like the cave salamander, spend their whole lives in total darkness, losing their eyes entirely.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how salamanders differ from frogs, then explain their moist skin needs.

name: The Secretary Bird
teaser: The secretary bird is the snake-stomping raptor of the savanna, a tall, elegant bird with a crest of long quills behind its head that reminded early observers of a secretary with pens tucked behind their ear. It is built for walking — up to 30 kilometers a day on long legs — and it hunts on foot, stomping snakes, lizards, rodents and insects with powerful, rapid kicks delivered from a height of over a meter. Its thick, scaly legs are protected against snake bites. The secretary bird strikes so fast that the impact is several times its own body weight, and it has been known to dispatch venomous snakes with precision blows to the head.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover how secretary birds kill snakes, then explain their long legs.

name: The Serval
teaser: The serval is the long-legged acrobat of the cat world, a slender spotted hunter built like a basketball player. Its legs are the longest, proportionally, of any cat, and its neck is stretched to match, which lets it see and leap over the tall grass of African wetlands. The ears are the giveaway to its hunting style: they are enormous, rotating like satellite dishes to pinpoint the rustle of a rat or frog hiding below. Then comes the serval's signature move — a vertical pounce of up to two and a half meters straight up, coming down exactly on the prey with a whack of both front paws.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how servals hunt by sound and pounce, then explain their oversized ears.

name: The Shoebill
teaser: The shoebill is the statue-like bird with a clog-shaped bill, a tall, grey, stork-like bird of African swamps that stands so still it is often mistaken for a statue. Its enormous bill — wide, hooked and shaped exactly like a wooden clog — is its hunting weapon: the shoebill stands frozen for long stretches, then lunges forward with startling speed to seize lungfish, frogs and even baby crocodiles, sometimes ripping them in half. It can strike so fast that its head moves almost faster than the eye can follow. The shoebill is solitary, silent except for a rare bill-clattering display, and it has become an internet favorite for its intense, unblinking stare.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover how shoebills hunt, then explain why they stand so still.

name: The Shoebill's Bill
teaser: The shoebill's bill is one of the most extraordinary beaks in the bird world: wide, deep and sharply hooked, shaped so precisely like a wooden clog that the bird is named after it. It is an ambush weapon — the shoebill stands motionless in shallow swamp water, then lunges with explosive speed to grab prey with the hooked tip. The bill can seize lungfish, catfish, frogs and even young crocodiles, and the sharp edges slice through struggling prey. The shoebill's head moves so fast during a strike that its vision blurs, and it is one of the slowest, most patient hunters in the bird world, often waiting an hour between lunges.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how the shoebill uses its bill, then explain the lunging catch.

name: The Shrew
teaser: The shrew is the tiny mammal with a huge appetite — one of the smallest mammals on Earth, some species weighing barely two grams, yet eating up to twice its own body weight in insects, worms and spiders every single day. Its heart beats up to 1,200 times a minute, and it must eat constantly or starve within hours. The water shrew can hunt underwater with a venomous bite that paralyzes prey, and some shrews carry toxic saliva — among the few venomous mammals. Shrews are so aggressive for their size that they will attack animals much larger than themselves, and they are active day and night, year-round.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover why shrews eat constantly, then explain their fast heartbeat.

name: The Sifaka's Leap
teaser: The sifaka is the lemur that dances — a silky-furred primate of Madagascar whose way of moving across the ground looks like a joyful sideways dance: it stands upright, throws its arms out for balance, and hops sideways on its hind legs in a series of graceful bounds. It's a sight so charming it's been nicknamed the 'dancing lemur.' That dance is really an escape tactic: on the ground, the sifaka is vulnerable, so it bounces quickly between trees, then leaps through the canopy in vertical, acrobatic jumps — sifakas can cover ten meters in a single leap.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how sifakas move on the ground, then explain why they bound sideways.

name: The Skink
teaser: The skink is the smooth shiny-scaled lizard, a large and successful family of over 1,500 species found on every continent except Antarctica. Skinks are built like little torpedoes — sleek, streamlined bodies with tiny legs and glossy scales that help them slip through grass and soil, and many species have reduced legs or none at all, moving like snakes. Most are fast, secretive and harmless, hunting insects and spiders in leaf litter. The blue-tongued skink of Australia is famous for flashing a bright blue tongue to startle predators, and the sand skink swims through loose sand as if it were water.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover why skinks have smooth scales, then explain their burrowing.

name: The Sloth Bear
teaser: The sloth bear is the insect-eater of the bear family — a shaggy, dark-coated bear of India and Sri Lanka that has abandoned much of the bear lifestyle for a diet of termites and ants. It's built for the job: a long, flexible snout, no front teeth (letting it suck insects in like a vacuum), a long tongue, and nostrils that can close to keep dust out. The bear's most striking feature is its habit of 'smacking' — it sucks air noisily through its snout, a sound that carries through the forest and lets a bear find insect colonies, and its loud snuffling can be heard from far away.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how sloth bears eat insects, then explain their unusual lips.

name: The Sloth's Algae Coat
teaser: A sloth's fur is a tiny ecosystem: green algae grows in it, along with moths, beetles, and fungi, giving older sloths a greenish tinge that makes them blend into the rainforest canopy. The relationship is symbiotic — the algae gets a home in the sloth's specialized, grooved fur, and the sloth gets camouflage, which helps it hide from eagle-eyed predators that hunt by sight. It may even get a snack: sloths have been seen licking the algae, possibly gaining extra nutrients from it.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover why sloths grow algae, then explain what both get from the partnership.

name: The Sloth's Slow Life
teaser: The sloth is the slowest mammal on Earth, and every part of its life is built around that choice. Its metabolism is roughly half the speed of other animals its size, its body temperature can drop and rise with the air, and its top speed is barely a few meters a minute — it would take a sloth all day to cross a soccer field. That slowness is a survival strategy: by moving so little, a sloth needs almost no energy, so it can survive on a diet of leaves that other animals can't digest at all, and its slow, quiet life makes it nearly invisible to predators.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn why sloths move so slowly, then explain how they avoid predators.

name: The Snowshoe Hare
teaser: The snowshoe hare is the hare with built-in snowshoes: its huge hind feet, up to 18 centimeters long, spread its weight so it can run on top of deep snow that would swallow other animals. It is also a master of camouflage — its brown summer coat molts to pure white in winter, so it matches the snow exactly. The transformation is triggered by daylight length, and a hare caught halfway through the change stands out dangerously against either background. Snowshoe hares are famous for their population cycles, exploding and crashing on a roughly ten-year rhythm tied to their predators, the lynx and the great horned owl.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how snowshoe hare feet work, then explain the population cycles.

name: The Snowy Owl
teaser: The snowy owl is the white owl of the arctic tundra, a ghostly hunter of the far north that breeds above the Arctic Circle and hunts in 24-hour daylight. Its white plumage camouflages it against the snow, and males are whiter than females, which keep dark barring. Snowy owls are among the largest owls in the world, with a wingspan over 1.5 meters, and they are powerful enough to take lemmings, arctic hares and even geese. In years when lemmings are scarce, snowy owls sweep south in dramatic irruptions, appearing across North America and Europe — the same birds that starred as Hedwig in the Harry Potter films.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover how snowy owls live in the arctic, then explain their feather color.

name: The Spadefoot Toad
teaser: The spadefoot toad is the digging toad of dry places, a desert survivor that spends up to ten months of the year buried underground. It is named for the sharp, hardened spade on each hind foot, which it uses to dig backwards into the soil, and it can tunnel several meters deep. When rain finally comes, spadefoots erupt from the ground and race to temporary pools to breed within days — eggs hatch, and tadpoles can metamorphose into toadlets in as little as two weeks, beating the drying mud. Some can stay buried for years waiting for rain, and they seal themselves in a waterproof cocoon of shed skin to survive.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover why spadefoot toads are called that, then explain their fast breeding.

name: The Spectacled Bear
teaser: The spectacled bear is the only bear in South America, and its name comes from the pale, cream-colored patches around its eyes that look like glasses — a pattern unique to each individual, like a fingerprint. Living in the Andes, from cloud forests to alpine meadows, it's also called the Andean bear, and it's one of the most arboreal bears, building nests in trees and climbing to reach fruit and bromeliads. It's mostly vegetarian — fruit, berries, and plant stems make up most of its diet — and it's remarkably adaptable, moving up and down the mountains as the seasons change.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover why it is called the spectacled bear, then explain its climbing skill.

name: The Spider Monkey
teaser: The spider monkey is the acrobat of the canopy, so named because its long, thin limbs and tail make it look like a spider dangling from a web. It has the prehensile tail perfected — a muscular fifth limb with a bare, fingerprint-like pad on the underside that grips like a hand, letting the spider monkey swing through the treetops with its whole body in motion, arms and tail working together. Spider monkeys move so fluidly that they rarely come to the ground at all, and they travel in large, noisy groups that split and rejoin, communicating with loud whinnies and barks.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover how spider monkeys move, then explain their unusually long limbs.

name: The Spoonbill
teaser: The spoonbill is the wader with the spoon-shaped bill, a striking white or pink bird that feeds by sweeping its flattened, spatula-tipped bill through shallow water from side to side. The bill is packed with sensitive nerve endings, and the spoonbill snaps it shut the instant it touches prey, filtering out tiny fish, shrimp and insects without needing to see them. The roseate spoonbill of the Americas is vivid pink, colored by the shrimp in its diet. Spoonbills nest in noisy colonies, often alongside herons and ibises, and their slow, rhythmic bill-sweeping is one of the most distinctive feeding styles of any bird.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how spoonbills sweep for food, then explain the bill sensors.

name: The Springbok's Pronk
teaser: The springbok's signature move is the pronk — a series of stiff-legged vertical jumps that can carry it up to two meters into the air, back arched and legs straight, landing to bounce again. It's one of the most joyful-looking displays in the animal world, and the springbok does it both when alarmed and when simply feeling good. Beyond the fitness-signal theory, springboks also pronk in groups, and some researchers think the bouncing herd may confuse predators or signal the alarm to the rest of the group.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how high springboks leap, then explain the theories behind pronking.

name: The Star-Nosed Mole
teaser: The star-nosed mole is the fastest eater in the animal kingdom and one of the strangest-looking: its snout is ringed with 22 pink, fleshy tentacles that form a star. Those tentacles are packed with over 25,000 touch receptors, making the star the most sensitive organ in the animal kingdom — so sensitive that the mole can identify and swallow prey in a quarter of a second, faster than any other mammal. The mole hunts underground and underwater, and its tentacles constantly twitch and probe, tasting the world by touch. It can detect a worm and eat it before the worm even reacts.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how the star-nosed mole hunts, then explain the touch tentacles.

name: The Stork
teaser: The stork is the big nesting bird of the rooftops, a long-legged, long-necked wading bird that has shared villages with humans for centuries — across Europe, pairs build enormous stick nests on chimneys, rooftops and church towers, returning to the same nest year after year and adding to it until it can weigh hundreds of kilograms. The white stork is the legendary bringer of babies, a story that may come from its habit of nesting near homes. Storks are silent birds — they have no true voice — and communicate by clattering their bills loudly. They migrate thousands of kilometers between Europe and Africa, soaring on thermals.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn where storks nest, then explain the baby stork legend.

name: The Sugar Glider
teaser: The sugar glider is the gliding possum that loves sweets, a small Australian marsupial that can glide over 50 meters between trees using a membrane of skin stretched between its wrists and ankles like a parachute. It is nocturnal, spending the day sleeping in a nest of leaves inside a tree hollow, and at night it glides from tree to tree, lapping nectar, sap and insects with its long tongue — the 'sugar' in its name comes from its love of sweet sap and nectar. Sugar gliders are intensely social, living in family groups of up to seven that groom each other and even 'puddle' together to keep warm, and their soft chirps and rattles keep the group in touch.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how sugar gliders glide, then explain their social life.

name: The Sun Bear
teaser: The sun bear is the smallest bear in the world and one of the strangest — a stocky, short-snouted bear of Southeast Asia's rainforests with a golden or cream patch on its chest that gives it its name (the 'sun' mark). It's built like a living toolbox: a tongue so long it can extend 25 centimeters to reach honey deep inside hives, huge claws for climbing and tearing into logs, and skin so loose that if a predator grabs it, the sun bear can twist around and bite back. Sun bears are the most arboreal of bears, spending much of their lives in the trees, and they're ferocious when cornered.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover how the sun bear got its name, then explain its long tongue.

name: The Surinam Toad
teaser: The Surinam toad is the flat frog that carries eggs in its back, one of the strangest reproductive strategies in the animal kingdom. During mating, the pair rises in the water and tumbles while the eggs are fertilized and pressed into the female's back, where her spongy skin grows over them, embedding each egg in its own little pocket. The young develop there for months, protected from predators, and eventually hatch as fully formed baby toads that push themselves out of their mother's skin and swim away. The toad itself is a flat, almost leaf-like creature with tiny eyes and a triangular head, a master of camouflage on the muddy river bottom.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how Surinam toads carry young, then explain the skin pockets.

name: The Swallow
teaser: The swallow is the agile insect-catching bird of summer, a small, streamlined bird with forked tail and long wings built for speed and maneuverability. It spends its days wheeling and diving after flying insects, catching them in mid-air with its wide gaping mouth, and a single swallow can eat thousands of flies, mosquitoes and aphids in a day. Swallows are famous migrants: the barn swallow travels up to 14,000 kilometers between its breeding grounds and southern Africa, returning to the same barn, sometimes the same nest, year after year. Their arrival is one of the classic signs of spring.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how swallows catch insects on the wing, then explain their migration.

name: The Swan
teaser: The swan is the elegant long-necked water bird, among the largest flying birds in the world — the mute swan can weigh over 14 kilograms with a wingspan of nearly 2.5 meters, yet it takes off and flies with powerful, measured wingbeats. Swans pair for life, and their courtship is a ballet of synchronized head-bobbing and mirrored swimming. The mute swan, despite its name, is not silent — it hisses, snorts and makes a rhythmic throbbing sound with its wings in flight. Swans are fiercely protective parents, and a swan defending its cygnets can injure a dog or even a person with its powerful wings and beak.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how swans feed, then explain their long necks.

name: The Swift
teaser: The swift is the bird that barely lands — it may stay airborne for ten months straight, eating, sleeping, drinking and even mating on the wing. Common swifts feed entirely on flying insects caught in their gaping mouths, and they sleep in flight by shutting down half their brain at a time, gliding on their swept-back wings. They drink by skimming water with their beaks, and young swifts may not land at all until they are two years old and ready to breed. When they do land, they cling to vertical surfaces with tiny feet, and their legs are so short that they can barely walk.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover how swifts sleep in flight, then explain their aerial life.

name: The Tamandua
teaser: The tamandua is the anteater of the trees — a smaller, climbing cousin of the giant anteater, with a short, prehensile tail that grips branches and lets it move through the canopy in search of nests. Also called the lesser anteater or collared anteater, it's about the size of a small dog and wears a dramatic black 'vest' over its cream fur. The tamandua is a specialist in one thing: finding ant and termite nests, which it does with a sense of smell so powerful that it can detect a colony through a meter of soil.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how tamanduas climb, then explain their powerful smell.

name: The Tapir
teaser: The tapir is the pig-like browsing mammal with a trunk, an ancient animal that has changed little for 50 million years and is more closely related to rhinos and horses than to pigs. Its short, flexible trunk is a prehensile nose that can grasp leaves and fruit, and it works as a snorkel when the tapir walks along riverbeds — tapirs are excellent swimmers and often cool off in water. The Malayan tapir is boldly black and white, while South American tapirs are plain brown. Tapirs are important seed dispersers of the rainforest, and all species are threatened by habitat loss and hunting.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn what a tapir's snout is for, then explain its rainforest life.

name: The Tarsier's Giant Eyes
teaser: The tarsier has the largest eyes relative to its body size of any mammal — each eyeball is about as big as its brain, and the whole eye is roughly the size of a human's, packed into a head the size of a fist. The eyes are fixed in their sockets, so the tarsier cannot roll them; instead it rotates its entire head almost 360 degrees, like an owl. Tarsiers are nocturnal hunters that leap between trees, grabbing insects, lizards and even birds in mid-air, and their enormous eyes give them superb night vision. These ancient primates of Southeast Asia are among the smallest primates alive, some weighing under 100 grams.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn why tarsier eyes are so large, then explain how they hunt at night.

name: The Tarsier's Rotating Neck
teaser: The tarsier has a superpower most mammals can only dream of: it can turn its head almost a full 180 degrees in each direction — a total range that nearly lets it see behind its own back. The ability is a direct consequence of its enormous eyes: because each eye is locked rigidly in its socket (there's barely room for eye muscles), the tarsier can't glance around like other primates, so its neck has evolved to do all the work instead.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover how far tarsiers can turn their heads, then explain the special neck joints.

name: The Tasmanian Devil
teaser: The Tasmanian devil is the scrappy marsupial with a powerful bite, a stocky, black carnivore of Tasmania whose jaws are so strong that pound for pound it has one of the most powerful bites of any mammal — strong enough to crush bones. Its screeching, snarling feeding frenzies and foul temper earned it the name 'devil'. Devils are nocturnal scavengers that eat almost anything, including carrion, and a group feeding can be heard from kilometers away. They are threatened by devil facial tumor disease, a contagious cancer, and conservationists are working to save them, including establishing healthy populations on offshore islands.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn why Tasmanian devils are named as they are, then explain the facial tumor disease.

name: The Tern
teaser: The tern is the slender sea bird that dives for fish, a graceful, swallow-like seabird famous for its effortless flight and its long migrations. The Arctic tern holds the record for the longest migration of any animal: it travels up to 90,000 kilometers a year, breeding in the Arctic summer and wintering in the Antarctic, seeing more daylight than any other creature on Earth. Terns hover over the water, then plunge to snatch fish near the surface. Common terns nest in noisy colonies on beaches and islands, and they are fearless defenders of their nests, dive-bombing anything that approaches, including humans.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover how terns dive, then explain the arctic tern's migration.

name: The Thrush
teaser: The thrush is the spotted songbird of the woodlands, a medium-sized bird famous for its rich, fluting song — the song thrush repeats each phrase two or three times, a signature pattern. It feeds on snails, and its clever trick is famous: it finds a favorite stone and uses it as an anvil, smashing snail shells against it to reach the soft body inside. The mistle thrush, a larger relative, got its name from guarding mistletoe berries through winter. Thrushes sing at dawn and dusk, and their clear, musical notes carry far through the woods, making them among the most celebrated singers in Europe.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover how thrushes find snails, then explain the anvil trick.

name: The Tortoise
teaser: The tortoise is the slow long-lived land turtle, a walking fortress that has outlived empires — giant tortoises can live more than 150 years, and some individuals alive today hatched before the telegraph was invented. Their domed shells, fused to their skeletons, are made of living bone covered in plates of keratin, and they can pull their heads and legs inside for protection. Tortoises are surprisingly strong and can push through brush and even climb ramps, and they have excellent long-term memories, remembering watering holes and even familiar humans for decades. Some species hibernate underground for months at a time.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how tortoises differ from turtles, then explain their long lifespans.

name: The Tortoise and the Hare
teaser: The fable of the tortoise and the hare — slow and steady wins the race — has been told for 2,500 years, and it is rooted in real animal behavior. Hares and rabbits sprint in short, explosive bursts and tire quickly, while tortoises are endurance walkers that can keep moving steadily for hours without stopping. A tortoise can walk several kilometers a day, and its slow, relentless pace is perfectly sustainable, while a hare's bursts of speed are all-or-nothing. Real tortoises also have a hidden speed: some can sprint surprisingly fast when motivated, and the story's lesson — persistence beats raw speed — holds up.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn the fable's lesson, then compare real tortoise and hare speeds.

name: The Toucan's Beak
teaser: The toucan's beak is one of the most striking structures in the bird world: up to a third of the bird's total length, bright orange, yellow, green or red, and made of a light, foam-like keratin sandwich with a honeycomb interior. Despite its size, the beak weighs very little — about one-twentieth of what it looks like — and scientists have discovered it works as an air-conditioning system: blood vessels near the surface dump heat, and the toucan can adjust its beak temperature to keep its body cool. The beak is also a tool for reaching fruit on thin branches and a courtship display.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover what the toucan's beak is for, then explain the cooling theory.

name: The Tree Kangaroo
teaser: The tree kangaroo is the kangaroo that climbed into the trees, a marsupial that swapped the plains of Australia for the rainforest canopy of New Guinea and far north Queensland. It looks like a cross between a kangaroo and a lemur — long hind legs and a powerful tail, but short, broad feet with rough soles and long claws for gripping branches. Tree kangaroos are surprisingly agile climbers that can leap up to nine meters between trees, and they descend to the ground tail-first, moving backwards down trunks. They are shy, solitary and threatened by deforestation, and several species are among the rarest mammals on Earth.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how tree kangaroos climb, then explain their long tails.

name: The Tree Porcupine
teaser: The tree porcupine is the climbing spiky rodent of the Americas, a nocturnal animal that spends its nights high in the canopy, unlike its ground-dwelling cousins. It has a long, prehensile tail that wraps around branches like a fifth hand, letting it climb confidently, and it sleeps curled in a ball in tree hollows by day. Its quills are modified hairs, up to 30 centimeters long in some species, and when threatened it raises and rattles them, stamping its feet before charging backward into the attacker. Tree porcupines eat leaves, bark, fruit and seeds, and they are surprisingly nimble despite their armor.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how tree porcupines climb, then explain their prehensile tails.

name: The Treecreeper
teaser: The treecreeper is the spiraling bark-probing bird, a tiny, brown, woodpecker-like bird that climbs tree trunks in a distinctive spiral, working its way up and around the trunk, probing bark crevices with its thin, down-curved bill for insects and spiders. When it reaches the top, it flies down to the base of the next tree and starts again — treecreepers almost never climb downward. Their camouflaged, streaky brown backs blend so well with bark that they seem to vanish when they stop moving. They nest behind loose bark or in tree cavities, and in winter they sometimes roost communally in a tight cluster to keep warm.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover how treecreepers probe bark, then explain their curved bills.

name: The Tufted Titmouse
teaser: The tufted titmouse is the crested relative of the chickadee, a small, gray, big-eyed bird of eastern North American woodlands, named for its prominent pointed crest. It is a bold and curious visitor to feeders, often the first to investigate something new, and it has a scratchy, whistled song and a famous scolding call. Titmice are intelligent: they hide seeds and acorns in caches across their territory and remember where they stored them, and they have been seen plucking fur from sleeping animals to line their nests. Pairs stay together for life and defend their territory year-round.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover how titmice store food, then explain their crest signals.

name: The Turkey Vulture
teaser: The turkey vulture is the common scavenger with a sharp sense of smell, one of the few birds with a well-developed sense of smell — it can detect the scent of a dead animal from kilometers away, following the faint odor of rotting meat on the wind. It soars with wings held in a shallow V, rocking side to side, and its bald red head is an adaptation for carrion feeding, keeping feathers clean. Turkey vultures eat only dead animals and are vital to the ecosystem as nature's cleanup crew, removing carcasses that would otherwise spread disease. They are silent except for hisses, and they cool off by urinating on their own legs.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover how turkey vultures find food, then explain their smell advantage.

name: The Turkey's Display
teaser: The wild turkey's courtship display is one of the grandest in the bird world: the male struts with his tail fanned into a wide, iridescent wheel, his wings drooped, his head and neck bare and flushed with reds, blues and whites, and he gobbles, puffs his feathers and drags his wing tips along the ground, sometimes in circles around a female. The display shows off the male's health and size, and the red, white and blue head colors shift with his mood. Turkeys have superb eyesight — up to three times better than humans — and the strut is a spectacle that females inspect carefully before choosing a mate.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover how turkeys court, then explain the tail fan.

name: The V Formation
teaser: Geese and other large birds fly in a V formation for one simple reason: energy. Each bird's wingtip upwash reduces the air resistance for the bird behind it, so the whole flock saves up to 25 percent of its energy compared to flying alone. The birds take turns at the front, the hardest position, rotating so no single bird does all the work, and the flock honks constantly — research shows the calls help the formation stay synchronized. The V shape also keeps every bird in sight of the leader, maintaining the flock as one unit. It is one of the clearest examples of cooperation in the animal world.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover why geese fly in V formation, then explain the slipstream benefit.

name: The Variety of Bird Nests
teaser: Birds build homes in astonishing variety: the weaver bird weaves grass into a hanging, waterproof basket; the ovenbird of South America sculpts a fortress of mud that bakes as hard as clay; the hummingbird builds a tiny cup bound with spider silk that stretches as the chicks grow; and the emperor penguin carries its egg on its feet, with no nest at all. Woodpeckers chisel tree cavities, swallows plaster mud under eaves, and the hornbill seals its mate inside a tree. Nests range from a scrape in the gravel to the great bald eagle's stick platform, which can weigh a ton and last decades.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover how different birds build nests, then explain the materials used.

name: The Viscacha
teaser: The viscacha is the chinchilla cousin of the high Andes, a chunky, rabbit-sized rodent that lives in the rocky slopes of the mountains at elevations up to 5,000 meters, where the air is thin and the nights freezing. It looks like a rabbit with a long, bushy, curled tail, and its thick fur keeps it warm in the cold mountain air. Viscachas live in colonies among boulders, sunbathing on rocks like cats in the morning and retreating to crevices at night. They are shy and rarely seen, but they are famous for their endearing round faces and long whiskers, and they have become an internet favorite.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover where viscachas live, then explain their rock dwelling.

name: The Wallaby
teaser: The wallaby is the smaller kangaroo cousin, a marsupial of Australia and New Guinea that comes in dozens of species, from the tiny rock-wallaby to the swamp wallaby the size of a large dog. Wallabies hop on powerful hind legs with the same energy-saving spring as kangaroos, and the rock-wallabies are remarkable climbers that bound across cliff faces with astonishing agility.
